#6307. The 8 Best RV Generators Give You Go-Anywhere Power

Having the juice to power your appliances and electronics makes a mobile home feel truly homey.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Driving an RV lets you bring the comforts of home along on your road trip, but having a portable generator is essential. It powers your electric appliances and charges electronics, like your phone and laptop. If your RV doesn’t come equipped with a built-in generator, then you’ll need to bring one along.

To be clear: There are no official, task-specific “RV generators,” but some portable generators are better-suited to the task than others. For starters, most RVs have a 30-amp (A) outlet that lets you provide power to your entire RV, charging its batteries while running everything from lights to the air conditioner. The best RV generators need to be fairly beefy–powerful enough to keep multiple appliances running with juice to spare–but also portable enough to pack and, often, move in and out of the RV door.

An RV generator is a big investment, but an important one. We’ll help you find the right option for your setup and walk you through the shopping process and recommend the best models we’ve found and tested. With our picks, you can keep the power flowing wherever you roam.

Looking for more backup power solutions? Here are our reviews of the best portable generators, the best solar generators, and the best home generators.

This rock-solid block of generator excellence from Champion is as perfect for RVing as it gets. Its 4,500-watt output is more than enough to run your entire RV, including the air conditioner. At the same time, it’s surprisingly quiet, clocking in at just 61 decibels—the same volume as a dishwasher.

While it’s heavy at just over 100 pounds, it's fairly compact—the size of a couple of car batteries—and an integrated handle and wheels make it fairly easy to move around. It offers up to 14 hours of runtime on a single tank of gas (2.25 gallons), and you can expand the power capabilities by pairing it with a compatible generator using an optional parallel kit.

Champion has a whole line of inverter generators, but we recommend this one because it features a remote starter with a range of up to 80 feet, which we appreciate when we don’t feel like messing around with a generator in the cold or dark.

The Wen DF360iX offers quite a bit of utility for an affordable price. For starters, there is the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane at up to 3,600 or 3,500 starting watts, respectively, and either 900 or 2,600 running watts. (Propane generates slightly less power than gas.) That’s enough electricity for small to mid-size RVs.

At 49 pounds, this generator's relatively lightweight, but it doesn’t cut back on ports to keep the price low. It has a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV, two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. It also has an auto-shutoff feature if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t be too noisy for public areas like a campground.

There are some drawbacks to a generator at this price range, however. The size of the gas tank may be a concern. If you’re using gas and need it to run overnight, you’ll need a generator with a larger tank. At just 1.5 gallons, you only get up to five hours of usage with a half-load runtime (though using a 20-pound propane tank as your fuel can get that up to 14 hours). But if all you need is something basic, this gives you what you need at a good price.

Previously, we recommended the Pro version of this power station—mainly because it was highly portable with wheels and a telescoping handle—but Jackery has since discontinued it. Its replacement, the HomePower 3000, isn't quite as easy to move around, but it makes up for it with more power: It can generate up to 3,600 watts for 3,072 watt-hours of power capacity, and uses a LiFePO4 battery, which is more efficient and longer-lasting than the previous model.

While the HomePower 3000 no longer has wheels, it does have handles and weighs just under 60 pounds. There are larger portable power stations out there, but many are even more cumbersome than this one, making them exponentially more painful to lug in and out of your RV’s storage area.

More importantly, when paired with a pair of 200-watt SolarSaga panels, you can recharge the station in around 9 hours under sunny conditions. Of course, it can also be pre-charged much faster using an AC outlet, but when using solar, you can take yourself off-grid for longer periods.

It’s got all the connections you’ll need to power your RV, including a 30-amp outlet, plus four AC outlets, a 12-volt receptacle, and four USB ports should you need them. Other nice features include an app that allows you to monitor its power levels and output from your phone, and a battery management system that protects the station from power surges, overcurrent, and even extreme temperature conditions.

Dual-fuel generators are very nice to have on an RV, because the two types of fuel work well in different scenarios: gasoline is easy to obtain just about everywhere you go, so it's great for long, isolated trips or living off-grid, but makes a lot of noise. Propane isn’t quite as accessible, but it allows your generator to run more quietly.

We like the GD400BN specifically because it's powerful, quiet, and portable. With its 4,000-watt output, it’s more than capable of powering your entire rig, with the air conditioner, but it’s built solid and weighs less than 50 pounds. Another plug or two would’ve been nice–its single AC outlet limits things a bit if you have any reason to plug in power tools or equipment. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator and comes at a decent price to boot.

At this point, the Honda EU2200i is nothing short of a campsite icon. You see them all the time at campsites, and with good reason: They are renowned for doing pretty much everything right.

Weighing in at just over 46 pounds and not much larger than a couple of stacked shoeboxes, this is about as portable as RV-capable generators get. It’s also one of the quietest options in its class, purring along at 47-58 decibels, or about the same volume as a normal conversation. Test Editor Brad Ford found the same thing in his testing, calling the EU2200i “remarkably quiet.”

“The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on,” he wrote in our guide to the best portable generators.

And its durability is outright famous: I have personally spent years on end bumping and bashing one all over the place, and it just won’t break.

The primary downside is its 2,200-watt outage, which makes sense for its size but is relatively small if you’re powering an RV. Still, given how often you see it around, RVers are clearly okay working around its limitations.

I can report firsthand that the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra is an absolute performance monster, with massive output (7,500 watts) and enormous capacity (6,500 watt-hours), which you can expand further by adding extra 6,000-watt-hour batteries.

I recently had one along for a cloudy camping trip where solar panels would have been useless, but it didn’t matter because its charge lasted a solid three days (though it was cool weather and I wasn’t using my a/c—for that you’ll need solar). It also charges very quickly: I charged mine via a wall outlet in about 2 hours. I could easily use this generator to back up my entire house, so needless to say, it can store and produce enough energy to handily power an a/c and everything else you may need in your RV—particularly with a good solar setup.

The downside to carrying a generator like this around, of course, is the weight. At just over 180 pounds, it’s way too heavy to move in or out of an RV solo. It’s more portable than you might think, though: You can remove the batteries from the generator, then carry it out in more manageable parts. Plus, the power station has wheels to help you move it around. Ultimately, the Delta Pro Ultra is probably overkill for most RVers, but it pushes the boundaries on what you can expect from an RV-compatible generator.

When we tested the Bluetti Elite 300, we were impressed that this compact station boasted an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper. It’s not quite enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

We were also pleased with its solar recharging capability. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. It worked well when we paired it with a 250-watt portable panel.

The only thing we didn’t like was the inability to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 delivers a lot of power and runtime, but is still very portable and easy to store in an RV.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

If you want to be a good neighbor at your campsite, this generator from Westinghouse keeps the rumble to a minimum. Thanks to a special throttling system that only produces as much power as needed, it spins down when you aren’t drawing much rather than constantly roaring at full speed. That keeps the volume down, dropping to a decibel level akin to generators half its size at low usage. I’ve used older versions of what were essentially the same model; they were very quiet then, and reviews indicate the volume has gone down even more.

Its hefty 4,500-watt output is substantial, considering the lack of racket, and capable of powering an entire RV without issue. It also has a remote starter, which allows me to fire it up from the comfort of indoors.

This Westinghouse is fairly heavy, though a retractable handle, wheels, and lifting handles make it easier to move around. And its relatively compact shape passes through an RV door without too much trouble. All in all, it provides ample power while keeping the noise to a minimum.

We’ve used RV generators in all shapes and sizes for decades, and regularly test new models from both top manufacturers and up-and-coming startups. Our current selections are the result of all that experience. To supplement that experience, we compared our findings against a variety of expert reviews and those from real-world buyers at retailers like Amazon.

The recommendations below span a range of price points, portability, and operating specs, and situational needs, and after much testing and consideration, we are confident that these are truly some of the best RV generators you can buy right now.

Size matters–in watts (W), that is. Though power needs of RVs can vary widely, we generally suggest that most RVs need at least 2,000 watts at any given time—enough to power an air conditioner, fridge, lights, and a few devices. However, with just 2,000 watts, you’ll have to be careful about running the a/c along with other appliances, or you might run out of power quickly. If you’re spending a fair amount of time inside and plan to use your a/c often, look for a larger generator that can put out upwards of 3,500 watts.

If you’re using a solar generator (i.e., a power station connected to solar panels), you also need to consider your generator’s capacity, or its ability to store energy that’s been harnessed by a solar panel. To power an RV, you should look for a power station that can store at least 3,000 watt-hours (Wh), which is enough to power a fridge, lights, devices, and small appliances for a couple of days. And it needs to have an output of at least 2,000 watts, which allows it to power said essentials simultaneously.

Keep in mind that solar generators generally cannot generate as much juice as gas or a direct electrical hookup. Unless you have an extraordinary solar panel array and perfect sun to keep the power flowing, you probably won’t be able to power a full suite of appliances on solar alone.

Many RV generators run on gasoline, but there are also dual-fuel generators that allow you to use gas or propane. The advantage of propane is that it can run for longer when using, for example, a 20-pound tank (sometimes twice a long as the gas tank). It will also allow the generator to run more quietly. The disadvantage of propane is that it will deliver slightly less wattage.

A solar generator, a battery-based power station that you can recharge using a set of solar panels, is an increasingly popular and attractive option as well. You’ll need both to harness the power of the sun. While it takes time to fully charge a power station via solar panels, they’re more sustainable and work well if you’re camping off-grid. Plus, if you need to charge it in a hurry, all power stations can recharge by plugging them into a wall outlet.

Remember: It is never safe to run a gas or propane generator inside your RV. They emit carbon monoxide, which is deadly when allowed to build up indoors. Power stations, however, are safe to use indoors.

In addition to the standard 30-amp/120-volt outlet that you want to properly hook up your RV, the best RV generators will have a variety of plugs that will allow you to power or charge other devices directly. We usually look for standard AC outlets, like you’d find at home, which come in handy for plugging in power tools, outdoor appliances, or whatever else. Many generators also come with USB-A and USB-C ports to charge laptops, phones, and other tech.

If you plan on running everything off your RV, port variety may not be as important. But it’s a very nice value add if you plan to use the generator away from your RV.

Since any RV enthusiast is bound to find themselves in a campground or RV park during their travels. The locations often have rules around noise levels and won’t allow noisy generators to bother other guests. The National Park Service, for example, prohibits “operating motorized equipment or machinery that exceeds a noise level of 60 decibels.” This is based on a range of 50 feet. That gives you a little wiggle room, but we recommend 65 decibels or lower.

Traditional, fuel-based generators are often louder than this, so for RV use, we recommend using inverter generators. Not only do these run much quieter, but they provide more stable current, which is important if you are powering sensitive devices such as TVs, laptops, and microwaves. Meanwhile, power stations run virtually silently, so noise level is never an issue for them.

There’s no “set it and forget it” RV generator: You will need to move it around often, so it needs to be light enough for one to two people to carry in and out. In general, lighter is better, but we’d generally look for one around 40-50 pounds for a 2,000-watt generator, or 50-100 pounds for 3,000-4,000 watts. Some generators feature built-in wheels and handles, which makes life easier when moving them around.

All this moving also means the generator needs to be durable enough to take a few bumps here and there. Plus, you want it to last as long as possible without needing repairs. It’s hard to gauge durability on spec, but certain brands have reputations for strong build quality and sturdy construction. Even then, it always pays to look at user reviews and find out if your pick has a reputation for holding up over time.

Portable gas generators run anywhere from 6 to 18 hours, depending on their fuel capacity. When properly well-maintained, you should be able to run it until the tank runs dry, fill it back up, then start over. Never attempt to refill the gas tank while the generator is running, which can lead to fires.

Power stations, sometimes referred to as solar generators, can run for several hours to several days, depending on the capacity of the battery and how much power you are using. Once depleted, the battery can take 1-2.5 hours to recharge using AC power, or 9 or more hours using solar panels.

Various experts recommend that fuel-based (gas and propane) generators be placed anywhere from 5-25 feet away from the RV or home, but we’ve found that 5-10 feet is about right. Just make sure the generator is clear of doors and windows. You don’t want to run the risk of carbon monoxide blowing into the RV. Also, it shouldn’t push up against a wall or other gear–you’re your generator well-ventilated on all sides.

Because they don’t emit any exhaust fumes, power stations can be set up wherever you like; however, if you are pairing them with solar panels, you’ll need them to be within cable distance of the panels, and your panels will need to be positioned to capture sunlight.

You can, but you shouldn’t. Electricity and water don’t mix, and running a generator in the rain can have unpredictable results. At best, it may fry the generator or your RV electrical system. At worst, it could cause a fire or electrocute someone.

#6306. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

Standing desks have become a go-to upgrade for anyone who works from home. Swapping your desk chair for a standing desk seems like an easy fix for a day spent slouched over a laptop, but standing still and upright for hours isn’t much healthier than sitting all day.

A 2024 study from the University of Sydney found that standing more didn’t lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, or heart failure, and it was linked to a higher risk of circulatory problems like varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis. To get the most out of your standing setup, you also need to sit for parts of the day.

If you work at a bar countertop or have a standing desk that can’t be lowered, a standard desk chair won’t work. The solution is an adjustable desk chair made for higher surfaces. It’s there when you need a break, and it’s easy to roll or slide out of the way when you’re ready to stand again.

If you’re looking for a standing desk chair that doesn't sacrifice style, then this drafting chair could be the perfect fit. It comes in seven colors to match any interior design scheme and adjusts up to 33 inches in height to fit any standing desk setup.

To rest your legs and feet, you need a chair that reaches the right height, supports your feet when you’re seated, and gets out of the way when it’s time to stand.

Measure from the floor to the top of your desk at your usual standing height, then subtract 10 to 12 inches. That’s roughly the seat height you want, leaving room for your thighs under the desk. Faux leather and vinyl are easy to wipe clean and usually cost less. Mesh breathes better if you run warm, and molded polypropylene or plastic seats are the lightest and easiest to move around. The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

#6303. Nov. 4, 1922: Tutankhamun’s tomb is discovered

When archaeologists peered inside Tutankhamun’s tomb a few weeks after its discovery on Nov. 4, 1922, they found antechambers packed to the brim with thousands of artifacts: statues, furniture, jewelry, clothes, chariots, paintings. Among these possessions was an iron dagger — just over one foot in length and crafted from an iron meteorite.

The cosmic source of the iron in the late pharaoh’s dagger was confirmed when a team of Italian researchers analyzed its elemental composition for the first time in 2016. While Earth-based iron contains about 4 percent nickel, the team found that the blade’s higher nickel concentration (and trace amounts of cobalt) was instead consistent with space rock.

Four years later, aided by the Grand Egyptian Museum’s conservation center, Takafumi Matsui, director of the Chiba Institute of Technology’s Planetary Exploration Research Center in Japan, and his colleagues used a portable scanning X-ray fluorescence instrument to map out the elements on the surface of the blade. They found not just iron, nickel, and cobalt, but also chlorine and manganese, among others. They also found that the bumpy, black spots along its edges and center likely originated from troilite — a mineral commonly found in iron meteorites. Further research released in 2022 investigated the how and where the blade was forged after its raw materials fell to Earth.

#6302. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6300. The Mystery of Life’s Origin on Earth Just Got More Mysterious

Hydrogen cyanide was crucial for early Earth chemistry. A new study says comets almost certainly didn’t deliver it like we’d previously thought.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Since time immemorial, humanity’s greatest thinkers have wrestled with what is arguably the most burning question of our inquisitive species: Why are we here? Over the millennia, the proposed answers have meandered from the divine to the demonstrable. Then, in 1953, the famous Miller-Urey experiment made it seem increasingly plausible that life emerged from the complex chemistry of early Earth.

However, exactly where life’s building blocks came from remains an open question. Some scientists favor “panspermia,” the idea that life didn't begin on Earth at all. In this view, hardy microbes rode here aboard comets, asteroids, or rocky debris blasted off other worlds, survived the trip through space, and seeded our planet. A softer version of the idea says space rocks delivered life’s raw ingredients rather than life itself, in the form of organic molecules made in the protoplanetary disk around our young sun. Still others argue that Earth needed no outside help and produced everything life required on its own.

But just as important as pinpointing this much sought-after answer is ruling out a few choices. To that end, a new study led by scientists at the University of Cambridge and published in the journal Scientific Reports models the possibility that comets ferried chemicals, specifically hydrogen cyanide (HCN), to the planet’s surface during its infancy more than four billion years ago. A 2022 study found that cyanide on early Earth likely served as a critical reductant (an electron donor in a chemical reaction), and the cyanide also served as a vital intermediate in Stanley Miller and Harold Urey’s famous experiments by producing amino acids when exposed to electricity (possibly from volcanic lightning).

Cometary bombardment is one of the leading theories of how HCN arrived on Earth (though other studies explore whether Earth's own chemistry could have produced the molecule). So the Cambridge team, led by Richard Anslow, modeled whether comets could have delivered it. They found the opposite of what the theory predicts: The chances of comets delivering HCN intact to the surface are vanishingly small, bordering on impossible.

“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon- and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get-out-of-jail-free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” Anslow said in a press statement. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”

The theory that comets provided the chemical substrate of life runs head first into two major problems. Anslow’s previous work showed that “bouncing comets”—comets whose speeds are impacted by the gravitational influence of multiple planets—could arrive gently enough to deliver their fragile cargo intact. But these new models suggest that such a billiard-ball effect likely didn’t occur in Earth’s neighborhood. Using advances in comet-impact simulations and a better understanding of comet-atmosphere interactions, the researchers concluded that comets usually traveled too fast and at too sharp an angle. On the off chance that HCN did survive the journey, the concentrations would often be too low to be useful, and prebiotic chemistry would need to occur quickly upon arrival. Together, these two requirements push the comet-delivery theory from plausible to a “one-in-a-million” occurrence, Anslow says.

“We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way,” Anslow said in a press statement. “But it seems to be a really rare occurrence—at best, a one-off fluke.”

Strangely, Earth’s planetary neighbor Mars would’ve had an easier go of it because it’s smaller and its atmosphere is less thick. This would’ve increased the likelihood of comets actually reaching its surface in higher numbers, but the dissolution of the Red Planet’s magnetic field roughly four billion years ago doomed the world to a lifeless existence (as far as complex life goes, that is).

Neither Anslow’s previous work nor this new study rules out the possibility that comets helped deliver life’s ingredients elsewhere in the Milky Way or beyond. But when it comes to the age-old question of why we’re here, these icy wanderers are likely not the answer.

Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

The new toothbrush still needs to be tested in further safety trials.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

#6298. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6297. Van Gogh’s Starry Night shows a real night sky, study suggests

For decades, art historians and astronomers have wondered whether the sky of Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night shows real stars or imagined ones. A new study argues the stars are real — and that Van Gogh likely saw them a month later than most scholars thought.

The study, published Oct. 22 in Scientific Reports, comes from a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of the South Korean telescope maker SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University’s School of Space Research in Yongin.

By combining astronomical data, historical primary sources, and statistical analysis, the team narrowed the celestial alignments shown in the painting’s sky to a handful of late-July mornings.

They further suggest Van Gogh likely painted the eastern sky as seen from his asylum room in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, around 3 a.m. on July 22, 1889. That morning, a waning crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades — the V-shaped star cluster in Taurus the Bull — were all gathered in the same small patch of sky.

RELATED: Exploring the solar system through space art

In May 1889, Van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, a former monastery outside Saint-Rémy. The previous December, after a falling-out with fellow painter Paul Gauguin, he had cut off his left ear, and more breakdowns followed. At the asylum he kept working, producing some 150 paintings, including famous works like Almond Blossom and The Starry Night.

On June 18, he wrote to his brother Theo that he had begun “a new study of a starry sky.” For most scholars, that line anchored the painting to the mid-June sky.

In 1984, art historian Albert Boime argued the painting likely shows the dawn of June 19, with the constellation Aries at its center. Two years later, astronomer Charles Whitney used weather records to rule out the 19th and suggested the sky was actually a composite. With the two theories at odds, the idea that Van Gogh painted real stars faded to what the authors call a “marginal minority view.” Most scholars granted only that the bright point near the horizon was likely Venus.

Kim’s team thought the stars were most likely real, and that the early studies were incomplete. No one had tested the painter’s field of view, the shape of its pattern of stars, and the historical record together. Plus, on the morning of June 19, the Moon was a waning gibbous, past half and nothing like the slim crescent depicted on the canvas.

Rather than assuming a date, the researchers asked whether the sky Van Gogh painted could occur, and when. Their method has two core steps. First, they compare a painted sky with astronomical simulations to see whether its arrangement is even possible. Then, they use a statistical method that measures the similarity between two shapes — called Procrustes analysis — to see how faithfully the painting’s star patterns matched real ones. When more historical data is available, the team also works to reconstruct the artist’s field of view from the landscape and check candidate dates against weather records and letters.

As a proof of concept, they applied the method to a handful of other night paintings. A 2011 study had argued that the stars in German painter Adam Elsheimer’s 1609 The Flight into Egypt weren’t copied from a single real sky, and the team’s test agreed. The painting’s Big Dipper sits at an angle to the Milky Way that never occurs in the night sky.

French painter Jean-François Millet’s Starry Night, painted between 1850 and 1865, has no letters, weather records, or known painting site to draw on, so the team ran only the core astronomical tests. The painting’s depiction of Orion — including the bright star Rigel — and Sirius revealed the tightest fit of any painting in the study to an actual star pattern.

Van Gogh’s own 1888 Starry Night Over the Rhône and Café Terrace at Night were next. Because their painting sites in Arles still stand and his letters and local weather records survive, they got the full treatment. The Big Dipper in Starry Night Over the Rhône matched the real sky with what the authors call “relative precision,” and the Summer Triangle in Café Terrace at Night fit even more closely.

RELATED: How Galileo blended science and art before his death 380 years ago

Then came The Starry Night. Van Gogh is thought to have based the painting’s village on an earlier sketch he had completed of Saint-Rémy. After locating a ridge near the asylum whose view matches the drawing, the team found the sketch captures a zoomed-in slice of the landscape. Measured diagonally, from one corner of the frame to the opposite corner, the field of view spans about 18°. They then made an assumption: that Van Gogh likely framed the painting’s night sky the same way. If he did, there should be a morning on record when the Moon, Venus, and a recognizable star pattern all fit inside that narrow frame and are arranged as painted.

Only three dawns in June and July 1889 put the Moon above Venus, as in the painting, inside that field of view: June 23, July 22, and July 23. Only the July mornings also placed the Hyades in view, and on July 22, the Moon and Venus sat in opposite corners with the cluster in between.

At the center of the canvas, a cluster of stars forms a lopsided V that closely resembles the shape of the Hyades cluster. But any handful of dots can coincidentally look like a V. The team had to evaluate whether these stars were intentionally painted as the Hyades or just happened to resemble the cluster’s shape.

They reasoned that if Van Gogh had painted the real cluster, each painted star should have a real counterpart in the same spot. That is, the star at the point of the painted V should match the star at the point of the real V, and so on down each arm of the cluster. Matching them up that way should give a better fit than any other possible combination. So the team tried every possible way of pairing the five painted stars with the five real ones — 120 combinations in all — and measured how well each fit. The natural, point-to-point pairing was the most accurate.

The match was close, but it wasn’t perfect. Of all the paintings the team tested, The Starry Night fit its stars with the lowest statistical accuracy. The authors also acknowledge that a close shape match alone can’t identify a star group. Some other constellations score as well or better and are ruled out only by other evidence, such as where they sat in the sky that morning. Nevertheless, the combined evidence still suggested July 22 as the most likely date.

One objection to this scenario remained. Historians have long held that a severe seizure in mid-July left Van Gogh unable to work. But after rereading his letters alongside weather records from that summer, the team argues the seizure may have struck later, in the last week of July, leaving Van Gogh free to watch the dawn sky on July 22.

The authors argue that the fact that so many clues converge on one morning makes it “hard to reconcile with the premise that the sky on the canvas is an arbitrary creation.” The simpler explanation is that the painting’s sky is rooted in actual observations of the sky on that morning in July — and the burden of proof now falls on anyone who says Van Gogh invented it.

Because the core test needs nothing but the star positions, the team argues it could be turned on other night paintings, including many no one has yet examined. “I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-Rémy paintings, and at Van Gogh’s movements that summer,” Kim said in a statement. “Our conversation with Van Gogh’s other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one.”

Stellarium, the free planetarium software the team used to cross-check its simulations, lets you simulate the night sky from any place and date. Enter Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, and set the clock to a couple hours before sunrise on July 22, 1889. If the sky looks too bright, turn off the atmosphere in the view settings (or press the keyboard shortcut, A).

Then search for the Hyades cluster. Brilliant Venus sits on one side, a slim crescent Moon slightly higher on the other, and between them the V of the Hyades. You can scroll through the hours to watch the scene wheel up from the horizon before dawn. Then step back a day to July 21, or ahead to July 23 and 24, and watch the Moon slide toward Venus. Or compare the view with June 19, the date Boime proposed, and judge for yourself which sky best fits the canvas.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6296. The Real Ark of the Covenant May Be Hiding in Ethiopia—and Only One Man Alive Is Allowed to See It

According to an ancient Ethiopian epic, the biblical relic was stolen in a 3,000-year-old temple heist—and now sits in a tiny chapel guarded by a single monk for life.

Next to the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in the ancient city of Axum, Ethiopia, stands a small, fenced-off sanctuary called the Chapel of the Tablet. Entry is forbidden to everyone on Earth except one man: a lone monk appointed for life to watch over its contents.

According to believers, he’s guarding one of history’s most sacred and sought-after relics: the Ark of the Covenant.

In the Hebrew Bible, the Ark is described in precise detail: a rectangular chest of acacia wood overlaid inside and out with gold, measuring roughly four feet long by two feet wide and high, and crowned with two golden cherubim with outstretched wings. Forged at Mount Sinai to house the Ten Commandments and serve as God’s literal throne on Earth, the Ark guided the Israelites through the wilderness, toppled enemy armies, and eventually became the sacred centerpiece of King Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem. Then, during the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.E., this ultimate seat of divine power vanished from the biblical record without a trace.

For millennia, its disappearance has fueled endless archaeological quests, conspiracy theories, and pop-culture touchstones like 1981’s Raiders of the Lost Ark. Yet according to the Kebra Nagast (“The Glory of the Kings”), a revered 14th-century Ethiopian national epic, the Ark was never lost at all. Instead, it was smuggled out of Jerusalem nearly 3,000 years ago by Menelik I, the son of King Solomon and Makeda—better known outside Ethiopia as the Queen of Sheba.

According to the epic, Menelik grew up in Ethiopia before traveling to Jerusalem in his early twenties to meet his father, carrying a royal ring Solomon had left with his mother as proof of his lineage. Solomon recognized the young man immediately—he was the spitting image of his grandfather, King David—and begged his favored son to stay and inherit the throne of Israel.

Menelik insisted on returning home to rule his mother’s kingdom. Reluctantly, Solomon agreed, but on one condition. The firstborn sons of Jerusalem’s highest-ranking nobles, priests, and military commanders were ordered to accompany Menelik as his new royal court to establish a “second Israel” in Ethiopia.

That decree sealed the Ark’s fate. Devastated at the thought of leaving the presence of God behind, the young elites conspired to pull off an ancient inside job. The heist was masterminded by Azariah, son of the High Priest Zadok. Prompted by an angel in a vision, Azariah commissioned an exact wooden replica of the Ark. Under cover of night, he and his co-conspirators slipped into the Temple, swapped the genuine Ark for the decoy, and hid the real relic in their luggage.

When Menelik’s caravan departed the next day, the Kebra Nagast claims the Ark’s power lifted their wagons and animals off the ground, propelling them toward Ethiopia at supernatural speed. By the time Zadok discovered the counterfeit and Solomon’s army gave frantic chase, the Ethiopians were long gone.

Christianity was still centuries away, so as tradition has it, the relic was first kept on Tana Qirqos, a remote island on Ethiopia’s Lake Tana, where priests guarded it for 800 years. Then around 340 C.E., when King Ezana of the Aksumite Empire converted to Christianity, the Ark was ceremoniously moved to the newly built Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum, permanently linking the ancient Israelite covenant with Ethiopian Christianity.

Over the centuries, whenever invaders threatened Axum—including Queen Gudit’s forces in the 10th century and the devastating Adal War in the 16th century—monks spirited the Ark away to mountain strongholds and island refuges until the cathedral could be rebuilt. In the 1960s, Empress Menen Asfaw, wife of Emperor Haile Selassie, funded the dedicated Chapel of the Tablet next door. According to local monastic lore, the move was necessary because a divine “heat” radiating from the Ark was cracking the ancient stone walls of its previous sanctum.

Because the Ethiopian Orthodox Church forbids anyone—including scholars, archaeologists, and even the church’s own patriarch—from laying eyes on the relic, its authenticity remains impossible to verify scientifically. Only one outsider in modern history has claimed to get a look. In 1941, British army officer Edward Ullendorff—later a prominent professor of Ethiopian studies—allegedly used his military clout and fluency in classical Ge’ez to talk his way inside the sanctuary. In a 1992 interview, Ullendorff claimed the chest he saw was merely a “middle- to late-medieval construction.”

However, Ethiopian officials and historians quickly pointed out a flaw in Ullendorff’s scoop: every church in Ethiopia keeps a replica of the Ark, known as a tabot, for ceremonial use. If Ullendorff saw a medieval wooden box, believers argue, he was simply fooled by a decoy—the exact same trick Azariah used on King Solomon 3,000 years ago.

And so, while treasure hunters continue to scour subterranean tunnels in Jerusalem and desert caves across the Middle East, millions of Ethiopians believe the search is already over. The world’s most famous lost treasure isn’t buried in a secret vault—it’s sitting right on a street corner in Axum, hiding in plain sight.

Magma and a possible environment for ancient life might be present on Mars in the region of a large volcano on the Red Planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A noxious gas found seeping through cracks on Mars hints that there may be magma flowing beneath the Red Planet's surface — and perhaps even an environment similar to habitable ones on Earth, a new study suggests.

Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft spotted a possible signal of hydrogen chloride gas leaking from rifts in the region of Alba Mons, the largest volcano on Mars in terms of surface area. (Mars' famous Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in terms of height.) Scientists interpret this gas as emissions from hot magma below the regolith of Mars.

Although more research is required to confirm the emissions, the team suggested that Alba Mons may host an environment similar to hydrothermal vents on Earth, where life once likely arose and continues to thrive today.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances Wednesday (Nov. 4), is not the first to suggest that magma may be flowing on Mars; NASA's InSight lander interpreted its presence through seismic observations and modeling earlier this year. But the new findings are the strongest evidence yet of gases being released by dormant volcanoes on Mars, first study author Alexander Trokhimovskiy, at Russia's Space Research Institute, told Live Science.

"Our study offers a complementary and potentially independent line of evidence [of Martian magma]: Atmospheric observations that reveal a possible signature of gas release from a subsurface magmatic system," Trokhimovskiy wrote in an email.

TGO first detected hydrogen chloride gas in Mars' atmosphere in 2021, but scientists were hesitant to link it to volcanic activity. The gas appeared to be seasonal, its distribution was not localized at a possible volcanic region, and other signs of volcanic gases, like sulfur, were not present, study co-author Kevin Olson, a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford who studies Mars gases, told Live Science in a separate email.

A photo of Mars with the Tharsis region centered.

Further work, however, suggested that the gas wasn't just popping up in the warmer spring and summer in Mars' southern hemisphere; it also appeared in the winter in the northern hemisphere, he noted.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"I managed to catch two observations from the start of northern winter in the first Mars year of our mission, and a single observation the next year," Olson said, adding that a year on Mars is closer to two years on Earth due to the planet's wider orbit. "These out-of-season measurements were close to one another in location and time in both years, which was rather surprising. We then set about creating a campaign of special, targeted measurements at this time and place."

That campaign lasted two Mars years — roughly four Earth years — and increased the likelihood that scientists are seeing "an injection" of hydrogen chloride into the atmosphere from volcano-adjacent vents, Olson said.

The scientists confirmed the unseasonal observations in the northern hemisphere, finding a "distinct and pronounced signal" that then diminishes and falls below the spacecraft's detection threshold. "This inconsistency is more suggestive of a puff of gas entering the atmosphere than of regular atmospheric chemistry," he said. "While the link remains a hypothesis, we have now seen this gas appear locally, and nowhere else, over four Mars years of observations."

Daniel Mège, also a co-author of the paper and a professor who studies planetary geology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, identified the fissures where the gas may be emerging. He said the complementary evidence from InSight (on the ground) and TGO (circling above) helps give the study weight: InSight spotted activity in the crust, while TGO detected the emissions in the atmosphere.

Although magma activity is not in itself a sign of life, Mège noted that Earth's first life-forms came from sites like hydrothermal zones, which have a similar confluence of materials and energy as the potential vents on Mars. But conditions would need to be favorable in that area for at least millions of years to allow life to form, he cautioned.

"If these requirements are met at local scale, at the scale of the seepage structures, then living organisms might wait for us to discover them," he told Live Science in an email. "But maintaining stable conditions over such a long period at a very local scale is not obvious."

#6294. A 1,600-Year-Old Artistic Marvel Seemed Physically Impossible to Recreate. Until One Scientist Did.

It took the better part of two millennia to figure out the science behind how this ancient glass cup could change colors.

Roughly 1,600 years ago, ancient Romans crafted one of the most pristine—and scientifically advanced—works of glass art, a cup that shifts colors between jade green and ruby red. We’ve never adequately replicated the creation, but that’s all changing thanks to the scientific process used in a University of Sheffield project aimed at mimicking the Romans.

“Although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting,” said Lisa Hollands, a team leader at the university’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, in a statement, “they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’”

Roman color-changing glass first appeared in the fourth century C.E., and the Lycurgus Cup offers the most glamorous example of it. Now on display at the British Museum, it’s one of 40 surviving glass cage cups. Its exterior depicts the mythical Thracian king Lycurgus ensnared in vines. The cup appears green in reflected light and red when light shines through it.

It’s a spectacular museum piece, but it’s long puzzled glassmakers and historians. How did the Romans create this color-shifting trick, now known as the dichroic effect? And why has every modern attempt to reproduce it failed? The leading explanation is that Roman artisans embedded trace amounts of gold and silver in the glass, forming nanoparticles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. Because these particles are smaller than the wavelengths of light, they don’t just let light pass through. They absorb and scatter certain colors depending on their size and shape, so the glass looks different depending on how light hits it.

“I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass,” Hollands said. “I’ve studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I’ve gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve.”

Hollands partnered with Caroline Jackson, a leading Roman glass expert, to learn about Roman-era glassmaking and to understand the materials they might have used. “Then came the more difficult part of trying to get small amounts of gold and silver into the glass in the right form,” she said.

Hollands experimented with different furnace types, starting materials with varying oxygen levels, and even sugar. Eventually she hit on a recipe that works: Her glass looks opaque green in reflected light and glows red when light shines through.

This magical effect occurs because when gold and silver join the molten glass mixture, nanocrystals grow. Because the nanoparticles are smaller than the wavelengths of light, Hollands told The Guardian, the electrons in their atoms can block certain colors under the right conditions. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through,” she said. “If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see.”

With the recipe finally cracked, the team asked Elliot Walker to use it in a contemporary sculpture. Walker is one of the UK's foremost glass artists and won season two of Netflix’s Blown Away. “It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one,” Walker said. “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass. It’s like shaking their hands.”

Walker gave the sculpture a classical form to echo the Lycurgus Cup, and he included a blown-glass element to show off its color-shifting effect. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture,” he said, “with the globe replaced by a cup.”

The new creation goes on display at the university’s Festival of the Mind on November 6 before shifting permanently into the school’s Turner Museum of Glass.

The Sheffield team said that although the recipe is mainly meant for decorative glass, the science behind it could lead to new photonic materials, which control light, and to advanced glasses for storing radioactive waste. Already, the project has contributed to research on immobilizing complex nuclear waste in glass and understanding the conditions that cause crystals to form, which helps maximize how much waste can be safely locked away.

“What Lisa and Elliot have managed to achieve has surpassed all our expectations,” said Christina Metcalfe, the school’s Molecular Photonic Breadboards project manager. “The incredible historic narrative rally captures people’s imaginations, and I like to think we’ve created something that people will marvel at for years to come.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6293. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”
