#6272. The Best New Restaurants in NYC Come in All Cuisines and Sizes

New York City has a new restaurant flinging its doors open seemingly every hour—and that's on top of the time-worn institutions, from old-school steakhouses and delis to bagel shops run by the same family for decades.

When it comes to the new, we're spoiled for choice: One week, it's a fabulous Korean small-plates bar with a commendable natural wine list downtown; the next it's an imported taverna from Argentina in the Village where the steaks are juicy as hell and, well, there's even more great wine to work your way through. To help you parse through all the opening news and find the buzzy spots worth fighting for a reservation at, our editors are eating out night after night, trying new Mexican mariscos joints and modern Indian fine-dining spots, to report back on the ones that stand out.

This is our Fall 2026 status report on the best of the new—the places to try your luck walking into, or commit to a Friday night dinner at, whether you're a NYC local or a visitor in town for just the weekend. These are the best new restaurants in New York right now.

The best new restaurants in New York City stretch across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island. Every business on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has personally tried the restaurant in question. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of the city. We’re always looking for standout dishes, a great location, and warm service—as well as serious sustainability credentials. In terms of how we define ‘new,’ we've chosen to focus on restaurants that have opened within a year of the publish date. When you work your way through the list, check back in: We'll update this guide regularly as new restaurants open in New York City.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: Martini hour and Shrimp Voodoo

After around seven years of living in Williamsburg, I’ve finally found the moody, cozy refuge this pocket of the neighborhood was missing. Booth’s Extra Fine, which just opened on October 9, feels like a sexy little secret. Hidden behind discreet oxblood curtains, the space simulates a vintage 20th-century supper club with dark walnut, rich leather booths, and deep, amber, brain-massage-like lighting. The heart of the restaurant stems from chef Nick Pfannerstill’s grandfather, Booth—an effortlessly stylish Milwaukee car salesman whose 1920s-50s photos line the walls.

Lean into the nostalgia and splurge on the porterhouse steak for two (or three—it's massive), but don't skip the Caviar Royale or the chef’s-kiss Shrimp Voodoo appetizer, cooked and swimming in Creole garlic butter. Personally? I can't wait to return and try the dry-aged Extra Fine Burger and a nice martini. Speaking of martinis, look out for Booth's "martini hour" launching soon, putting $12 cocktails—gin or vodka—at your disposal. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

Neighborhood: Hudson Yards, ManhattanGo for: A standout egg curry

Indienne, a tasting-menu-driven Indian restaurant, comes from chef Sujan Sarkar, who has worked in kitchens across Mumbai, New York, and San Francisco and runs a Michelin-starred restaurant of the same name in Chicago. Sarkar’s shtick? In his words: he reimagines Indian cuisine by “blending classical Indian flavors with refined European technique.” Think: deconstructed and then reconstructed. It takes a couple of courses to get a feel for what Sarkar is doing. The dhokla, for instance, isn’t spongy; it’s cubed, dehydrated, crackly, and tinged with white chocolate. The zingy passionfruit pani puri arrives in the shape of an oyster shell over reindeer moss. But once you get past the initial surprises, things really pick up. The “egg curry”—a whole steamed egg sitting on top of curry foam encrusted with potato sev and topped with caviar, served with buttery babka pao and house-churned butter—is an absolute standout. Things get a little more traditional with the chicken makhani that my husband got: chicken, three ways (chicken breast topped with spiced chicken mince wrapped over malai mousseline), served with buttery dal and even butterier naan. I didn’t miss the meat for a second, being on the vegetarian tasting menu myself, because my celeriac kebab was smoky and melt-in-your-mouth. And then came another surprise: the ghewar, a traditional Indian sweet that arrived like a mini layer cake with edible gold leaf (there’s a lot of this) and a bouncy coconut foam. A Penicillin-adjacent drink made with apricot whisky, mead, and ginger kept me company along the way. As we left, we were shown Sarkar’s other venture in the same premises, the British-Indian chophouse Elder, that was busy on a Tuesday night. —Arati Menon, global digital director

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ribeye among many other things

From the man (Pablo Rivero) behind one of Buenos Aires's most iconic steakhouses (Don Julio) comes Graciela—an Argentine tavern on a cozy corner in the West Village, where the wine list is long and commendable, the food is fire-cooked, and the room is star-studded in that quiet, in-the-know way. All the hype made me suspicious, but if you're expecting a Corner Store or Carbone experience, this is not that. It's just fantastic cooking that is elevated and pristinely executed enough to be covetable, with an experience that stays focused on the food. And the space, with dried herbs hanging from the ceiling and heavy wooden furniture and warm, low light, feels both moody and inviting; cool yet welcoming.

It's easy to rack up a major bill here, because every corner of the menu is worth exploring—from a red pepper dip with wood-fired oven-made bread, to the sliced bondiola coppa with lemon zest and olive oil (a very true must), to, of course, the salty, sizzling steaks. (The iconic whole tomato starter has been lost to the turning of the seasons, but I am certain something autumnal will replace it.) Some flavors are more complex, but much of what you'll find are crowd-pleasers, like the milanesa neapolitana which our serve aptly described as being "like a pizza milanesa" which is impossible to complain about. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Roti, actually, to accompany the beef cheek panang curry

The preponderance of new restaurants in the West Village specifically should be studied—sometimes it feels like we could dedicate a whole list to that neighborhood alone. The best of them, like Hommali, take the cuisine of choice and present it in an eminently stylish, upscale dining room. Every time I asked general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin where something—the stemware, any number of the vividly colorful paintings on the walls—had come from, the answer was JJ Market, or Chatuchak Weekend Market, in Bangkok. It just looks good in there, I can't stress it enough. And then there's the matter of the food, which is buoyant, delightful, and oftentimes a wonderful introduction to Thai flavors for many Americans. I'm talking about a cold tom yum seafood cocktail, a heavily-spiced beef tartare on tripe cracker, and tao jiew lon, a fermented soybean-coconut dip scooped up with fried veggies. The mains are enormous and well-priced, and the best bite of the evening was not the beef cheek panang curry (although that was great on its own), but rather the piece of delicate roti used to scrape up the last remnants of sauce. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: SoHo, ManhattanGo for: sashimi and sake pairing

For this toro-obsessed tuna lover, Noury’s torotaku tartare topped with uni was love at first bite. As I greedily piled the pale-pink tuna belly, pillowing orange uni, and pickled yellow daikon radish with a dash of sushi rice onto a sheet of toasted nori to make a DIY handroll, I knew at once that I had reached appetizer ambrosia. And the saké pairing? Divine nectar.

I had high expectations for chef-and-sommelier duo Alex Chang and Lina Goujjane, who opened Kiko together in 2024, which I believe remains one of the city’s most underrated restaurants simply because of its isolated locale in so-called Hudson Square. Now, with Noury the pair finally has an address to match their ambitions in prime Soho, on Sullivan Street between West Houston and Prince.

While Kiko is cozy and chic, Noury is stylish and sexy. The restaurant is modeled after a Japanese “izakaya,” relaxed dining establishments that serve shareable plates and drinkable tipples. As such, small bites, raw seafood, and saké are the star, but the vibe isn’t so puritan as an omakase counter. In addition to the daily changing sashimi and futomaki, there are also non-fish entrees like the steak haché (not my favorite bite, but a popular crowd pleaser) and pork and cheese mille feuille katsu; plus a surprisingly addictive chrysanthemum salad. To pull it all together, Chef Alex tapped Joji Miwa as Noury’s chef de cuisine, whose career spans award winning restaurants like Sushi Sanshin in Osaka and Sushi Noz in New York. That’s where he first met Lina, the mastermind behind the beverage program, which includes both extremely rare and accessible sakes and a selection of shochu cocktails and refined spirit-free options. Like at Kiko, the service at Noury is knowledgeable and their hospitality kind. Come. Eat. Drink. Be merry. —Hannah Towey, news editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ox tongue

Somssi, like Arthur, is new but doesn't feel it. It's a West Village restaurant with no flash or bombast, just a short and clever menu that jumps off from operator Ahris Kim's Korean origins and a casual, dimly-lit couple of dining rooms with lace accoutrements and eclectic hanging art giving the most comfortable feeling that you're at a friend's supper club rather than a sterling food and beverage operation. There's the semi-viral "Potato, Potato, Potato and Caviar" croquette, which is what it sounds like and will appeal to all, but more fun is to be had with things like the Grilled Ox Tongue, which comes undisguised as such on the plate with its uneven triangular shape atop romesco. I only gagged once while eating it, when my teeth came too close to my own tongue and I thought too hard about what I was eating, but then quickly continued my feast for love of the novel and tender dish. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Nolita, ManhattanGo for: crudo spotted with stracciatella and a late night

It was fitting that I ended up at Tashca just a few days after returning from Portugal, because I could fully appreciate how plucked-from-Lisbon this special spot in the LES is. Open only on Thursdays (the space is available for private events on other nights), this breezy little restaurant feels like being at a friend’s slightly chaotic but very endearing dinner party. Your table may or may not be ready when it’s supposed to be (we were given sparkling wine when ours took 30 minutes longer than planned, which is a trade I would have willingly made), and on that note, all reservations are made by Instagram DM (and you will need one; I saw several walk-in hopefuls turned away). But when you do flit through the open doors into the dining room, you won’t want to leave. Candles burn low throughout the night, and flowers hang from light fixtures—and the food, most importantly, sings, toeing the line between beauty and comfort, with distinctly Portuguese dishes that feature great seafood, bright produce, and a long list of tasty wines to pair. On the night I visited, there was a $95 prix-fixe made in partnership with visiting chef Joao Magalhaes Correia (who is usually in the kitchen at his Lisbon spots like Bar Alimentar). It featured a couscous bathed in squid ink and topped with a perfectly charred skewer of grilled octopus; melon draped in presunto ham; and a crudo topped with globs of stracciatella that I never could have imagined would work as well as it did. Come early, and plan to stay late. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: NoMad, ManhattanGo for: fried chicken, actually!

When the Jungsik team closed sleek offshoot Sea in NoMad in May, it wasn't to abandon ship. They worked with commendable quickness to open a new concept, Mūje, by July. Like Jungsik proper, Mūje serves a tasting menu. Unlike Jungsik proper, Mūje is casual and focused on Asian food more generally rather than Korean exclusively. It's also more affordable at $150 for eight courses (Jungsik will cost you $335 for 10). There's a lot of fun to be had here with such a premise, like the tender short rib that comes with four different wraps nodding to Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese approaches, respectively. The best bite by a mile is the chicken wing, which is insane. It comes deboned and stuffed with pork, a Chinese technique, but is fried with the Korean Prinkle seasoning (a combination of cheese and onion and other good stuff) to create something really special. You only get one, so savor it. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Greenpoint, BrooklynGo for: an immaculate and affordable champagne list, plus the half chicken of the moment

I loved being at Arthur. With its lively and long dining room, buoyant soundtrack of soul music, and warm service, it's a place that feels like it's been around for a long time despite having opened in April. Food and drink are reasons to visit, in equal measure. Charlotte Mirzoeff's wine list is extensive and counts the French along with the Corsican and Portuguese, with a Champagne list 30-plus bottles deep (Mirzoeff is obsessed with the stuff, wants us all to be drinking more of it, and has two options for less than $100 to help make that happen.) Kevin Finch's food is rustic and comforting, the type you want to eat on the regular, but never boring—escargot comes grilled on a skewer beneath a bed of chives so ample it looks like a wig, for example. Two favorites: the kohlrabi with anchovy, herbs aplenty, and hazelnut (sop up the sauce with the pillows of housemade brioche) and the sasso chicken, with its crispy skin served atop crispier rice. Burgerheads take note: they've got an excellent one, with dijon, blue cheese, caramelized shallots, and a thick brisket patty between a sesame seed bun, but it's only available on Wednesdays. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Dumbo, BrooklynGo for: oysters broiled with bone marrow butter

Mexican food is back in the former Gran Electrica space on Front Street, a stretch of Dumbo real estate bustling with tourists moving to and from the Brooklyn Bridge vantage point. This time, the operation is run by Alan Delgado, the chef behind Fort Greene burrito spot Los Burritos Juarez, with drinks from bartender Ivy Mix. The great backyard garden patio remains, although I enjoyed my meal in the front dining room, which manages a moody mise en scène with its terracotta walls and glowing light despite lovely, huge windows overlooking the street and its passersby. Mix's beverages are stellar and inventive, in particular the rotating micheladas and frozen beverages that are tart and perfect. On the food front, the must-order comes first in the oysters, which are broiled a delicious brown color in bone marrow, and arrive bubbling. It's the perfectly decadent start. People talk about the fish tacos in particular, but I preferred the suadero, a confit brisket with guac on a corn tortillas rather than the flour Delgado is known for (and which can be purchased plain on the side, something I recommend.) There are flashier entrees, but the Chile Colorado—a braised pork shoulder with pinto beans and pickled onions that takes on a stew-like consistency, is subtly smoky, extremely filling, and something I'll be returning for. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: potato bread, celery salad, and a breezy dining room

In the location of the former Llama Inn, a beloved modern Peruvian eatery in Williamsburg, the new Cafe Bar J.F. has arrived. Despite a name that feels designed to be confused and/or forgotten (both of which I keep experiencing), the space inside—and the food they serve—is an honorable replacement for Llama Inn. The concept, which comes from the Llama Inn team and is spearheaded by chef Francisco Castillo, is a “South American Tavern”. To me? It feels like eating at one of the many breezy, design-eyed restaurants I love to splurge at in Lima or Buenos Aires, with dishes that build on beloved foundations like ceviche and asado. Madrid-based Plantea Estudio has elevated the room from the plant-filled corner it once was to a more demure combo of dark-wood and metal furniture (and while the rooftop remains open, the interior is so lovely I chose to stay indoors). The prices will get ya if you don’t pay attention, but certain items—the potato bread and the celery salad, two surprising ones—really lingered. Go for a date night, or a celebratory dinner with a friend, and take the excuse to work through the satisfying cocktail menu. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Guinness, oysters, and whatever seafood special is on the chalkboard

My friend Sarah put it best. There we were—me leaning back in a booth, she perched on a stool—at Dean's, the lively new pub from King team leaders Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi, the windows flung open in celebration of one of spring's first sunny days, and she says, “This feels like what the Hamptons is supposed to be like.” The parts that make it so: a location in the Village and the according clientele, nautical stylings (lots of dark wood and blues of the navy variety), abundant seafood done the British way. All to say that, somehow, we felt as though we'd stumbled into something of a seafood shack. The halcyon weather won't be a constant, of course, but the place will do just as well comforting the cold in winter with its pies and beers—the stargazy pie, a hopefully perennial special, is strikingly fish-forward when it appears on your plate, head and tail of a milky-eyed mackerel protruding. Whether or not you eat its eyeballs, the rest of the dish beneath the buttery crust is basically chowder, not at all intimidating but very much delicious. It's also rather heavy, so if you want to try as many dishes as possible while also downing excellent Guinness pour after excellent Guinness pour, perhaps stick to such happy hits as the oysters, fish and chips, and scallops in malt vinegar. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6271. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#6270. American Resumes Service to Haiti After Two-Year Pause

American Airlines on Sunday restarted service to Haiti after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince.

The carrier is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haitien, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

The inaugural flight on Sunday was staffed by an all-Haitian, Creole-speaking crew, the airline said.

“The connection between the United States and Haiti is incredibly meaningful, which is especially true in South Florida,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “We know the critical role air service plays in linking countries and communities, so we’re beyond proud to reinstate such a consequential connection for so many.”

U.S. airlines suspended service to and from Haiti in 2024 amid a rise in gang violence. Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince was temporarily closed after bullets struck aircraft taxiing on the tarmac.

So far, American is the only U.S.-based carrier to have resumed service to the country.

#6269. Faye Travel Insurance: The Best New Company Out there

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#6268. 11 Gorgeous Mountain Cities in the US, Plus Where to Stay

Whether you're seeking snow that's smooth as butter or high altitudes that keep summer comfortably cool, there's nothing quite like America's mountain cities to scratch an itch for the outdoors. With over 100 distinct mountain ranges across the US, there are endless peaks to summit and après-ski offerings to enjoy. The possibilities range from astoundingly good omakase in Salt Lake City to heliskiing in Colorado's San Juan mountains.

Whatever your vibe is, there's something for you—it's not all log cabins and snow shoes in the country's best mountain cities. These are year-round destinations that offer world-class art, adrenaline-pumping slopes, and family-friendly activities. From Appalachia to the Rockies, these are the mountain cities to call home for your next adventure, plus our favorite, editor-approved places to stay.

Nestled in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains’ Ten Mile Range, Breckenridge is one of the country's most treasured ski towns, home to five peaks peppered with skiers of all abilities come winter. The once crown jewel of Summit County's mining towns, its lined streets are hugged by weathered saloons and colorful homes harking back to its boomtown days. Breck's—as regulars call it—real claim to fame though, is its nearly 3,000 acres of lift-served terrain. After you hit the slopes, there's plenty to love beyond the skiing, whether you're looking crawling through its craft beer and distillery scene or appraising the thriving arts district.

Stay here: A new kind of boutique hotel tailored to outdoor enthusiasts, the dog-friendly Gravity Haus Breckenridge draws out-of-towners with a wide variety of guest rooms (from bunk rooms to two-bedroom suites), a Japanese-inspired onsen, private ski lockers, and an in-house team to help you explore outside.

As Crested Butte lies just 24 miles from Aspen, the two are practically next-door neighbors, but you'd be remiss to skip this hidden gem because of that fact. There's something that feels more intimate about Crested Butte’s historic downtown, which looks like it was stolen out of a snow globe or used as the set of a holiday Hallmark movie, but it can keep up with the best of them. There's the world-class skiing and mountain biking with some memorable restaurants and watering holes to boot. In other words: all the beauty and nightlife, none of the pretense.

Stay here: If you want to stay an arm's length away from it all, check into Old Town Inn, which sits three miles away from Lake Grant and two miles away from Peanut Lake. The property also offers free shuttle service to Mount Crested Butte.

Mountain cities nearby a national park are automatic winners, but Whitefish somehow goes a step above the rest. Being steps away from Glacier National Park certainly helps as travelers gain access to some incredibly beautiful lakes and glaciers, but there's also the namesake ski resort in town that plus tons of summertime activities like hiking and zip-lining; and its mountain-backed, saloon-lined downtown has more than enough Old Western vibes to fill an entire vacation.

Stay here: Larch House is a new 39-key hotel is the first design-forward boutique hotel of its kind in Whitefish. It’s in the heart of downtown’s historic Railway District, a short walk away from all the town’s shops, restaurants, and bars.

Aspen, Colorado’s reputation precedes itself; it’s the quintessential mountain city that's been winning praise since 1879 (when it was originally founded as Ute City). Why? Its surroundings are simply awe-inspiring—snow-capped peaks in winter that turn into perfect hiking weather in summer—and its comfortably small footprint makes your whole itinerary easy to reach, from the famed slopes to downtown's designer boutiques and top-notch restaurants. Aspen has long been a hotspot for skiers searching for fresh powder and a lively après scene, but the town has been on a roll more recently with all types because of its worldly mix of cultures on display at institutions like the Aspen Art Museum. In addition to those seeking snow, Colorado's premier mountain city welcomes families, food lovers, and design seekers alike.

Stay here: There’s an inimitable charm to Aspen’s Hotel Jerome. From rustic to high fashion, the 135-year-old historical landmark sits in a perfect location for both rest and play. Offering both complementary hotel-to-hill transit and walkable proximity to designer shops, a stay at the Jerome is as convenient as it is decadent.

Two years after Hurricane Helene descended on Asheville, the creative spirit of the artsy Appalachian city is back and better than ever. With hundreds of artists bringing life to repurposed spaces, whether it's a glass studio, ceramics workshop, or open gallery, Asheville is abuzz again.it seems Asheville's pure energies are vibrating at a higher frequency than ever, even as it continues to rebuild. As Jeffrey Burroughs, a local jewelry designer shared with Condé Nast Traveler, “What music is to New Orleans art is to Asheville,” and visitors come here for much more than the bucolic scenery.

Stay here: Enfolded within the grounds of the opulent Biltmore Estate, the Inn uniquely summons what it was like to be a guest at the Vanderbilt family’s magnificent 19th-century mansion, but with 21st-century luxury and comfort.

Ouray calls itself the Outdoor Recreation Capital of Colorado, and it's an epithet well-earned. See why on the Perimeter Trail, a 6.5-mile loop that hugs the rugged mountain city. Set aside (at least) four hours for the full hike; shortly after your ascent, you'll be taken aback by views of the entire box canyon—a sight that continues along much of the journey. Among the trail’s highlights are the towering Cascade Falls, its Baby Bathtubs (smooth, carved rocks kids can play on), and the Box Canyon Falls high bridge. Because the Perimeter Trail is never more than a half mile from town, there are several points where hikers can cut the walk short and head back into Ouray.

Stay here: The adults-only Beaumont Hotel and Spa is made for those looking to rejuvenate their bodies after long days spent romping around Ouray's thrill-seeking offerings. Plan to spend a day soaking in the property's hot springs, which has been soothing visitors since 1886.

Salt Lake City is becoming something of a cultural haven in the Mountain West. Foodies flock to the city for its inventive dining—from speakeasy cocktails to picture-perfect omakase—while the mountains are never far for skiing or hiking—don’t miss out on the quirky annual events like Winter Roundup skijoring (skiers and snowboarders get towed by horses through the snowy streets) and the ultra-hip, indie-forward Kilby Block Party Music Festival. Boutique shopping and independent galleries are emerging alongside long-standing museums, lending downtown an even more vibrant, walkable energy. Between all the buzz, postcard mountain views, swanky bars, and hotels that balance history, style, and service, Salt Lake City has genuinely become a place you’ll want to return to—not just pass through.

Stay here: Downtown Hyatt Regency SLC is the city’s workhorse: spacious, modern rooms, consistent service, and direct access to the convention center and buzzy streets. It’s perfect for business travelers or anyone valuing convenience and reliable amenities.

The powder here is perfect, and so is the quirky, small-town vibe. But it’s when the mercury starts to rise that this historic mining community in the San Juan Mountains really shows off its shine: Warmer temperatures bring vibrant wildflower blooms, its famed film festival, and beloved bluegrass performances to Telluride. Come for the robust art scene where you’ll find a mix of creatives, outdoorspeople, blissful retirees, and the odd celebrity or two (Oprah Winfrey is among those who reportedly own a home here). Even with all the new hype, Telluride has gracefully managed to hang onto its authentic character and remains a favorite, down-to-Earth Colorado destination.

Stay here: The Madeline Hotel & Residences, Auberge Resorts Collection, located at the base of Telluride Ski Resort, is an ideal basecamp for your trip. This updated 83-room alpine retreat, which also features 71 residences, is surrounded on three sides by the San Juan Mountains and offers stunning views from its 4,000-square-foot outdoor terrace, complete with a heated pool, massive hot tubs, fire pits, and an al fresco lounge.

Jackson Hole is the epitome of why they call this region of the country big sky country. There are endless open spaces to admire the handsome soaring mountains, and it's no secret what makes so many first-time visitors never want to leave. The resort skiers and adventurous outdoorsy types have been coming for decades, and in recent years, the dining scene has only been getting better. All of which gives it an outsized place in the mind of travelers. Jackson Hole brings in a whopping 2.6 million visitors every year; the entire state of Wyoming has a population under 600,000. It’s a gateway to the National Parks, a winter wonderland, and an idyllic paradise year-round.

Stay here: Four Seasons Resort Jackson Hole, nestled at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Teton Village, is the only ski-in/ski-out hotel in the village, and comes with unobstructed views of the Tetons, full-service alpine spa, an outdoor pool and jacuzzi (open year-round), ski concierge, and all the pampering you’d expect.

If the air feels lighter in Silverton, maybe because the landmarked former mining town rests at a cool 9,300 feet above sea level. The scene here feels closer to the industrial history than many of Colorado's other rehabbed mining outposts, with a good number of its colorfully painted storefronts catering to passengers from the out-and-back, steam-powered train from Durango. It's the perfect home base to spend a couple of days hiking and fishing in nearby San Juan National Forest. In the winter, this is one-horse town completely transforms into a mecca for serious backcountry skiers.

Stay here: For a real step back in time, step through the threshold of The Bent Elbow Hotel, whose façade nods to the Victorian architectural style that was rampant in Silverton's hey-day. Paired with the mountain-view balconies, you might just wonder which century you're in. But worry not about the loss of modern amenities, the rooms come equipped with special comforts from complimentary streaming services to white noise machines to complete your wind-down ritual.

Townsend is called the “peaceful side of the Smokies” for a reason. Instead of neon lights and chain brands, you'll find a small downtown area alongside the Little River with easy access to the national park. The eastern part of town is closest to the park’s most incredible waterfalls: Meigs Falls and Spruce Flats Falls. The Smokies lay claim to more than 700 fishable rivers, including the Little River, that can be visited with Townsend-based Little River Outfitters. In Townsend, Dancing Bear Appalachian Bistro is a local favorite, with seasonal Appalachian-inspired dishes like striped bass and sorghum glazed chicken on offer.

Stay here: Head to nearby Walland for Blackberry Farm, a Relais & Châteaux resort spread over 4,000 acres—and hands down the most notable stay in these parts. It has James Beard award-winning restaurants including The Barn (which accepts reservations from non-guests), known for its dishes crafted from seasonal and local ingredients.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6267. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6266. Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and I've loved redeeming my World of Hyatt points over the years on everything from cheap and cheerful Category 1 airport hotels to luxurious bespoke properties on idyllic Greek islands.

I knew that the program had expanded the ways to redeem points beyond hotel stays to experiences via its Find experiences platform. But I've never given it much thought, assuming the value (or the experiences themselves) wouldn't be that great.

So, when Hyatt recently invited me to an event that it sponsors, the Laver Cup tournament at London's The O2 arena, I jumped at the chance to go as a tennis enthusiast. I'd been to The O2 countless times for concerts and thought I knew the venue pretty well. But Hyatt was auctioning off a luxury experience in the ultra-VIP Legends Club, a space I didn't even know existed that turned out to be on a completely different level of luxury, in part due to its courtside seats for watching the action.

Seeing how few Hyatt points the winning bids went for, especially given this impressive level of premium hospitality and access, I came to the realization that this might just be the most valuable way to redeem World of Hyatt points.

Related: This is how you do a luxury all-inclusive: Zoetry Mallorca, bookable with Hyatt points

Find is World of Hyatt's experiences platform, where members can book everything from fitness workshops and chef's table dinners to Broadway tickets, paying with either cash or World of Hyatt points. You don't need to stay at a Hyatt hotel to take part, though some experiences include accommodations.

Most Find experiences are advertised with a fixed price — and that's where you might struggle to get outsize value. When TPG travel writer Rachel Craft tested a fixed-price Find dining package in Denver, it delivered less value than TPG's valuation of World of Hyatt points at the time, and she concluded that members would probably get more value redeeming their points for hotel stays.

Auctions work differently. A small number of limited-time experiences, often tied to Hyatt's sports sponsorships, go to the highest bidder, with members bidding in points rather than paying a set price.

Before you bid, it's worth knowing the rules:

Auctions are usually only a small portion of the Find options available at any one time, so here's how you can find them:

The Laver Cup packages were a savvy example of just how much value a Find auction can deliver.

Each of the three packages Hyatt auctioned included:

Starting with priority, fast-track entry to the venue, the Legends Club was a significant step up in luxury from anything else I've seen at The O2. It even surpassed my impression of the Virgin Red Room, a corporate suite at The O2 that can be booked with Virgin Red points.

The two-level hospitality suite (usually hidden behind the stage at traditional concerts) was huge and opened onto the arena, with a perfect view down the baseline.

Before the play started, there was even a Q&A with tennis legend Andy Murray, which isn't something you get with a regular ticket.

Premium food and drinks were included from 90 minutes before the session until the final ball, and the Champagne kept flowing the entire time.

When it was time for the tennis, I headed down to my own courtside seat in the second row. I was so close to the current No. 3 player in the world, Carlos Alcaraz, that I could almost have reached out and touched him.

I didn't stay at the Park Hyatt this time, but having toured the hotel, I can see why it would make the package even more appealing, with spacious rooms, marble bathrooms, views over the Thames and a 65-foot indoor pool.

Published all-in prices for a single Legends Club ticket ranged from $1,329 to $2,652 for Friday night and from $1,461 to $2,916 for either Saturday session, depending on the seat.

Standard rooms started at $633 per night when TPG reviewed the Park Hyatt, and the hotel's 60-minute "Back to Brilliance" massage cost $279 per person. Add the two-night stay and hotel credit, and I estimate each package was worth between $5,000 and $8,000 before assigning any value to the transfers.

A search engine index of Hyatt’s official Find homepage shows Hyatt auctioned off three Laver Cup packages with Legends Club single-session tickets and Park Hyatt accommodations (plus the above-mentioned inclusions) with winning bids of 81,583, 120,560 and 160,000 points, although the closed listings are no longer visible on the live page.

TPG's October 2026 valuations assign a value of 1.65 cents to every World of Hyatt point. By that valuation, the winning bids were worth about $1,346, $1,989 and $2,640, respectively. Even using the low end of my estimated package value, those redemptions delivered about 6.1, 4.1 and 3.1 cents per point, respectively, or roughly 1.9 to 3.7 times TPG's valuation, a spectacular result.

Put another way, the Category 8 Park Hyatt London River Thames costs 35,000 to 75,000 World of Hyatt points per night for a standard room, so two nights can cost 70,000 to 150,000 points. The two lower bids were below the 150,000-point threshold required for two standard award nights on top-priced dates, while the highest bid was only 10,000 points higher.

Of course, not every auction will deliver this much value. Popular experiences, such as Formula One races, can attract plenty of competition, and you have no control over where the bidding ends. However, you can decide up front what an experience is worth to you and stop bidding if the price goes past that amount.

World of Hyatt members earn points on eligible Hyatt stays and Find bookings paid for with cash, but a credit card can be the quickest way to build your balance for an auction.

You can choose between two cobranded cards:

Or, you can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt from the following cards:

Chase Ultimate Rewards points held in Chase Sapphire Reserve and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business accounts transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio.

Points held in Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred accounts transfer at a 4:3 ratio, meaning 1,000 Ultimate Rewards points become 750 World of Hyatt points.

Bilt Points currently transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio through Dec. 31, 2026. The ratio will drop to 4:3 on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: How many Hyatt points do you need to transfer before the Sapphire Reserve beats the Sapphire Preferred?

Fixed-price Find experiences still would not usually tempt me away from a hotel redemption, but auctions are a different story.

This was easily the most luxurious sporting experience I have ever attended, from the VIP entry to the spectacular views and the hospitality of the Legends Club, which offered everything I could imagine, including proximity to some of the world's best tennis players.

Factor in the accommodations, transfers, food-and-beverage credits and other perks, and it's clear this is an exceptional way to redeem World of Hyatt points. You'll potentially considerably exceed our valuation of these excellent hotel points by redeeming them this way.

The 2027 Laver Cup will be played at the Intuit Dome near Los Angeles from Sept. 24 to 26, 2027. As the official hotel partner, look out for Hyatt Find experiences and auctions for next year's tournament.
