Rewards cards are frequently rolling out high-value welcome offers. If you're a travel enthusiast like us at TPG, it's likely you're keeping your eyes peeled for standout bonuses.

This month, we've compiled six of our favorite cards with stellar offers right now. These range from top-tier business cards to cobranded options for your next trip — and you won't want to miss out on the value.

Plus, there are even more limited-time offers available, so don't stop your search here if none of these currently suit your needs.

*Welcome offer value is determined using TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer.

Related: Easiest credit card welcome bonuses to earn

Chase's premium business card offers multiple benefits, including useful statement credits and travel perks.

Welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Sapphire Reserve for Business combines premium travel perks with strong earning potential for business owners who spend heavily in some of its bonus categories.

For TPG founder Brian Kelly, the card's earning potential on advertising purchases has been particularly valuable. "The Sapphire Reserve for Business has let me consolidate my spending and keep earning beyond those limits, which is a big deal for growing our TPG brand," he said.

The card earns 3 points per dollar spent on social media and search engine advertising purchases (capped at $1 million in spending each anniversary year beginning Nov. 15), and Brian has also gotten significant value from its travel benefits. He has used The Edit to book luxury hotel stays with on-property perks such as daily breakfast for two and property credits, while also taking advantage of Chase's Points Boost for select hotel and airfare redemptions.

To learn more, read our full review of the Sapphire Reserve for Business.

Apply here: Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business

The Amex Platinum is one of our favorite luxury travel cards thanks to its long list of useful benefits, including airport lounge access and valuable statement credits.

Welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Why we love it: TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak finds solid value in the Amex Platinum's benefits. Specifically, Olivia enjoys receiving the up to $155 Walmart+ statement credit per calendar year (up to $12.95 monthly, plus applicable taxes) that covers the cost of a monthly membership when paying with the Amex Platinum (on one membership, subject to auto-renewal; Plus Ups excluded).

Walmart+ includes a complimentary Paramount+ subscription (separate enrollment is required), which allows her to avoid paying out of pocket for the streaming service.

She also uses the card's up to $300 Lululemon statement credit per calendar year at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online (allocated as up to $75 per quarter) and up to $400 Resy statement credit per calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter; simply pay with your Amex Platinum at an eligible U.S. Resy restaurant; no reservation is required).

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Platinum.

Apply here: American Express Platinum Card

The Capital One Venture Rewards is a straightforward travel rewards card that earns at least 2 miles per dollar on every purchase and gives cardholders access to Capital One's airline and hotel transfer partners.

Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, receive a $300 credit to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year upon account opening.

Why we love it: The Venture Rewards offers a simple earning structure and flexible redemption options for a reasonable $95 annual fee.

Cardholders earn at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, so there's no need to keep track of bonus categories. For potentially greater value, you can transfer your miles to Capital One's airline and hotel partners.

TPG points and loyalty lead writer Katie Genter has held the Venture Rewards for years and values it for many of the same reasons. "I like the Venture's straightforward earning structure, and the fact that it earns versatile yet valuable Capital One miles," she said.

The current offer is particularly appealing because the $300 Capital One Travel credit comes on top of the 75,000-mile bonus, making an already strong offer even more rewarding in the first year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

The United Explorer is a solid option for travelers who fly United several times a year and want valuable airline perks without paying a premium annual fee.

Welcome offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Explorer offers several useful United benefits, including a free first checked bag for the cardmember and one companion (when the flight is purchased with the card), priority boarding and two United Club one-time passes each cardholder year.

TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak has held the Explorer for years and particularly appreciates how easy it is to get value from the card's United-specific benefits.

"The biggest reason I tout the Explorer as often as I do is because of how easy it is to get meaningful value from it without needing to use merchant credits that may not fit your spending habits," she said.

With a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150), the Explorer could be particularly appealing to travelers who regularly check bags or use United Club access.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer Card.

The Hilton Honors Aspire is a premium hotel card that offers valuable benefits for travelers who regularly stay at Hilton properties.

Welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

Why we love it: The Aspire offers automatic Hilton Honors Diamond status, an annual free night reward and up to $400 in statement credits for eligible Hilton resort purchases each calendar year (up to $200 biannually).

For Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site strategy, the free night reward and resort credits are among her favorite credit card benefits. Both she and her husband hold the Aspire, allowing them to take advantage of two sets of these benefits each year.

The card's perks can help offset the card's $550 annual fee, particularly for travelers who can redeem their free night rewards at high-end Hilton properties.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Aspire.

The United Gateway is an entry-level United credit card that lets travelers earn MileagePlus miles without paying an annual fee.

Welcome offer: Earn up to 50,000 bonus miles: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Gateway offers a straightforward way to earn United miles on everyday purchases while avoiding an annual fee. It's a strong option for occasional United flyers who want to build their MileagePlus balances but don't need the more extensive travel benefits of the airline's higher-tier cards.

TPG credit card writer Becky Pokora appreciates the card's everyday earning opportunities: "I keep my card linked to my toll road and Parkmobile accounts, since it earns extra miles on local transit and commuting charges and defines those categories broadly," she said.

Becky also uses the card for inflight purchases to receive a 25% statement credit on eligible purchases, another perk that adds value without an annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Gateway Card.

These offers can help you boost your transferable points and miles balance or unlock meaningful discounts on your next trip.

As always, be sure to factor in each issuer's unique set of application restrictions and ensure you can meet any spending requirements to earn the bonus.

But with so much value on the table, you won't want to miss out on adding one of these top credit cards (and its bonus) to your wallet.

#6243. Review: Emirates 777-300ER “Game Changer” First Class Dubai To Brussels

Seven years after my first flight in Emirates’ fully enclosed Boeing 777 first class suite, I returned to the same route and same flight, EK183, from Dubai to Brussels. The “Game Changer” suite remains extraordinary, but this flight demonstrated that even a superb seat cannot compensate for disappointing service, though perhaps my exceptions were too high? My latest review follows, with the original 2019 review preserved below for comparison.

I first reviewed this product in 2019 and came away impressed. Returning in 2026, I was curious whether it would feel quite as special after experiencing more of the world’s leading first class products. The suite certainly did. The experience around it was less consistent, especially compared with my excellent Emirates A380 flight from Mumbai to Dubai.

As I explained in the introduction to this trip report, I booked Mumbai–Dubai–Brussels for 102,000 Emirates Skywards miles and approximately $700 in taxes and fees. That included my A380 flight the day before and this flight to Brussels on a Boeing 777-300ER featuring Emirates’ “Game Changer” first class suites.

I took an Uber from my hotel to DXB. Emirates has a dedicated terminal for business and first class check-in and within area, there’s a posh first class check-in lobby.

However, with so many first class passengers, there is not the sort of personalized ground service you might experience with Air France or Lufthansa. After checking in, I was on my own to get through security, passport control, and to the lounge.

I visited both the Concourse A and Concourse B Emirates First Class lounges before my flight.

I reached the gate (further than I thought) about 30 minutes prior to scheduled departure and the flight had fully boarded, with a “final call” announcement from the gate agent and on the monitors.

I settled in onboard, noticing the cabin was booked full. What war?

The first class cabin has six suites in a 1-1-1 configuration with the middle suites having virtual windows (with a live feed of the world outside).

My suite, 1K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush “dentist” chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look…it’s just so odd that after all these years Emirates has only retrofitted nine jets with this product.

There’s also a flip-up cabinet with a mirror that houses the amenity kit skin products and a cool souvenir notebook and pen.

The suite has universal A/C, USB-A, and USB-C power (plus HDMI for those still living in 2012).

There are also plenty of lighting options.

Within the suite, you can customize your experience not only via adjusting the seat from upright to reclined to fully-flat, but you can adjust the temperature and lighting (even the color of the lighting).

I didn’t need to sleep on this daytime flight to Brussels, but I ended up taking a 4-hour nap: the bedding is superb and the 79-inch bed very comfortable in 180º lie-flat mode.

In terms of the hard product alone, this seats beats out the JAL A350-1000 suite. But of course a flight is about more than the seat, especially in first class….

Emirates’ “ICE” entertainment system includes hundreds of movies, TV shows, live TV, music, and games…more than enough for a journey around the sun, let alone a quick trip to Europe.

Noise cancelling headphones are from Bowers & Wilkins.

While this flight did not have Starlink Wi-Fi, the OnAir internet was complimentary and worked reasonably well, even if it felt more like dial-up than high speed.

It was also a lovely day just to look out the window, especially as we neared Brussels.

Upon boarding, I was offered a refreshing glass of Champagne and chose Dom Rosé 2010.

Menus were distributed prior to pushback, with a la carte breakfast and lunch choices available throughout the flight. along with an exceptional collection of wine and spirits plus a “movie snack bar” menu.

I thought the breakfast choices were limited. My omelet was fine, but I’ve had much better omelets on other carriers and even had a better one out of Mumbai on Emirates the day before.

Service began with fresh fruit, a cappuccino, orange juice (with ice cubes?), rhubarb yogurt, and delicious bakery items like a cinnamon bun and almond croissant.

The omelet had beans, potatoes, and cooked spinach with it…utterly forgettable.

After waking up from extended nap, it was time for the main feast. While my meal was being prepared, I was offered mix nuts and hydrated with some sparkling water.

The caviar course was excellent and I had more Dom Pérignon Rosé with it.

Next came fabulous Arabic mezze with humus, grape leaves, tabbouleh, falafel, kibbeh, and fattoush salad..everything was great.

With time running out, I skipped the soup and went right for my main course: pan-fried lamb loin and cutlet, served with olive caramel sauce, tomato fondue, beetroot jus, potato pavé with pistachio dukkah-crusted kale, and blanched sugar snap peas.

Sadly, it was so overdone that I did not finish it. However, I did enjoy some excellent garlic bread and red wine (a Bibi Graetz Colore 2015 from Tuscany) with it.

Lunch ended with a cheese course and chocolate truffle cake (with roasted hazelnuts and pistachios). The cheese included:

The “new” 777 has two lavatories in the front of the cabin, shared by crew. They are spacious, though not like upstairs on the A380:

I was never proactively offered an amenity kit. When we landed, I asked about it and was told, “They are on request only.” So be aware of that…

Slippers and pajamas (what Emirates class loungewear) was proactively offered. I took size medium, which fit me (I’m 6’1″) and was very comfortable.

As I mentioned above, skin products from Byredo were present in the suite.

I’ll repeat what I wrote in my first impressions of this flight.

After breakfast, my dishes sat for over 20 minute untouched. Not the service I was expecting.

I woke up a couple hours before landing for the meal and was totally ignored for almost 30 minutes (and my suite door was open). I realize that I could have just pressed the call button (and eventually did), but I don’t think that should be necessary in first class…I think that the FAs should have been far more proactive in monitoring the cabins.

When I did call the FAs to begin meal service, there was 90 minutes left in the flight, which in theory should have been time for everything. I provided the full order and the caviar came quick, but once again the crew was not attentive. I finished the caviar and waited. Finally, the mezze came and I finished it…and waited. I waited and waited for the main course and it came (having been left in the oven far too long).

I waited again. The captain announced our descent into Brussels. My glass was empty, my plate was pushed way, but no one was coming.

Do I really have to push the call button after I finish each course? That’s not the kind of first class service I like.

With 40 minutes left in the flight, I finally flagged a FA down and asked her to bring the cheese and dessert at once. She seemed very agitated, not in the hostile sense, but because she was so stressed…because it wasn’t only me trying to finish my lunch, but the other four in the cabin (it was booked 5/6).

She brought over the cheese and dessert and I ate it…it was fine…but I felt too guilty ordering coffee with so little time left…again, not a feeling I should have in first class. Drink refills were not offered.

The pre-arrival service could have been so much better executed. The service flow was so perfect on my A380 flight because the flight attendants took charge and proactively executed service. Not so on this flight and it wasn’t because the FAs were too busy: they were chatting in the galley.

So was it was the best flight ever? Nope. The A380 flight the day before was perfect…this one was not.

I think it’s always appropriate to mention here that I am incredibly grateful to fly first class on Emirates and this sort of “first world problem” is not meant to condemn Emirates or gripe so much as it is to offer an honest comparison between this and other premium cabin products. Comparatively speaking, Emirates fell short here.

Despite the questionable service, what a pleasure it was to fly on this product and enjoy the beautiful suite and multi-course meals. I look forward to doing this again. Next time, though, I think I’ll skip breakfast and just have one meal in the middle of the flight.

The review below was originally published on June 7, 2019, and covers my earlier flight from Dubai to Brussels.

I booked my ticket from Dubai to Brussels a couple night before the trip using Emirates Skywards. The points transfer on a 1:1 basis from American Express Membership Rewards and the trip cost 85,000 miles and about $420 in taxes/fees. The same trip would have been 75,000 miles with Qantas, which has now been added as an American Express transfer partner.

I began the day with a 4:00 A.M. cab ride to Dubai International Airport from the Park Hyatt. Although I tired to sleep, I was too excited for the upcoming journey. Pulling up to the Emirates premium class check-in area Dubai, a line of uniformed staff were waiting to assist with luggage, but today I was traveling only with hand baggage.

Inside, I  found myself the only passenger in a huge terminal…it felt a bit surreal. After checking in, I proceeded down a long hallway toward the security checkpoint and passport control.

After a couple hours in the first class lounge, I headed to the gate for boarding, which began ahead of schedule about an hour prior to takeoff.

B1 is used for aircraft departing from remote stands and passengers were being funneled down a single escalator and onto a waiting bus. I tried to board but was told to wait and that first class boarding would begin “soon”. So I waited. And waited. And waited. 25 minutes passed. I was getting antsy. So were the three other first class passengers. We were the only ones left in the gate area.

Finally, we were invited to head downstairs where our “first class” bus was awaiting. I don’t know if “first class” was the right word, but the bus was very comfortable. We soon began what turned out to be a 15-minute bus ride to the aircraft…which seemed to be parked in Abu Dhabi (I jest…). Upon reaching the aircraft, we were invited to carry our own bags up the fairly steep air stairs onto the 777-300ER that would shortly be departing for Brussels.

Onboard, three FAs were waiting at the door. After a warm welcome, one escorted me to my suite.

I was grinning ear-to-ear as I stepped into the beautiful six-seat cabin. Wow, this was spacious! The cabin is arranged in a 1-1-1 configuration with four window/aisle suites and two suites in the middle, one with an entrance on aisle one and the other with an entrance on aisle two.

My suite, 2K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ latest first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look.

What I appreciated most about this new cabin was the attention to detail Emirates placed in making it practical. For example, my rollerboard carry-on fit perfectly in the cabinet, which was so much more convenient and aesthetically pleasing than having to leave it under the ottoman (like in Singapore or Etihad First Class) or store it in a closet (Lufthansa First Class) or overhead bin (Air France First Class).

There was also a closet that easily accommodated my garment bag and clothes on a hangar and smaller storage cabinets along the window.

A power port and USB charger was conveniently located within arm’s reach, as was a USB-C charger (which my laptop has…).

Adjacent to my seat was a touch panel that allowed for control of the lighting (including customizable mood lighting) and the temperature of the suite. The armrest also had a four-button seat control.

In addition the drink cabinet, there was a basket with snacks sitting on the table along with beautiful orchids:

But the attention to detail went even further. The careful stitching on the seat and embroidered Ghaf (prosopis cineraria) tree above the window further showed how much thought Emirates put into this cabin. And the overhead lights were shaped like diamonds.

Each suite had binoculars to look out. These were not souvenirs; FAs collected them as we approached Brussels.

The suite across the aisle from me stayed vacant, so I had a chance to check out the “fake” windows”. Kudos to Emirates for trying, but I was not impressed.

I structured the flight around a nap…not because I wanted to sleep through a pricey flight, but because I slept poorly the previous two nights and wanted to try out the bed and bedding.

Thus, shortly after my post-takeoff breakfast flight attendants prepared the bed for me while I changed into my pajamas. The bedding is simply tremendous, with a satin-like finish that was soft and so comfortable.

Window shades lower by button (sheer blinds and blackout) but Emirates also added real curtains. While I figured these were purely for aesthetic reasons, light seeped through one of my three windows so it turns out the curtains were quite practical.

The only annoying thing was that I could not figure out how to shut off the small band of blue light overhead:

I slept for about 3.5 hours, asking the FAs to shake me awake with about two hours to go until landing.

Prior to pushback, I was offered a drink of choice and chose orange juice, which was freshly-squeezed. Later on in the boarding process, I was also offered Arabic coffee and a choice of dates.

After takeoff, I examined the menu for today’s flight:

Having had steak for “breakfast” I was actually in the mood for some eggs, but only a light continental breakfast was offered. No problem…I wasn’t all that hungry. The purser, Ashwin, came by to introduce himself and took my breakfast order. I just wanted some fruit and yogurt along with a cappuccino. Almost immediately, my table was prepared by Tetiana and I was offered more orange juice along with a basket of warmed breakfast breads.

The table folds out from the console in front:

Mixed nuts were also offered and I enjoyed a glass of Dom Pérignon 2008 Champagne.

I do try to stay away from these fatty carbs, but the croissants smelled so good I ended up eating two of them…and some danish. So much for my light breakfast…

The fruit, yogurt, and cappuccino (notice the chocolate powder stencil art is the Emirates logo?) were all tasty and the whole breakfast service took only about 20 minutes. I still had plenty of time for sleep and a big feast prior to landing.

I was presented with a hot towel after my breakfast dishes were cleared.

After my nap, Tetiana again set up my tray table for lunch.

Hot bread from the oven and my favorite Isigny Sainte-Mère butter from France were offered.

I started the meal off with some more Dom, though this time some Dom Pérignon Rose 2006. It was served at the perfect temperature and was a spectacular accompaniment to the meal which would follow.

I began with caviar, admittedly more so for the trip report than because I felt like it. Still, I ate it and enjoyed it. I appreciated that Emirates warmed the blinis.

While I was eating my soup, Maria brought over my next course, a green salad with French dressing.

For my main course, I ordered a beef filet with asparagus and boiled potatoes. The dish was beautifully presented and the asparagus with truffle hollandaise sauce was spectacular…even better than Lufthansa First Class.

But the beef filet? Not so much…it was served beyond well-done and I ended up only nibbling at it. Such a shame that it was served overcooked. Tetiana was concerned that I did not eat and offered to bring me something else, but by this point I was already full and there were still two courses left.

As you can read in the menu above, the cheese course was quite extensive. I had a sample of each piece, but could not finish it.

Finally, I completed my meal with warm chocolate cake with raspberry sauce and another cappuccino.

Kudos to Emirates for an excellent dining experience in first class.

Emirates does not offer amenity kits on daytime flights. That said, there were several toiletries available in the lavatory and a box at each seat contained Byredo (Swedish) amenities like eye cream and skin toner. The amenities were “hidden” away in a cabinet along the table that folded up to reveal a mirror with lights. A leather-bound notebook and writing pen were also present.

Pajamas were available by request. Emirates uses “breathing” pajamas that are supposed to help the body stay ventilated. While that may just be a gimmick , I loved the soft pajamas and they have become my new favorite airline pajamas…my old favorites were also from Emirates.

Finally, the slippers were also quite comfortable and also large enough for my feet.

Ok, this is what surprised me the most. I knew the flight would have wireless internet, but like all (and I do mean ALL) my previous Emirates flights, I just assumed it would not work. Boy was I wrong. Not only was the internet functional and free (as a Skywards member), it was FAST!

Make sure your Skywards number is associated with your reservation in order to take advantage of the complimentary wi-fi.

On the other hand, the IFE was no surprise. I knew Emirates would offer a comprehensive library of movies, TV shows, live TV, games, and music and of course it did. There were even two cameras to allow for live views from outside.

What did impress me, however, was the wireless remote in the suite and the detachable tablet that served as a secondary IFE device, especially suited for games and music. When detached, it was totally wireless and also controlled the seat, could summon FAs via video conference for service, and easily controlled my customized soundtracks.

Newspapers were offered prior to takeoff.

Lastly, the Bowers & Wilkins noise-cancelling headphones were comfortable and worked very well.

Two first class lavatories were compact, but kept very clean and offered towels, Buglari toiletries, and other amenities like toothbrushes and combs. There were even little bars of soap like airlines used to offer decades ago.

Tetiana, Maria, and Ashwin provided excellent service from start to finish. Tetiana and Maria primarily took care of me and were not only lovely and charming, but highly polished. I appreciated how precisely the table was set, drinks were poured, and food served. I never had to wait long between courses and plates and utensils were always promptly cleared. Throughout the flight, I was addressed by last name.

Upon landing in Brussels I requested a picture of the flight crew and they happily obliged:

The only problem with this flight was that it ended so quickly. 6.5 hours was not enough time to fully enjoy the wonderful hard and soft product onboard. I was simply ecstatic throughout the flight…Emirates takes first class to a whole new level.

Was this my best first class flight ever? I don’t know if I’d go that far, but it was absolutely the best first class hard product (suite) I have ever experienced. While the old Emirates suite is still very nice, the new suite is even more spacious, even more comfortable, and even more cutting-edge.

Emirates has room for improvement with its first class ground product, but its in-air product is top-notch.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Awesome photos!!! That suite looked very spacious. I agree with you that 6.5 hours doesn’t seem to be that long. I hope EK will have this hard product on their A380s someday or at least have their 777 planes with the new F fly ultra longhaul on a regular basis.

You didn’t try the ’01 Mouton Rothschild? Epic fail!

The Rolex of wines – good quality and carefully made, but prices are sky-high because it’s collected by fanatics and therefore maintains a certain mystique. There are more interesting wines out there for less money.

Curious, why do you not like the video windows?

Thank you very much Matthew. I am overwhelmed seeing the great pictures you took on our flight. It was a pleasure having you as a guest on-board. I hope i’ll welcome you again soon on one of our trips again. Regards Ashwin.

These are great photos. Did you use a wide-angle? What camera?

Matthew my wife and I are travelling with Emirates from Brisbane to Madrid First Class. We are flying from Brisbane to Dubai on a 777-300ER are you aware if Emirates have upgraded their 777 from Brisbane. From Dubai to Madrid we are in an A380 in First Class we have flown in the A380 First Class before but not the 777. From your review we are hoping for the upgraded 777 experience.

Sadly, it looks like your 777 will have the old first class. It won’t be so bad, though. 😉

Hi Matthew Late posting but I wonder can you help? Flying from Singapore Dublin via Dubai on 10 March. Have a few options on that day to Dubai. Any new 777’s on the route? Also if I take the morning one I have 1.30 transfer time in Dubai. Do they offer any ground service? I’ve never had any help on the ground before but never had such a short transfer

Hi Annie, new first class does not operate to Singapore at this time. Ground services are lacking in Dubai. You’ll have lounge access, but no escort from flight to lounge to flight. If you are departing from a remote stand, you’ll have a private bus.

Matthew, Thanks for the comprehensive review…. notwithstanding the envy I have for your flight. My question is a very mundane item (although I consider it to have enough weight to differentiate EK’s new F suite), since the suite is totally enclosed and you are able to control the suite temperature… how cool and how warm can the suite be set? Regards

Michael, I prefer cool cabins (with heated seated if available…not here, unfortunately) and I noticed my suite was noticeably cooler than the aisle/lavatory.

Do they not board out of the lounge for the 777? When I took the A380 we boarded out of the lounge.

Its been a while since I read a review of this and I actually now think the AF cabin is more elegant. AF First soft product is miles ahead of what you had here

You said in the review they’ve only retrofitted 9 jets with the game changer. I thought the real issue was that it’s only on the last 9 delivered 777’s and they’ve actually retrofitted zero jets with it. Which isn’t really forgivable given they have retrofitted many 777s with a new business class. So the delays of the 777X can’t really be used as an excuse given they retrofitted so many of the jets, just not with the game changer first. Such a let down I think.

#6242. 17 Trips You Should Book a Year in Advance

I'm a firm believer that holidays need a balance of organization and freedom, so that you can enjoy all the long-awaited activities without feeling like they're obligations. Starting to organize and book excursions well in advance can make your experience considerably better, especially when planning trips to particularly popular destinations. Though, that's not the only reason why you should already be thinking about what to add to your 2027 travel bucket list.

Planning a trip a year in advance, long before your suitcase ever leaves the closet, offers up a very particular and potent type of dopamine hit. The moment you confirm a flight or secure a coveted reservation delivers its own quiet thrill, a reminder that the joy of travel lives not only in the trip itself, but in the anticipation that precedes it.

With 2027 shaping up to be a year of more personal, experience-led travel, there's even more reason to start planning ahead. According to Booking.com's 2027 travel predictions, 77 percent of travelers are interested in taking a holiday that pushes them beyond their comfort zone, while 81 percent would choose a destination based on how they want to feel rather than simply where they want to go.

Booking early has myriad practical advantages, too. It can protect you from soaring prices, guarantee access to peak-season experiences, and ensure a plethora of accommodation options that often fill up months before departure. The extra planning room also allows you to seek out lesser-known routes and time your visit to seasonal spectacles. Plus, it offers the underrated delight of months filled with small frissons of excitement every time you think about what is to come. Whether you’re dreaming of spotting wildlife in East Africa or weaving through the Peloponnese in Greece, here's your guide to planning a trip a year in advance for 2027.

This gallery has been updated since its original publish date.

England’s landscapes offer a surprising breadth of adventure for such a compact country, from the rugged drama of the Lake District to the chalk cliffs and wildflower-strewn downs of the South East and the mellow, biscuit-hued villages that string all of this together. A rich tapestry of moors that feel wonderfully remote, market towns that hum with independent food producers, and stretches of coastline where seals bob with the rhythm of the waves can all be woven together, with the added ease of just being able to ring up and book. Outdoorsy types can opt for hiking along windswept coastal paths in Cornwall, paddleboarding through still-water estuaries in Devon, or following ancient woodland trails in the New Forest, while those who prefer a slower pace can settle into long lunches at quaint English vineyards (Chapel Down in Kent and Rathfinny in Sussex, to name a few), wander through sculpture parks or spend languid afternoons in honey-stone villages where the loudest sound is often the church bell.

For those seeking the same sense of escape on a gentler scale, a clutch of estates across England is quietly rethinking the country house stay. Just outside London, The Grove in Hertfordshire is a firm family favorite, amid rolling parkland and its own championship golf course. The addition of two quaint cottages tucked into the grounds in 2025 offers a more private way to experience the estate, with access to its extensive grounds and family-friendly activities, from mini Land Rover rides to archery and woodland walks. Further north, The Tawny in Staffordshire offers a more immersive relationship with the landscape, where architecturally considered treehouses and lakeside retreats complement woodland gardens, dining at The Plumicorn restaurant, and paths to explore across its two adjoining estates. While in Hampshire, Avington Park Estate leans into its historic setting, pairing grand riverside scenery with elegant accommodation and access to fishing, wild swimming, and a range of wellness experiences, including a lakeside sauna pod.

All this, though, with the caveat that some of the most sought-after Great British stays can fill up well ahead of peak weekends and school holidays, so it's worth getting your reservation in early if you have your heart set on a particular property or date in 2027.

The Peloponnese invites a slower, deeper kind of Greek escape, one built around winding coastal roads, mountain passes scented with wild herbs, and ancient sites that appear almost without warning. This southern peninsula feels far removed from the island throngs, yet it offers a richness that rivals any Aegean hotspot. Planning ahead is key, particularly if you want to secure small guesthouses, family-run inns, or farm stays in popular coastal areas during July and August. For a 2027 trip, consider traveling in May, June, or September, when temperatures are generally more comfortable for sightseeing and the roads are less crowded than at the height of summer.

A favorite among avid road trippers, routes here weave through layers of history and landscape. One moment you’re exploring the fortified town of Monemvasia, built on a towering rocky islet connected to the mainland by a narrow causeway, and the next you are wandering through the ruins of Mycenae or the venerable theater at Epidaurus. The distances are manageable with a well-planned itinerary, which leaves ample time to pause at quiet coves, watch fishermen haul in their morning catch, or break for lunch under vine-covered pergolas in medieval villages. Allow at least a week if you want to explore several parts of the peninsula rather than rushing between archaeological sites, and consider choosing a handful of bases, such as Nafplio, Monemvasia, the Mani peninsula, or Pylos, to make the most of the journey.

The Mani peninsula is stark and dramatic, dotted with stone towers and rugged beaches that glow at sunset. To the west, the region opens into long ribbons of sand, olive groves that stretch toward the horizon, and wetlands alive with birdlife. Near Pylos, the Gialova Lagoon is an important stopping point for migratory birds, while the nearby crescent-shaped Voidokilia Beach makes a particularly tempting stop on a coastal drive. Inland, the mountains of Arcadia offer cool respite in summer and timeless hiking trails that trace the contours of rivers and valleys. If you're traveling in 2027, book your preferred accommodation early for peak summer dates, but leave enough room in the itinerary for spontaneous detours. In fact, for travelers drawn to the romance of the open road, there are few places as rewarding or as effortlessly cinematic as the Peloponnese.

For couples planning a celebration trip, Hawaii remains one of the most evocative places to unwind together. The archipelago pairs volcanic drama with serene beaches, vibrant reefs, and an open spirit, while its deeply held sense of community gives romance a grounded, almost effortless quality.

For a romantic escape, the choice of island is just as important as the hotel. On Big Island, volcanic landscapes and stretches of coastline set the scene for a slower-paced holiday, while Oahu combines beautiful beaches with Honolulu's lively restaurants and nightlife. The hotel scene offers plenty of tempting options, from the traditional-style, thatched-roof hale at Rosewood Kona Village and the extensively renovated Mauna Lani, Auberge Collection, to smaller gems such as White Sands Hotel and Surfjack in Waikiki.

For a honeymoon or anniversary trip, it's worth booking your preferred resort and flights in advance, particularly if you're traveling over Christmas, New Year, or during the summer holidays. And if you're hoping to explore more than one island, allow enough time for the additional flights rather than trying to squeeze too much into one trip.

The landscapes of Utah are full of sandstone spires, rust-red cliffs that glow in the late-afternoon light, and labyrinthine slot canyons that twist into shadow and sun. Geology becomes a storybook, particularly at Utahraptor State Park, home to one of the most significant dinosaur bone sites in North America. Located around 15 miles northwest of Moab, the park protects the Dalton Wells Dinosaur Quarry, where thousands of dinosaur bones have been discovered, including those of its namesake predator. Further south, the astonishing petroglyph panels at Newspaper Rock offer a rare glimpse into centuries of Indigenous history, with carvings attributed to Basketmaker, Ancestral Puebloan, and Ute peoples. The rock surface is carved with scenes that feel as vivid today as when they were first etched.

Both sites can be reached from Moab, a small desert hub that continues to evolve. From April to early November 2027, Canyon Spirit, formerly Rocky Mountaineer's Rockies to the Red Rocks service, is scheduled to operate its two-day train journey between Denver and Moab, with an overnight stay in Glenwood Springs. With panoramic windows framing Colorado's mountains, river valleys, and dramatic red-rock canyons, it is a journey that turns the simple act of moving from one place to another into an experience in its own right. Winter, too, brings a different kind of spectacle to Utah, when canyon walls catch the low light and snowfall softens the edges of its famously rugged terrain. For a 2027 trip, it's worth securing your preferred train departure and accommodation in Moab well ahead, particularly if you're traveling in spring or autumn, when temperatures are generally more comfortable for exploring the desert on foot.

Vancouver Island offers a rare kind of quiet that settles over old-growth forests, wild shorelines, and mountain lakes so still they resemble polished stone. It is also a place where Indigenous presence remains central. The lands of the Kwakwaka’wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth, and Coast Salish peoples continue to shape the island’s identity, and planning ahead allows travelers to seek out experiences rooted in cultural respect rather than commercial interpretation. Ferries can fill up quickly during summer, making advance bookings worthwhile on reservable routes and giving you time to curate a thoughtful route. BC Ferries generally opens reservations six months ahead and recommends booking at least four to six weeks before long weekends, so it's worth planning your crossings early if you're traveling with a car or camper van.

On the water, you can join marine excursions informed by generations of coastal knowledge or explore the Salish Sea with Indigenous guides who share their knowledge of the region's history, wildlife, and cultural traditions. Fishing trips with Indigenous-owned outfitters offer another way to experience the island's coastal traditions, while storytelling walks and wildlife encounters reveal how land, sea, and culture are intertwined. Vancouver Island’s landscapes match this richness. Orcas pulse through cold channels, black bears forage along shorelines and in forest clearings, and mist drifts between cedar trees that have stood for centuries. Whether you pitch a tent north of Campbell River or take a slow-rolling road trip in a camper van, this is a destination where the outside world becomes the centerpiece. Summer is a particularly rewarding time to explore, with longer days for hiking and kayaking, while whale-watching opportunities vary by location and season. If you're planning a 2027 escape, check campsite reservation opening dates and arrange popular guided wildlife excursions and Indigenous-led experiences ahead of your visit, particularly for July and August.

Your kids might learn about the rainforest at school—but there’s nothing like seeing it in real life to nurture their interest in nature and inspire their curiosity. Costa Rica is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world, with more than a quarter of its territory protected for conservation, and it’s not just children who are enchanted by bright butterflies, noisy green macaws, bead-eyed tree frogs, and sloths. It’s a relatively small country, so it’s possible to take in the rainforest canopy, pineapple plantations, sandy beaches, and mist-topped mountains all in one trip. From spotting wildlife on guided rainforest walks to exploring hanging bridges around Arenal or watching the waves roll in along the Pacific coast, there are plenty of ways to turn a family holiday into an adventure.

The best eco-lodges, home rentals, and hotels in Costa Rica are worth booking well ahead, particularly for Christmas, Easter, and school holidays. The Pacific coast's dry season generally runs from December to March, with April marking the transition towards the rainy season, making these months popular for beach holidays and outdoor adventures. The Caribbean coast follows a different rainfall pattern, with September and October often among its driest months. Plan in advance and book into one of the country's famous eco-friendly stays—we like the Victorian-style bungalows at Aguas Claras in Puerto Viejo or the luxurious Lapa Rios Lodge on the Osa Peninsula. Aguas Claras welcomes children aged three and over and can arrange activities such as surfing lessons and wildlife excursions, while Lapa Rios, which accepts children aged six and over, offers guided rainforest experiences and opportunities to learn about conservation. For a private stay, there are some truly fantastic Airbnbs in Costa Rica, including treehouses surrounded by tropical greenery and villas near the beaches of Santa Teresa.

For a 2027 family trip, it's worth planning your route as carefully as your accommodation. Winding mountain roads and travel times between regions can make an ambitious itinerary tiring, particularly with younger children. Choose a few bases rather than trying to see everything, and book popular guided activities ahead of time. Some national parks also require advance online tickets, so check the relevant booking arrangements before visiting.

Where to stay: Best Hotels in Costa Rica; Best Rentals in Costa Rica

Though Seoul is famous for its café culture and culinary scene, the kitchens in South Korea's southern regions are drawing travelers down and out of the capital, with tour operators designing itineraries that guide guests through the ingredients, culture, and history of each recipe. Responsible Travel has put together an eight-day experience with departures available throughout much of 2027, inviting travelers to experience regional specialities, spend a night at a Buddhist temple near Gyeongju, explore traditional food markets, and learn to make kimchi. On the coast, Jeollanam-do spotlights fresher, lighter flavors straight from the ocean such as ganjang gejang (soy-marinated crab), plus richer dishes like beef-rib soup. You can also stay in a temple at Baekyangsa, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan (of Chef’s Table fame) has a meditative approach to Korean cooking. The temple offers a separate overnight experience featuring a demonstration of her temple cuisine, with sessions generally held monthly and dates released around a month in advance.

Most arriving by air will travel through Seoul at some point—so factor in a few days to check out chefs such as Jungsik Yim and Mingoo Kang, who have been putting the city on the Michelin-starred map with their internationally-acclaimed menus. Kang's restaurant Mingles holds three Michelin stars in the 2026 guide, while Yim's Jungsik has two, making both tempting additions to a food-focused itinerary. For an authentic stay, book into a hanok in Seoul, perhaps in the historic Bukchon neighborhood, where traditional tiled-roof houses sit alongside galleries, tea rooms, and small boutiques. Be aware that tourist sightseeing is restricted between 5 p.m. and 10 a.m. in designated residential streets, so check the local rules before visiting.

Ask most people what’s on their travel bucket list, and you can guarantee that a trip on Belmond's Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is up there. Long associated with romance and timeless glamour, there are few things as enjoyable as a journey on one of these famous trains through Europe. Thanks to a focus on slow travel, you can now justify your ticket as a greener way of getting around. From the moment you arrive at the station and the lacquered dark blue carriages come into view, you feel like you’ve stepped into the pages of an Agatha Christie novel.

There are 70 routes to explore, including Paris to Verona and Amsterdam to Venice. On the Florence to Paris route, squeeze in a stay at Castello di Casole beforehand so you can start your trip with freshly cooked pizza from the hotel’s 16th-century pizza oven and glasses of wine from their vineyard while watching the sun set behind the rolling Tuscan hills.

Once on board and directed to your cabin, there’s little to do but sit back, sip Champagne, and watch as the train station melts away and towns and fields speed past you. A three-course lunch in one of the three 1920s dining cars is next, followed by an afternoon drinking cocktails in 3674, the train’s Art Deco bar car, before dressing in your finery for the evening.

Time slips away as quickly as the snow-capped mountains whizzing past the window, and after a decadent dinner followed by martinis in the bar car—accompanied by the tinkling of a piano and, if you’re lucky, a sing-song from the bar staff—it’s time to climb into bed and let the movement of the train (and aforementioned martinis) lull you to sleep.

If you don’t quite manage the 6 a.m. wake up to see the sunrise over Champagne, then you’ll stir as the train pulls into Paris and coffee and pastries arrive promptly at your cabin. All that’s left is to wonder how quickly you can save for your next Venice Simplon-Orient-Express adventure. With 2027 journeys already available to book, it's worth reserving early if you have a particular route, date, or cabin category in mind.

Uruguay’s summer runs from December to February, although warm weather and beach holidays can extend into March, so it’s a popular winter break for sun-starved travelers (and when seasonal restaurants and hotels are most likely to be open). While Montevideo offers a mix of city beaches, markets, and culture, further along the coast, José Ignacio—a former fishing village turned bustling beach town—draws a fashionable crowd of locals and foreigners. The area has become a magnet for art lovers, foodies, and design enthusiasts, with places such as Posada Ayana, home to James Turrell’s Skyspace installation, and Luz, a wine lodge surrounded by vineyards and olive groves, around ten minutes' drive from José Ignacio. Guests at Posada Ayana can experience Turrell's Ta Khut installation at sunrise and sunset, while Luz offers wine tastings and culinary experiences that make it worth venturing away from the beach.

Seafront favorite Playa Vik continues to attract visitors with its striking architecture, art-filled interiors, and views over Playa Mansa. Just out of town, the high-design Sacromonte Landscape Hotel offers a more secluded escape in the wild sierras of Maldonado, where contemporary cabins overlook the surrounding vineyards and countryside. Although Francis Mallmann’s restaurants Chiringuito and Bodega Garzón are on many bucket lists, few know that visitors can also stay at Casa Anna, the chef's charming guesthouse in nearby Pueblo Garzón. Alongside regular accommodation, Casa Anna offers separately arranged hosted culinary experiences with Mallmann, including shared meals and opportunities to discover his distinctive approach to open-fire cooking.

If you're planning to spend the last of your annual leave in the South American sunshine, aim for late December to experience José Ignacio at its buzziest, but be prepared for higher prices and limited availability at the most sought-after hotels. February and March can offer a quieter alternative, although some seasonal businesses begin winding down as summer draws to a close. For the festive period, booking in advance is particularly worthwhile, especially if you're hoping to secure one of the area's smaller, design-led retreats.

The ski-in-ski-out Park Hyatt Niseko Hanazono boasts Molière Montagne, a restaurant from three-Michelin-starred chef Hiroshi Nakamichi, an impressive selection of restaurants and bars, and hot-spring bathing facilities for unwinding after a day on the slopes. Sansui Niseko offers a fully serviced alternative to townhouses by Kasara or Airbnb (the latter of which are particularly high quality here), with direct ski access to Grand Hirafu's Family Course, an onsen, and spacious suites for those traveling with family or friends.

The outskirts of Sapporo are stunning in the fall, with koyo (the appearance of autumn leaves) at its most colorful around mid-October, but winter is when Niseko really comes into its own. The 2026 to 2027 ski season is scheduled to begin on November 28, with some ski areas planning to remain open into early May, depending on snowfall. January and February are generally the best months for the famously light, dry powder that draws skiers and snowboarders from around the world, although snow conditions can never be guaranteed.

For a trip during the winter season, booking accommodation, ski lessons, and equipment rentals well in advance is a good idea, particularly over Christmas and New Year's Eve. With four interconnected ski areas, a thriving restaurant scene, and plenty of opportunities to warm up in an onsen after a day in the snow, Niseko is the kind of destination where a little advance planning can make all the difference.

Another blockbuster backdrop, Jordan’s archaeological city of Petra was named one of the new seven wonders of the world in 2007 for its extraordinary rock-carved architecture and the Al Siq canyon. A couple of hours' drive from Petra, the sliver of Red Sea coast around Aqaba draws visitors for its sun, souks, and scuba-diving opportunities, with colorful coral reefs and warm waters making it a favorite among underwater explorers. Beyond the coast, the extraordinary landscapes of Wadi Rum are another reason to add Jordan to your 2027 travel wish list. Here, towering sandstone formations and vast desert valleys provide the setting for guided excursions with local Bedouin communities and nights spent beneath the stars at desert camps.

Spring and autumn are among the best times to visit, with milder temperatures making it easier to explore Petra's archaeological treasures and venture into the desert. If you fly into the capital, Amman, a metropolis of ancient tradition and entrepreneurial spirit greets you, alongside a slew of social enterprises such as SEP, a fashion and lifestyle brand working with Palestinian refugee embroiderers, and Beit Sitti, a cooking school founded by three sisters where visitors can learn to prepare traditional Arabic dishes alongside local women.

For those hoping to combine Petra, Wadi Rum, and the Red Sea in one trip, planning ahead allows time to arrange local guides, accommodation, and transport between the country's most spectacular destinations. It's also worth looking into the Jordan Pass, which includes admission to more than 40 attractions, including Petra, and a tourist visa fee waiver for eligible visitors who purchase it before arrival and meet the relevant stay requirements. With travel schedules and regional conditions subject to change, check the latest official advisories before confirming your 2027 plans.

Antarctic travel is still trying to strike a balance between overtourism and sustainable travel, with the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators recording more than 113,000 tourists traveling to the region during the 2025 to 2026 season. Once accessible only to wealthy explorers or well-funded scientists, it’s exciting that this stark, striking landscape is now attracting a growing number of adventurous travelers, although its increasing popularity raises important questions about protecting one of the world's most fragile environments. Many choose to visit during the austral summer (November to March), when there’s less sea ice and more sun (ideal for kayaking, wildlife watching and, on certain specialist expeditions, skiing and snowshoeing).

From vast penguin colonies and seals resting on ice floes to humpback whales feeding in the Southern Ocean, Antarctica offers extraordinary opportunities for wildlife encounters, both on land and at sea. For many travelers, a polar cruise is one of the most rewarding ways to experience the continent, with expedition vessels offering guided shore landings and Zodiac excursions, while larger ships may provide scenic cruising without disembarkation. Choosing an operator committed to responsible tourism is essential, although even carefully managed expeditions have an environmental footprint. Consider a vessel with hybrid-electric propulsion, such as Ponant’s Le Commandant Charcot, the first hybrid-electric polar exploration ship powered by liquified natural gas, which also carries two onboard scientific laboratories. Or, book with an operator such as Abercrombie & Kent or White Desert, which offers a different way to experience the continent through its fly-in expeditions and luxury land-based camps, including Whichaway Camp.

With the Antarctic travel season concentrated into just a few months and places on specialist expeditions limited, planning a year ahead is particularly worthwhile. Travelers hoping to visit during the popular summer months of December and January (or to secure a place on a small-group expedition) should start comparing itineraries and booking well before departure.

Trekking in the Himalayas comes with its own set of logistical, financial, and physical challenges, so booking well in advance can make a huge difference. Big groups will struggle with spontaneity, and allowing yourself several months to train and prepare for long days on the mountains is well worth the effort. But physical preparation is only part of the equation: Ladakh's high altitude means visitors also need to allow sufficient time to acclimate, particularly when arriving in Leh, which sits at around 11,500 feet above sea level. Local tourism authorities recommend at least 48 hours of rest before heading to higher-altitude areas.

If you’re determined to spot the region’s elusive snow leopard too, a good local guide is essential, and they book up fast. Hemis National Park is one of the world's best-known places to search for these big cats, with experienced trackers scanning the rocky slopes and valleys for signs of movement. Unlike conventional trekking holidays, snow leopard expeditions are best undertaken during the colder months, generally between November and April, when specialist wildlife tours operate in the region. The conditions can be challenging, with freezing temperatures and unpredictable mountain weather, but the rewards can be extraordinary. Ladakh is at its loveliest, and busiest, during the warmer months, from June to September, for those interested in exploring its Buddhist monasteries.

Consider booking through Voygr Expeditions, andBeyond, or Responsible Travel, all of which offer specialist snow leopard expeditions with experienced local guides or trackers. Some itineraries also incorporate visits to local communities and conservation initiatives, including andBeyond's support for the Snow Leopard Conservancy. With several 2027 departures already sold out, securing a place six to 12 months ahead is advisable, especially for those hoping to travel during the peak winter months.

For decades, safari trips centered around Big Five game, but Rwanda has something that Kenya, Zambia, and Botswana do not: silverback mountain gorillas. As a country, Rwanda has been a champion of ecotourism since long before the term went mainstream, with reforestation, conservation, and caps on visitor numbers protecting the environment and the wildlife within it. These efforts have contributed to a remarkable conservation success story, with the mountain gorilla population across the Virunga Massif, which spans Rwanda, Uganda, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing from 480 in 2010 to 604 in 2016. In the Virunga Mountains, only eight people may trek to visit a particular gorilla group each day, with encounters limited to one hour. Visitors are told to stay at least 23 feet away to protect the gorillas from human diseases, although the animals themselves may occasionally approach more closely (recall David Attenborough’s encounter in 1978, when he commented, ‘There is more meaning and mutual understanding in exchanging a glance with a gorilla than any other animal I know’).

A collection of established luxury lodges, such as Magashi Camp, Singita Kwitonda Lodge, One&Only’s Gorilla’s Nest, and Nyungwe Tea Forest Resort have proven themselves to experienced safari-goers. While Magashi offers traditional Big Five game drives in Akagera National Park, Singita Kwitonda and Gorilla's Nest provide luxurious bases for gorilla trekking, and Nyungwe Tea Forest Resort is ideally placed for exploring the rainforest and tracking chimpanzees. For those wanting to venture beyond the forests, Lake Kivu offers a completely different perspective on Rwanda's landscapes. The Kivu Queen uBuranga, which began welcoming guests in December 2023, takes travelers across the lake aboard a luxury floating hotel, with opportunities to explore its islands and discover local communities and traditions.

Gorilla trekking permits currently cost $1,500 per person for most international visitors, and with only eight visitors allowed per habituated gorilla group each day, booking several months in advance is strongly recommended, particularly during the drier seasons from June to September and December to February. Those hoping to combine gorilla trekking with a stay at one of the country's most exclusive lodges should start planning even earlier, especially if traveling during peak holiday periods.

A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6241. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6240. Frontier Airlines Warns Of Scam Emails With Real Booking Codes And Fake Refunds

A fraudulent airline email is easier to dismiss when it gets your trip details wrong. What happens when it includes your actual flight information and confirmation number? Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting precisely that, with scammers using real reservation details to solicit credit card information. Frontier has confirmed an active phishing campaign, and the obvious question is how the scammers obtained the data.

View From The Wing highlights a concerning report that Frontier customers have received fraudulent emails offering refunds or claiming an existing reservation has a payment problem.

The troubling part is that passengers say the messages contain genuine confirmation numbers and flight details. Some report entering their credit card information into the linked websites.

One version promises a refund after the passenger verifies the card used for the booking. Another creates urgency by suggesting payment for an upcoming trip has not gone through.

The latter is a scammer’s dream: someone expecting to travel soon may be particularly inclined to resolve what appears to be a ticketing problem.

Frontier has published a warning on its website, acknowledging an active email phishing campaign targeting customers.

The airline says it will not email passengers asking them to revalidate a reservation, reconfirm credit card information, or provide payment details to obtain a refund.

The critical point is that a correct confirmation number does not make an email legitimate.

If the passenger reports are accurate, someone has obtained information that should not be available to a random scammer. That raises the possibility of unauthorized access to a reservation-related system, compromised credentials, or misuse by someone with legitimate access.

An inside job is one possibility. A breach at the airline or a service provider is another. Compromised passenger email accounts could also expose booking confirmations, though it seems too coincidental if this has been happening on a larger scale and only with Frontier.

We do not yet have enough evidence to identify the source, establish how broadly information was exposed, or conclude that the access happened recently. Older stolen data can still be used in a new scam campaign.

There is, however, a relevant disclosure. In an October 2, 2026 notification, Frontier described a security incident involving its customer care database and information submitted through its customer care form. The airline said it updated the database configuration and improved monitoring in response.

That disclosure does not establish that this phishing campaign is linked to that incident, but it makes the question of where these reservation details originated even harder to ignore.

Warning passengers is necessary…but it would be nice if Frontier was a bit more transparent about the source of the leak.

I recently questioned Lufthansa Group’s decision to require a Travel ID account for online check-in. My objection was to making passengers create an account to complete a basic task after buying a ticket.

This Frontier story gives me reason to consider the security side more closely.

A booking reference and surname are convenient credentials, but they can be copied from a confirmation email or exposed elsewhere. Requiring additional authentication before allowing access to sensitive reservation information could offer passengers protection, even if it still strikes me as a bit heavy-handed like the incessant two-factor-authorization to log into Air Canada Aeroplan or United MileagePlus.

I’m not convinced Lufthansa introduced its requirement for this reason, or that its particular implementation would prevent the Frontier scam. Still, I would be more receptive to an account requirement accompanied by a clear explanation of what it protects and why the existing process is inadequate. Communication goes a long way in just about everything…

Frontier has confirmed a phishing campaign, while passengers report that fraudulent messages include their real booking details. For now, verify any supposed payment problem or refund through the airline’s official website or app. Do not trust a message merely because it contains your personal details.

But the burden should not fall entirely on passengers to spot convincing fraud. Frontier needs to explain, to the extent its investigation can establish, how scammers obtained the information that makes these messages so believable.

#6239. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

#6237. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.
