#6236. Eurostar Premier (First Class) Review: Better Than Flying, But Hardly A Luxury Experience

My first Eurostar Premier journey took me from Brussels to Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, where I connected to a KLM flight to Los Angeles. The train itself felt older than I expected, but the quiet carriage and productive journey made it a pleasant alternative to flying.

I sometimes enjoy trying a new travel experience without researching every detail beforehand. There is a certain irony in that, considering how much of this blog is devoted to helping others know what to expect. Eurostar was one of those experiences. I had long wanted to try it, and an award booking provided the opportunity.

I booked Brussels to Los Angeles through Air France/KLM Flying Blue for 60,000 miles in business class (plus $478.13 in taxes and fees). The itinerary included a Eurostar train from Brussels-Midi to Amsterdam Schiphol, followed by KLM World Business Class to Los Angeles. I could have booked a departure from Brussels Airport for the same mileage price, but chose the rail connection to try something different.

The cabin description was confusing. My ticket indicated business class, while KLM’s Air&Rail information referred to a “premium” experience for those connecting in business class. Eurostar’s actual classes are Standard, Plus, and Premier. At check-in, the agent confirmed I was booked into Premier.

Rather than use the actual Eurostar check-in desk, Brussels-Midi has an Air France-KLM ticketing office and rail check-in counter located in the rear of the station.

My train departed at 5:53 am and I showed up at 5:15 am to check-in…where I found a massive line and only one agent on duty. One passenger in the front of the line was traveling on SNCF to Paris but had a ticketing issue which the lone agent was trying to resolve. But time was ticking and the line grew longer.

Finally at 5:30 am I walked to the front of the line to ask for assistance, noting my train departed in 20 minutes. I did not mean to be the ugly American, but it was just what the agent needed to ask the frazzled traveler from Côte d’Ivoire (I noticed her passport) to step aside. Within a few minutes she had cleared the line and I was on my way upstairs to the rail platform.

There was a Eurostar lounge in Brussels, but it did not open until 6:00 am during my visit, so I could not use it…though I would have access to it had my train departed an hour later.  Not that I ended up having a lot of time to spare, but it woudld have been nice to have a cup of coffee there before the train departed.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in Coach 11, the very last cabin designated as Premier.

Stepping onboard felt more like entering an older TGV first class carriage than the sleek, modern interior I had imagined. Old is, not necessarily a bad thing, but the cabin showed wear. My footrest was broken and the cabin just look tattered and well past its prime.

In the very rear of the cabin was a compartment with seating of four that remained empty throughout the journey.

The bigger advantage on this particular departure was how quiet it was: there was only one other passenger in my carriage and even as we neared Amsterdam there was never more than five in the cabin.

A nearly empty premium cabin is not something you can count in Premier, but it made this an especially pleasant setting to work ahead of a long flight in which I did not want to open my computer.

The lavatories in the Premier cabin were very typical European train toilets with metal toilets, a small sink, but fairly spacious.

We departed on time, and an attendant welcomed us and offered me breakfast menu shortly after pushback, along with a packaged moist towelette.

Sandwich IGP Bayonne ham, AOP Comté cheese, with dill picked cucumbers

Fruit Kampot pepper and verbena apples, gala melon, watermelon

Both were accompanied by yogurt, a croissant, juice, and coffee. I chose the fruit, though I would have liked both (and my request for both was politely declined).

It was a modest meal, but I enjoyed it. The fruit was good and the coffee was decent, as was the croissant.

I preferred this breakfast to the catering KLM serves on its short intra-European flights and the presentation was far nicer. It did not need to be elaborate to be satisfying at that hour and I had a second cup of coffee and some cold pressed berry juice prior to arrival at AMS.

The onboard internet worked well, allowing me to be productive during the ride. For this trip, I valued that more than a particularly luxurious cabin, though I was initially concerned that I would be capped at 500 MB of data.

Thankfully, even though I quickly exceeded the cap the internet continued working…

In-seat power was also available so I arrived in AMS with my devices fully charged.

The attendant’s welcome and breakfast service provided a pleasant start to the morning. Sure, it would have been nice to have the sandwich as well (I was still hungry and the cabin was empty), but she denied my request in a very kind way!

At one point I took a walk through the train to check out the Café Car which offers food and drinks for purchase.

Looking at the menu, I’d say I would have been fine with a falafel wrap and Lavazza coffee had I been booked in coach.

My destination was Schiphol Airport, not Amsterdam Centraa, whcih thankfully meant no backtracking a regional train to the airport.

Next came my KLM lounge visit and onward flight to Los Angeles.

For my itinerary, I was happy to have Premier included in the Flying Blue award.

Whether I would pay a substantial premium for it separately is another question and the answer is probably not. Eurostar lists extra-spacious seating and lounge access among Premier’s benefits, but I could not use the Brussels lounge on this departure.

It is also important to compare the correct route. Eurostar’s class descriptions distinguish between London services and continental routes. For example, the included meal in Premier on a London-route would have included a multi-course hot meal.

For a separate purchase, I would compare the actual fare difference and the benefits available for the particular trip (like the lounge), probably paying no more than €50 for the upgrade on this particular route.

Eurostar Premier was less polished than I expected, but I enjoyed the journey. The worn interior and broken footrest deserved attention, while breakfast and reliable internet helped make the ride worthwhile. For this Brussels–Schiphol connection, I was glad I chose the train. It gave me a quiet, productive start to the trip home and left me interested in trying Eurostar again.

For some reason, I pictured something more like a modern Japanese or Chinese high speed rail carriage.

The seating is awful – Regiojet, our local carrier, used these same coaches as a lowest (sub-economy) class.

I take all lines of the Eurostar fairly frequently, and for context you took an older model of what was Thalys – the high speed train connecting Belgium to France and the Netherlands. They merged with Eurostar a few years back, but the experience remains quite distinct. Eurostar to/from London requires going through security and passport control, and is in a completely different part of the train station, and a lot more like getting in a flight. Overall. I’d recommend Plus. The price difference is rarely huge with economy, and you get more or less the same as Premium but without the lounge access or meal. Most routes max out at less than 3 hours, so I’d buy something before or after leaving, or as noted get a coffee on the train. I’ve taken Premium a few times and while it’s a nice upgrade, I’d not spend my own money on it, and the two times I’ve chosen it with the option of Plus were because I had urgent work and needed the lounge as a quiet office space. Overall, it’s a good review and reflective of the experience. Fingers crossed the new rolling stock freshens things up when it arrives, and I’m glad you could try things in this part of Europe.

I love that you include choo-choos (even though this is Live and Let’s…FLY). That photo in the reflection… *chef’s kiss*

The red Eurostar trains are Ex-Thalys TGV sets modified for different voltages across Europe, which is why they look/like tired old TGV trains. The Eurostar Siemens trains that usually run Brussels-London service are more similar to German ICE trains.

I can’t see any Kampala pepper on that fruit salad,

Eurostar have (just) new trains on order, and while they’re conflating their purchase with their cross channel services, they are exactly the right number to replace their aging ex Thalys fleet. So don’t expect any immediate improvement

Gone are the days of the “sure thing” complimentary upgrade. But, for those who find themselves on the road more than once a month, top-tier elite status can mean the difference between being there for that special family event or a disappointing night in an airport hotel.

Due to a ton of work travel, I currently hold top-tier status in the Big Three US airline elite programs. As a Northern Virginia resident, United is my primary airline, and I earned its invitation-only Global Services status again this year. As I was trying to figure out which of these three status levels was the most rewarding, I realized I may not even have the best elite status in North America.

No, I’m not talking about Southwest Airlines A-List Preferred status. I think there’s a reasonable argument for looking north.

Air Canada Aeroplan Super Elite status may actually be better for many frequent travelers, even if it seems complicated as a U.S. resident.

Here are a few reasons to consider earning Super Elite status.

One area where Aeroplan really shines is lounge access — a perk that even top-tier elites at most U.S. airlines can't count on when flying domestically.

Super Elite members can bring immediate family into any Maple Leaf Lounge as well as an additional guest. Delta Diamond, United 1K and American Executive Platinum members get no complimentary lounge access as a benefit of their status.

While Aeroplan doesn’t grant access to their Signature Suites lounges, Super Elites can enjoy lounge access with partner airlines such as Emirates and Virgin Australia. They also have access to an arrivals lounge at London Heathrow.

Arguably one of the most valuable benefits of Super Elite status is Priority Rewards. With few exceptions, a Priority Reward can be redeemed for a 50% discount on a one-way or round-trip flight, including on partner airlines (and Air Canada has a lot of partners).

Aeroplan members can earn these rewards multiple times each year as part of Milestone Benefits.

If you hold 25K status, your Priority Rewards are valid on economy flights in Canada and the United States (including Hawaii). However, Super Elites can redeem them for all cabins up to and including business class, including on partner airlines.

When you consider the pricing of international business class award flights, it’s not hard to imagine saving 100,000 Aeroplan points or more when redeeming a Priority Reward on a round-trip ticket.

You can book a flight for someone else, even if they’re not immediate family, so long as you use your Aeroplan points.

If you travel as much as I do, you might consider the Air Canada Concierge Service to rival Priority Rewards in value. Super Elite members get access to a personalized concierge service.

Reports from Super Elite members indicate that Air Canada concierges have a healthy amount of autonomy to fix problems while you’re traveling, including moving you to other airlines to get you to your destination as quickly as possible. In many major airports, Air Canada has local concierges, so the support is right where you need it.

This level of service used to be commonplace with the U.S. carriers. While invitation-only levels such as United Global Services offer more flexible rules during irregular operations, my personal experience over the past few years is that many tools that used to be available to those agents have been restricted or removed.

How does a U.S. resident earn Super Elite status? It’s a bit complicated, but you have options. Cabotage restrictions prevent an airline like Air Canada from flying you between New York and Los Angeles, even if you connect in a Canadian gateway.

However, if you travel internationally, especially in a premium cabin, Air Canada is well situated to get you to many places in Europe and Asia. With hubs in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, AIr Canada can connect you to Europe and Asia. It may be easy to forget Toronto as an option if you live in Ohio or Indiana and need to fly to France.

The Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (see ) is also a great way to accelerate your quest for Super Elite status. Just holding the card gives you 5,000 Status Qualifying Credits each calendar year and entry-level 25K elite status. Spending on the card can earn another 20,000 Status Qualifying Credits. That means the credit card alone can get you 20% of the way to Super Elite.

Top-tier elite status is largely similar among American, Delta and United. While Air Canada shares many of the same benefits with them, Aeroplan has a few key benefits that set Super Elite status apart.

Priority Rewards allow your mileage balance to punch above its weight. Lounge access and a dedicated concierge service can make travel much smoother, even on the toughest days. And a few business class tickets to Europe can quickly put you in the range of Aeroplan Super Elite status.

#6234. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6233. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

#6232. In Luxor, Ancient Egypt feels newly alive

The water is cold and clear. Half-hidden amid the palm-tufted grounds of the Mortuary Temple of Seti I, this sacred sunken lake on Luxor's west bank was once the domain of ancient Egyptian priests. More than 3,000 years later, women from nearby villages still come, hoping its waters will serve as a fertility aid or a balm for their sick children, says my guide Ahmed Hassan, who was born and raised on this side of the Nile. It's one of the area's many miracles, he adds: No one knows where the water comes from, but it hasn't run dry since those priests of antiquity first bathed here. Hedging my bets, I submerge my hands.

It can be difficult to know what to believe in this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, 410 miles south of Cairo, where the Nile exudes a life force of its own; the mountains cradle secret treasures; and the light, particularly at golden hour, plays tricks, almost convincing you that you have traveled back in time. The line between the real and the mystical feels flimsy, whether you are considering the scale of the approximately 1,000-ton, 65-foot-tall colossus of Ramses II, inexplicably carved from a single piece of granite and lying prostrate at the king's statuesque funerary temple, the Ramesseum; or observing the unnerving precision of the hieroglyphs in the tomb of Ramses V and VI, in the Valley of the Kings, that has proved immune to the ravages of time.

Formerly ancient Thebes, Luxor—whose name comes from the Arabic Al-Uqsur (The Palaces)—served as Egypt's capital during the New Kingdom, from circa 1550 BCE to 1070 BCE. On the west bank of the Nile, sugarcane and banana plantations lead to a limestone canyon topped by Al-Qurn, or The Horn, a natural peak shaped like a pyramid. The rulers of the New Kingdom decided that this would be the ideal spot to protect their richly decorated tombs from grave robbers—a failed exercise, since every tomb in the Valley of the Kings was looted in antiquity, bar that of now legendary boy king Tutankhamen.

“There are many sites that have an impressive amount of ‘stuff,’ but what you have in Luxor is truly monumental,” Mennat-Allah El Dorry, from the American University in Cairo's department of sociology, Egyptology, and anthropology, tells me. “You have Karnak and Luxor temples on the east bank, and the mortuary temples on the west, as well as Valley of the Kings. It is such a dense area.”

I take her recommendations, balancing the quiet of the lesser-visited, only partially restored Mortuary Temple of Seti I and the Ramesseum with the many-splendored tombs at the Valley of the Kings, where voyeuristic crowds swell to see the diminutive mummy of Tutankhamen languishing 26 feet below ground. By contrast, the tomb of Ramses V and VI close by is deserted. A toothless, djellaba-wearing guard smiles conspiratorially before letting me behind the barrier. He takes my phone and assumes the practiced ease of a fashion photographer directing his next magazine cover: “Come closer; go there; look over your shoulder.”

Much of Luxor feels like it hasn't changed in centuries. At sunset the sails of felucca boats trace a timeless scene on the Nile's surface. Amid the clip-clop of horse-drawn carriages, the call to prayer tumbles from minarets and the sky settles into strips of apricot and lavender.

Matching the restraint of Arax is the stripped-back Marsam Hotel and discreet yet stately Habu Hotel, the latter just feet away from the Medinet Habu Temple. But Hotel Al Moudira sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. Founded by Italian Lebanese artist Zeina Aboukheir in 2001, and originally designed by famed Egyptian architect Olivier Sednaoui, the hotel revels in its maximalism: a whimsical interplay of domes and arches embellished with terra-cotta plaster, frescoes, and antiques. In 2022, Aboukheir sold the hotel to its new owner, Florian Amereller, but she still guides its creative direction, most recently in the design of six new villas. I stay in one of the five rooms in the salmon pink Villa Casbah, where hand-painted silhouettes of gazelles trip skittishly across the walls.

Chef Gioconda Scott at The Moudira Farm Kitchen

Under its new ownership the now five-star Al Moudira has expanded to include a huge swath of surrounding farmland. It's here, in an open kitchen engulfed in greenery, that I find British Spanish chef Gioconda Scott in the midst of a busy lunch service. In 2025 she launched The Moudira Farm Kitchen, where she transforms the fresh produce grown on-site into an unfussy, seasonal menu inspired by the Mediterranean. “This is simple cooking,” says Scott, who populates her kitchen with young chefs from the local tourism college. “Every element has to be good. If you don't have a good olive oil or a good tomato, there's no hiding.”

The restaurant itself is filled with products made by artisans on the farm. Crockery, rendered in a range of earthy tones, was crafted by potters whom guests can join for classes. I can hear the distant clack of the loom that wove the jaunty turquoise tablecloth, while, in other corners, artisans carve alabaster, blow glass, and upholster furniture.

The same crafts inhabit the decks of Al Moudira's new, 180-foot Nile Canopus, a nostalgia-infused nod to historic travel along this evocative waterway. Open-air decks with safari-tent-style coverings, a cozy library, and rooms fitted with brass beds and bespoke teak and rattan furniture are designed to evoke the age of Amelia Edwards, author of the seminal 1877 travelogue A Thousand Miles Up the Nile.

There has been a proliferation of new dahabeahs on the Nile, which offer more intimate, personalized experiences than do the hulking, 50-cabin motorboats that also ply these waters. Laden with modern conveniences, today's dahabeahs are admittedly no longer sprightly enough to be harried along by wind and sail; instead they are pushed and pulled by dinky-looking tugboats. On the inside they are increasingly elaborate. Karine Hassoun called on Egyptian painters, professors, and artisans for her eight-cabin dahabeah, Nile Divine, a celebration of contemporary Egyptian craft. In the nine-cabin Oro, a dark wood exterior pays tribute to the dahabeahs of old but with a dramatic brass wall in the reception area, a plunge pool extending out over the deck, a full-fledged bar up top, and suites with private terraces and hot tubs. Oberoi Hotels and Resorts will join the fray later this year with two seven-suite dahabeahs featuring interiors by Karim Mekhtigian, founder of Alchemy Design Studio, while Waldorf Astoria Hotels and Resorts' new, 29-suite Nile cruiser will bring to the water all the elements of its land-based hotels, including its Peacock Alley brasserie.

Change is underway on land too. I see the cranes hovering over the east bank, pinpointing where a Four Seasons Hotel, due to open in 2027, is rapidly taking shape. The much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter's base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery and where Agatha Christie was inspired to write parts of Death on the Nile—recently closed for a renovation and will reopen as a Mandarin Oriental in July 2027, exactly 120 years after its official inauguration, hopefully with original features and charm fully intact.

That's only weeks before next year's solar eclipse: On August 2, Luxor will witness the moon masking the sun for its maximum duration, a total of 6 minutes and 22 seconds. Just enough time for that line between the real and the mystical to grow even flimsier.

A few feet from Habu Temple, recommended for its deeply etched hieroglyphs and particularly well-preserved colors, is a property with its own historic pedigree: the unassuming, 17-room Habu Hotel was one of the first hotels to open on Luxor’s West Bank in the 1920s. It has been given a smart revamp, its public areas now filled with antiques, including stately granite busts and wooden statues from the 1800s. Sundowners on the hotel’s charming rooftop terrace bring you close enough to the temple’s chiseled interior that you can admire its exterior engravings from the comfort of your lounge chair.

A day spent tirelessly exploring Luxor’s sites is best ended in the spa at Hilton Luxor Resort and Spa, where treatment rooms look directly over the Nile and the infinity pool is one of the best spots in the city to catch Luxor’s famous sunsets. This is an ultra-convenient base if you want easy access to the historic sites on Luxor’s East Bank—Karnak Temple, in particular, is within walking distance. A private breakfast on a felucca offers a fresh perspective of the Nile, especially if you time it to coincide with hot-air balloons rising majestically over the Valley of the Kings.

For a stripped-back stay that’ll make you feel like an Egyptologist of old, head to Marsam Hotel, which started life as the excavation house for the University of Chicago, before being converted into a hotel in 1939. There’s (very intentionally) no swimming pool or TVs; the 29 pared-back rooms and five suites are designed for guests who are serious about exploring the many sites that surround this historic hotel. Whether or not you spend the night, make time for lunch at Marsam’s farm-to-table restaurant, where the menu changes daily and you’ll be serenaded by the resident donkeys, camels and horses.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6231. Alaska Airlines Cuts Jobs As $700 Million Loss Looms, CEO Admits Overhead Costs Grew Too Fast

Alaska Air Group is cutting about 200 jobs as CEO Ben Minicucci warns the company could lose as much as $700 million this year if current conditions persist. Higher fuel prices are the immediate problem, but Minicucci also acknowledged that overhead has grown too quickly. That is a sobering backdrop for an airline pursuing an ambitious international expansion.

According to Reuters, which reviewed Minicucci’s employee memo, the reductions affect non-contract positions, including 125 in Washington and 48 in Hawaii. No frontline, non-management positions are being eliminated. Affected employees will finish working November 13 but continue receiving pay through December 31, with severance and other support.

The cuts represent less than 1% of the group’s roughly 32,500 employees. That makes them relatively small across the company, but certainly not small to the people losing their jobs…

Minicucci warned employees that, if conditions persist, Alaska Air Group could record its first adjusted pretax annual loss outside the pandemic since 2003. That is a warning about a potential full-year result, not a $700 million loss already reported. It also concerns the parent group, which includes Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

In its October 20 earnings release, Alaska forecast a full-year adjusted loss of $5.00–$5.50 per share and said fuel would cost $1.8 billion more than its original annual plan. Its fourth-quarter forecast assumes fuel at $4.65–$4.85 per gallon. Third-quarter revenue rose 14% to $4.3 billion, but that commercial growth has not been enough to deliver the annual profit management expected.

Those numbers help explain why simply selling more tickets is not solving the problem.

There was another revealing part of Minicucci’s message:

“We must return to the financial discipline that has long been a key competitive advantage.”

He also acknowledged that overhead expenses had grown disproportionately to revenue in recent years, adding these costs had “grown at a disproportionate rate to revenue.”

Fuel prices are largely beyond an airline’s control, but the size and cost of its management structure are not. The question is why overhead was allowed to grow that way and whether these reductions address the problem or merely provide some near-term savings. Cutting 200 positions cannot will certainly not offset a fuel bill running $1.8 billion above plan.

It also puts management in the uncomfortable position of asking employees to absorb the consequences of spending decisions those employees may have had no role in making.

I have been following Alaska’s efforts to become a more substantial global competitor, including its latest European expansion to Athens and Paris and investment in premium cabins and lounges.

These job cuts do not automatically mean that strategy is wrong, though Alaska cannot cut its way to growth. It needs a product passengers will choose and a network that gives them a reason to return. Pulling back on customer investments when conditions deteriorate could leave Alaska with the costs of expansion but less ability to earn a premium.

Still, growth deserves scrutiny when the company is losing money. Management must be willing to adjust if demand or achievable fares do not justify the investment. Ambition is useful, but it cannot become an excuse to keep spending on something that is not working, though with every investment, it takes time for a sappling to grow into a tree and the “no pain, no gain” mantra certainly applies here too.

Minicucci intends to continue investing in the fleet, customer experience, and network while tightening spending elsewhere. That is a defensible approach…and it could be that these jobs are no longer needed with AI and simply a low-hanging fruit to trim unnecessary expense in order to focus on what is more important.

Alaska Air Group is cutting about 200 jobs while warning of a potential $700 million annual loss. Fuel costs explain much of the pressure, but management’s acknowledgment that overhead grew too quickly deserves attention too.

I want Alaska’s expansion to succeed. Heck, I want JetBlue and Alaska to merge. A stronger competitor is good for passengers. But the company needs to demonstrate that its growth can produce sustainable earnings, and employees losing their jobs should not be the only ones held accountable for restoring financial discipline.

I don’t want to see any business fail but you have to recognize that 2 of the 3 major drains on AS are and were within their control and you can’t be surprised when fuel – which spikes at least once per decade and we are on round two this decade – raises its head.

and, yes, Andy, Delta has had the lowest rates of growth since covid and is posting the biggest earnings. Ok, so, all I read is… “Some of you may die, but it’s a sacrifice I am willing to make.” (Lord Farquaad in the 2001 animated film Shrek) except it’s more like… ‘I’m rooting for some airlines that compete with my preferred carrier may go under, but as long as Delta survives, it’s all good to me.’

I really think AS is getting leaner and meaner so they can take on Jetblue as a pre-packaged bankruptcy and merger partner……

A lot of the Pacific and, to a lesser extent, Atlantic bleed should start to stem if they get in the AA Joint Ventures.

When Alaska Airlines was a relatively small domestic airlines, its pilots earn less than UAL and Northwest, helped keep operating cost low. Now, as Alaska Airlines scale up, the wage has to be more comparable. It is tough to compete with Delta or UAL on long haul routes, especially to Europe, or Asian cities without partner airlines on the other side. I wish Alaska management re-plan next year long haul routes. While Anchorage to Tokyo is likely a win, Seattle to Seoul may not earn money outside of summer peak season.

Salaries & benefits are a tiny drop in a giant ocean of fuel, fuel, fuel.

Transoceanic flying has been a 1 percent drag on unit revenues, which is less impactful than Hawai‘i storms. Prior to the war, some of the transpacific routes were already starting to turn profitable. Alaska’s strategy is correct if they want to remain the dominant carrier in Seattle; failure to evolve would have left them like JetBlue. They’ve been unlucky with timing, given that fuel costs have skyrocketed and they’re paying more than anyone else. The MAX 10 delays, 787-9 Starlink STC delay, Singapore fuel spike, and Hawai‘i storms have all been factors out of their control that uniquely affected their profitability this year. But strategies aren’t measured by years. If Alaska can weather this storm, they look well-poised to emerge as a stable, profitable entity with the strongest product portfolio in the country

@Tim Dunn–I think you gave a hangup about the Virgin America buyout. That was a long time ago and did not cause AS any harm, other than sime stupidity around use of the Virgin brand name, fir which they are stull forced to pay for a name they haven’t used in years.. It definitely dud not cause the current issues. Neither did buying out HA. That total deal was $1.8 billion (including assuming HA’s debt). Matthew and Tim–the major culprit remains fuel costs–extra fuel costs are the same amount, $1.8 billion, all of it absorbed in the same year as opposed to amortized costs of theHA buyout. That number alone is more than twice the projected loss for the year.

@Matthew–One more point. I don’t think AS should be looking to merge with or buy another airline right now. You pointed out that fuel costs alone don’t account for the projected loss, even though $1.8 billion is the same amount paid for HA when accounting for taking on HA’s debt. It’s very complicated for an airline to buy and integrate another airline but AS has done pretty well. Still, I don’t know why they would want to go through that again with JerBlue. It would mean less commonality the fleet, more union contracts to deal with, and a lot more complexity. I think they have their hands full trying to stay profitable while executing their growth plan. I don’t see another merger helping them, especially right now.

Steve, AS spent a lot of money for Virgin America only to dismantle most of what they acquired. Yes, it was a drag.

The same thing is happening w/ HA; they have dismantled HNL-Asia flying only to try SEA-Asia/Europe.

Fuel IS ALWAYS a major cost for airlines and it is far from consistent in price. Building a business plan that can accommodate huge fuel price swings is what managements are supposed to do.

Alaska is most impacted by fuel prices due to its West Coast concentration. They had started to diversify their fuel sources by investing in tankering fuel from Singapore. Unfortunately, Singapore fuel prices more sharply than even West Coast fuel prices in H1 2026. That’s not an indictment of the business plan; it’s a uniquely unlucky headwind

#6230. 15 of the Coolest Marathon Courses Around the Globe, From the Arctic Circle to the Great Wall of China

The TCS New York City Marathon is consistently one of the best days of the year in the city—it's emotional, it's inspiring, and it shows off the best of humanity. If you're a runner or a spectator who got the itch for more this past weekend, you're in luck: There are tons of incredible courses around the world, and while they may not traverse NYC's five boroughs, they will take you to world wonders, through safari lands, and across borders.

As someone who regularly travels for halfs, I spend a lot of my time researching and bookmarking races. For me, running through a new place one of the best ways to get to know a destination—you get the lay of the land, see what the community is like, and notice things you might not see from a car or public transportation. And as destination races grow in popularity, the courses offered are getting even more spectacular. The races on this list—halfs, fulls, 10Ks, and more—prove it. Below, I’ve rounded up 15 of the most spectacular races happening in the next year or so, all of which are well worth traveling for.

Date: March 13, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 10K, 3.5K

What to know: If you haven't run a Rock ‘n’ Roll marathon yet, you're missing out on a good time. As the name suggests, these music-centric runs make for an extremely lively course—bands and DJs fill the roads and the after party. Locations change each year, and in 2027, the series is going to Taitung on Taiwan's east coast; runners will move between the mountains and the Pacific Ocean on a flat, smooth route. After the race, be sure to check out the area's night markets, hot springs, and endless good eats.

Where to stay: Luxury hotels near the starting line include the Sheraton Taitung Hotel, which has an outdoor swimming pool, and Formosan Naruwan Hotel, with a spa and saltwater pool.

Date: April 25, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, 21-miler, 11-miler, 12K, 5K

What to know: With a cliffside, oceanview course running from Big Sur to Carmel along California’s iconic Highway 1, it doesn’t get much more scenic than this. It’s a Boston qualifier race and has a six-hour time limit, along with several course length options, making it a good one to run with a group, even if your ideal mileage differs.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at a few different properties in Monterey, closer to the finish line. Of course, there is no shortage of luxury hotels in the area—Alila Ventana Big Sur, Post Ranch Inn, and Carmel Beach Hotel are a few Traveler favorites.

Date: April 4, 2027Registration: The 2027 lottery entry has taken place; check back in May for the 2028 race; charity bibs are still availableDistances included: Half-marathon

What to know: As the name suggests, the course runs past several London landmarks, including Big Ben, the Tower of London, the London Eye, and Somerset House. It’s a lively course—musical performances, DJs, dancers, and themed cheer stations can be expected—and even better, it's a flat one, with 238 feet of total elevation gain.

Where to stay: In 2026, Blue Orchid Hospitality and the Clermont Hotel Group offered discounts for race weekend stays at properties like The Wellington Hotel, The Tower Hotel, and Thistle Trafalgar. We’ll update that list once 2027 partners are announced. For luxury stays near the starting line, consider Raffles London at the OWO or the Corinthia London.

Date: April 04, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half marathon, 10K

What to know: Okay, I'll get the cons over with first (for most, I'd presume): This is a cold and snowy course. Once you've got that fact out of the way, you can weigh the very unique pros. This Finnish Lapland course kicks off in Santa Claus Village square (!) in Rovaniemi, starting exactly on the line of the Arctic Circle. It's put together as part of a five-day running program with log cabin lodging, each with a private sauna, as well as activities like husky sledding, Northern Lights excursions, and an Ice Pool Experience. It all wraps up at a trophy dinner with—wait for it—Santa Claus himself. This is peak whimsy, friends.

Where to stay: Lodging is included in the tour package.

Date: May 15, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 8.5K

What to know: This race lets you run along one of the seven wonders of the world. It’s a strenuous, hilly course, but if the views alone don’t keep you going, the residents in local villages cheering you on along the route just might.

Of note, to register, you must sign up for a tour package; the starting price is $790 and includes race entry plus two nights of accommodations. It’s sponsored by Albatross Adventure Marathons, which also puts on The Big Five Marathon (more details below) and the Iceland Volcano Marathon, among other adventurous runs.

Where to stay: Hotels must be booked along with the packages. For a relaxing post-race stay, check into the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, with its award-winning spa (after a massage, consider the tea meditation too) and standout dining options, from Italian to dim sum.

Date: May 16, 2027Registration: Open now and quite affordable—the most expensive distance is €39 ($44)Distances included: Half-marathon, 10K, 5K (paved course); 17K, 8K (trail)

What to know: Set in Tossa de Mar, a beautiful, historic seaside town on Spain’s Costa Brava, these runs are all about the coastal views. Of course, that does mean a challenging, hilly course for all but the 5K, which boasts a flat route in the town’s center. Of note, the maximum time is on the shorter end: 2 hours 35 minutes for the half, 1 hour 15 for the 10K, and 45 minutes for the 5K.

Where to stay: Zel Costa Brava, about a 10-minute drive from the starting line, was mentioned in our list of the Best Places to Go in Spain and Portugal in 2026. It has a funicular to take guests down to the beach, a huge pool with plenty of lounge chairs to kick back on, and a spa with a thermal circuit, ideal for soothing sore legs.

Date: June 11-12, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 5K

What to know: Running around America's first national park, near sites like the Grand Prismatic Spring, is bound to be a highlight for any outdoor-loving runner. While not inside the bounds of the park, the views from the Custer Gallatin National Forest and the Hebgen Lake Ranger District are still impressive. The half marathon starts bright and early at 6 a.m. and has a four-hour course limit. There are five aid stations along the way, and 552 feet of elevation (of note, there are some technical, rocky sections to contend with).

Where to stay: The Lazy Duck Inn is the most convenient choice, given it's location near the start and finish line. To pad out the rest of your trip, check out our guide to where to stay in and near Yellowstone.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon

What to know: The name says it all: You might just see the big five while you run! The course takes runners through the South African Savannah on the Entabeni Game Reserve. It is a smaller race, with a maximum of 300 participants, in a moderate climate (expected to be in the 60s to 70s this year) along a sand and gravel trail. Past participants rave about this one, calling it “The ONLY marathon I have wanted to run twice!” and “the best adventure ever.” Like the Great Wall course, registration requires selecting a tour package, starting at $3,560 for the seven-day package, which includes accommodation, meals, game drives, bush walks, and more.

Where to stay: At the end of any package, you’ll be transferred to Johannesburg International Airport. Give yourself a night to decompress at the Park Hyatt Johannesburg, where peacocks roam the grounds, rooms overlook serene gardens, and Sunday brunch comes with a side of live music.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 10K, 5K, kids race

What to know: The Tromsø, Norway, race begins at 8:30 p.m.—but thanks to the midnight sun the event is named after, it’s still light out. One of the northernmost races in the world, with a course surrounded by mountains and fjords, it boasted 9,000 runners from an impressive 88 countries last year. Of note, the maximum time limit is 5 hours and 30 minutes for the marathon and 3 hours and 30 minutes for the half.

Where to stay: Right in Tromsø, St. Elisabeth makes for a lovely stay, especially if you take advantage of the spa’s thermal bath, pool, and saunas. A bit further out (45 minutes or so), the Yggdrasiltunet Farm Hotel offers an even more blissful setting for a post-race escape with its wood-fired barrel sauna, guided ice bathing, hot tub overlooking the sea, and yoga classes.

Date: June 20, 2027Registration: Open now (half marathon is already sold out; sign up for 2028 notifications on the website)Distances included: Half marathon, 10K

What to know: The race website dubs this “the most beautiful run on the planet,” and honestly, that might not be so hyperbolic. Running through Canada's first national park sounds like a dream, especially when the course passes by the Vermilion Lakes, Legacy Trail, and Bow Valley Parkway, with wildlife likely to be spotted along the way. It's not a particularly hilly course, with a total elevation gain of 418 feet, but do note the elevation, which maxes out at 4,620 feet.

Where to stay: The official host partner is Banff Lodging Company, which operates 16 hotels across Banff, Canmore, and Lake Louise, including Hotel Canoe & Suites and Otter Hotel. Guests can receive a 15% discount on these rates. Afterward, consider a wellness-centric stay at the stunning Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise.

Date: July 03, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon, 10.55k

What to know: Designed for adventure-seekers, this Northern Iceland race explores one of Earth's geological hot spots—you’ll run along the rim of two volcanic craters and over black lava rock, with steaming geysers taking your mind off the miles ahead.

Unless you’re an Icelandic resident, you’ll need to book the six-day tour package, which is around $3,100 and includes accommodation, transportation, meals, a celebratory post-race dinner, and some activities, with add-ons like whale-watching and waterfall chasing available too. Of note, race entrance is not included in that fee ($350 for the half and full, and $223 for the quarter marathon).

Where to stay: Our resident Iceland expert and contributing writer Erika Owen highly recommends one of the tour lodging options, Fosshotel Glacier Lagoon, saying that it “embodies the best of Iceland: seclusion, surrounding nature, and beds topped with Icelandic wool blankets.” On your way out of town, consider a stay at The Retreat at Blue Lagoon; beyond the must-dip-in thermal baths, the tasting menu at Michelin-starred Moss is well worth a splurge.

Date: July 18, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half-marathon, 5K, The Pairing (both!)

What to know: A 13.1-mile route through Napa and Sonoma’s wine country, this course is surrounded by farms, vineyards, and ranches—yes, there are gently rolling hills, but it’s not an overly challenging course. The real prize for the 3,000-ish participants is at the finish line: At the post-race wine festival, top local vineyards reward you with wine tastings, and your goodie bag includes a commemorative wine glass.

Where to stay: Several hotels partner with the race to offer discounted stays, including the Westin Verasa Napa Hotel, notable for its Hyperice Recover & Recharge Kit available at the front desk. (Heads up for other future runs: Hyperice and Normatec products can be found at most Westins across the US! I swear by the Normatecs and Hypervolt for post-race recovery.) Just across the street from the starting line sits Carneros Resort and Spa, a seven-time Readers’ Choice Award winner; down the street is Stanly Ranch, Auberge Collection, a resort with a gorgeous outdoor pool that’s exactly where I’d want to park myself post-race.

Date: October 15–17, 2027Registration: Opens January 1, 2027Distances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler, kids races

What to know: This is one course that’s absolutely on my running bucket list, and one I hope to tackle in 2027 (which happens to be the event's 50th anniversary!). It’s the only US race I’ve found that crosses borders: After starting in downtown Detroit, runners cross over the Ambassador Bridge into Windsor, Ontario, before returning to the US through the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel (yep, an underwater mile!). Uniquely, this means you will have to carry your passport during the marathon and international half.

Where to stay: The AC Hotel Detroit at the Bonstelle is minutes from the start line, and well-situated to other places of interest (Little Caesar’s Arena, Fox Theater, the Detroit Institute of Arts). For a post-race treat, stop by Warda Pâtisserie. JW Marriott Detroit Water Square, opening in February 2027 near the Riverwalk, is sure to be a lovely place to stay too.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, 10K, 5K

What to know: History buffs will love this course in Greece, which, according to legend, follows the original marathon route Pheidippides ran way back in 490 B.C. when he brought news of victory from the battlefield of Marathon (it’s also the course used in the 2004 Olympics). The marathon course stays open for eight hours and passes by landmarks like the Athens Concert Hall, Eleftherias Park, the Presidential Palace, and the National Garden. There are packages available if you want transportation, accommodations, and tour options baked into your visit; they’re not required for entry, but individual registration tends to sell out first, so plan accordingly.

Where to stay: The race starts in the town of Marathon, northeast of central Athens. For a stay close to the finish line with an excellent spa and both indoor and outdoor swimming pools, consider Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel. A bit further south, the seaside One&Only Aesthesis offers a touch of coastal glamour, plus a Guerlain spa.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler

What to know: The course begins in downtown Tulsa, weaving through neighborhoods and the University of Tulsa campus. Along the way, you'll encounter lots of support from the community, with block parties hosted along the course to cheer runners on. Of note, this is a Boston Qualifier, and race day temperatures tend to sit around the 50s.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at several partner hotels, including Brut Hotel, a charming boutique hotel a short drive from the start line with an outdoor pool, rooftop bar, and spa. I’m eyeing the Olympian Massage, designed to “relieve tension and restore mobility by utilizing deep tissue and sports massage techniques.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6229. United Airlines CEO Insists He Runs The “World’s Best” Airline. Does That Title Even Matter?

Scott Kirby believes United Airlines is the best airline in the world (he has for quite some time). I understand his argument, and there are aspects of United that compare favorably with just about any competitor. But the claim raises a more interesting question: what actually makes an airline the best? The answer depends on much more than the seat or the route map or any other single quality…and maybe that’s asking the wrong question anyway.

In his recent Cheeky Pint interview with John Collison and Ben Thompson, Kirby made a case for United that deserves more than an eye roll.

His argument is not that United serves the best food or offers the most luxurious seats. He acknowledges that Asian and Middle Eastern competitors do better on the physical product and probably service. He also identifies schedule as the primary reason people choose an airline. But he believes United’s technology changes the overall assessment:

“I say schedule is the number one reason people pick an airline. But, everything else matters for brand-loyal customers. It’s service, product, reliability, and technology. The Asian and Middle East carriers do better than the US airlines on product for sure, and probably service too. I think we do a really good job, but they have different cultures for service, so they do better on that. But I think technology is the differentiator.

“United, that’s why I now believe that United in totality is the best airline in the world, and it’s because of technology. It’s exponentially getting better. Things like being able to do this for customers when there’s a delay and tell them what’s going on. We started it this summer. AI allows us to institutionalize this. But if you’re going to have a delay, like sending customers weather radar maps. In Chicago, there was a day where the weather was over the horizon, but you had to fly. It was sunny at the airport, but you had to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and so the routes were closed. You couldn’t—

“We sent half the people the normal weather delay, which they think you’re lying… Because it’s sunny outside. You must be lying to me. We sent half a picture with the radar map, and you have to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and the routes are closed because of outside. The people with a 1-hour delay, I think the numbers were negative 60 NPS on the normal way of sending it, plus 60 when we send a picture of the map. A 120-point difference.”

His case for United rests on technology: better tools for managing travel, clearer communication during disruptions, and connectivity that makes time onboard more useful. For example, he describes sending passengers radar maps to explain why distant thunderstorms were delaying flights even though the weather at their airport looked fine. His point is that passengers respond much better when they understand what is happening.

Thus, Kirby is acknowledging that competitors outperform it in some traditional measures of onboard quality, but arguing that United’s technological advantages outweigh those shortcomings.

I think he is right that these things matter. I am less convinced that they settle the question.

Start with the most obvious consideration: an airline is not particularly useful if it cannot conveniently take you where you need to go. I love trying new products and will sometimes take an absurd routing to do so. Most travelers understandably do not approach their trips that way.

A nonstop flight at a convenient time can be more valuable than a better seat reached through a connection. Frequency matters too. An airline with several flights a day gives you more options, particularly when something goes wrong.

This is a substantial part of United’s appeal. Its network gives me reasons to fly it that have nothing to do with whether another airline serves better Champagne.

But the best network for me may be largely irrelevant to someone living elsewhere. A traveler in Taipei and a traveler in Chicago are starting with very different choices. There is no universal route map that works best for everyone.

Emirates is a good example of why an airline’s reputation may need to be separated from the particular experience you are buying.

Mention Emirates and many people think of luxury (massive first class suites, showers, and bars onboard with beautiful flight attendants serving you extensive food and beverage offerings). That “halo effect” reputation is understandable.

But someone booking business class on an older Boeing 777 may encounter a product that falls well short of that image. The retrofitted 777s improve the situation with a 1-2-1 layout and direct aisle access, but I would not put that seat ahead of the leading business class products elsewhere.

Singapore Airlines illustrates this as well. Its reputation for service, built in part around the Singapore Girl branding, is extraordinary. Yet some travelers strongly dislike its longhaul business class seats, particularly their sleeping position.

A beautifully presented meal and gracious service cannot entirely compensate for a bed in which you struggle to get comfortable. Singapore’s new cabin reveal on Friday, November 6, will be particularly interesting for that reason.

My recent Emirates 777 first class flight demonstrated the reverse problem: a superb suite paired with service that did not live up to it. I loved the space, but the experience still fell short.

So what about Kirby’s argument that technology is most important?

We sometimes talk about technology as if it is separate from the passenger experience. But an app that lets you solve a problem without standing in line is providing service. A clear explanation of a delay is providing service. Working internet can determine whether a long daytime flight is productive or frustrating.

US airlines deserve credit here. Their digital tools can be excellent, and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it. But even the Alaska, American, and Delta apps are–comparatively speaking–much better than their non-US peers.

To be clear, that does not mean every American airline leads every foreign airline or that an attractive app excuses indifferent employees. It does mean that evaluating service solely by how someone pours your wine misses a large part of what an airline does for its customers.

Connectivity is especially important to me. Extra legroom and a better meal are welcome, but painfully slow or non-functioning Wi-Fi can materially change how I feel about a flight. For someone hoping to disconnect and sleep, it may barely register. The features can be measured. The importance each passenger assigns to them cannot be universal.

I also recognize the limitations of my own perspective. Much of my coverage focuses on premium cabins, and those experiences influence my preferences. But what does the airline offer someone in economy?

Some Asian carriers offer a more appealing combination of legroom, meals, and attentive service than their US counterparts. That deserves weight, even if the business class cabin lacks the latest suite.

At the same time, the aircraft still matters. So do the fare restrictions, baggage allowance, and cost of choosing a seat. A generous meal does not tell us whether the ticket represents good value.

For a family paying for several tickets, the best airline may be the one offering a tolerable nonstop journey at an affordable total price. For a tall passenger, a little more legroom may matter far more than the entertainment selection.

An airline cannot claim superiority for everyone based on what it provides a small number of passengers at the front of the aircraft.

A great airline should operate reliably and treat passengers well when it fails.

Those are related, but separate, expectations. I want to arrive on time. When that is impossible, I want an honest explanation and practical assistance.

No airline can prevent every weather delay or mechanical problem. But how it prepares, communicates, and recovers tells me much more than a polished promotional video.

American Airlines is a useful example from my own flying. I would argue that some of my recent meals on American have been the best among the US network carriers. Its free Wi-Fi has also tends to work very well for me. Those are real strengths.

Nevertheless, my experiences with inconsistent service and operational problems place American well below Delta and United in my overall assessment. That is not a claim that every American flight is bad or every Delta flight is good. It is the cumulative effect of repeated experiences. A carrier earns my confidence over time, and it can lose it the same way.

The loyalty program belongs in this discussion too.

Award availability, redemption prices, and the usefulness of elite benefits all affect how much value I receive from an airline. A good program can persuade me to choose one carrier when the alternatives are otherwise similar.

But I try to separate the airline I enjoy most from the program in which I find the most value.

An excellent redemption does not make an uncomfortable seat comfortable. Status does not make a canceled flight depart. Conversely, a wonderful airline can have a loyalty program that gives me little reason to engage with it. Ideally, the program reinforces a relationship the airline has already earned through its service.

Qatar Airways and STARLUX are among my favorites because I have found their overall experiences so compelling. The appeal extends beyond a seat or a meal: I look forward to flying them because of the reliable Wi-Fi, excellent service, and quality in everything.

Air France has also come such a long way. Its newer business class seat is excellent, and the addition of Starlink on equipped aircraft addresses something that matters greatly to me. Combined with the food and service I enjoy, that makes it an increasingly attractive choice.

Yet I still have many reasons to fly United. Its network and technology have practical value in my life that an exceptional flight on another carrier cannot always replace.

That is why my favorite airline and the airline I choose for a particular trip need not be the same…maybe the point is that talking about which carrier is “best” is ultimately futile and our focus instead should be rewarding carriers who do things well and not patronizing those that continually disappoint.

Kirby’s claim is worth discussing because he recognizes that being the best involves more than having the fanciest cabin. Technology and network utility deserve more credit than they sometimes receive.

But I would not crown United the best airline in the world on that basis alone. The seat still matters. So does the person serving you, the reliability of the operation, and what happens when your plans unravel.

For me, the best airlines are the ones that bring those elements together consistently, but at the same time I realize how arbitrary my own evaluation can be. Thus, I tend to think asking “who is best” is the wrong question versus asking “who does X,Y, and Z well?”

What makes an airline the best for you—and which airline comes closest?

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

In Kirby’s world, as long it is said with enough superlatives it must be true

Pretty much. IT is one factor for sure but United is not remotely the best based on it alone and to state the painfully obvious United is not the best airline regardless.

Friends, who cares what a CEO says; I think many of them are going to soon be ‘put in their place.’ Basic consumer protections are long-overdue. No more of this blustering, attention-seeking, etc. Just run a reliable operation.

I live near a United hub so of course United gives me the greatest access to destinations. If I lived near an American hub then American might be the best airline for me. I don’t give a rat’s about IFE, who designed the seat, and whether or not the FA smiles at me when giving me my drink and snack (just that they not show outright hostility to me, like Delta FAs). #6228. Getting to Know New York Through Its Sandwiches

“By the end of our time together, I will be asking you again: ‘So, what is a sandwich?’”

An expert-led tour that starts by questioning its own object of inquiry is unconventional. But then, so is our guide. Ben Gollan, known to his Instagram followers as A Man and His Sandwich, has spent the last nine years reviewing sandwiches across New York City. Gollan moved here from Australia in 2016, after nearly a decade as a government lawyer. For about as long, he has run an Airbnb Experience that turns a food crawl into a two-hour pilgrimage to the city’s best sandwich slingers.

It was a pastrami sandwich at Harry & Ida’s, a former deli in the East Village, that turned Gollan into a professional sandwich hound. “It was a fourth-generation Jewish deli that broke every rule of pastrami sandwiches: it was thick-cut and fabulous,” he says as we dash across Bowery. We’re scuttling over from a coffee shop in Cooper Square that served as our meeting point and into the East Village—a neighborhood of contrasts that still manages to connect New York's past and present. There are 12 of us in total, mostly locals, a couple of newer transplants, and just one traveler. “It’s usually mostly visitors, so this is different,” he says.

It’s a great introduction to the city. After all, New York runs on sandwiches, and there’s no shortage of great ones, whether it’s a classic Italian deli sub you’re after or a grab-and-go banh mi. They’re economical, versatile, delicious and, as is the point of Gollan’s tour, telegraph the city’s greatest personality trait—its diversity. So is there such a thing as a New York sandwich? “Not really,” he says, "but the chopped cheese, born in East Harlem, might come closest.”

The Bono at Via Della Scrofa, a small family-owned joint that wouldn't look out of place on the streets of Rome

“We start here because it’s closest to what we think of as a traditional sandwich,” says Gollan, before filling us in on the origins of what is the modern-day sandwich. It involves John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who, in the 18th century, gave his title to the now-ubiquitous food. Gollan loves to talk and think about sandwiches as much as he eats them. “Although I've learned never to trust history, especially when rendered by colonizers,” he muses. “Do we really think it took us till the 1700s to invent the sandwich?”

Named after a Roman street, Via Della Scrofa is the kind of bottega or alimentari you might find in Rome, with a tiny counter selling tiny espressos and focaccia, as well as imported groceries from Italy. “It's small family-owned joints like this that make New York what it is,” says Gollan. While the rest of the group gets to try the Porcodeddena panini (made with porchetta), I’m getting a Bono: grilled eggplants sweetened with sun-dried tomatoes, with arugula and buffalo mozzarella, in a warm roll that’s toasty on the outside and soft and warm on the inside. The bread is perfect—it’s a rosetta (or michetta), a traditional Roman bread roll. I wash it down with a Crodino, a popular non-alcoholic bitter aperitif from Italy.

Around us, the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House, an annual event, had taken over the street, adding personality to our time with its bands, pop-up stalls, and lively crowds. Gollan regales us with stories of owner Giovanni Bartocci, describing him as a real character with “a man bun, suspenders, tattoos, and naturally, a Harley," and I look around hoping he'll show up. I ask Gollan why he isn’t eating with us. “I never want to tire of these sandwiches, and if I keep eating them, I will.” The wind picks up and blows over the canvases at an art stall, but the band is undeterred, playing “New York, New York.”

A spicy Pakistani rendition of the chopped cheese at Nishaan

The writer and her chopped cheese sandwich, the chapli kebab replaced with Impossible Meat.

Order: A chopped cheese, but make it desi

An 11-minute walk up 1st Avenue and a few blocks later, we spot our next sandwich spot. A cobalt-blue sign reads Nishaan; bags of rice are piled high along its exterior; and a long line snakes out of what I can only assume is a tiny space inside. Nishaan began as a pop-up at the weekly open-air food festival Smorgasburg and went on to win season 18 of The Great Food Truck Race. While there are other dishes on the menu (elote chaat, mango lassi), it’s Nishaan’s twist on that great New York City bodega staple, the chopped cheese, that many are after: a spice-laden chapli kebab, chopped up on a griddle with peppers and onions, then enhanced with a zingy cilantro sauce and tamarind chutney. When it opened in August 2025, it was one of the most talked-about new restaurants in New York City, which has emerged as a hub for a new generation of Pakistani eateries. “New York belongs to everyone, and so does the sandwich,” proclaims Gollan.

In a city that runs on pastrami, vegetarians like me don’t faze Gollan; he orders me a version with Impossible Meat. We tuck ourselves out of the wind and into an alley and dig in. I can’t stop eating, making a mess as I go along. “Half the fun of a sandwich is the experience of eating it,” Gollan adds.

Regulars love the pho sandwiches at Sunny and Annie’s—sandwiches stuffed to the brim with pho ingredients, minus the broth.

Sunny and Annie’s is a 24/7, 365-day-a-year kind of neighborhood classic with 92 items on its sandwich menu.

“We’re taking a detour,” says Gollan, frantically looking around him. It’s the day of the Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade, and the crowds around us are building, as are the dogs in costume—cheese boards, UPS drivers, and, suitably for the occasion, hot dogs. We ditch the idea of cutting through the park and work our way around the revelers.

Our destination? Sunny and Annie’s, a 24/7, 365-days-a-year kind of neighborhood classic that has been open since 1997. There’s no front door here, because there’s always someone around. Inside, past the candy, chips, and dish detergent, we’re greeted by what must be the most extensive sandwich menu I’ve ever encountered, all written out on brightly colored sheets of paper stuck to the glass counter. There are 92 handheld options in total, some named after politicians and celebrities, like the Jackie Chan—bulgogi, cilantro, avocado, lettuce, jalapeños, and onions, served on a roll or hero. There’s also a chicken cutlet sandwich called the Australian. It’s not named after Gollan.

This is not a place to linger, so we keep it moving. Outside, the crowds have thickened, and Gollan instructs us to head to a neighborhood bar called ABC Beer Co., which often features at the end of his tours. As someone who has spent many a night in an East Village bar, I’m disappointed I’ve never been here before. It’s spacious, has a backyard, and is equally welcoming to couples on dates and families with little ones.

The writer's sandwich tour ended at ABC Beer Co, a hybrid beer bar and store with a particular focus on NYC breweries.

Gollan appears with our pho sandwiches, wrapped in spinach tortillas. They smell like pho, taste like pho; only the avocado throws me off.

Some of us get ciders and wine, and the conversation winds back to where we started: So, what really is a sandwich? “I want this to get contentious: bang the tables, let’s have a food fight," Gollan says, egging us on. Hot dogs? Quesadillas? What about a hamburger? A pizza folded in half? Does it have to have a carb? What about a lettuce wrap instead of bread? Gollan briefs us on a famous 2006 Massachusetts lawsuit—White City Shopping Center vs. Panera Bread—which legally answered an age-old culinary debate: Is a burrito a sandwich? The judge ruled that a burrito is, in fact, not a sandwich, clearing the way for the Mexican fast-casual joint to open in the vicinity of Panera Bread. “A sandwich court case is my Roman Empire," he says. “When this question goes to the Supreme Court, I will be there.”

The point of this tour—and the posed question—Gollan says, was never to walk away with an answer, but to open our minds and palates. So, what are Ben Gollan’s own rules for a sandwich, I have to ask. He lists the following:

And then he adds: “Take those rules and throw them in the bin.” And with that, class is dismissed.

The NYC Sandwich Tour can be booked directly on the A Man and His Sandwich website, as well as on Airbnb. Tours run every day of the week, with the exception of Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Ben Gollan, who proudly calls himself the Chief Sandwich Officer, often leads the experiences himself, but he also has co-hosts to help guide fellow sandwich enthusiasts on these two-hour outings. Along the way, guests sample three standout sandwiches—from the classic to the “slightly unhinged”—before finishing up at a bar to settle the debate over what really counts as a sandwich. While my tour focused on the East Village, Gollan also leads sandwich tours around Williamsburg. And word on the street is that he has his eye on opening a sandwich shop of his own one day.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6227. JetBlue Raises Baggage Fees Again, Now Charges Up To $140 Roundtrip For One Checked Bag

JetBlue has raised checked baggage fees again, and bringing one ordinary suitcase can now add as much as $140 to a roundtrip ticket. With holiday travel approaching, this is another reminder that the fare you see when shopping may be far removed from what your trip actually costs.

JetBlue has increased baggage charges for new bookings made on or after November 3, 2026. The airline’s updated fee schedule lists a first checked bag starting at $50 each way. The price depends on when you travel and when you pay.

For passengers without an included baggage allowance or waiver, these are the new charges within the United States, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Canada. All amounts are per bag, each way:

You can see more particulars here, including pricing for Mosaic elites.

Upcoming peak periods include November 19–January 18. If you booked before November 3, check your reservation for the applicable charges (old rates apply). Here’s the full chart of peak dates over the next year:

That means one suitcase costs $100 roundtrip even at the lowest new rate. On peak dates, it costs $110 when paid in advance or $140 when purchased within 24 hours of each departure.

Consider a family of four traveling over Thanksgiving, with each person checking one suitcase and no baggage benefits.

Pay sufficiently early and the roundtrip baggage bill is $440. Wait until check-in for both flights and it becomes $560.

When does it become cheaper just to buy new clothes at your destination? We certainly try to pack efficiently when traveling with our children, but one standard checked bag per person hardly strikes me as an extravagant amount of luggage, especially for a longer holiday trip.

At these prices, baggage can materially change which airline offers the best deal. A cheaper JetBlue ticket may cease to be cheaper once you add the luggage you actually need…though it would not surprise me to see others follow.

Mosaic 1 members receive one checked bag, while Mosaic 2–4 members receive two. Eligible JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders receive one bag. Premium-cabin allowances depend on the fare purchased: Base fares include one bag, while standard and Flex premium fares include two.

Those benefits become more valuable every time the underlying fees rise, though it’s still not a loyalty program or credit card product I can get enthusiastic about.

JetBlue’s latest increase pushes the cost of one checked suitcase to $100–$140 roundtrip for passengers without an exemption. For families, the additional expense can reach hundreds of dollars.

Compare the total cost before booking, and if you know you will check a bag, pay more than 24 hours before departure. I want JetBlue to succeed, but charging passengers more to bring their belongings does little to make it an airline people actively want to choose. Quote the contrary, JetBlue is doing a great job of alienating passengers during its great time of need.

Customers will tolerate different prices when talking about pre-paid verses paying at the airport, but this peak non-peak charge is how you drive customers away because they can see through it and know it’s sham. It doesn’t cost JetBlue more money to load baggage on peak days verses non-peak days.
