#6226. Breeze Airways Cancels 11 Nonstop Routes: See Map & List Now

Airlines regularly adjust their route networks, and Breeze Airways is no exception. The US low-cost carrier has been making several changes to its network recently. It has discontinued at least 11 nonstop routes since the beginning of this year. Most of these are domestic services connecting destinations in states such as Florida, Colorado, and New York.

However, the airline has also ended its service between Providence and Cancún, which was the Rhode Island airport's only international connection. Breeze had planned to resume the service on December 19, 2026, ahead of the Christmas holiday period, and continue operating until March 20, 2027. However, it has since removed all flights from its schedule, and the route is no longer available for booking.

Breeze launched its first international service earlier this year in January, connecting Norfolk International Airport (ORF) in Virginia with Cancun International Airport (CUN) in Mexico. It subsequently introduced additional international routes throughout February and March. One of these was a weekly Saturday service from Rhode Island TF Green International Airport (PVD) in Providence to Cancún, which began in February.

However, the route was never intended to operate year-round. At the time of its launch, the airport described it as an eight-week trial scheduled to run through April, allowing Breeze to test demand before committing to a longer-term service. Indeed, the trial delivered disappointing results.

According to data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT), the low-cost carrier carried just 1,364 round-trip passengers on the route and recorded an average load factor of 49.8%, meaning fewer than half of the available seats were occupied. It also captured less than 11% of passengers traveling from Providence to Cancún.

Many continued to use connecting services or traveled to Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) for nonstop flights. Interestingly, Frontier Airlines previously operated nonstop flights between Providence and Cancún in 2022 and recorded a similarly low load factor of 50.2%.

Although Breeze has expanded into international markets, domestic flights still account for the majority of its operations. It serves more than 90 destinations across the United States, focusing largely on underserved markets. However, not every route has attracted sufficient demand, and the low-cost carrier has discontinued several domestic services this year. In fact, some of those were fairly new.

One of those is its service between Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) and Ogdensburg International Airport (OGS) in Upstate New York, near the Canadian border. Breeze launched the route in September 2024, but it recorded an average load factor of just 28.2% through July 2026, according to DOT data.

Average Load Factor (According to DOT, through July 2026)

Further ahead, the budget airline is preparing to end its nonstop service between Washington Dulles and Tri-Cities Airport (TRI) on November 30, 2026, less than a year after launching the route in December 2025. The service was introduced following a regional economic development initiative led by BRIDGE.

This raised more than $2 million in local funding to help attract Breeze to the Tri-Cities market, serving Johnson City, Kingsport, and Bristol. However, passenger numbers have remained relatively low. According to DOT data, Breeze carried 4,453 passengers on the route through July and recorded an average load factor of just 49.3%, equivalent to approximately 68 passengers per flight on its 137-seat Airbus A220-300.

Underused seasonal links have crumbled under poor loads while the airline pivots its fleet toward bigger Myrtle Beach plans.

While Breeze is withdrawing from underperforming markets, it is also preparing to launch several new routes. The airline has been particularly active in filling gaps left by Spirit Airlines. One such airport is Myrtle Beach International Airport (MYR) in South Carolina, where Breeze has become one of the largest carriers in terms of destinations served.

In February next year, the low-cost carrier plans to introduce nonstop flights connecting Myrtle Beach with BOS and Arnold Palmer Regional Airport (LBE) in Latrobe, Pennsylvania. It will also launch a service between Latrobe and Orlando International Airport (MCO). Notably, Latrobe lost its scheduled passenger services following Spirit's withdrawal.

Elsewhere, Breeze is expanding its international network from Tampa International Airport (TPA). The airline plans to introduce flights to Montego Bay, Jamaica, in December, followed by Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, in June 2027. These will complement its new Tampa–Cancún service, scheduled to begin on December 18, 2026.

Online shopping portals can help you save money on everyday purchases, and some let you earn rewards on top of the points or cash back you already get from your credit card.

Capital One Shopping takes a slightly different approach: It combines shopping rewards with coupon codes, price comparisons and deal alerts.

You don't need a Capital One credit card or bank account to use Capital One Shopping. The free service is available through its website, browser extension and mobile app, and you can redeem eligible Shopping Rewards for gift cards rather than cash or travel points.

Here's how Capital One Shopping works, how to earn and redeem rewards, and what to know before using it.

Capital One Shopping is a free online shopping tool that helps you find lower prices, apply available coupon codes and earn rewards at participating retailers. It can also compare prices across merchants and alert you to potential savings.

Unlike a traditional airline or hotel shopping portal, Capital One Shopping doesn't directly award airline miles or hotel points. Instead, eligible purchases and promotions earn Capital One Shopping Rewards, which can be redeemed for select retailers' electronic gift cards.

Capital One Shopping is separate from Capital One Offers, which provides shopping promotions to eligible Capital One cardholders.

You can shop through the Capital One Shopping website, install its browser extension or use its mobile app.

Keep in mind that rewards aren't necessarily credited immediately. Capital One Shopping says eligible rewards typically post within 30 to 90 days after making a qualifying purchase or completing a promotion's requirements, although some may take longer.

Returns, cancellations and other exclusions can affect reward eligibility. Using another shopping portal or applying an unlisted coupon code may also interfere with tracking, so be sure to review the offer's terms before completing your purchase.

The Capital One Shopping browser extension can help you find savings without having to manually check the portal before every purchase.

Once you've installed the extension and signed in, you can shop at participating websites as usual. Depending on the retailer, the extension can alert you to available Shopping Rewards, search for coupon codes and compare prices.

I keep the Capital One Shopping extension installed on my browser, so whenever I'm shopping online, I can easily see if any rewards are available. Even if an offer isn't always available, it's nice to know when I might be able to earn something extra on a purchase I was already planning to make.

Before checking out, review the terms of any available offers, including minimum spending requirements and product exclusions. It's also worth comparing the final price after discounts and shipping rather than choosing a retailer based solely on its advertised rewards rate.

Capital One Shopping also offers price-drop notifications for eligible products, which can be useful if you're planning a larger purchase and have some flexibility about when to buy.

Unlike traditional cash-back shopping portals such as Rakuten and TopCashback, Capital One Shopping lets you redeem your rewards for electronic gift cards at participating retailers rather than cash.

When you're ready to redeem your rewards, sign in to your Capital One Shopping account and navigate to the "My Rewards & Savings" section. From there, select "Redeem Now" to browse available gift cards and complete your redemption.

Available retailers and redemption amounts may vary, so check your account for current options.

Keep in mind that Shopping Rewards aren't the same as cash. If you'd prefer rewards that can be deposited into your bank account, a traditional cash-back shopping portal may be a better fit.

You don't need a Capital One credit card to use Capital One Shopping, so consider using a card that earns a strong rewards rate on everyday purchases or online shopping.

You can generally earn credit card rewards on eligible purchases in addition to Capital One Shopping Rewards, allowing you to earn rewards through both programs on the same purchase.

Personally, I like using my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card for online purchases. While it doesn't offer bonus rewards specifically for online shopping, it earns at least 2 miles per dollar on purchases, so I know I'm getting a solid return on my spending.

For example, if I make a $200 purchase through Capital One Shopping using my Venture X, I'll earn 400 Capital One miles in addition to any eligible Shopping Rewards.

Related: The best credit cards for online shopping

Capital One Shopping is a free tool for finding online discounts, comparing prices and earning rewards that can be redeemed for gift cards.

You don't need a Capital One credit card to use it, and eligible purchases can earn Shopping Rewards on top of your usual credit card rewards.

If you regularly shop online and don't mind redeeming rewards for gift cards rather than cash or travel points, Capital One Shopping is worth trying out. Just be sure to compare prices and review offer terms before making a purchase.

#6224. There's a New Luxury Sleeper Train Route Coming to the French Riviera Next Spring

As someone who travels a lot for work, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train—even if that means spending eight hours on the rails.

Thankfully, it's easy to travel Europe by train at nearly any price point. And although I am a big fan of modern high-speed routes, the most romantic way to see the continent is certainly aboard one of Belmond's gorgeous luxury trains, which travel to destinations such as the British countryside, the Amalfi Coast, and the Scottish Highlands.

But in 2027, my bucket-list Belmond journey is a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of itineraries: the French Riviera.

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express offers three cabin types: Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites.

On May 10, 2027, the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is launching a new route from Paris to Monaco, traveling to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history.

The journey, which will become a regular addition to the train's annual schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality.

The new route will take travelers to Monte Carlo for the first time in the train's history.

The experience begins in Paris, where passengers will board the train's distinctive midnight blue carriages before settling into their accommodation for the night. There are several options to choose from, including the classic Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites, each drawing inspiration from the train's Art Deco heritage.

For those looking to really splash out, there's also L'Observatoire, an exclusive carriage created in collaboration with French artist JR. Designed as a private sanctuary on the rails, it comes complete with a bedroom, an en-suite bathroom featuring a freestanding bathtub, a spacious living area, a library, and even a secret tearoom.

As evening approaches, guests can enjoy dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord and L'Oriental, before heading to the famous Bar Car 3674 for cocktails and live piano music.

But perhaps the most exciting part of the new journey comes the following morning. After waking up to breakfast served in their cabins, passengers will be treated to sweeping views of the Mediterranean as the train makes its way along the Côte d'Azur. The route passes the red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and travels through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice. The train will then continue towards Monaco before arriving at Monaco-Monte-Carlo station.

Breakfast served aboard the Venice-Simplon Orient Express.

Monte Carlo also has a surprising connection to the train's history. In 1977, two original train carriages were purchased at an auction in the principality, helping set in motion the project that would eventually become the luxury train we know today.

“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival,” says Pascal Deyrolle, Belmond's Europe area managing director for trains. “There's also something rather special about coming back to Monte Carlo, given the role it played in the train's history.”

The new journey is part of Belmond's expanding collection of European rail experiences, alongside the second year of its “Villeggiatura by Train” itinerary, which connects the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express with Belmond hotels in Italy.

Of course, a journey this luxurious comes with a price tag to match. Tickets for the new Paris-to-Monte-Carlo route start from €4,870 (approximately $5,450) per person, based on two people sharing a Historic Cabin. The fare includes the overnight journey, all meals with sommelier-selected wines, unlimited soft drinks, transfers, and 24-hour steward service.

#6223. Delta Air Lines CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow Move That Separates It From Virgin Atlantic

Delta Air Lines is fighting Heathrow Airport’s decision to move it away from Virgin Atlantic, warning that separating the partners will hurt passengers and undermine years of investment. I understand why Delta is upset. But whether that should entitle it to remain in Terminal 3 is a more complicated question.

Heathrow plans to move Delta from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, while Virgin Atlantic remains in Terminal 3. The decision would split an operation the two airlines have spent years integrating.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian issued an unusually pointed public statement on November 2, calling the decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.” He argued that sharing Terminal 3 supports convenient connections and a consistent premium experience. Delta intends to challenge the move, saying it “will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision.”

“Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers. For more than a decade, our airlines have served millions of customers through our co-located operation in Terminal 3, offering travelers convenient connections, premium amenities and access to an expanded global network.

“Delta and Virgin Atlantic provide UK consumers with a valuable competitive alternative across the Atlantic. Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal. We are committed to preserving the seamless travel experience for which Delta and Virgin Atlantic are known and will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision. We urge Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider their decision in favor of a more prudent and thoughtful outcome that puts travelers first and allows competition to flourish at Heathrow.”

Terminal assignments can sound like an obscure airport planning issue until you are the passenger trying to make a connection.

A traveler arriving on Delta and continuing on Virgin Atlantic would face a terminal transfer that is unnecessary today. The same applies in reverse. Unfortunately, terminal transfers are not easy at LHR and moving between terminals introduces another step and more opportunity for something to go wrong.

For someone simply flying Delta to London and heading into the city, the effect may be less consequential. But Delta and Virgin sell their partnership as an integrated travel experience. Separating their airport operations makes that promise harder to deliver.

There is also the premium experience. Eligible Delta passengers currently benefit from Virgin Atlantic’s Terminal 3 facilities, including its Clubhouse. Those facilities are part of what makes the partnership attractive, especially when choosing between similarly priced business class tickets.

If the move happens, I would assume that a Delta flight departing from Terminal 4 will not include access to Virgin’s Terminal 3 facilities, at least in any practical capacity. However as I mentioned in my earlier story, integrating with Air France/KLM in Terminal 4 makes a lot of sense (far more connecting itineraries) and the lounge is not bad at all.

Still, replacing something that already works well requires money and effort. I can understand why Delta would prefer not to start over.

Heathrow’s decision follows a three-year terminal review. The airport says the changes will improve its use of existing capacity and operational resilience, while creating room for growth.

Heathrow also says airlines representing 81% of its passengers support the outcome (that is a share of passenger traffic represented by supportive airlines, not a survey showing that 81% of travelers approve).

Delta is not the only carrier being asked to move. The wider reshuffle also affects Finnair, Japan Airlines, LATAM, and China Southern.

An airport cannot necessarily give every airline its preferred location. Keeping one partnership together may mean imposing constraints or additional costs elsewhere. Delta’s investment deserves consideration, but it should not automatically settle how Heathrow should allocate scarce terminal space.

Bastian also presents the shared terminal as supporting competition across the Atlantic. I accept that a more cumbersome ground experience could make Delta and Virgin less attractive to some travelers. A passenger comparing connections may reasonably prefer an itinerary that avoids a terminal transfer.

But claims that the move will weaken competition or drive up fares need more support than the fact that Delta dislikes it. Heathrow is changing where Delta operates, rather than announcing that it must stop serving London or taking slots away. Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult. That deserves a substantive answer but there’s undeniable logic in the shuffling.

Delta has good reason to challenge a Heathrow move that would separate it from Virgin Atlantic. Sharing Terminal 3 offers practical benefits, and I understand Bastian’s anger. But Heathrow must manage the airport as a whole. I would be more persuaded by a clear account of what this reshuffle improves and why those gains outweigh the disruption.

For now, this is a dispute over a planned 2028 change..itt does not mean your next Delta flight has moved to Terminal 4. I hope the eventual outcome preserves as much of the current passenger experience as possible, but I’m still not convinced Delta is being unfairly picked on by LHR and I am convinced that whether Delta wins or loses this battle, its passengers will enjoy a great ground product at Heathrow for many years to come.

Not to defend Delta, but why would anyone connect from DL onto AF/KL at LHR. It just adds complextity and cost versus flying DL to AMS/CDG and connecting from there. I doubt they have anything to gain by being co-located with AF/KL rather than VS. Also T4 is worse than the T2/T3 complex for ground transport or self-connecting options.

Is terminal 4 underutilized or are they shifting the problem of crowding from T3 to T4? With LHR ruling out the prospect of new slots at LHR in 2028 when Heathrow’s Management says this move will lead to gains the question they haven’t answered is gains for who, for which airline.

If this move is really about alleviating congestion in T3 then go for it. But if this move is part of a broader plan that will see Delta capacity at T3 replaced by another carrier then Delta has every right to throw a fit.

T4 is operating significantly under capacity and since BA needs to move additional capacity into T3 to relieve T5, it has to be one of the larger T3 tenants who moves out.

Delta doesn’t adult very well and tends to react particularly poorly when told no. Not everyone is going to come out a winner and they just need to deal with the fact that this is a loss for them.

A better solution would be to move all SkyTeam out of Terminal 3 into Terminal 4, move all OneWorld and its partners into Terminals 5 and 3 and distribute the non-aligned between Terminals 2 and 3 as space allows. Terminal 4 is much more modern than Terminal 3 so there should be little complaint on that one.

I tend to agree and the current two-level Qatar lounge would make a great new Clubhouse. LHR should do this and just help VS/DL pay for it…

Yep. This was the obvious move by LHR if that’s your end game. End of the day this will be about compensating DL/VS for the move to T4. But VS(/DL) gets no brownie points for renovating the current Clubhouse in a transparent attempt to forestall this. LHR told VS/DL that this was the likely outcome – if VS(/DL) wanted to waste their money playing a game of chicken, that’s on them.

Are there really that many people connecting in LHR to Asia on Virgin?

While the clubhouse is nice I wasn’t overly wowed by it. And since flights are day time west, it’s not as important having a lounge meal like eastbound when you’re trying to maximize sleep. The Air France lounge in T4 looks nice enough anyways. I think the biggest loss for anyone flying D1 is the arrivals lounge, especially if you’re heading straight into the office.

Maybe Delta should have listened to their pilots a few years ago and stopped outsourcing so much of their international flying to partners…

” Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult.”

Heathrow is proposing to level the playing field between the two major US-UK Joint Ventures at the airport. Virgin had the chance to move, as well. It’s not as though Delta doesn’t have the cash to build a reasonable ground experience at T4. LHR isn’t even anything close to a transfer hub for DL. Those hubs are AMS and CDG — CDG, an airport where DL/AF customers have to change terminals and clear security between terminals. what a concept for Delta.

I get why Delta is upset but it doesn’t seem very persuasive to be mad about “connections” when LHR isn’t much of a connecting airport for their Joint Venture. But as usual… Delta and Virgin Atlanta love to cry foul when asked to do what AA/BA do today…

#6222. Delta CEO Calls Heathrow Move ‘Short-Sighted’

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is pushing back against a planned terminal move at London Heathrow, calling the airport’s decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.”

In comments posted Monday on LinkedIn and published by Delta, Bastian objected to Heathrow’s decision to relocate the airline from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4. The move, planned for 2028, would separate Delta from joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which would remain in Terminal 3.

Bastian said the airlines’ shared operation has served millions of passengers for more than a decade, providing connections, premium amenities and access to their combined networks. He argued that splitting the carriers would undermine years of investment and the benefits of operating from the same terminal.

Delta will “pursue all available remedies to correct this decision,” he said, urging Heathrow to reconsider. Bastian did not outline specific legal or regulatory steps.

Virgin Atlantic has also challenged the plan. CEO Corneel Koster said separating the two airlines would complicate journeys, weaken competition and reduce passenger choice. The carrier is considering its options to contest the relocation, Sky News reported.

Heathrow says the changes will help ease congestion and make better use of its terminals. The airport began notifying airlines of the outcome of its terminal occupancy review on Oct. 27.

A Heathrow spokesperson told Sky News that the plan followed consultation with airline customers and would improve the passenger experience, strengthen operational resilience and provide room for growth.

Delta is one of five airlines slated to change terminals. Finnair and Japan Airlines would also move from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4, while LATAM would relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 2. China Southern would move from Terminal 4 to Terminal 5.

Delta consolidated its Heathrow operation in Terminal 3 in September 2016 to operate alongside Virgin Atlantic. In announcing that move, Delta cited easier connections and last-minute flight changes, along with access to Virgin Atlantic’s premium facilities for eligible passengers.

#6221. On Location: How Coastal Newfoundland Set the Scene for Netflix's No. 1 Series ‘Below’

A mysterious sea creature is captivating audiences on Netflix as the Josh Hartnett-led series Below remains the No. 1 show in Netflix’s global rankings. The six-episode thriller paints an eerie image of small-town life in Newfoundland, and viewers are intrigued by the mystique of the striking Canadian backdrop.

Despite the fictional giant squid terrorizing Snook’s Arm, the show pulls on elements of reality, from climate change affecting the Atlantic Canadian sea life to the government-run resettling of remote fishing towns, which started in 1954 and continues to this day. It’s that history that drew production designer Emmanuel Fréchette into the project.

“When I found out that more than 300 towns in Newfoundland had been resettled, I was amazed,” he tells Traveler. “The script is very interesting, mixing that reality with the mundane life in Newfoundland—and this creature!” After all, creator Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy) had frequented the region for years, inspired to bring an authentic depiction of its culture to the screen.

That started behind the scenes as the cast and crew engaged in Newfoundland and Labrador’s most famous tradition. Visitors, who they called CFAs (or Come from Aways—this is also where Broadway hit musical draws its name), get “screeched in” by kissing a cod to become honorary citizens. So they all went to St. John’s Christian’s Pub to pucker up. “The guy there is such a great character, and he has a routine and speech that’s very entertaining," Fréchette says.

When it came to filming locations, the remote regions posed practical challenges, so the majority of the sets were built by production, a joy for Fréchette, who was trained as an architect. “I was stunned by the humble architecture, built by boat owners and builders,” he says of the homes’ low ceilings. “The structures are very endearing and make you think of a boat, so I wanted to follow that thread.”

That’s also what helped root the fantastical storyline into reality. “This was vernacular architecture—architecture without architects—just following the needs of the people out of survival, and I found that so beautiful,” he says. “So I really tried to mimic what I was seeing all around me that survived the decades.”

And it’s clearly had an effect on audiences. According to data provided by Booking.com, not only have searches for the province’s capital of St. John’s risen 16.9% by Americans on the platform compared to last year, but the coastal town of Twillingate, home to the floating icebergs, has skyrocketed 123.7%.

Here, Fréchette shares the filming locations from the popular Netflix series Below.

The show is set in the actual resettled town of Snook’s Arm, which had a population of 10 when it was approved for resettlement in 2017, according to the CBC. But its remote location would have been difficult to film in with such a big crew, so Brigus South—a town with a population of about 700 at last count in 2021—stood in.

“We picked that place because it had a connection with the water,” Fréchette says of the inlet going deep into the land. “Lots of the characters are dragged into the water, so it was great to have this presence for the eeriness.”

But to get the cozy town ready for its close-up took work, as the crew designed and built about 80% of what appears in the series, including the fish plant, Fishermen’s Hall, and wharf. The Penneys home was an existing home they covered, and the church was also a house that they retrofitted, adding the bell tower.

When Fréchette was scouting locations, he stayed in a hostel by the sea in Twillingate, about 275 miles northwest of the capital. “We’d be having a coffee with the window open, and suddenly we were freezing,” he recalls of a sudden drop in temperature from 68 degrees Fahrenheit to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s when they’d look up and see an iceberg floating their way. “It lowers the temperature all around the bay—it’s such an amazing phenomenon.”

As it turns out, the Atlantic town sits along Iceberg Alley, where from late April through July, the remnants of broken glaciers glide down the coast. Many of the shots of Calvin (Hartnett) harvesting icebergs were actual footage from these massive blocks of ice naturally floating along.

The capital served as the home base for the cast and crew, who were spread out across hotels and home rentals during filming. But its Ocean Sciences Centre, about 30 minutes north of downtown, found the spotlight as one of the most striking structures in the series, the marine research center where Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) worked.

While Fréchette admits it took some work to convince the operating facility to shoot there, he’s excited it worked out because “it really adds production value and is a great location.” After all, the circular wooden structure reflects that government building architect of the 1960s and early 1970s, “at a time we were dreaming and imagining things beyond what was possible to build today.” Reminiscent of designs by Canadian architects like Arthur Erikson, he adds that “it was ambitious, but it had a vision—and is fantastic!”

About 20 miles north of St. John’s at the top of the Avalon Peninsula sits Pouch Cove, a town of about 2,000 residents. The art director told Fréchette about the Pouch Cove Heritage Society, a historical building that was closed since they were fundraising to preserve it, so one weekend, they went up to visit. “The floor was sunken in and it was structurally unsafe,” he says.

The show’s head carpenter and engineer got to work, fixing it up, temporarily transforming it into the interior of Below’s Fisherman’s Hall, while permanently restoring it for the community. “It was a win-win because they were happy to get the money from the location, but also the work we did on it was helpful for them.”

When Calvin returns to his abandoned childhood town of Little Pot Rock, that dilapidated setting was an actual resettled town, about a 30-minute drive down from Pouch Cove on a dirt road that the production had to grade in order to shoot there.

“It was quite tricky, but just stunning—really wild and rugged,” Fréchette says, calling it “the most amazing location.” All that was there was one tiny house, about 12 by 20 feet, but it never showed up on camera. Instead, the production custom built all of the Budgell family’s dwellings. But the area can be visited as part of a 4.3-mile hike along the East Coast Trail.

The fishing village of Bay Bulls is home to North America’s largest Atlantic puffin colony, as well as a prime whale watching destination. But for Below, it was all about the functional purpose of its Pennecon Marine Base. Though it never shows up on screen, its industrial harbor was essential in order to dock the boat used as the research vessel since it had a draft (depth) of nearly 10 feet, and they needed an appropriate spot that the cast and crew could board. Also shot here were the exterior scenes of the submersible, which was hung from the boat by a crane and lifted onto the dock.

Pittman’s fish farm played an integral part of the plot, as Calvin confirmed that the sea creature was real—but it turns out the location was landlocked. “It was very complicated to do this on the sea because we’d have to deal with tides and storms, so we decided to cheat it on a lake in Brigus,” he says of the town that’s actually about 60 miles northwest from Brigus South. There was no actual fish farm there, so they custom-built the floating dock and cabin.

While the outside of Linda’s Bar was filmed using a retrofitted Brigus South home, the interior was actually the Rising Tide Convenience shop in the town of Harbour Main, about 33 miles southwest of St. John’s. The local business, best known for its homemade ice cream, “looked great inside, so we dressed it up,” Fréchette says, taking extra care to ensure the exterior entrance they built flowed seamlessly between cuts. As for Noah (Kaleb Horn)’s on-screen screech-in? That was a prop, but an actual frozen fish to ensure the fish kiss was genuine.

#6220. Flying Blue Delays 50% SAF XP Price Hike After Admitting “We Didn’t Handle The Rollout Well”

Flying Blue has postponed an abrupt devaluation to the elite status credit members earn through sustainable aviation fuel and charitable contributions. I remain skeptical of the underlying scheme, but program chief Tiffany Funk deserves credit for acknowledging the botched rollout, listening to members, and giving them time to adjust.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue initially changed its earning rates on November 2, 2026, without advance notice. For cash contributions toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the cost increased from €10 per XP to €15 per XP, a 50% increase.

XP, or Experience Points, determine Flying Blue elite status. Members who had incorporated these contributions into their qualification plans suddenly faced a more expensive path to their goal.

Now, as One Mile At A Time also reports, Flying Blue has postponed the changes until December 1, 2026. The previous earning rates return effective November 4, and contributions made since November 2 will also receive credit at the prior rates.

Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, addressed the reprieve:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I appreciate the candor. Funk acknowledges that Flying Blue handled the rollout poorly and offers a practical correction. Members now have a transition period, including protection for contributions made during the initial rollout.

To be candid, I consider this arrangement a greenwashing revenue-generating measure. Awarding elite status credit for an environmental contribution is a convenient way to monetize the pursuit of status while wrapping the transaction in a sustainability message, a win-win for both Flying Blue and frequent travelers but probably not for the environment.

We don’t have to litigate that here and I readily acknowledge SAF can play a role in reducing aviation’s lifecycle emissions, but purchasing a contribution does not make a passenger’s flight emissions disappear. And I suspect the additional XP is the deciding factor for many members who participate, not altruism for Mother Earth.

Flying Blue certainly understands the appeal. Someone approaching a qualification deadline may find paying for a contribution far more convenient than taking another flight. But my skepticism about the arrangement does not diminish the importance of treating participating members fairly. Flying Blue offered an opportunity, and members planned around it. Their reliance was entirely foreseeable.

Flying Blue owes no one a permanent opportunity to acquire additional XP at a particular rate. It can decide that the existing formula is too generous or that it wants a different balance between flying and other qualification methods. Members can then decide whether the revised offer is worthwhile.

My larger objection, as with most devaluations, concerns candid communication and advance notice. Tell us what is changing. Give us time to adjust plans made under the existing rules. Please spare us the suggestion that a reduction in benefits is an “enhancement” inspired by member feedback.

Funk avoids that familiar gaslighting here. She does not claim members asked to pay more for their XP. She acknowledges that feedback exposed a problem with the rollout and explains what Flying Blue will do about it.

That is a much more credible use of member feedback.

Consider someone who booked travel expecting to earn a certain number of XP from flights and make up the remainder through SAF contributions. An overnight change can upset that calculation after the flights have already been purchased.

That member is not necessarily demanding that the rules remain unchanged forever. The objection is that a plan made in good faith has become more expensive without warning.

The additional time gives members an opportunity to complete contributions at the previous rate or reconsider their qualification strategy. Crediting contributions made since November 2 at the old rate also avoids penalizing those who happened to transact during the botched rollout.

Neither measure eliminates the devaluation. Both make its introduction fairer.

I commend Funk for listening and adjusting. Management can respond to criticism without abandoning the underlying business decision. Here, a relatively straightforward concession makes loyal customers  feel heard rather than taken for granted.

I remain skeptical of Flying Blue’s SAF contribution scheme, and the higher cost per XP will make it less attractive. Heck, I remain skeptical of status in general as a proud free agent for two years running. But the program has corrected the avoidable failure of introducing that change without clear communication or notice.

Funk acknowledged what went wrong and gave members time to prepare. Flying Blue is entitled to revise its earning rates. Members who planned around those rates deserve a reasonable transition, and they now have one. That is a welcome response…I never thought Funk would make the program more generous as other loyalty programs cut and devalue, but measured and clear changes with advance notice to members are all anyone can ask for.

#6219. 5  Boeing 787-9 Fleets With At Least 40 Business Class Seats

This list examines five carriers operating Boeing 787-9s with at least 40 business class seats, comparing their layouts, seating products, and approach to premium travel. The order follows the number of business class seats, but the figures alone do not tell the whole story. And one configuration in particular raises an interesting question about just how much of a Dreamliner's cabin an airline is willing to reserve for its most valuable passengers.

Qantas’ 236-seat 787-9 has 42 business seats in a 1-2-1 layout, each with direct aisle access. Australian Aviation reported that the cabin also includes 28 premium economy seats and 166 economy seats. The first of Qantas’ 787-9s arrived in October 2017, and the business seat is the Thompson Aero Vantage XL, an evolution of the suite Qantas already flew on its Airbus A330s. Business Traveller’s review adds that the 42 seats are split between a 30-seat forward cabin and a 12-seat secondary cabin, with a galley and lavatories in between.

Business class accounts for about 18% of the aircraft's total capacity, a relatively modest share compared with the other configurations in this countdown. Simple Flying examined how the 787-9's range lets Qantas operate long-haul routes directly from Australia instead of relying as heavily on hubs such as Singapore and Hong Kong. The aircraft also allows the airline to match capacity to demand without needing to fill an Airbus A380, which matters when a jet has so few seats to sell. It is a small business cabin with big ambitions, designed for passengers who can spend most of a day in the air.

Qantas is not standing still. AwardLocker notes that the airline advertises an evolved suite with a sliding door for new 787-9 deliveries from fiscal year 2028. Simple Flying examined how the carrier is reshaping its fleet without grounding. Today's Qantas suites have no doors, so the upgrade represents a significant change to the passenger experience. Still, 42 seats are enough to make the aircraft a serious long-haul proposition. The next airline takes that premium investment further, with a cabin that offers considerably more personal space.

The shortest 787 flight is a domestic connection of under 90 minutes.

All Nippon Airways' 206-seat 787-9 layout has 48 business seats in The Room FX. According to ANA, the seats alternate between forward- and rear-facing positions, and each is self-contained, with a door and a large 24-inch (61 cm) 4K monitor. ANA says it is the largest business class seat for a mid-sized aircraft, KarryOn reported, and the seat was developed with Safran Seats and Acumen. Pre-reclining the seat creates a sofa-like position, while adjustable leg rests turn it into a bed. The Points Guy adds that the 48 pods are split between the forward and rear cabins, with six rows each.

The dimensions help explain the attention surrounding the product. AwardFares reported a bed length of 76.5 inches (194 cm) and a waist width of 27 inches (69 cm), while Aircraft Interiors International says the sofa end is 41.5 inches (105 cm) wide. The same report adds that each of the 48 seats has a door, and that ANA plans a gradual rollout from 2026 on major long-haul routes. In effect, the seat offers more living space without adding weight, a clever trade for a mid-sized jet. Business class accounts for roughly 23% of the aircraft's 206 seats, giving the premium cabin a substantial share of the available capacity.

There is an important catch, however: not every ANA 787-9 has The Room FX. ANA’s cabin pages show that its 215-seat and 246-seat 787-9s use the Business Staggered seat instead, which also gives every passenger direct aisle access. ANA's cabin pages list each option by aircraft layout, so identifying yours takes only a minute. Checking the seat map before booking is essential, particularly when the difference between configurations can change the entire experience. With 48 business seats, ANA has already moved well beyond Qantas' more restrained layout. The next airline, however, manages to fit even more premium seats into its Dreamliner.

American Airlines' premium-heavy 787-9P has 51 business seats, made up of eight Flagship Suite Preferred seats and 43 standard Flagship Suites, all with doors, according to The Points Guy. The eight Preferred seats sit in the front row of each of the two business cabins. To keep the layout efficient, View From The Wing reports that the pitch is 42 inches (107 cm) at the windows and 44 inches (112 cm) in the center seats.

The Preferred suites offer up to 19% more bed space and 42% more living area, per AirlineGeeks. The whole aircraft seats 244, which makes business class about 21% of the cabin. Simple Flying explains that the premium-heavy version's forward mini-cabin offers the most exclusivity. Simple Flying also compared American's new Flagship cabin with United Polaris, a rivalry that is shaping US long-haul travel.

American also gives the 787-9P 32 premium economy seats, so the premium cabins together hold 83 seats. AwardWallet’s onboard measurements put the entertainment screens at 17.5 inches (44 cm), competitive with other US carriers, and every seat offers wireless charging.

The first 787-9P entered service in spring 2025 on transatlantic routes from Chicago and Philadelphia, and American has been receiving Flagship Suite 787-9s since then, with 30 scheduled in total, Aviation Business News reported. But beware: AwardLocker warns that American also flies a 285-seat 787-9 with only 30 business seats. So, the 787-9P is a very different proposition from the airline's more conventional Dreamliner configuration. Its 51 seats put it firmly among the most premium-heavy aircraft on this list, although a Japanese competitor manages to squeeze in one more.

What's it like onboard American Airlines' Boeing 787?

Japan Airlines flies two versions of the 787-9 with more than 40 business seats. Its 203-seat layout has 52 Sky Suite III seats, a reverse-herringbone design in a 1-2-1 layout where every seat angles toward the window and has direct aisle access, according to JAL’s announcement. The cabin grew from the 787-9’s previous 44 business seats to 52. The Milelion says the business cabin splits into 28 seats in rows 1 to 7 and 24 seats in rows 8 to 13, and the Sky Suite III bed measures about 78 inches (198 cm). That design first appeared on JAL’s Boeing 777-200ER in mid-2016, before it moved to the 787-9 in 2017, according to Executive Traveller. Business class takes up roughly 26% of the 203 seats, a huge share for a Dreamliner, and one reason corporate travelers pay attention to this jet.

Why? Japan’s Impress Watch reported that the denser layout let JAL answer strong corporate demand while keeping lie-flat comfort. The older, 195-seat layout has 44 original Sky Suite seats in a 2-2-2 layout, where window seats are staggered, so every passenger can still reach the aisle. Each seat is about 20.5 inches (52 cm) wide, per The Milelion. Both versions carry 35 premium economy seats, so the difference is felt up front, not in the back.

JAL also flies a third 787-9 layout, but with fewer business seats, it does not qualify. The Milelion notes JAL operates three configurations of the jet, so check the cabin count before booking. For a comfort-first ranking instead, Simple Flying’s list of five comfortable 787 business seats is worth a look. Now for the US airline that answered United’s push, and how far it went.

United Airlines' newest 787-9s carry just 222 seats, and 64 of them are Polaris business suites in a 1-2-1 layout across 16 rows, according to One Mile at a Time. Eight are the larger Polaris Studio suites at the front of the business cabin. The Blue Board’s fleet guide says each is roughly 25% larger than a standard Polaris seat, with a sliding door and a 27-inch (69 cm) 4K OLED screen. The suites also add a companion ottoman for dining with a guest and wireless charging, details that make them feel closer to a first-class product.

The Elevated configuration represents a major departure from United's conventional 787-9. As of late September 2026, The Blue Board counted just 11 Elevated aircraft among United's 59 787-9s, with most still flying 48 Polaris seats. FlyMag’s analysis says the Elevated version has one-third more Polaris capacity than United's conventional 787-9, which seats 257 passengers, even though it carries 35 fewer people overall. That is a substantial shift in how the airline uses its long-haul aircraft, prioritizing premium capacity over the number of passengers carried.

The jets entered service on April 22, 2026, between San Francisco and Singapore, and Inside Flyer reported that from October 24, 2026, United will base them in Houston for flights to São Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo. United plans to have 33 Elevated 787-9s flying by 2028, Airways Magazine reported. The aircraft is still relatively uncommon, but its planned expansion should make the configuration increasingly visible across the airline's international network.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

With 64 business class seats, including eight larger Polaris Studio suites, United takes the top spot in this countdown. Its Elevated Dreamliner carries more business class passengers than any of the other configurations examined here, while also dedicating nearly 45% of its total capacity to business and premium economy. The difference between the 42-seat Qantas cabin at the beginning of this list and United's 64-seat configuration is striking. It also shows just how much flexibility Boeing's 787-9 offers airlines: the same aircraft can be configured for long-distance efficiency, distinctive private suites, or a much larger premium operation. For passengers, however, one lesson is worth remembering before booking any of them: always check the aircraft configuration, because the 787-9 name alone does not guarantee the cabin you expect.

#6218. Why the Algerian Sahara Should Be Your Next Off-Grid Adventure

I woke up in the small hours of the night. Orion’s Belt was directly above where I lay on a thin roll-up mattress, zipped into a canvas sleeping bag. The hunter’s three luminous studs stood out in a canopy awash with stars from horizon to horizon, the Milky Way a glittery paint stroke across the scene. Aside from an occasional shuffle or snuffle from my fellow campers, the night was draped in a thick blanket of stress-shrinking quiet. It’d been days since I had cell reception. I could practically hear my nervous system thanking me.

A breathtaking canopy of stars illuminates the vast Algerian Sahara.

You don’t need to sleep al fresco while camping in the Sahara Desert—I could crawl back inside my own pop-up dome tent at any time—but I’d certainly recommend it. It was a highlight of my trip to Algeria’s tranche of this continent-spanning desert.

I was in the Sahara on a nine-day tour with Explore Worldwide, a UK-based small-group tour company, which began running trips to Algeria earlier this year, partly as a reaction to the country’s new, albeit cautious, encouragement of tourism. I wanted to find out what that development looked like on the ground and experience the desert region that hopes to attract new visitors.

Algeria is one of our Best Places to Go in Africa in 2026. Find our full guide here.

Africa’s largest country is hard to miss on a map, but all but one of the 10 well-traveled people in my group (mostly British and 60-years-plus) were first-timers in Algeria. Traditionally, the economy here has been driven by the oil and gas sector, and the development of tourism has been of little interest to the government. This has led to a fraction of the arriving tourists received by other North African countries such as Morocco or Egypt; roughly a third of its visitors are members of the diaspora coming to visit and stay with family. But recently, a push to diversify the economy has led to the launch of an ambitious “master plan” to increase arrivals four-fold by 2030, with a special focus on desert tourism.

Although the majority of projects (such as much-needed new hotels) remain in-progress, the government has introduced visas on arrival for people spending the majority of their time in the Sahara—an option taken by nearly 39,000 visitors since 2023, contributing to an uptick in arrivals. I took advantage of the scheme myself. After an hour or so in the capital Algiers’ Houari Boumediene International Airport—queuing, waiting, and nervously watching an official wander around with my passport—I paid my fee in cash ($150 for 10 days), my passport was stamped, and I was warmly welcomed to Algeria.

Algiers' iconic Casbah is the most ancient quarter of the city—and well worth exploring for its winding alleys and traditional Ottoman-style architecture.

The trip kicked off with an Algiers city tour, giving us a brief but necessary taste of the country’s culture and history before we flew into the desert. I arrived early for a little solo exploration, allowing me to wander the cool, peaceful paths of the lush Hamma Botanical Garden, and enjoy a bowl of rechta (thin noodles with chicken in a clear broth) in the intimate lounge of El Walima Restaurant.

With our tour guide Wassim Messgo, we walked through the narrow lanes of the Casbah—the UNESCO-listed historic center—past a smattering of souvenir stalls, and visited the hard-hitting National Museum of the Mujahid—dedicated to the bloody war for independence from France between 1954 and 1962. I could’ve spent longer in Algiers and want to return to see other cities in the north. Messgo recommended Constantine: “You get Roman ruins in other parts of the region,” he said, “but not in a city like this.”

But my focus for this trip was the Sahara.

The Algerian government has introduced visas on arrival for people spending the majority of their time in the Sahara.

Algiers to Djanet—a little oasis town in Algeria’s southeast near the Libya and Niger borders—is a two-hour flight, usually scheduled in the middle of the night (to avoid desert winds during the day, so I was told). On arrival, I was reminded of Algeria’s high levels of security, partly due to fluctuating tensions with neighboring countries, particularly Morocco at present. Our passports were collected and our names ticked off against a list that linked us with our guide: Aissa Khirani, a Djanet native who’s spent the past 20 years leading tours locally and across Africa. Khirani told me that guides have to submit their plans to the military, including the identities of guests and staff, along with car registration numbers.

In addition to being a military hub, Djanet is the tourism gateway to this swathe of the Sahara. Our flight was perhaps half tourists—but for the five days we were in the desert, we encountered only six other vehicles. This was a benefit of traveling with a guide who knew his way around, while having a flexible itinerary so we could avoid other travelers—and account for unexpected weather events.

Djanet is a little oasis town in Algeria’s southeast near the Libya and Niger borders, and a gateway to the Sahara.

As we drove around the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau over the following five days, the landscape varied with surprising frequency—Mars-like rocky flats; sandy canyons edged by colossal rock formations; sweeping seas of peachy dunes with crisp ridgelines and wind-rippled faces. Camels, many belonging to Touareg nomads, grazed on sparse patches of vegetation. Caves and overhangs here have protected at least 15,000 examples of rock art, some thought to be 10,000 years old, depicting people hunting or dancing, giraffes, cattle, and jars possibly for carrying water as the region dried up.

We eased into desert life with two nights at something close to a glamping site—shared with a couple of other guests—which had tents you could stand up in, thick mattresses, even charging units. For the following three nights, we camped among the dunes and at the base of hulking rockfaces that resembled elephant skin. Our mobile set-up consisted of basic tents, a dining table by the campfire, and a “bathroom”—a chair with a cut-out seat in a canvas cubicle.

Camping at the base of the hulking rockfaces of the Algerian Sahara

Tents come with comfortable mattresses, extra seating, even charging units

“To be honest, I don't want Algeria to be like Morocco or Tunisia or Egypt,” Khirani told me, as we drove out of Djanet in a convoy of four Toyota four-wheel-drives, echoing sentiments Messgo had also shared. Both guides spoke about how relaxed Algeria currently feels for visitors; when I visited Djanet’s market, for example, we’d been greeted but otherwise left alone to browse the stalls of jewelry and fabrics.

As for the desert, Khirani continued, it still feels remote. “The desert to me means peace of mind,” he said. “It’s a sensation like emptiness, but with it a kind of happiness that you cannot describe.” He hopes to protect that experience, while encouraging tourism “in a smart way.”

The shifting shades and surfaces of the desert dunes

Caves and overhangs in the region have protected at least 15,000 examples of rock art, some thought to be 10,000 years old.

While I had precious moments of solitude—sitting on a dune at sunrise, submerged in quietness as the sand turned cool beige to warm caramel—many of my favorite memories are of people: Hemaya baking bread in the sand under hot coals; driver Ali Lazghem playing the same four songs on repeat and letting other drivers know exactly how he felt when they stalled at the top of a dune he was powering up; the whole team excited to see a locally famous and yet unnamed rock formation that features on the cover of Lonely Planet’s latest Algeria guide for the first time.

Back in Djanet, at the end of our off-grid adventure, I was finally able to shower again. I knew one wash wouldn’t be enough to fully de-grit my hair—at that stage, almost solid with desert debris—and that I’d be tapping out orange sand from my shoes for days. But that’s the thing about time in the desert. It tends to stick with you, in more ways than one.

I traveled with Explore Worldwide on their nine-day Algeria’s Sahara Desert Adventure tour, which begins and ends in the capital Algiers. Prices start at $2,410 (excluding international flights, which are typically via hubs such as Paris or London). The package includes accommodation, most meals and activities, including a day-tour of Algiers and five nights camping in the Sahara Desert; don’t expect guides to keep strictly to the itinerary, but you’ll certainly spend plenty of time in scenic parts of the Sahara, see several examples of rock art, and be treated to warm hospitality and tasty food throughout. If you want to explore the northern cities too, you can do Explore’s two-week Ancient Algeria and the Sahara Desert tour. In Algiers, the comfortable El Aurassi is considered one of the best hotels, though service and style fall short of a standard five-star experience. For a visa on arrival, tour operators will provide the required authorization letter—otherwise you can apply for a visa from your nearest Algerian embassy. Bring dollars to exchange for Algerian dinars when you arrive (ATMs are unreliable), as cards aren’t commonly accepted. Exporting dinars is prohibited. Also note that it’s illegal to carry binoculars and drones into Algeria.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6217. But Our Flag Was Still There

Imagine a time when Americans could be arrested by soldiers and imprisoned without the ordinary opportunity to challenge their detention before a judge. When a former congressman could be tried by a military commission for a political speech, then banished from the country. When newspaper offices could be occupied by troops and publication stopped. Imagine an editor imprisoned in the very fortress his grandfather had immortalized in a song about American freedom.

O say, can you see By the dawn’s early light

I woke up this morning thinking about the question at the beginning of our national anthem.

After an election, we tend to look for answers. This morning, I find myself more interested in what we can still see.

I see a country in which people cast ballots and those ballots have consequences. A country in which officeholders can be challenged and voters can change the direction of government. I see people who care enough to argue, sometimes bitterly, about the future of a place they still believe is worth fighting for.

That is an exhausting way to govern ourselves, but what a remarkable inheritance!

What so proudly we hailed At the twilight’s last gleaming

The president in those opening examples was Abraham Lincoln.

His administration’s restrictions on civil liberties are part of our history, even if they sit uncomfortably alongside the achievements for which we rightly honor him.

Beginning in 1861, Lincoln authorized the suspension of habeas corpus, the means by which a detainee can ask a court to examine the legality of detention. The Constitution permits suspension in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it. Whether the president could exercise that authority without Congress was fiercely contested. The practical consequence was that people could be held by military authorities without the ordinary judicial protection against unlawful imprisonment.

In September 1862, his proclamation, circulated by the War Department as General Orders No. 141, subjected people discouraging enlistment or engaging in broadly described disloyal practices aiding the rebellion to military trial. It also suspended habeas corpus for those detained by military authority.

These were sweeping powers, with consequences far beyond the battlefield.

Whose broad stripes and bright stars Through the perilous fight

In 1863, a former Ohio congressman was arrested after delivering an antiwar speech, tried by a military commission, and convicted. Lincoln changed his punishment from imprisonment to banishment into Confederate territory.

Another critic, a Baltimore newspaper editor, had been arrested in 1861 and confined at Fort McHenry. His grandfather was Francis Scott Key. Think about that for a moment. The grandson of the man who wrote the words we sing about the land of the free became a political prisoner inside the fort associated with those words.

He was a Southern sympathizer. The former congressman’s politics were deeply objectionable in their defense of a slaveholding order. But we do not need to admire either man’s cause to take seriously the government’s treatment of him. Constitutional protections have little substance if they depend on our approval of the person invoking them.

O’er the ramparts we watched Were so gallantly streaming

General Ambrose Burnside ordered the suppression of the Chicago Times in 1863. Lincoln intervened to have that order revoked. That correction belongs in the account as much as the original abuse.

But in 1864, after the New York World and Journal of Commerce published a forged presidential proclamation, Lincoln himself ordered military action against the papers, including seizure of their printing establishments and the arrest of their editors and publishers.

The forgery was serious. So was the use of military power against newspapers.

All of this happened while the country was fighting a rebellion rooted in slavery, with its survival genuinely in doubt. That context is essential to understanding Lincoln’s decisions. Even so, it does not place those decisions beyond scrutiny and reminds us today there is nothing new under the sun.

I can regard Lincoln as a great president and still recoil at some of the powers exercised under his administration. An honest affection for America must leave room for that.

And the rockets’ red glare The bombs bursting in air

Our anthem was born of an actual bombardment. The danger was physical, and the outcome could not yet be known.

We sometimes speak of our own political moment as though we alone have discovered uncertainty. Every alarming development becomes unprecedented. Every election becomes the final opportunity to save the country.

Some warnings deserve our attention. Rights can erode, and institutions can fail. History offers plenty of evidence for the absolute necessity vigilance.

This country has been torn apart by civil war. It has tolerated profound injustice while congratulating itself on liberty. It has denied the protection of its promises to people who had every right to claim them.

And Americans have challenged those failures…often at great personal cost and against a majority quite comfortable with the way things were.

The work has never been easy, and progress has never been secure. The end of slavery did not prevent the injustices that followed. A constitutional promise could exist for generations before people received anything approaching its protection.

But the promise gave people something to demand. It still does.

Gave proof through the night That our flag was still there

I won’t comment on the outcome itself, but I have great hope after an election like this. The system is working. Imperfectly, unevenly, and with people understandably dissatisfied by its results. Yet democracy remains alive. Voters can register disapproval and impose consequences. Political power remains something that must answer to the public.

One election cannot certify the health of an entire republic. It can, however, demonstrate that the mechanisms of accountability still operate. I think we should allow ourselves to recognize that today, across political lines.

I spend much of my life traveling beyond our borders. That has made me more conscious of how much I value the ability to criticize my government openly and expect another opportunity to vote. Neither should be taken for granted.

We have built something very special here. Its failures are real, and so is its capacity for correction.

Repairing what is broken will require patient work long after the election coverage ends. Some damage will take years to undo. Some losses cannot be restored to the people who suffered them.

Still, Americans before us have undertaken that work under circumstances far more desperate than ours. We can honor them by continuing it.

This morning, I feel grateful that the country remains ours to shape. Grateful that disappointment can find expression at a ballot box. And I’m hopeful that we retain enough humility to recognize our mistakes and enough resolve to address them.

The anthem ends with a question. After all this time, it remains a question worth asking ourselves.

O say, does that star-spangled banner yet wave O’er the land of the free and the home of the brave

Earlier this year, JetBlue raised its checked bag fees and kicked off a wave of fee hikes across the industry. United followed. Then Delta, American and Southwest.

Seven months later, JetBlue is leading the fee-hiking charge again.

The carrier on Tuesday raised its bag fees for the second time in 2026.

Going forward, customers will pay at least $50 per bag. That’s a 28% jump from the lowest fee the airline previously charged its customers.

Passengers who don’t pre-pay for their bag will pay $60 for their first piece of checked luggage.

And because JetBlue uses a dynamic baggage-pricing system, flyers will pay even more for their checked baggage on peak travel days.

In a statement about the airline's second bag-fee hike this year, the carrier pointed to rising fuel and operating costs.

“This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one,” a spokesperson said.

Here’s how JetBlue’s bag fees will shake out, going forward.

These fees will apply to flights booked starting Nov. 3.

So if you had already purchased a JetBlue flight prior to Nov. 3 — including trips for the holidays — the previous fees would apply to your trip.

As noted above, JetBlue also raised the fees customers will pay for their second checked bag, too.

Here are the days where JetBlue's "peak" baggage fees will apply, through October 2027.

JetBlue does continue to offer free baggage perks as a benefit of certain cobranded credit cards. Plus, its Mosaic elite status members each get at least one free bag.

Customers flying in JetBlue’s premium Mint cabin are still entitled to their first bag free. The same goes for flyers who book the carrier’s new domestic first-class (BlueFirst) seats, which are set to debut on some flights next month.

As JetBlue raises its baggage fees, the biggest question for consumers is how the rest of the airline industry respond.

If history is any indication, we’re about to see another wave of fee hikes across the industry.

After JetBlue raised its bag fees in late March, it took only weeks for nearly every major U.S. carrier to follow with their own fee hikes.

This would be the latest case of sticker shock for travelers, who are simultaneously battling surging fares.

Even budget airline Frontier last week reported customers had paid 71% more in fares over the prior quarter.

All of this comes as airlines have had to contend with sky-high jet fuel costs in 2026 — which they’ve aggressively passed onto customers.

But while jet fuel costs may eventually fall, it’s unlikely flyers will see any future relief when it comes to baggage fees — typically, once those go up, they don’t come back down.

While JetBlue has raised its baggage fees, it is worth noting that passengers do have freedom to bring a full-size carry-on bag on JetBlue flights, regardless of the fare type. The airline no longer bars its Blue Basic (basic economy) passengers from using the overhead bins.

Of course, the belongings packed in any carry-on bag must meet the Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy.

#6215. What Is the UNESCO Tentative List, and How Do You Get on It?

With a total of 27 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the United States is peppered full of sites of wonder. There's the Statue of Liberty, the patinated icon that has served as the first face millions of immigrants saw once they reached the country's shores and the San Antonio Missions in Texas which were first constructed the 18th century. Beyond manmade wonders, UNESCO has also recognized natural sites such as the Florida Everglades and the Grand Canyon. There's no shortage of modern marvels and breathtaking landscapes to behold in the US, which leads us to ask, how does a destination gain recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The process begins with the UNESCO Tentative List, which puts the best of the best up for consideration.

The Tentative List, as the name suggests, comprises natural and cultural properties that a country considers to have the potential to be recognized as World Heritage. It is not a confirmation that a site has been selected for inscription, only the first step towards a formal nomination, which is drawn up subsequently in the process. To qualify for World Heritage status, a property must demonstrate Outstanding Universal Value (OUV), meaning its cultural or natural significance ought to be considered exceptional from an international perspective. A site’s inclusion on the Tentative List places it in the position to be examined further for its potential OUV. This process enables a stronger foundation of vetting for the final nominations that a country draws up.

Even if a site included in a Tentative List is not nominated during one evaluatory round, there’s always a chance in the future that it may be added back to the list and considered for a nomination. The list is updated at any time per the country’s discretion, but each included site must undergo a separate nomination and evaluation process before qualifying for the World Heritage List. Once a site is inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage, it is removed from the Tentative List.

At the heart of UNESCO’s World Heritage process is the concept of Outstanding Universal Value (OUV). In simple terms, this means a place must be significant beyond its own country, and its cultural or natural importance must be exceptional enough to matter to people around the world, including future generations. A site must demonstrate this value against at least one of UNESCO’s 10 selection criteria, whether for its contribution to human history and culture, its geological features, its ecological processes or its biodiversity.

The cultural criteria include sites that represent exceptional examples of human creativity, demonstrate an important exchange of human values, bear testimony to cultural traditions or civilizations, or illustrate significant stages in human history. They also cover traditional settlements and landscapes, as well as properties associated with events, living traditions, beliefs, and works of outstanding universal significance.

The natural criteria consider exceptional natural beauty, significant stages in the Earth’s geological history, ongoing ecological and biological processes, and habitats important for conserving biodiversity.

Meeting one or more criteria is not enough on its own. A proposed property must also satisfy the relevant conditions of authenticity and integrity, alongside requirements for protection and management. Its inclusion must make a case for why its significance is exceptional in a global context, including through comparisons with similar properties.

It’s important to note that UNESCO’s 10 criteria are regularly revised to reflect the evolving understanding of World Heritage.

Countries identify properties they consider to have potential OUV and may eventually nominate for World Heritage status. UNESCO encourages them to involve a broad range of stakeholders in preparing their Tentative Lists, including site managers, local communities, government bodies, and non-governmental organizations. The process is led by each country, so the extent and nature of consultation can vary.

Currently, the US has 17 sites on their Tentative List, with nominations dating from 2008 and 2017. The US has submitted both cultural and natural sites for consideration with locales raning from the country's Pacific territories to Alabama. Below are the current contenders on the Tentative List, according to the National Park Service.

The country must still decide whether to proceed with a formal nomination and prepare the documentation required to demonstrate the property’s OUV. This includes establishing how the site meets the relevant selection criteria, documenting its authenticity and integrity, outlining the measures in place to protect it, and presenting a management framework. The nomination must also explain how the property compares with other sites of similar significance.

The country, not UNESCO, decides which properties to nominate for World Heritage status. Once a site on the Tentative List is formally nominated, independent advisory bodies assess its significance and conservation measures. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee then makes the final decision on whether to inscribe it on the World Heritage List.
