#6201. This Train Offers a Front-Row Seat to One of Colorado’s Greatest Natural Wonders

“Locomotives all have their own attitudes and personalities,” says Adam Clawson, the 24-year-old engineer at the helm of Royal Gorge Route Railroad, as our train winds along the Arkansas River. “They are their own living, breathing machines, and you have to learn their personalities.”

It’s a warm Saturday afternoon in October, and Clawson is at the controls of a locomotive he knows well: “Black Betty,” a jet-black, 3,000-horsepower diesel-electric unit that runs along a 12-mile stretch of tracks in Southern Colorado. Clawson is a third-generation railroader, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and great-grandfather, who both worked along this same route.

The Royal Gorge Route Railroad winds along the Arkansas River in Colorado.

As he eases the rumbling locomotive through the gorge, he offers a running commentary on the geology and history unfolding outside the window. Millions of years ago, he says, as the Rockies rose above the plains, the Arkansas River began carving its ancient path through the emerging peaks. Over time, the water wore away the hard granite, cutting a narrow, V-shaped gorge that plunges as deep as 1,250 feet in places.

The result is the Royal Gorge, a geological wonder nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of the Arkansas River.” Visitors can experience the dramatic 10-mile-long chasm from several perspectives: From above, while gazing down from the Royal Gorge Bridge, the tallest suspension bridge in the nation (or for more adventurous travelers, while rock climbing a 5-hour via ferrata); and from below, while paddling the Arkansas’s roaring rapids on a whitewater raft. But for travelers looking to sit back and savor the scenery passing by, there's no better viewpoint than the Royal Gorge Route Railroad's open-air car, standing face-to-face with the staggering canyon walls.

The writer's view aboard the Royal Gorge Route Railroad

This train line is as historic as it is scenic. Though the tourist train didn't launch until 1998, the route itself has been here for nearly 150 years—but it was close to never being built in the first place. In the late 1870s, a pair of competing railroad companies—the Denver & Rio Grande and the Santa Fe—duked it out for the chance to build tracks through this narrow canyon. Their two-year battle, which involved everything from court injunctions to sabotage to gun-slinging hired guards, became known as the “Royal Gorge War.” Eventually, the two companies signed a treaty and the Denver & Rio Grande prevailed, building tracks that eventually reached the lucrative mining hub of Leadville.

Decades later, the train still threads through the same Old West landscape, but the ride is decidedly more comfortable. Today passengers can choose from three classes: Vista Dome, which offers nearly unobstructed views of the gorge from glass-enclosed dome cars; Deluxe Class in the vintage dining car, where four-top tables with cushioned booth-style seats and a bar are nestled against the large windows; and Coach Class, with four-person table seating and the option to order food and drink from the casual grill menu and bar. On select dates, there are also First Class dining tickets available for lunch and dinner, with elevated menus and wine pairings. Regardless of where you sit, all ticket holders have access to the open-air car, which is standing-room only. With Clawson or one of his fellow engineers at the controls, all travelers have to do is sit back and let the scenery unfold.

The journey begins roughly an hour south of Colorado Springs in Cañon City at a historic depot originally completed in 1914. A few miles later, a dilapidated pipeline comes into view, running along the canyon wall just above the river. Completed in 1910, this eight-mile-long, mostly wooden structure provided water to Cañon City until 1973. As the train passes under the Royal Gorge Bridge, Clawson encourages me to open the cab window, lean back, and look up. The wind whips my hair as I stare at the bridge some 1,000 feet overhead. It’s 18 feet wide, according to Clawson, but from this vantage point, it looks like a thin wire that’s been strung across a gaping expanse.

As the train works its way through the river gorge, water rushes past and red rock walls tower on both sides.

Next, the train squeezes through the gorge’s narrowest and deepest section, the towering red granite walls growing taller and more imposing as they tighten around the tracks. Then we chug over the famous “Hanging Bridge,” which was an engineering marvel when it was completed in 1879—and remains one even today. At this point, the chasm narrows to just 30 feet wide, creating a bottleneck that required a little ingenuity to get a train through. Engineer C. Shallor Smith came up with a brilliant solution: He designed a 175-foot-long bridge that’s suspended above the rushing water by A-shaped supports anchored to the canyon wall.

Soon after, Clawson spots a pair of plastic kayaks hauled out on a small beach on the other side of the waterway. “We might get mooned,” he warns, referencing how paddlers traditionally greet the train when it passes. But when we spot the kayakers standing on the bank a few minutes later, they simply smile and wave. Clawson blares the train’s horn in response.

Eventually, the train reaches its western terminus, the town of Parkdale. Clawson hits the brakes and we jump down onto the tracks. Standing in front of the train up close, I’m struck by just how imposing she is. Thinking back to Clawson’s personality comment, I imagine her as fiercely independent—a self-assured, no-nonsense type of gal who’s not easily pushed around.

We clamber back into the cab and the train heads in reverse, retracing the route toward Cañon City. I relax back into my seat, letting the engine’s vibrations and the rhythmic drone of the wheels lull me into a pleasant daze. Outside, the rocky surfaces of the gorge’s walls alternate between light and shadow while the river glints in the midday sun. High overhead, I spot a turkey vulture circling on a thermal, its wings arching in a shallow V as it glides without flapping.

Clawson follows my gaze. “You can’t make this up,” he says. “Somebody might type into AI, ‘Take this picture of me and make it look like I’m in paradise.’ [But] all I gotta do is step outside."

#6200. How Much Premium Economy Costs On London-New York Flights In 2026

Premium economy on a London-New York flight can cost more than twice as much as an economy ticket, but the difference between the two cabins and business class can sometimes be surprisingly small. For passengers facing an approximately eight-hour transatlantic journey, a wider seat, extra legroom, better meals, and extra baggage can be appealing, but does the experience justify the added cost?

In 2026, passengers traveling between London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and New York JFK Airport have several airlines to choose from, including British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and JetBlue. Those flying to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) have fewer nonstop options, primarily British Airways and United Airlines. With different premium economy products, competing fares, and varying baggage allowances, how much should passengers actually expect to pay for a more comfortable transatlantic journey?

Premium economy on the London-New York route typically costs approximately $1,000 to $1,300 for a return journey, compared with around $500 to $600 for a standard economy ticket. This means passengers can expect to pay roughly twice as much for the upgraded cabin, although the difference depends on the airline, travel dates, departure airport, and availability.

According to our analysis of premium economy fares in 2026, the transatlantic market demonstrates how airlines position their intermediate cabin between standard economy and business class. Premium economy has become a major revenue opportunity for carriers, letting them charge more for added comfort without offering the considerably more expensive lie-flat seating associated with business class.

However, the difference between cabins isn't always consistent. A NerdWallet comparison of British Airways fares found that one evening departure from New York JFK to London offered premium economy for $1,162, more than twice the $532 economy fare. Business class was available for just $1,222, meaning passengers would have saved only $60 by selecting premium economy instead. Another comparison showed a return premium economy fare of $1,459 against $737 in economy. These examples raise an important question: how much competition exists between airlines on the route, and where can passengers find the best selection?

The greatest selection of nonstop services is available between London Heathrow and New York JFK. According to FlightConnections, five airlines serve the route: British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and JetBlue. The route covers approximately 3,440 miles (5,536 kilometers), with flights generally taking around eight hours.

However, passengers should distinguish between the airlines operating the route and those offering a dedicated premium economy cabin. British Airways calls its intermediate product World Traveller Plus, Virgin Atlantic markets its cabin as Premium, and American Airlines offers Premium Economy on eligible long-haul aircraft. Delta also operates Premium Select on eligible international services. JetBlue, meanwhile, offers its Mint business class and Even More Space economy seating rather than a conventional dedicated premium economy cabin.

The situation is different for passengers traveling to Newark. According to FlightConnections' LHR-EWR route information, British Airways and United Airlines operate nonstop flights between the two airports: United's intermediate product corresponding to British Airways’ World Traveller Plus is called Premium Plus. The route covers approximately 3,454 miles (5,559 km), with an average flight time of seven hours and 55 minutes.

British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American, Delta, JetBlue

World Traveller Plus, Premium, Premium Economy, Premium Select

Such a variety of airlines at JFK makes it attractive to travelers seeking schedule flexibility and competitive fares. Nevertheless, more airline options do not automatically mean cheaper premium economy tickets. British Airways and Virgin Atlantic offer useful examples of what passengers can expect to pay.

A closer look at the price bump that is required to fly in BA's Club cabins.

British Airways and Virgin Atlantic are two of the most prominent competitors on the London-New York market, and both offer dedicated premium economy cabins on their long-haul services. Their current fares demonstrate that passengers departing London can sometimes find considerably more attractive prices than those booking an equivalent journey from the United States.

Virgin Atlantic's official website provides a particularly useful snapshot of its pricing. For a return journey from London Heathrow to New York JFK between November 17 and November 22, 2026, the airline advertised Premium fares starting at approximately $1,529. Its published offers for selected dates in May, July, and August 2027 also showed starting fares of approximately $1,542 to $1,549. These are advertised starting prices, not guaranteed fares for every departure.

The airline's official Premium flight deals page also provides information about its cabin and included services. British Airways, meanwhile, allows passengers to compare World Traveller Plus fares through its official website.

Furthermore, the KAYAK sample for February 5–12, 2027 provides another useful comparison point during low season, with prices slightly lower than those for immediate departures within two weeks, although those dates fall outside the 2026 calendar year. With the fares set, the next question is what passengers get for spending more than £1,000 on a return ticket.

One of the main advantages of premium economy is extra personal space, which can make a big difference on an overnight transatlantic journey or for passengers with health issues. British Airways' World Traveller Plus cabin features wider seats, additional legroom, greater recline, lumbar support, and adjustable headrests and footrests. Passengers also receive an enhanced meal service, complimentary bar service, personal entertainment systems, and priority boarding.

Virgin Atlantic's Premium cabin offers a similarly upgraded experience, although the precise seat specifications depend on the aircraft operating the flight. According to its official cabin information, the airline offers up to 38 inches of seat pitch, additional room to stretch out, and a footrest. Its onboard experience also includes restaurant-inspired meals served on porcelain dishware, a welcome glass of bubbly, and additional snacks on selected aircraft.

Baggage is another important consideration when calculating the actual cost difference between economy and premium economy. Virgin Atlantic Premium includes two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds (23 kg) each, plus a 22-pound (10-kg) hand luggage allowance. British Airways World Traveller Plus also provides two checked bags on most routes, while some economy fares are hand-baggage-only tickets. According to NerdWallet, adding two checked bags to certain British Airways economy bookings can cost up to $175 each way.

These additional services make premium economy more than simply an upgraded seat. However, the cabin doesn't offer the same experience as business class, especially for sleeping arrangements and airport lounge access. This distinction becomes important when the price difference between the two cabins starts to narrow.

The price difference between premium economy and business class fares is not always huge. Airlines use dynamic pricing systems that adjust ticket prices according to demand, remaining inventory, booking patterns, and the number of seats available in each fare category. As a result, a premium economy ticket can occasionally approach the price of a discounted business class seat, especially when demand for the intermediate cabin is high.

NerdWallet’s British Airways example illustrates this well. One New York JFK departure offered premium economy for $1,162, compared with $532 for economy and $1,222 for business class. In this comparison, choosing premium economy instead of business class saved only $60. For passengers seeking the additional comfort of a fully flat bed on an overnight flight, that relatively small difference could make business class a more attractive option.

Passengers also have another option when considering British Airways: using Avios. According to Award Travel Finder's London-New York redemption analysis, a one-way off-peak World Traveller Plus redemption requires 46,750 Avios, increasing to 66,000 during peak periods. Economy requires 27,500 Avios off-peak and 33,000 during peak periods. Taxes and charges are additional, meaning passengers must compare the monetary cost of an award ticket with the cash fare before deciding whether redemption represents good value.

Available loyalty points and occasional business-class promotions make comparing all three cabins especially important. Nevertheless, for passengers without enough points or who can't find attractive business class fares, premium economy remains an interesting middle ground. The question is whether the added comfort justifies the higher cost on this transatlantic route.

Premium economy occupies an interesting niche in the London-New York market because it provides a noticeable improvement over standard economy, often without the substantial expense of business class. On an approximately eight-hour journey, additional legroom, wider seats, improved dining, and priority airport services can make a meaningful difference for some passengers.

However, the financial case weakens when the fare approaches business-class pricing. A passenger paying $1,162 for premium economy when business class costs $1,222 is arguably better off considering the higher cabin, provided the business class fare is genuinely available for the same itinerary and booking conditions. Conversely, Virgin Atlantic's advertised return fare of $1,529 for November 2026 demonstrates that premium economy can be considerably more accessible than some of the higher-priced examples found in the US market.

Competition also gives passengers some flexibility. Travelers to JFK can compare British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American Airlines, Delta, and JetBlue, while Newark offers British Airways and United as nonstop options. Checking both New York airports, comparing departure dates, and examining the differences between economy, premium economy, and business class can reveal opportunities that aren't immediately apparent when searching for a single airline.

Premium economy isn't automatically worth twice the price of economy, but the cheapest available ticket isn't necessarily the best option. The deciding factor will be the actual fare difference on the selected dates, the baggage and onboard benefits included, and how much passengers value additional comfort during their transatlantic journey.

#6199. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

#6198. 10 Magical Christmas Traditions Around the World

Living far away from family is hard at the best of times, but it becomes particularly difficult around the holidays. If there's one thing that makes it a little easier for me, it's being able to mix and match festive traditions from different countries to create something that's uniquely ours. As an Italian living in France with a British husband, I love bringing together the best of each culture for a rather extravagant Christmas. On Christmas Eve, we have oysters and Champagne, as per French tradition, followed by an Italian feast and plenty of Christmas crackers—although I draw the line at Christmas pudding, preferring a simple pandoro over anything else.

Whether, like me, you spend Christmas far from your family, are planning to chase the sun this December or are driving home for the holidays, one of the great joys of Christmas is making memories and indulging in nostalgic traditions. All over the globe, different countries and cultures celebrate the season in different ways, marking the holiday with long-established rites and rituals or merging heritage to create beautiful new traditions. Below, we run through some of our favourite Christmas traditions around the world, and ask the Traveller editors about their own personal festive rituals. From seafood feasts on Christmas Day in Australia to surfing Santa’s taking to the waves in SoCal, these are the most wholesome traditions for some festive joy this season.

Christmas is not recognized as a national holiday in Japan, but the festive season is still celebrated—albeit slightly differently from how you’d expect. As part of a marketing campaign launched in 1974, a few years after KFC first opened in Japan, the brand came up with the slogan ‘Kentucky for Christmas’, and it stuck. On Christmas Day, many Japanese families tuck into a full feast of fried chicken—a tradition so popular that you often have to order weeks in advance to make sure you’ve got your bucket guaranteed for the big day. The original Christmas meal even came with a bottle of wine. Christmas cake is just as surprising in Japan, too—strawberry shortcake, made with layers of sponge, whipped cream and fresh strawberries, is a festive favourite.

As you might imagine, food is at the heart of Christmas celebrations in Italy. Every region has its own traditions and dishes, enjoyed on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and throughout the festive season. While northern Italians might tuck into tortellini in broth and other comforting dishes, in the south we go all out. In my family, we have twelve different dishes—mostly fish-based—served for Christmas Eve dinner, before indulging in traditional desserts and an unholy amount of nuts while playing tombola. If there is one tradition that the whole country shares, it's the rather quirky tradition of La Befana – a witch-like old woman who flies through the skies on a broomstick on the night of January 5, leaving gifts for children to discover on the morning of 6 January, known as Epiphany (Epifania in Italian). Well-behaved children receive sweets and presents, while naughty ones get coal – although these days it's usually sweet, sugary charcoal, which is actually delicious.

The real difference between the Scottish festive season and that of much of the rest of the world is Hogmanay. Once Christmas Day is done and dusted, the focus is on New Year’s—or, as the Scots call it, Hogmanay. Street parties in cities such as Edinburgh roll on until the early hours, Robert Burns’ Auld Lang Syne is sung at midnight, and the ‘first-footing’ custom takes place—the first visitor to a home after midnight is believed to bring good luck for the year ahead (along with traditional gifts such as whisky, shortbread or a lump of coal, of course). Traditionally, a tall, dark-haired man is considered the luckiest first-footer.

While much of the Northern Hemisphere is wrapping up against the cold, Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer, meaning festive celebrations often revolve around the beach, sunshine and outdoor gatherings. "The traditional Christmas lunch in Australia is usually seafood, a roast ham served cold, lots of salads and then a pavlova for dessert," explains Lauren Burvill, CNT’s senior commerce writer and resident Aussie. "After lunch the classic traditions are to play cricket in the backyard, or if you're lucky, on the beach. It's not unusual to see Santa on the beaches as well, often riding on an inflatable rescue boat from the local surf club. On Boxing Day the country's favourite pastime is to watch the cricket or the Sydney to Hobart yacht race."

Forget snowy landscapes and cosy fireplaces—in Southern California, you might spot Santa Claus swapping his sleigh for a surfboard during the festive season. "I grew up in greater Los Angeles, and though December isn't typically beach weather, something uncanny almost always happens on Christmas," explains Megan Spurrell, Conde Nast Traveler US’s associate articles director. "The temperatures spike to the mid-70s Fahrenheit with shining sun and many families, including my own, end up at the beach. But we also go to look out for a very SoCal figure, known as Surfing Santa. We keep our eyes out at Manhattan and Hermosa Beach, especially near the piers, though I've heard of surfing santas in Malibu and Santa Monica, too. Most are just local dudes with a Santa suit who reliably hit the waves on Christmas morning to entertain their neighbours (and get a surf session in)."

While many Western traditions see Santa leaving lumps of coal in stockings for badly behaved children, in Austria it's the terrifying Krampus who comes to punish them. As the folklore goes, the Krampus is a fearsome horned figure with a long, snake-like tongue, who accompanies Saint Nicholas on 5 December, otherwise known as Krampusnacht, the eve of Saint Nicholas Day. While Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with sweets and small gifts, Krampus is said to frighten or punish those who have been naughty. Today, the tradition is celebrated with Krampuslauf parades, during which people dressed in elaborate horned masks and furry costumes take to the streets, particularly in Alpine towns and villages. The folklore even inspired a Christmas comedy horror film in 2015, starring Adam Scott and Toni Collette.

In Peru, Christmas Eve, known as Nochebuena, is the main event, with families gathering for a festive dinner and celebrations that often continue well past midnight. "We alternate years of spending Christmas in Southern California with my mom and sisters, and going to Lima, Peru, with my husband's family" says Megan. "Though Peru has plenty of traditions tied to Christmas, perhaps my favourite is the sheer fact (shared in many Catholic and Latin American countries) that the whole affair begins at midnight on the 24th. It can be torture waiting until midnight proper to dig into the feast of turkey and arroz arabe that sits out waiting, but the entire city explodes in fireworks when the clock strikes 12. And then the party doesn't stop until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes at a family member's house or at the city's bars and clubs. It almost feels like a preview of New Year's Eve, just a few days earlier."

Dumplings are a major part of Polish cuisine day to day, and Christmas is no exception. The traditional Christmas Eve supper, known as Wigilia, begins when the first star appears in the sky, with families gathering around the Christmas table for a feast that traditionally includes 12 meatless dishes. "My favourite part of seasonal eating has never been the Great British Christmas Roast, but instead 'Polish Christmas', celebrated by my family on Christmas Eve, a haphazard tribute to the Polish side of my family tree," says Olivia Squire, Traveller's features editor. "When I was a child, my grandmother used to make pierogi (Polish dumplings filled with mashed potato and cottage cheese) from scratch, which in more recent years has been taken over by my mum and I and usually involves a lot of swearing and tears. It's all worth it when we sit down to eat them alongside a vegetarian version of bigos (hunter's stew—an insult to my meat-loving ancestors), breaded fish and holy wafers, soundtracked by Carol's at King's, my English dad's addition."

Forget spending a fortune on Christmas presents—in Germany, the tradition of Schrottwichteln puts a rather amusing twist on exchanging gifts, with friends and family swapping unwanted, bizarre, or downright useless objects instead.

"For gifts, we follow the German tradition of Schrottwichteln (literally 'junk Secret Santa'), where everyone brings something completely useless, unwanted or gloriously ridiculous, often something they were given once and never knew what to do with. The more pointless, tacky or absurd, the better," Karin Mueller, Traveller's visuals director, tells us. "Our children have grown up with this ritual, and what began as a cosy dinner has become the highlight of the year. They never miss it. Now that they’re young adults, they bring their partners along, and it’s turned into this wonderfully chaotic, joyful, very-London celebration that I’m pretty sure they’ll keep going long after we stop hosting."

Across England, Christmas is celebrated with familiar traditions, from exchanging gifts to tucking into mince pies and singing Christmas carols. But each county and neighbourhood has its own customs, too. In some seaside towns, brave locals take part in a Boxing Day dip—sprinting into the freezing sea to shake off the Christmas excesses, often while raising money for charity. There's also the age-old custom of burning a Yule log, traditionally associated with good fortune and protection from misfortune. In Cornwall, some communities gather in local pubs for a traditional Cornish ‘shout’, joining together to sing folk songs and sea shanties.

"In the hazy betwixmas period, the days of lounging on the sofa and gorging on Terry’s chocolate orange are punctuated by one magical evening at a local pub for a Cornish 'shout'", explains Lucy Bruton, CNT's social media manager. "A shout refers to the community coming together to sing sea shanties and folk songs in the pub, and the Lerryn (where my family live in Cornwall) shout is a particularly special one to me. The tiny pub feels packed to the eaves with people of all ages belting out some of my favourite Cornish songs – from "Trelawney" to "Lamorna" and, of course, “Cornwall My Home”. It’s dark, cosy and a real slice of the magic of Cornwall."

A version of this story originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

For anyone looking for a fun weekend getaway, Nashville almost always makes the short list of options. And for good reason, it’s a city packed with character, history, live music and excellent food.

I was lucky enough to grow up in the Nashville area, so the world of the Ryman Auditorium, the Grand Ole Opry and even excellent airport musicians will always feel like home. I recently went back for a short trip, and while I was there, I made sure to hit some of my favorite food spots — and check out some new ones while I was at it.

If you have Nashville on your list, don’t miss these favorite eateries. And for any food-focused trip, a card that earns on dining is worth having, like the Navy Federal Flagship Premier Visa Signature®. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases and 4 points per dollar on travel purchases, a strong combination for a trip like this, and all for just a $95 annual fee.

If you need a great travel and dining card, now is the perfect time to add the Flagship Premier card to your wallet. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 50,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 in the first 90 days from account opening. Offer ends Jan. 3, 2027.

Here’s how to use the card to make your food-focused weekend trip to Nashville even better.

I live on the West Coast now, so my go-to flight is usually a nonstop on Alaska Airlines, but I sometimes opt for another airline. With the Flagship Premier card earning on a wide range of travel purchases, I can compare prices and book whichever flight makes the most sense — no loyalty to one airline or travel portal required.

The Flagship Premier card can also help you save on your flight to Nashville with its $100 annual airline credit, which offsets the cost and gives you more flexibility when booking.

And when you’re at the airport, you’ll be thankful for Flagship Premier’s statement credit of up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck® to help you zip through security.

When it was time to choose my hotel, I knew I wanted to stay at The Thompson Nashville. It’s in the Gulch, making it within walking distance of many of my favorite dining and shopping spots.

Regardless of which hotel you choose, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar when you book on your Flagship Premier card. That means you’re free to pick whichever hotel you want, without worrying about staying within a single brand or portal to earn bonus points.

Flagship Premier tip: Earn 4 points per dollar on a wide range of travel spending — not just hotels and airfare. Ground transportation counts too, whether you’re in a rental car, on public transport or using rideshare services.

Nashville has quite the dining scene, and the list of standout spots seems to grow every day. To make sure I fit in as much as possible, I turned one day into my own food crawl, with a combination of old favorites and a few newer ones.

For a food-focused trip like this, the Flagship Premier card earns where it matters most. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, so you’ll earn bonus points wherever your taste buds take you.

Since moving away from Nashville, I’ve come to realize that few places make a better chicken biscuit than Biscuit Love. Biscuit Love is an iconic Nashville staple, but it was new to me, so I knew it would make the list when I saw it around the corner from my hotel.

It absolutely lived up to the hype. From the fun southern and country-music themed decor to the food worth writing home about, Biscuit Love has landed a permanent spot on my list of favorite Nashville eateries.

The menu spans southern staples like biscuits and gravy and shrimp and grits, as well as lighter options like oatmeal and omelets. I knew I wanted to try their Princess biscuit, a buttermilk biscuit topped with fried Nashville “Hot Chicken” and homemade pickles. I also added the summer special Sunshine latte to my order — an iced latte with tangerine, cinnamon and vanilla and topped with housemade salted honey cold foam. And, of course, a side of bacon.

The entire meal was excellent. The chicken was perfectly fried, the biscuit light and fluffy and the pickles delightfully tangy. And the sunshine latte, I discovered, is a favorite for a reason. It was the perfect morning treat to start the day.

After such a big breakfast, I had to wait a while before I could even think about lunch. But when the time finally came, I knew I was headed to Ladybird Taco for my favorite tacos in Nashville.

A location a few blocks from my hotel made it an easy walk. Wanting to pace myself a bit this time, I opted for just one brisket taco and a side of chips and queso.

While I haven’t been to all the taco joints Nashville has to offer, the Austin-inspired menu at Ladybird has been my favorite for years, and I was thrilled to be back for a taste. If you happen to be there for breakfast, be sure to check out their breakfast tacos and Crema coffee — I’m always surprised at how well their coffee and queso go together.

After lunch, I was ready for an afternoon pick-me-up. Living on the West Coast has raised my coffee standards pretty high, but Barista Parlor never disappoints.

I popped in for an iced whiskey-caramel latte as a post-lunch treat to keep me going through the rest of my day in Nashville.

While Jeni’s isn’t Nashville-exclusive, it's only available in select cities and is a spot I make sure to visit every time I’m in town for its creative, seasonal flavors. I originally went in for my favorite — Brambleberry Crisp — but was tempted by the new fall lineup on the menu, which included Pumpkin with Brown Sugar Blondies.

I took a risk and ordered a half scoop of each and was delighted to discover that they pair beautifully. (Just learn from my mistakes and be sure to eat your ice cream quickly if you happen to be there during a heat wave.)

To close out my food crawl day, I headed to The Optimist, a seafood restaurant from chef and restaurateur Ford Fry that was new to me. I love every restaurant of his I’ve been to, and so many of my friends had raved about this one that I wanted to see if it lived up to the hype.

One of my good friends joined me, and we set out to try some of the hottest dishes.

While we surveyed the menu, our server brought rolls for us to enjoy. They were soft and fluffy — and the perfect thing to snack on while deciding.

Per our server’s recommendations, we landed on the Alabama Blue Crab dip and a half dozen oysters, which were both an excellent start to the meal (and complement to our Champagne).

We then moved to the spicy kale salad, which was aptly named. While delicious, it was too spicy for either of us to enjoy more than a few bites.

For our main dish, we ordered the Crumbed Halibut (with brown butter, parsley and charred lemon) and a side of “Proper ‘Chips’” (with malt vinegar aioli). The Halibut was crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, and the brown butter made it sing. The fries were equally well-executed, and the aioli took them to the next level.

The verdict: The Optimist lives up to the hype. I’ll definitely prioritize going back the next time I’m in town.

Flagship Premier Tip: Earn 3 points per dollar on all dining, making this a great card to have handy when exploring local cuisines — from a nearby coffee stop to the splashiest seafood dinner in town.

A card that earns on both travel and dining makes a trip like this Nashville weekend a breeze, and that’s exactly what the Flagship Premier card does.

With the card, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar on your travel purchases — from hotels and flights to transportation while you’re there, without having to deal with booking through a travel portal.

The $100 annual airline credit and up to $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit (once every four years) take the edge off both the cost of flying and the airport experience.

No one likes to juggle multiple cards while traveling, and the Flagship Premier card keeps things simple. With 4 points per dollar on travel and 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, one card covers the two categories that matter most on a trip like this.

Plus, there are no limits on the rewards you can earn (other than your stomach at the end of your food crawl).

If you haven’t been to Nashville lately, be sure to add it to your list — along with these excellent food spots while you’re there.

And wherever your next trip takes you, the Navy Federal Flagship Premier card is worth bringing along, especially for trips centered on food and travel. Between the travel credits and elevated earning rates, it’s the perfect card for any trip.

#6196. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

#6195. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6194. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

Does anyone plan on buying Choice Privileges points?

#6193. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 9Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: In-ground pool, firepit, outdoor shower, dedicated office space, rooftop with mountain views

Don’t let the university neighborhood fool you—this south-of-downtown oasis is ideal for a quieter, family-friendly stay. It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. But perhaps the most lovable feature is the private backyard, which has a pool, firepit, and full dining table, all surrounded by lush greenery and sleek appliances.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Observatory Park, The Robert and Judi Newman Center for the Performing Arts, University Hills Farmers Market, University of Denver

Get groovy at this nostalgic studio apartment, which features an authentic disco ball and skyline views (including a peek at Coors Field, where the Colorado Rockies play) in the heart of Denver's Lower Downtown (LoDo) neighborhood. Lucky for its guests, this spot is within walking distance of downtown Denver’s hottest entertainment, shopping, and dining outposts for a day or night out on the town. Plus, it’s equipped with all the amenities of your dreams, including a spacious California king bed, a 13-foot vintage couch, and a fully equipped kitchen for whipping up meals.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Coors Field, Commons Park, Little Man Ice Cream shop, Ball Arena, 16th Street Mall, Larimer Square, McGregor Square, Denver Union Station

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, fully equipped kitchen, private backyard, in-unit washer and dryer, kid-friendly amenities

You and your crew are in for a treat when staying at this charming, historic Boulder home. With original woodwork, colorful wallpaper, a fenced backyard, and three spacious bedrooms, guests here will enjoy a stylish stay.

#6192. Ill-Fated Learjet Had Altitude Struggles Amid Severe Turbulence 6 Months Ago, ATC Audio Shows

The Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people onboard, had experienced a troubling encounter with severe turbulence just six months earlier. Resurfaced air traffic control audio from May 2026 reveals that the same aircraft struggled to maintain its assigned altitude near Newark, New Jersey, prompting a controller to challenge the crew's description of the conditions as merely moderate turbulence.

The revelation, originally reported by the Daily Express, raises questions about similarities between the two incidents, particularly in how the pilots characterized the turbulence they encountered. Before Sunday's fatal crash, the Learjet's crew also reported moderate turbulence despite altitude fluctuations of up to 700 feet. However, investigators have not established a connection between the incidents, and the identities of the pilots involved in the May incident remain unconfirmed.

The earlier encounter occurred in May, when the Learjet, registered as N722BD, was flying near Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). According to audio obtained by The US Sun, a controller noticed the business jet climbing unexpectedly and questioned the crew. A female pilot responded that they were "just about to call you," said they were experiencing moderate turbulence, and were unable to maintain their assigned altitude.

The controller immediately challenged that assessment and instructed the pilots to descend to 4,000 feet. The situation was particularly concerning because another business jet was operating nearby at a similar altitude, potentially creating a separation issue. A male pilot subsequently reiterated that the Learjet was experiencing moderate chop, but the controller insisted that an inability to maintain altitude indicated more serious conditions.

"If you can't maintain altitude, that's not moderate. That's severe turbulence."

The controller then explicitly asked whether the aircraft was encountering severe turbulence, prompting affirmative responses from both pilots. When questioned about possible injuries, the female pilot reported none, but confirmed that severe turbulence was continuing. The identities of the two pilots have not been established, and there is no confirmation that either was aboard the aircraft during its fatal flight six months later.

The May exchange highlights an important distinction in how pilots report turbulence. Under the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) turbulence classifications, moderate turbulence can produce changes in altitude, attitude, and airspeed, but pilots should retain positive control. Severe turbulence involves larger, more abrupt changes and can leave an aircraft momentarily out of position. The controller's concern was therefore consistent with established aviation terminology.

Slight, irregular changes in altitude or attitude

Changes in altitude or attitude, with positive control maintained

Large, abrupt changes; aircraft may be momentarily out of position

Aircraft violently tossed about; control practically impossible

This distinction matters in congested airspace, where aircraft must maintain assigned altitudes to preserve separation from other traffic. An unexpected climb or descent can create a potential conflict even when the deviation is caused by atmospheric conditions rather than pilot action. Accurate turbulence reports also help controllers warn following aircraft and coordinate alternative altitudes. However, difficulty maintaining altitude does not automatically establish a mechanical problem or loss of control.

For N722BD, the May recording indicates that the aircraft deviated up to 700 feet above and 400 feet below its assigned altitude of 4,000 feet. That suggests that the initial description of a "moderate chop" significantly understated the difficulties the crew was experiencing, and supports the controller's assessment of severe turbulence.

This article serves as reassurance that turbulence rarely poses a danger to passengers and requires little effort from pilots to navigate.

N722BD departed Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), bound for North Eleuthera Airport (ELH) in the Bahamas, carrying seven passengers and two pilots. While crossing South Florida at 35,000 feet, the crew reported light clear icing and turbulence, with altitude deviations of approximately 600-700 feet. The similarities to May are striking: once again, pilots aboard the same aircraft described "moderate turbulence" while experiencing substantial altitude fluctuations. Nevertheless, those fluctuations alone do not prove that the November conditions met the FAA's severe classification.

After encountering precipitation, the crew requested permission to climb to 37,000 feet, hoping to find smoother conditions. ATC approved the request, but less than 30 seconds later, the pilots reported an uncontrolled descent and declared an emergency. According to Flightradar24, the aircraft's reported descent rate exceeded 32,000 feet per minute before it crashed in Palm Beach County, killing everyone aboard.

The NTSB investigation has already uncovered evidence of an inflight breakup, including pieces of the aircraft's left elevator found between 1.3 miles (2.1 km) and 3.8 miles (6.1 km) from the impact site. Investigators are examining weather, aircraft systems, maintenance records, and flight communications. Although both encounters involved turbulence and difficulties maintaining altitude, no causal connection has been established. A preliminary report is expected within about 30 days, and the final investigation will likely take considerably longer.

#6190. New Cathay Pacific “Halo Suites” First Class For Boeing 777-9s

In late 2024, Cathay Pacific unveiled its new Aria Suites business class, which is progressively being introduced on the carrier’s Boeing 777-300ER fleet. While we know Cathay Pacific is introducing a new first class product, it’ll take some time before we see that in service.

In light of everything going on — the introduction of Cathay Pacific’s new business class, the delays to the Boeing 777X, the products being introduced by competitors, etc. — I’d like to cover the latest when it comes to Cathay Pacific’s new first class.

We’ve known for years that Cathay Pacific plans to introduce new first and business class products on its Boeing 777-9s. The airline has 35 of these aircraft on order, and they’re expected to become the carrier’s flagship aircraft.

Note that not all Cathay Pacific 777-9s are expected to get first class. The expectation is that somewhere around 20 of them will feature the cabin, while the remaining will feature business class, premium economy, and economy.

Initially the aircraft was supposed to enter service as of 2020, though due to delays stemming from a variety of reasons, the plane is now slated to be delivered in 2027 at the earliest.

Many airlines were planning on introducing new “flagship” products on their 777-9s, though the seven year delay has obviously not been ideal for that, and has caused many airlines to fall behind with their premium products. I would imagine that Cathay Pacific was planning on debuting its new business class on 777-9s, but now decided to install it on 777-300ERs.

While Cathay Pacific has moved forward with introducing its new business class, the airline only plans to introduce a new first class as of 2027, on Boeing 777-9s. Understandably, one major concern here is when 777-9s will actually enter service for Cathay Pacific.

At this point, the aircraft will enter commercial service in the second half of 2027 at the absolute earliest, and Cathay Pacific isn’t even the launch customer. So it could very well be 2028 before we see the first Cathay Pacific 777-9.

In 2023, Cathay Pacific applied for a trademark for “The Aria Suites,” which is the carrier’s new business class. The airline also applied for a trademark for “The Halo Suites,” and this is specifically intended to cover “luxury and first class air transportation services.”

For what it’s worth, the two patents were filed just a few weeks apart. While we can’t say anything with certainty, I’d be willing to bet with that this will in fact be the name of Cathay Pacific’s new first class product.

We know that Cathay Pacific has been working on developing its new first class product for many years (it was supposed to be ready in 2020, based on the initial Boeing 777-9 delivery timeline). We also know that Cathay Pacific is planning something truly spectacular. However, there hasn’t been any official indication as to what we can expect (though rumor has it that we could get a “tease” in the coming months).

Back in 2019, Cathay Pacific applied for a patent for a new first class product, and… wow! Let me emphasize that I can’t guarantee this will be Cathay Pacific’s new first class, though I think it’s very possible. I’d highly recommend reading the whole application, as it actually contains a couple of different concepts.

Below is the diagram that’s displayed, and if I’m understanding this correctly, the plan is that figures five through eight reflect what Cathay Pacific is hoping to offer.

This appears to be based on Paperclip Design’s Peacock Suites concept. The below pictures should give you a sense of just how spectacular this product might be (though I’d expect Cathay Pacific to have a customized version of this, so don’t expect it to be exactly like this).

This product looks absolutely wild, and I’m in disbelief that we could see anything like this introduced. It almost looks more like The Etihad Residence than a standard first class product. Heck, it almost looks more like what you’d expect on a private jet.

A couple of years back, former Cathay Pacific Chairman Patrick Healy has called the new product “mindblowing,” and “a really, really special product and very impressive.”

This would likely blow away the best first class products in the world, like Air France’s 777 first class, Emirates’ 777 first class, and Japan Airlines’ A350 first class. In terms of other first class products on the horizon, we know that Singapore Airlines will be unveiling a new first class shortly, and Qatar Airways is working on a new first class, but it’s not a sure bet yet.

Due to ongoing delivery delays with the Boeing 777-9, the carrier’s plan to transition its fleet is proving to be anything but straightforward.

Cathay Pacific is currently retrofitting its 777-300ER fleet with the new Aria Suites business class. As the airline retrofits its 777-300ERs, it’s also removing first class from those planes (assuming they have them). We’re seeing a combination of three-cabin aircraft reconfigured (with business class, premium economy, and economy), along with some four-cabin aircraft (with first class).

At this point, Cathay Pacific has just six planes remaining with first class. In the past, the airline has acknowledged that it may hold off on reconfiguring some jets, so that it can maintain even a small fleet with first class seats, for markets where it’s really needed. However, with the extent of the delays, one wonders if Cathay Pacific really wants to put the fleet retrofit project on hold, just to preserve a few dozen first class seats.

Cathay Pacific’s first class is an excellent, spacious product. While this isn’t the world’s most private first class, it is one of my favorites. On top of that, the soft product is very good.

Cathay Pacific plans to introduce a new first class product, though only on the 777-9, and not on the 777-300ER. You can expect this product to be introduced as of late 2027 at the earliest, assuming the Boeing 777X actually gets certified (that’s a big “if”).

Based on some filings, it would appear that Cathay Pacific will name its new first class “The Halo Suites,” and some diagrams suggest that this will be an unbelievably good product. I can’t wait to learn more. Rumor has it that we could get our first official tease of this product in the coming months, though who knows, that may be delayed yet again.

What do you make of what we know about Cathay Pacific’s new first class?

#6189. How everyday families can use the power of credit cards to support their lives

Many of us here at TPG love to leverage our favorite credit cards to enhance our travels. From trying out the newest lie-flat product to relaxing in an airport lounge, these products can go a long way in unlocking memorable experiences.

But for many Americans, credit cards represent a tangible way to support their household's bottom lines — especially in the face of rising costs and the unexpected hurdles that life can throw in their way.

Recently, TPG founder Brian Kelly sat down with three everyday families to help them maximize their wallets — and the conversations demonstrated the true power of making rewards work for you.

Here are some real-world stories that show just what credit cards can unlock for you.

One of the most under-the-radar benefits of credit cards is how they can build financial literacy and set your children up for success in the real world. No, this isn't about giving teens or young adults unfettered access to a big credit limit. Instead, it's the power of adding them as an authorized user to an existing credit card.

That's exactly what we recommended to Seungah Jeong for her 14-year-old daughter, Emi. She just started high school and is starting to spend her own money. By becoming an authorized user on her mom's card, she can start building up a credit history for when she's ready to go off on her own.

Even better? Some cards allow you to set individual spending limits for your authorized users, so your kids can learn about budgeting in a controlled environment.

Everyone has different needs when it comes to credit cards, and making the most of your everyday spending requires two important items. Put simply, you need to know:

If you never eat out, a credit card with a bonus on dining purchases won't do you any good. If you're a frequent international traveler, you don't want to swipe a card and incur foreign transaction fees. And if you focus on earning rewards with a single travel provider, you may be missing out on more flexible rewards.

We saw this play out with all the families we met.

Take the Goralczenkos. Parents Andrew and Tracy have quadruplets who are heading off to college, and both were laid off two years ago when the company they worked for suddenly went out of business. They had been collecting rewards on their favorite theme park credit card for years, but in their current situation, that's not doing much for them.

Instead, they can shift their focus to cash-back rewards, picking up a new card that awards them 3% back on some of their biggest purchases — like gas and groceries.

It was a similar story with Seungah, whose 18-year-old son Oliver was heading off to Greece for college. Our recommendation was to get a new travel rewards card, specifically one that offers flexible rewards and waives foreign transaction fees. That means Oliver won't be hit with up to 3% in fees every time he swipes the card in Europe.

Finally, there was Renee Lewis-Mance. She and her husband, Chris, are retired, but she's very into the points game, focusing primarily on a single airline and a single hotel loyalty program. While these programs can be valuable, Renee is missing out on one of the biggest benefits of being retired: flexibility.

That's why we recommended adding a new transferable rewards card to her wallet. Earning points or miles in one of these programs provides an array of redemption options when she's planning a trip. She's not locked into a single airline or hotel chain, which could limit her options.

Beyond earning with your everyday spending, most popular cards offer one-time bonuses for new applicants (subject to minimum spending requirements). This allows you to take home a big haul of points, miles or cash-back rewards up front while picking up a new card that better fits your spending habits.

This was particularly appealing for the Goralczenkos. The card we recommended came with a $100 welcome bonus, plus 3% back on some major everyday spending categories. That won't get them a flight to Europe, but in their current situation, cash back is much more appealing.

Chris Mance found himself in a similar boat. He was able to grab a one-time, $200 cash-back bonus on a new card that was also a better fit for where he spends his money each month.

But even more importantly, this new card will help him address the final strategy ...

Here at TPG, we like to joke that there's no "point" to using cash for your everyday purchases — but there's certainly risk. Carrying around a bunch of cash leaves you vulnerable to theft, and even if you opt to swipe a debit card, you're generally earning no rewards on those purchases.

That's the exact situation that Chris Mance found himself in. While his wife (Renee) loves playing the points game, Chris usually pays cash or uses a debit card for his regular trips to Home Depot and the grocery store. However, by shifting those purchases to a cash-back credit card, he can unlock some significant rewards.

Based on our estimates, his grocery purchases alone could turn into $250 in cash back every year.

In addition, since Chris was spending a good chunk of money on home improvement purchases — tools, gardening supplies, plants — we recommended a card that will allow him to customize his rewards by picking a category to earn 6% back in the first year. That alone should net him around $300 in rewards.

The best part? This card had no annual fee.

In both cases, Chris isn't spending more money than he already planned to spend. He's just switching to a payment method that rewards him for his existing spending habits.

The world of credit cards features an array of products to meet the needs of virtually every American. Sure, there are options geared toward luxury travelers with a variety of benefits to help elevate their next trip. But many others can be a great fit for everyday pursuits, like shopping at the grocery store or building your child's credit history.

Ordinary families can easily take advantage of cash-back rewards to support their household bottom lines, and can boost their earnings by carefully analyzing their spending habits to select the best card(s) for their wallets.

And as long as you're responsibly managing your credit and spending within your means, the only way to lose is by not participating at all.
