#6188. Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

With just two months left in 2026, time is running out to qualify (or requalify) for Delta Medallion elite status.

If you have not done so already, check your elite qualification metrics, tally up your travel for the rest of the year and see where that puts you in terms of elite status for next year. If you're short of your goal, you still have time to close the gap. There are plenty of ways to earn Delta status — and they don't all involve flying.

Here are some ideas to help you earn what you need by the end of the year and reap the benefits of Medallion status in 2027.

Related: Reciprocal earning coming soon from new Delta-Hyatt partnership

Remember that as of Jan. 1, 2024, Delta consolidated all Medallion status earning activities into Medallion Qualification Dollars, axing Medallion Qualification Miles and Medallion Qualification Segments.

Now, flyers earn MQDs not just on eligible travel purchases with Delta and its partners, but also on other activities, such as spending on Delta-issued credit cards and vacation packages. You'll need to reach the following MQD thresholds for each Medallion status tier:

Of course, the most obvious route to status is by booking paid flights through Delta: You'll earn 1 MQD per dollar on the ticket price of any Delta-marketed flight operated by Delta or its partner airlines (except in basic economy, which doesn't earn miles or MQDs). However, Delta's new "basic" premium fares still earn MQDs.

However, there are plenty of other ways to earn MQDs without setting foot on an airplane. Here are some last-minute strategies to help put you over the top for Delta elite status in 2026.

One of the best changes to the SkyMiles program in recent years is that Delta award tickets booked in Main Cabin or higher now earn MQDs. This can make earning status much cheaper.

If you have a stash of SkyMiles in your account, consider redeeming them to close the gap to your desired status tier. The number of MQDs you'll earn is calculated by dividing the number of miles redeemed by 100. (And remember, holders of select Delta American Express cards automatically save 15% on Delta-operated award tickets.)

There is one major exception to keep in mind: Only Delta-ticketed award flights earn MQDs. Your award ticket must be booked with Delta SkyMiles through a direct Delta channel in order to qualify (though it does not need to be operated by Delta). For example, using Air France-KLM Flying Blue miles to book an award flight operated by Delta won't earn MQDs, even if you add your SkyMiles number to the itinerary.

Related: Your complete guide to the Delta SkyMiles program

Since achieving Delta Medallion status now requires hitting spending thresholds, mileage runs are not the useful tool they once were if you're flying on Delta metal. On the bright side, you can still leverage partner fares to earn MQDs quickly. This is because these flights earn MQDs based on a percentage of the flight distance rather than the ticket price.

If you go this route, know that earning rates vary depending on which carrier and fare class you fly. For example, an Air France flight in full economy will earn MQDs based on 20% of the miles flown, while a full economy WestJet ticket will earn 15% of the miles flown. Remember, MQDs are not to be confused with SkyMiles.

You can also earn 1 MQD per dollar spent on Delta Vacations, the airline's platform for booking all-in-one vacation packages. However, Delta Car Rentals and Delta Stays bookings no longer earn MQDs.

Some Delta cobranded credit cards allow cardholders to earn MQDs. The following cards give you an automatic 2,500 MQDs each year (known as MQD Headstart), plus additional MQDs when you spend on the card:

It may be worth applying for one of these cards to close the gap for next year's Medallion status. If you already have one and your everyday purchases won't get you close enough to your desired status level, you might consider ways to increase your spending temporarily — such as paying your rent or mortgage with your cobranded card or making purchases for a friend and having them pay you back.

Just be aware that purchases on these cards must post to your account in 2026 to help you qualify for elite status in the 2027 status year. Purchases made in late December may go toward the following year instead, depending on the transaction date submitted to American Express by the merchant (which may differ from the date when you made the purchase). For example, if you make a purchase on Dec. 31 and the merchant lists the transaction date as Jan. 1, the MQDs you earn will count toward next year instead of this year.

Related: Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex card review

Delta SkyMiles has historically been one of the most generous programs when it comes to status challenges. After temporary unavailability during recent program changes, the SkyMiles Medallion Status Match Challenge has returned. This means travelers who hold elite status with another airline can request a match through Delta Medallion. If approved, you'll receive the equivalent Delta status for three months, along with a status challenge to extend your shiny new Medallion status.

In 2025, Delta also offered a new program called Elevate Your Status that allowed members to make a one-time MQD purchase to reach the next Medallion status tier, as long as they already had the required number of MQDs to qualify. This limited-time promotion has ended, but keep an eye out in case Delta brings it back for 2026.

Delta's Choice Benefits for Platinum and Diamond members include MQD Accelerators to help you get closer to next year's status. In 2026, Platinum members can select this Choice Benefit to boost their MQDs by 1,000, while Diamond members can earn an extra 2,000 MQDs this way. These MQDs typically take six to eight weeks to deposit into your account — so, if you plan to use this route to achieve next year's status, now is the time to make your Choice Benefit selection.

Another Choice Benefit option allows you to gift Medallion status to other members. Platinum Medallions can choose to gift Silver Medallion status to four people, and Diamonds can gift Gold status to four people. So be nice to friends or family who might be able to give you a hand up into the club.

Note that Platinum status members can select one Choice Benefit, and Diamond status members can select three benefits. You can select your Choice Benefit as soon as you earn status, and you have until Jan. 31, 2027, to select your 2026 benefits.

Related: The ultimate guide to Delta Choice Benefits

This option is probably not feasible for most travelers, but it's worth mentioning.

Thanks to Delta's partnership with Wheels Up, a private jet subscription service, Wheels Up members can receive one Diamond Medallion status for every $100,000 spent in a Wheels Up Fund during a calendar year. If you don't have a subscription, you can still get one Diamond Medallion status after making at least $125,000 in flight spend. However, travelers who earn status either way will not get access to Choice Benefits.

This is obviously not the cheapest option for earning Delta elite status. However, if you or your business use the service anyway, it may be a good way to bypass the other requirements and go straight to the top.

Even though 2026 is coming to a close, there's still time to level up your Delta Medallion elite status so you can travel in comfort next year.

The most important thing is to know where you stand after accounting for the rest of your planned travel for this year. Once you determine how many extra MQDs you need, you can use these strategies to ensure you earn your desired elite tier for next year — and all the perks that come with it.

#6187. Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card Amex Offers Deal: Save $200 On $900+ Flight

The Amex Offers program frequently offers promotions that can save you money on flights, hotel stays, etc. There’s a new Amex Offers deal that seems to be specific to one co-branded Marriott card, and it’s incredibly lucrative.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) seems to have a new targeted Amex Offers deal whereby you can earn $200 back when you spend $900+ on airfare.

This is really straightforward — targeted members just need to register for the Amex Offers deal, and then spend $900+ across one or more transactions by February 28, 2027.

You can reach that spending threshold through one or more qualifying purchases, and the flights need to be booked directly with airlines (so not through a third party). There are no restrictions as to which airline you can book through, so you can use this both for US and foreign carriers, which is awesome.

Officially Amex Offers deals are all targeted, though this one at least seems to be pretty widely targeted. It seems that it’s specific to this card, and that most people with the card are eligible for the offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card has a steep annual fee. Personally, it’s a card that I have, and one that I find to represent a good value, thanks to the variety of perks it offers. However, an easy $200 in savings beyond the expected value sure helps even more with making the math work!

The card ordinarily earns 3x Bonvoy points per dollar spent on airfare, and I value those points at 0.7 cents each, for a 2.1% return. So if you spent exactly $900 on a ticket, you’d get a $200 statement credit plus 2,700 Bonvoy points, which I value at an extra $19 return, for a total return of around 24%. That’s excellent.

Even if you don’t have an immediate ticket you want to book, most major US airlines let you bank credit if you buy a ticket and then decide that you no longer want to travel. So you could typically buy a $900 (non-basic) ticket, and essentially pick up that much credit with an airline for around $700. That’s a great value, assuming you can use the credit before it expires.

Amex Offers has a new deal that can save you $200+ on the cost of an airfare purchase of $900+. This seems to be specific to the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, and it’s widely targeted. This is an easy opportunity to save well over 20% on the cost of an airline ticket with few strings attached, so it’s worth taking advantage of, if eligible.

Are you eligible for this Amex Offers deal, and do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6186. Why 17 Regional Gates Matter So Much To The Airline Carrying Over 60% Of Miami's Passengers

Paul Bickford | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Miami International Airport (MIA) is preparing for a major transformation, and one of its most important developments involves an area that many passengers would rather forget. The $1 billion D60 expansion will replace an outdated regional boarding facility at Concourse D with 17 traditional contact gates, bringing an end to the bus transfers and outdoor boarding arrangements that have long characterized this part of the airport.

While the investment is substantial, its significance extends well beyond improving the appearance of a boarding area. For American Airlines, which carries more than 60% of Miami International Airport's passengers, the project represents an important investment in the infrastructure supporting its largest international gateway.

With approximately 400 daily departures from Miami, the airline depends on the airport to connect passengers across the US, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe. Improving just 17 gates could therefore have considerable consequences for its operations, passenger experience, and future growth.

Miami International Airport occupies a particularly important position in American Airlines' network. Unlike many other major American airports, Miami provides the oneworld carrier with an extensive collection of connections to destinations throughout Latin America and the Caribbean.

Its geographical position makes it a natural gateway for passengers traveling between the US and numerous international markets, giving the airline a substantial competitive advantage in the region. American Airlines operates approximately 400 daily departures from Miami International Airport, making the airport one of its most important operational bases.

Its presence is also reflected in its passenger market share, with the airline carrying more than 60% of the airport's traffic. This concentration means that improvements to Miami's infrastructure have an especially direct impact on American Airlines compared with smaller operators using the airport. The largest airlines at Miami International Airport by market share, as per data from the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics, are outlined in the table below.

The importance of the hub is also connected to the wider economic significance of Miami International Airport. The airport handled 55.3 million passengers in 2025, ranking it among the busiest airports in the US. According to Miami-Dade County, its economic activity generates approximately $212 billion in business revenue annually and supports nearly 946,000 jobs.

This demonstrates how closely aviation is connected to the surrounding region's prosperity. For American Airlines, maintaining a strong position at Miami International Airport is therefore about considerably more than operating a large number of flights.

The airport supports connections between domestic markets and destinations across the Caribbean and Latin America, while also providing opportunities to attract international travelers connecting through the US. Infrastructure that accommodates growing passenger numbers is essential if the airline wants to preserve and strengthen this position.

The current D60 facility is unusual compared with the conventional boarding arrangements passengers experience elsewhere at major international airports. Rather than providing individual boarding areas connected directly to aircraft through passenger boarding bridges, the existing arrangement uses a shared boarding space serving 17 ground-level regional aircraft positions.

Passengers must consequently follow a less convenient process to reach their aircraft. For travelers, this can mean leaving the terminal building and boarding a bus before being transported to an aircraft parked outside the main concourse. In other circumstances, passengers use outdoor boarding arrangements, exposing them to Miami's heat, humidity and unpredictable weather.

Although such procedures are not unusual at airports serving regional aircraft, they are increasingly difficult to justify at a major international gateway. The shared boarding arrangement also creates practical challenges during busy operating periods. Passengers traveling on different flights must use the same general waiting area.

This makes the environment potentially crowded and confusing when several departures are approaching simultaneously. Managing boarding announcements, passenger movements, and flight delays becomes more complicated when multiple aircraft depend on a common facility rather than separate gate areas.

These limitations are particularly noticeable given the scale of American Airlines' Miami operation. An airport handling tens of millions of passengers annually needs facilities capable of supporting consistent passenger flows, including during peak departure periods.

The existing regional facility represents an increasingly outdated part of an otherwise extensive hub, making its redevelopment an important step towards improving the overall experience. American Airlines' regional flights are operated under the American Eagle brand. The carrier's regional subsidiary's flights are operated by the aircraft detailed in the table above, according to data from ch-aviation.

The modernization plan is expected to last five to 15 years.

The D60 expansion will transform the existing regional boarding area into a three-level extension of Concourse D. Rather than simply renovating the shared waiting space, the project will convert the 17 ground-level regional aircraft positions into 17 traditional contact gates, each featuring its own passenger hold room.

This will provide a considerably more conventional boarding experience for passengers departing from the facility. The new gates will be designed to accommodate larger regional aircraft and narrowbody aircraft, providing greater flexibility than the existing arrangement. This is particularly important for American Airlines because aircraft requirements can change as passenger demand develops across individual routes.

The ability to accommodate different aircraft types gives the airline additional options when allocating capacity and planning its future operations. Passenger facilities will also receive considerable attention. Each gate will have an individual boarding area, while the expansion will introduce additional dining and shopping opportunities.

An improved baggage handling system is another important component, helping the airport support the increased operational requirements associated with the expanded facility. Together, these improvements should make the experience considerably more comfortable and convenient. The project is scheduled to break ground in 2027, with completion initially targeted for 2030.

However, Miami International Airport's published capital improvement information also identifies 2033 as the scheduled completion date, illustrating that the delivery timetable remains subject to planning developments. The project is primarily financed through airport bonds, alongside $34 million in grants from the Florida Department of Transportation.

One of the most significant benefits of D60 will be the removal of the bus boarding process for regional flights. Although the $1 billion investment includes several major infrastructure improvements, this particular change is likely to be among the most immediately noticeable for passengers.

Instead of traveling through a shared boarding area and transferring to an aircraft outside, travelers will use individual gates connected directly to the concourse. This creates a more predictable journey from the departure lounge to the aircraft. Passengers will be able to wait in designated boarding areas, receive flight information at their individual gates, and board without relying on a bus transfer.

The improvement should also make the boarding process more accessible for passengers with reduced mobility, families with young children, and travelers carrying additional luggage. Weather is another important consideration in South Florida. Miami's tropical climate can bring intense heat, heavy rainfall, and thunderstorms, making outdoor boarding less comfortable than conventional terminal facilities.

Eliminating unnecessary exposure to these conditions will provide a more pleasant experience, particularly for passengers traveling during the summer months when temperatures and humidity can become especially challenging. There are operational advantages for American Airlines as well. Removing the need to coordinate buses and outdoor passenger movements could simplify certain aspects of ground handling.

However, actual improvements to turnaround times will depend on staffing, aircraft scheduling, and other operational factors. More importantly, individual gates will provide a more organized environment in which airline employees can manage boarding and assist customers. The busiest domestic destinations from Miami International Airport last year are outlined in the table above.

The most common aircraft type will operate 4,363 flights from Miami International Airport in April 2025.

An especially important feature of the D60 development involves its connections to the US Customs and Border Protection facility. The expansion will provide third-level connections to Concourse D's customs infrastructure, creating the capability to accommodate international arrivals.

This is significant because Miami is not simply a domestic hub for American Airlines but one of its most important international gateways. The additional connections will help integrate the expanded facility into the airport's international passenger processing arrangements. International arrivals require appropriate separation and secure passenger circulation before travelers reach customs and immigration facilities.

Incorporating these connections into the design means the new gates can offer greater operational flexibility as American Airlines develops its international network. This is particularly relevant to the airline's extensive presence across Latin America and the Caribbean. Demand between Miami and these destinations can vary considerably, while aircraft assignments and route requirements evolve over time.

Infrastructure capable of supporting international arrivals provides additional possibilities for managing flights, rather than restricting the facility to a narrower range of regional operations. The busiest international routes from Miami International Airport last year are detailed in the table above. For passengers, improved integration could eventually mean more convenient international travel through Concourse D.

The benefits will depend on how individual services are allocated and how the airport implements its passenger processing arrangements, but the underlying infrastructure represents an important improvement. It also demonstrates that D60 has been designed around the long-term requirements of an international hub rather than simply replacing an inconvenient regional boarding facility.

D60 is part of Miami International Airport's wider Modernization in Action program, a multibillion-dollar investment covering improvements across the airport. The broader program includes developments to passenger facilities, terminal infrastructure, baggage systems, and other essential airport services.

Consequently, the Concourse D expansion should be understood as one component of a much larger effort to prepare Miami International Airport for continued passenger growth. Other major projects include the development of Concourse K, which is scheduled to open in 2029, and the redevelopment of the Central Terminal, currently targeted for completion around 2031.

These developments will complement improvements to Concourse D by increasing capacity and modernizing facilities across different parts of the airport. The combined investment is intended to create a more efficient and passenger-friendly international gateway. For American Airlines, these improvements are particularly important because of its dominant position at Miami International Airport, ahead of its rivals, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.

An airport carrying more than 60% of its passengers on a single airline needs infrastructure that can support the demands of a major hub, rather than facilities designed around much smaller regional operations. Better gates, more comfortable boarding areas, and improved international connections all contribute to the airline's ability to serve its customers.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Ultimately, the significance of D60 lies in the difference between the airport American Airlines needs and the facilities it currently has available. 17 gates might appear relatively modest within an airport handling more than 55 million passengers annually, but their transformation addresses a longstanding weakness in one of the carrier's most important hubs. As such, Miami International Airport is making a substantial investment in the future of its busiest airline.

#6185. Condor Plans To Open First-Ever Lounge At Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3

Germany’s second largest airline, Condor, plans to open its own lounge for the first time ever. However, some more patience will be required, and details are also still quite limited.

Earlier this year, we saw Frankfurt Airport (FRA) open its new Terminal 3, which is the airport’s first new terminal in decades. We’ve already seen all airlines that previously occupied Terminal 2 move to Terminal 3.

The long term plan is that Terminal 1 will be exclusively for Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, while Terminal 3 will be for all other airlines. Meanwhile Terminal 2 may eventually be rebuilt, as Lufthansa hopes to take it over as well, but that’s a very long term vision.

As of now, the only airline that hasn’t yet completed the move to Terminal 3 is Condor, which is Germany’s second largest airline. The carrier still operates out of Terminal 1, and uses Lufthansa lounges for its customers, despite Lufthansa’s disdain for the carrier.

The expectation is that Condor will make the move to Frankfurt Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027. As part of that, the airline also plans to open two lounges in the terminal, as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. The expectation is that one will be a Schengen lounge, while the other will be a non-Schengen lounge.

The catch is that the lounges will only open later in 2027, due to the pace of construction. While the company’s CEO confirmed these plans in a meeting with employees, publicly the airline has only confirmed that “we are currently in discussions with our partners at Terminal 3 of Frankfurt Airport to explore the possibilities for Condor’s own lounge offering.”

No details are yet known about what kind of amenities the lounges will offer… I’m definitely curious to see what they come up with, as it’s always interesting when an airline opens a lounge for the first time!

Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 is getting quite a nice selection of lounges. As things currently stand:

On top of that, we know that Qatar Airways is opening two lounges in the non-Schengen area of the terminal, which will be for passengers traveling on oneworld airlines.

Condor is expected to move to Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027, as it’s the last (and largest) airline to make the move to the terminal. We now officially know that Condor is planning on opening two lounges in the terminal, though they’ll likely only open in late 2027.

It’s exciting to see the airline open lounges for the first time, and only time will tell how this plays out…

#6184. Is the Venture X Business worth the $395 annual fee?

The Capital One Venture X Business is a great option for small-business owners who want to earn miles on their spending. It features a solid welcome bonus and many of our favorite features found on its consumer counterpart, the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card.

One such similarity is the $395 annual fee. This is a bargain compared to some other premium business cards, such as The Business Platinum Card® from American Express with its $895 fee (see rates and fees).

Still, a $395 annual fee is a meaningful expense. Does the Venture X Business offer enough benefits and earning potential to justify that premium fee? Here's what you need to know if you're on the fence.

Currently, new Venture X Business applicants can earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit:

*To use within 16 months from account opening

This bonus is worth up to $6,550 when you factor in TPG's November valuations of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents and the travel credit.

If you can meet the steep minimum spending requirements, the bonus alone is valuable enough to justify paying the card's $395 annual fee more than 16 times over.

Related: How to maximize your Capital One miles

Beyond the Venture X Business welcome bonus, you'll earn:

And when it comes to redeeming your miles, you have options. If you want to keep it simple, you can redeem your miles for a statement credit to cover travel expenses (charged to the card within the previous 90 days). This option offers a value of 1 cent per mile.

To get more value out of your miles, you can also transfer your miles to any of Capital One's 15-plus hotel and airline partners, including valuable options like Air Canada Aeroplan, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer and Wyndham Rewards.

TPG values Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each when used with transfer partners, though the value you receive depends on your redemption.

This makes the Venture X Business an especially attractive option for big-spending business owners who don't want to worry about bonus categories.

With this card, you can feel confident knowing you're earning valuable rewards no matter what you're buying.

Related: Should you transfer Capital One miles to partners or redeem them directly?

Venture X Business cardholders receive $300 in credits each year for travel booked through Capital One Business Travel. This credit is automatic, making it relatively easy to use.

However, since the credit is limited to travel booked through Capital One Business Travel, you'll likely give up any hotel or rental car elite status perks. The drawbacks of booking through a portal can put a damper on the value of this annual credit.

Still, fully taking advantage of this perk will bring your effective annual fee down to just $95.

Related: How to decide whether to book travel directly or through a portal

The travel credit isn't the only annual perk you'll get as a Venture X Business cardholder. Every year, on your account anniversary, you'll also receive 10,000 bonus miles, worth $185 according to our valuations.

Even if you redeem these anniversary miles directly for travel at a rate of 1 cent per mile, this annual bonus is worth $100. This perk and the travel credit combined more than justify the card's $395 annual fee each year.

As a Venture X Business primary cardholder, you get unlimited access to Capital One Lounges, currently open at:

Capital One also operates dining-focused "Landing" facilities at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

This card also includes access to Priority Pass lounges.

Without an eligible credit card, you can pay $90 for a lounge day pass. Five visits alone would cost $450 out of pocket, so you'll make up the annual fee's value quickly if you can take advantage of your Capital One Lounge access.

Related: Capital One Venture X vs. Venture X Business

On top of these benefits, the Venture X Business includes additional travel perks:

These benefits are more difficult to quantify, but they'll provide added comfort and peace of mind during your travels.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers: Amex, Capital One, Chase and Citi

If you can take advantage of key Venture X Business benefits, such as the annual travel credit and anniversary bonus miles, you can offset the card's annual fee year after year.

However, if you can't maximize the annual travel credit or airport lounge access, you may want to go with another of our favorite business credit cards. You may also want to consider a different card if you anticipate struggling to meet this card's lofty welcome bonus spending requirements.

#6183. Park Hyatt Phu Quoc, Vietnam, Opening Soon, And I’m Intrigued!

Back in 2019, plans were announced for an exciting new Park Hyatt resort in Vietnam. The property has been massively behind schedule on its planned 2022 opening. Several months ago, the hotel started accepting reservations for stays as of March 2027. There’s now a positive update, as the timeline has been moved forward to December 2026, so it’s just weeks away.

The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 8, 2026. The delays on this property have been endless, so it’s nice to see the timeline moved forward for once. Here’s to hoping that there are no last minute delays.

For those not familiar with Phu Quoc, it’s Vietnam’s largest island, and half of the island is in a national park and UNESCO site. The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is expected to feature a total of 168 keys, including 114 rooms and suites, and 54 private pool villas. This is Park Hyatt’s first resort in Vietnam, and second property in the country, after the Park Hyatt Saigon.

The resort is located on the southwestern tip of Phu Quoc Island, and is developed on 160 acres of land, bordered by a mile-long white sand beach on one side, and lush hills on the other side. The Park Hyatt is a 30-minute drive from Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC).

Details about the property are fairly limited, though here are some things we do know:

Below are some renderings of the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc. Given that we’ve had the same renderings for years and the property has been delayed year after year, I can’t help but wonder if the actual property looks anything like the renderings.

With the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc bookable, what are rates like? If you’re looking to redeem World of Hyatt points, this is a Category 7 property, meaning that a free night redemption will cost anywhere from 25,000 to 55,000 points per night, assuming a standard room is available. I value World of Hyatt points at around 1.4 cents each, so that puts the “cost” of a redemption at $350-770 per night.

When it comes to cash rates, they seem to start at just over $700 per night, and that’s before the 13.4% in taxes and service charges, so we’re talking about entry level rates of over $800 per night all-in.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

Depending on the award pricing for the nights you’re looking at, redeeming points here could potentially be a very good value.

While I’ve visited major cities in Vietnam several times before, I’ve never gone there for a beach vacation, so I’m intrigued by this property, especially given the value of World of Hyatt points, plus of World of Hyatt Globalist status.

Based on what I’ve heard, currently the top properties on the island are the JW Marriott Phu Quoc, the InterContinental Phu Quoc, and the Regent Phu Quoc. Many people have told me that these properties are among the best of their respective portfolios.

I’m curious, though, for those who have been to Phu Quoc, is it worth a trek from the United States? I’m sure it’s gorgeous and I’ll certainly take Vietnamese food over Caribbean food, but is it otherwise worth traveling that far out of the way?

It’s funny how my preferences in that regard have changed over the years. 15 years ago, I’d almost exclusively take beach vacations in Southeast Asia, given the generally higher standard of everything (service, hotels, etc.), plus the more reasonable prices.

However, as I’ve gotten older, my opinion has changed. For one, the jet lag becomes more challenging the older I get, and can take away from relaxation. Furthermore, flight award options just aren’t as exciting as they were over a decade ago. Like, easily being able to always snag Cathay Pacific first class awards was a great reason to vacation in Asia, as far as I’m concerned. 😉 But that’s no longer so easy.

But I also have another motive here. I’m intrigued by airline startup Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is just taking delivery of some Airbus A330s. So if I can fly an ex-American A330 directly to here, I’d sure find that to be amusing! For that matter, I really love the Capella hotel brand, and I’ve heard the Capella Hanoi is among the best in the portfolio, so I’d really love to visit that, and pair it with a visit here.

A Park Hyatt property is expected to open in Phu Quoc, Vietnam, and it’s now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. This property has been under development for eons, and it’s over four years behind schedule on opening. With the opening being just weeks away, here’s to hoping that the timeline finally actually sticks.

Do you plan on checking out the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc?

Airport lounges can serve as oases from a busy, crowded or outdated terminal. Some lounges participate in membership networks like Priority Pass, while others, like the United Club lounge, are operated by individual airlines.

If you’re a loyal United Airlines flyer or frequent one of the carrier’s largest hubs, visiting a United Club lounge is probably already on your radar. However, the airline made some major access changes in 2025.

Here's what you need to know about accessing United's lounges.

The Chicago-based airline operates a network of standard lounges known as United Clubs, as well as more exclusive Polaris lounges for eligible premium-cabin travelers on select long-haul international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes. Both offer complimentary food, drinks and Wi-Fi, while Polaris lounges feature additional amenities, such as sit-down dining, relaxation areas and shower suites.

So, how can travelers gain access to United's network of lounges?

You'll need a same-day boarding pass to access United lounges. This can be a same-day boarding pass for a United-operated flight or a flight operated by a Star Alliance partner airline, like Lufthansa or Swiss.

Related: Best United Airlines credit cards

United now has two tiers of paid membership for entry to the Club.

This membership offers the primary member unlimited access to all 45-plus United Club locations. There are no discounts available for United Premier members. Individual members can pay to bring guests into the lounge on a one-off basis; a one-time pass costs $59 per guest and is subject to availability.

Individual members do not have access to Star Alliance partner lounges.

Annual fee: Varies depending on Premier status

All Access members can enjoy unlimited United Club access for the primary member and up to two adult guests, or one adult and any dependents under 18.

This membership also includes access to Star Alliance partner lounges and other select partner locations, subject to applicable access policies.

Lifetime United Club members have been converted to All Access memberships.

TPG values United MileagePlus miles at 1.2 cents each per our November 2026 valuations, so your best bet is to pay the annual membership fee with cash rather than miles.

Having an eligible cobranded United credit card can be the most cost-effective way to consistently enter the United Club.

You can get lounge access with the following cards (note that some cards only offer one-time passes):

*The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Unlike a paid Individual membership, a United Club membership earned via a cobranded credit card offers a unique access policy that includes entry for primary cardmembers, one adult guest and any dependents under 18 years old.

Cardmembers can unlock an All Access membership, which increases the guest allowance and provides access to participating Star Alliance partner lounges, by earning Premier Gold status or higher, or by spending $50,000 on eligible purchases with their United Club Card or United Club Business Card in a calendar year.

Since the annual fee on both the United Club Card and the United Club Business Card is $695, having a credit card to enter the lounge remains a more attractive option than outright buying a membership.

Additionally, the United Club Card and the United Club Business Card offer four one-time passes on each account anniversary. A pass can be used by one person accompanying the primary cardholder or an authorized user into the lounge.

If you’d prefer to avoid the hefty annual fee, you can opt for the entry-level United Explorer Card or the United Business Card, both of which include two single-use United Club passes each year. Note that these day passes don’t include guest access, nor can they be transferred to friends or family who aren't authorized users or accompanying a cardmember into the lounge.

Certain MileagePlus Premier and Star Alliance Gold members can access United Clubs when traveling on eligible flights.

United Premier Gold (and higher) members can access United Clubs when traveling internationally on United or another Star Alliance carrier, regardless of their class of service. They can also bring along one guest who's traveling on the same flight.

Travelers who earn Star Alliance Gold status through another member airline can access United Clubs when flying on any eligible Star Alliance flight, including domestic United flights. Again, guests must be traveling on the same flight as the elite member.

United’s invite-only Global Services members can enjoy lounge access on all United-operated flights, including those operating exclusively within the U.S. Note that this new perk only covers the Global Services member — you’ll only be able to bring a guest into the lounge with an All Access membership, eligible cobranded credit card or when flying internationally.

Travelers flying in certain premium cabins on United or its Star Alliance partners can also access United Clubs. However, eligibility and guest privileges vary by airline, route and cabin class, as outlined below.

If you don’t travel enough to justify an annual membership, you can also purchase a one-time United Club pass for $59 per person at United Club locations or through the United mobile app. Just note that day passes don’t guarantee entry when lounge is at capacity.

Travelers using a one-time pass can enter a United Club only up to three hours before their scheduled departure time. (This exclusively applies to departure flights, and there is no time limit for entry on connecting flights.) These one-time passes are not accepted at grab-and-go locations, United Polaris lounges, United Arrivals Lounges or partner lounges.

You can also earn complimentary one-time passes with select cobranded credit cards, including:

One-time passes issued through United cobranded credit cards must be redeemed by the primary cardholder, an authorized user or a guest accompanied by either. Each pass admits one person.

United’s lounges are open to a few other travelers, including:

Some premium-class passengers also have access to United’s Polaris lounges, which offer a more premium experience. You can expect modern furnishings, private spa-like shower suites and elevated culinary options.

Three types of passengers are eligible for Polaris lounge access:

In addition to United Clubs and Polaris Lounges, the carrier operates a grab-and-go lounge concept called United Club Fly.

The first such space opened at Denver International Airport (DEN) in November 2022, and a second one opened at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in 2025. Eligible travelers can enter Club Fly by scanning their boarding pass at the self-service entry gate.

Once inside, you can head to the snack bar that’s stocked with packaged and prepared foods. You can also order a coffee from the barista.

Given Club Fly’s focus on efficiency, the access policies are a bit different. Eligible United Club members and travelers flying in international premium cabins are eligible to enter, but they cannot bring any guests.

The Chicago-based carrier operates more than 45 United Club lounge locations. Of course, you’ll find a plethora of United Clubs in the carrier’s main hubs, including:

Apart from DEN, all of the aforementioned airports also have Polaris lounges.

There are other United Club locations scattered across the U.S., including in airports such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX), Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) and Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), among others.

Check out United's website for a complete list of the airline's Club and Polaris lounge locations.

United offers a variety of ways to access its United Clubs, both for premium-cabin frequent flyers and for those with a membership.

If you frequently travel with United, it’s worth analyzing which options offer the best bang for your buck to unlock a relaxing lounge experience.

#6181. Qatar Launches Two South American Destinations

Qatar Airways added two South American destinations on Wednesday, becoming the first Gulf carrier to serve Venezuela.

The new service flies from Doha to Bogotá, Colombia, then continues to Caracas, Venezuela, before returning nonstop to Doha. Qatar Airways will operate the route on Wednesdays and Sundays using a Boeing 777-200LR.

Flights are scheduled to leave Doha at 7:35 a.m. and reach Bogotá at 4:25 p.m. After a 90-minute stop, the aircraft continues to Caracas, arriving at 9 p.m. The return flight leaves Caracas at 11:30 p.m. and reaches Doha at 8:35 p.m. the following day. All times are local.

The airline originally planned to start flying the route in July but postponed the launch following an earthquake in Venezuela, according to Aviation Week.

Qatar Airways is also expanding its codeshare with LATAM to include domestic flights from Bogotá. The agreement will put Qatar’s code on LATAM flights to destinations including Medellín, Cartagena and Cali.

The additions bring Qatar Airways’ network in the Americas to 17 destinations. The carrier began serving South America in 2010 with flights to São Paulo.

#6180. What Is A Lifestyle Hotel? The “Cool” Hotel Trend That Means Nothing

It goes without saying that the hospitality industry has a lot of trends. At times there might not actually be much substance to these trends, but the idea is that executives in the industry think certain things are “hot,” and they perceive it to reflect consumer demand.

Along those lines, if you look at trends among the major hotel groups, the concept of “lifestyle hotels” has become incredibly popular. There are an endless number of brands like these that have emerged. I think one logical question is what the term actually means. What makes a property a lifestyle hotel, rather than an… umm, not lifestyle hotel?

I know I’m generally pretty verbose and use a fairly limited vocabulary when it comes to describing things, but that’s intentional. In part, my issue is that many of the descriptors used in marketing, particularly in the travel industry, are so beyond meaningless:

My point is, we’re completely desensitized to useless descriptions of every aspect of the travel experience… unless you’re currently enjoying a seasonal fruit plate served by a private Michelin star chef on a plane, in which case I can’t save you. 😉

Anyway, that brings us to lifestyle hotels, one of the hottest trends in the hotel industry. It’s easy to name brands that claim to be lifestyle hotels — we’re talking Hilton’s Canopy and Curio Collection, Hyatt’s Andaz and Thompson, IHG’s Kimpton and voco, Marriott’s W Hotels and Autograph Collection, etc.

I guess the best way to define a lifestyle hotel would be to step back for a moment, and separate out the two words. Generally a lifestyle brand is a company that sells products by associating them with a specific way of living, set of values, or identities, that customers want to adopt.

A lifestyle hotel is generally defined as a property offering the personalization of an independent boutique hotel, with the attributes of a chain hotel (meaning loyalty, distribution power, etc.). Generally (but not always) these properties have a strong food & beverage or social concept as a core pillar, since that’s a large attribute that can make a hotel popular with a certain guest profile.

The issue with the concept of lifestyle hotels is that hotels can choose how they want to market themselves, and I think some hotels take a “fake it till you make it” approach. If you ask me, the concept of a lifestyle hotel should come down to two factors:

We can of course create all kinds of more specific distinctions, but I think it’s unnecessary. I’ve already written in the past about the concept of “boutique” hotels, another term that means so little. As far as I’m concerned, a lifestyle hotel could be small or big, as the big question is how bustling it is relative to its size.

But this also gets at the issue of how hotel groups choose to label their brands. For example, Marriott labels AC Hotels, Aloft, Autograph Collection, Element, Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, and W Hotels, all as lifestyle brands. From my perspective:

I mean, I live pretty close to a Moxy, and I’ve never thought to myself “hey family, maybe we should go to the Moxy for dinner tonight” (as much as my older son would probably love going somewhere and being able to microwave his own dinner).

So to me, these are the hotels that very much fit into the “fake it until you make it” camp. Like, the major hotel groups want to convince investors and customers that these are somehow something they aren’t. I mean, I’ve also had pleasant stays at AC Hotels properties, and that’s described as “a lifestyle brand that celebrates a new modern aesthetic complemented by a European soul and Spanish roots.” I mean… really?

Hotel groups love to grow and market their lifestyle hotel brands, but I feel like they take a lot of liberties with how they define these. On the most basic level, the idea is supposed to be that lifestyle hotels offer a boutique hotel-style experience, while being associated with one of the major brands.

However, I’d say more accurately, it’s about how much of a “destination” a property is, as that also determines the vibe of the place. I’d love if someone could help me understand just how hotel groups can in good conscience categorize some brands as being lifestyle hotels. Like, how does Marriott include AC Hotels, Autograph Collection, EDITION, and Moxy, all under that same umbrella?

How do you define the lifestyle hotel concept?

#6179. Southwest Premier Business Card Review: Is The $149 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card is the more basic of the two Southwest business cards. This card has a $149 annual fee, and gets you a handful of valuable benefits when you fly Southwest, including complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating within 48 hours of departure and a free checked bag, among other things.

If you fly Southwest at least a few times a year and you qualify for a small business credit card, the Southwest Premier Business Card is worth considering. It’s worth an extra close look right now, because now is your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the airline’s valuable Companion Pass benefit. I’ll get into all that and more below in my comprehensive Southwest Premier Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card

Before getting into the Southwest Premier Business Card in detail, let’s take a broader look at the card’s main features:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Premier Business Card:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is Southwest’s entry-level business credit card. Let’s take a look at the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and annual fee, given that these are factors that many people consider when applying for a card.

The Southwest Premier Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each, as that’s roughly the rate at which you can redeem points toward flights. So by my valuation, 60,000 Rapid Rewards points are worth ~$720.

While this is a decent welcome offer, let me note that we’ve seen bigger limited time welcome offers in the past. So if you’re primarily after the best welcome offer, it could make sense to wait to apply.

The welcome bonus on the Southwest Premier Business Card isn’t available to those who currently have this card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), or any personal Southwest credit card.

Also remember Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, apply. With the 5/24 rule, you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the last 24 months. However, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a $149 annual fee. There’s no cost to add additional users to the card. You can set individual spending limits for additional cards, and you can earn points on their spending.

The Southwest Premier Business Card doesn’t charge any foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about racking up extra charges.

Obviously the rewards structure is an important factor to consider when applying for a credit card. So how does the Southwest Premier Business Card do on that front? In addition to offering bonus points in select spending categories, the card also offers the ability to earn status through spending, so let’s cover those details.

As far as the rewards structure goes, the Southwest Premier Business Card offers:

While these are some good bonus categories, I wouldn’t consider this to be an industry-leading rewards structure — there are better cards for airfare spending, and better cards for everyday spending.

Based on my valuation of Southwest points at 1.2 cents each, using the Southwest Premier Business Card to book Southwest flights gets you a 3.6% return on spending, while the 2x and 1x categories get you 2.4% and 1.2% returns on spending, respectively.

Spending on the Southwest Premier Business Card can count toward A-List elite status. Specifically, through the end of 2026 you can earn 2,000 Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward A-List for every $5,000 you spend on the card. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on the card will earn one TQP.

A-List status ordinarily requires 35,000 TQPs per year, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

However, Southwest has announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status. Earning it will require 35,000 TQPs (unchanged) or 25 qualifying flights (up from 20 today).

Personally I probably wouldn’t spend that much money on a credit card to earn A-List status, but for some people this could prove to be worthwhile, especially if you’re close to earning A-List status otherwise.

One of the very best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With Southwest Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket), and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal, and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest. The pass is valid for the rest of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the following full year, so the earlier in the year you earn it, the more it’s worth.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, though, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Business Card; it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that points from the current welcome bonus offer do count toward Companion Pass qualification for the rest of 2026 and through 2027, per Chase’s offer details, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a solid welcome bonus that’s especially valuable now that it’s your last chance to earn it and have it count toward the Companion Pass, but that’s not the only reason to consider this card. There are also several ongoing perks that can make your experience flying Southwest a little more comfortable.

One major ongoing perk of the Southwest Premier Business Card is that you earn 6,000 Rapid Rewards bonus points on your account anniversary every year. As mentioned above, I value Rapid Rewards points at around 1.2 cents each, so to me, that’s like $72 worth of value annually.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation.

If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can help you recoup the annual fee. For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way, so you could save $90 on a roundtrip flight. With two roundtrip flights with checked bags in a year, that already cancels out the $149 annual fee.

As a Southwest Premier Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat within 48 hours prior to departure, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight.

The Southwest Premier Business Card also gets you a 15% promo code each year on your account anniversary. You can use this to score a 15% discount on a Southwest flight, excluding Basic fares. This perk is another nice way the card can save you money when flying Southwest, especially if you book cash tickets in addition to award flights at least once a year.

Southwest Premier Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. This perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers 25% savings on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases on Southwest. Just charge your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for 25% of the purchase total, which should appear within two billing cycles.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a great welcome bonus, and the $149 annual fee can be largely offset by the 6,000 anniversary bonus points and other benefits. The welcome bonus can also go a long way toward earning the Companion Pass, which is all the more reason to get the card now before this opportunity ends.

That said, I don’t necessarily think the Southwest Premier Business Card is a great pick for everyone. If you’re not loyal to Southwest or you split flying across multiple airlines, it’s probably not the best card for you. And if you want flexible points that you can redeem with a variety of airlines and hotels, it could also be best to skip this card.

First, let me compare it to the more premium Southwest Performance Business Card, then I’ll share the points currency I recommend earning instead if you’re mainly concerned with booking award flights on Southwest, not extra perks with the airline.

The Southwest Performance Business Card (learn more) is the more premium sibling of the Southwest Premier Business Card. Overall it comes with more benefits — and in some cases enhanced versions of the same perks on the Southwest Premier Business Card.

Here’s a quick overview of how the Southwest business credit cards compare:

The extra 3,000 anniversary points are worth $36 by my valuation, so you’d need roughly $9,500 in Southwest spending for the extra point per dollar to cover the rest of the $150 fee difference, before counting the seating and Global Entry perks.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and you want as many perks and points as possible, the Southwest Performance Business Card could be worth the higher annual fee.

If your goal is to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points, but you don’t actually plan on earning the Companion Pass or Southwest status, there’s a much faster way to earn those points.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. You can earn points at a much faster rate with the following business cards:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is a good entry-level Southwest Airlines business credit card with a nice welcome bonus. The current bonus can earn you a lot of travel on Southwest, and can even help you earn Companion Pass — but only if you earn the bonus under the current offer, before the 2027 program changes take effect.

This card is definitely worth considering, though the only other consideration is that I think it could be worth paying the premium for the Southwest Performance Business Card, which has better ongoing perks. And earning Ultimate Rewards points with a Chase credit card could also make more sense unless you really value the Southwest-specific benefits.

Which Southwest business credit card do you prefer?

#6178. Qantas Is Retiring Its Airbus A380s 4 Years Early Because It Trusts Its A350-1000 & Boeing 787 Deliveries

The Airbus A380 should have no place in contemporary aviation's point-to-point model, made possible by advanced twin-jet aircraft. However, some airlines continue to fly the A380. Korean Air has pushed the type's exit back from 2026 to 2031, and Lufthansa won't start retiring the A380 until well into the 2030s.

Qantas has bucked this trend by bringing its scheduled A380 retirement date forward to mid-2028. The reason for this disparity lies in the aircraft that different airlines plan to use to fill the capacity gap left by retiring A380s. For instance, both Lufthansa and Korean Air have substantial Boeing 777X orders.

As such, they have been forced into an A380 extension by the ongoing delays plaguing the program. Meanwhile, Qantas has opted for the already-operational Airbus A350 and Boeing 787 programs. Able to fill capacity gaps with these jets, the airline can retire the A380 on its schedule. Qantas has declined to comment on this.

Qantas had previously planned to keep flying its A380 fleet into 2032. However, this August, it announced a pull-back to mid-2028, as reported by Aerospace Global News. The move has been facilitated by the successful deployment of A350s and the arrival of additional Dreamliners into the fleet.

The A380 retirements will be progressive, meaning that the first of Qantas' ten-aircraft A380 fleet will be retired in March 2028, with the rest following over the subsequent months. Qantas hasn't set any specific dates beyond its first A380 retirement, giving it a high degree of flexibility should circumstances change further.

Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson has said that the need to retire the A380s has been caused by the challenging economics of flying older four-engined aircraft in the second half of the 2020s. “The A380 is an older aircraft, and so the cost of those aircraft over time will increase in terms of maintenance,” she said. She hopes that eliminating this additional cost will contribute to improving the carrier's margins to 10% to 12% by FY2032.

The arrival of A350s and 787s will provide a replacement for Qantas' A380s. The carrier has firm orders for 24 A350s and 12 787s, Aerospace Global News reports. Half of the A350 orders are for the Airbus A350-1000ULR jets, capable of completing the nonstop Project Sunrise flights from Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and New York JFK Airport(JFK).

Qantas is also in active discussions with Boeing and Airbus to convert 20 existing purchase-right options into firm orders, with the jets arriving in 2030. The table below shows the carrier's current fleet (without the additional 787s and A350s), showing how it operates while the airline still flies A380s, based on data from Planespotters.net. When Qantas made the orders in 2023, Alan Joyce, Qantas Group's CEO at the time, said:

“Both the 787 and A350, and the GE and Rolls-Royce engines fitted to them, are thoroughly proven and extremely capable. (...) These are generational decisions for this company. The aircraft will be part of the fleet for 20 years."

It's important to note that, given the lower capacity of the A350 and the Dreamliner compared with the A380, these jets will not offer like-for-like replacement. However, they will be able to operate every route currently carried out by the A380, while also providing the flexibility needed to open new routes.

Both Qantas and British Airways are reconfiguring their A380s to cut economy seating.

The absence of 777Xs from Qantas' order sheet has provided an option, but that does not mean the decision to retire the A380 wasn't forced. Overshadowing everything has been a reduction in pre-tax profits. This has mainly been the result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has forced oil and jet fuel prices higher.

Fuel hedging has not been able to offset all of this increase. The table below uses data from Qantas' Investor Centre to show the airline's key results for FY2026. It shows hundreds of millions in profit reductions compared with last financial year.

A$2.064 billion ($1.45 billion) - down A$330m ($232 million)

A$1.29 billion ($907 million) - down A$319m ($224 million)

Qantas Domestic +7 ppts; Qantas International +5 ppts; Jetstar Domestic Flat; Jetstar International +6 ppts

Unpredictable fuel and maintenance costs have hit the A380 particularly hard, given that this enormous jet is unbelievably thirsty. Meanwhile, increasing the number of highly efficient twin-jet planes in the Qantas fleet will reduce its reliance on unhedged fuel supplies, making the airline much more resilient to geopolitical crises that upset the oil market.

Worse than having to retire expensive aircraft early due to poor profitability is being unable to retire these expensive jets despite poor profitability. Lufthansa is a notable example that has become stuck with the A380 while it waits for the 777X to arrive. Lufthansa's 777X delivery expectations remain in the first quarter of 2027, but that does not mean the airline thinks it will begin flying them that year.

Tygart Media reports that the Lufthansa summer 2027 schedule does not include the 777X. Worse than continuing to fly the A380 as a result, Lufthansa is also keeping its Airbus A340-300s flying to deal with the capacity gap. The table below shows the widebody Lufthansa fleet as it exists before the delivery of the 777Xs.

It's important to note the advanced age of these jets, with only the 787 and A350 pulling the average age down. As airlines feel increasing pain without their expected 777X aircraft, Boeing will suffer with them, even as some aircraft have already been built but may be undeliverable. Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr said:

"Like our friends in Dubai, we are in talks with Boeing about which of these airplanes we will not be accepting for commercial service and which of these aircraft will be able to be modernised. And then, of course, with the financial contribution of Boeing, we would be willing to take."

Time is running out for passengers wanting to fly on one of the Australian flag carrier's superjumbos, especially from Melbourne.

An airline with a slightly less acute A380 problem caused by 777X delays is Korean Air, which has five A380s in service. This airline also has an aging fleet of 15 747s. The original plan set for 2021 was for the A380 to retire by 2026 and the 747 to retire by 2031. This has been pushed back in response to delivery delays and Korean Air's takeover of Asiana (which had a fleet of six A380s), One Mile At A Time reports.

The carrier's A380s continue to selectively serve high-capacity routes. A capacity gap has emerged because of delivery delays. In August 2025, the airline made its largest order for new aircraft ever, as AviTrader reported at the time. The order included 20 Boeing 777-9s, along with 25 787-10s, 50 737-10s, and eight 777-8F.

Walter Cho, the Chairperson and CEO of Korean Air, said that "acquiring these next-generation aircraft is the core of our fleet modernisation strategy, delivering significant gains in fuel efficiency and enhancing the passenger experience across our global network." However, these benefits are meaningless while Korean Air waits for these planes to be delivered.

Lufthansa and Korean Air will find it hard to contemplate the retirement of their A380s until their ordered 777Xs start to arrive. After the official launch in 2013, the 777X was supposed to enter service in 2020. Yet, the program has faced numerous regulatory hurdles and setbacks.

Most recently, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has said that the 777X will not be certified this year, as it will follow the certification of the Boeing 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10. This new certification timeline puts the expected first deliveries of the 777X in 2027 at risk. Lufthansa will be uniquely impacted by the change in schedule. It is the launch customer.

Production standard 777X jets have already been built for Lufthansa. In May 2026, the first one built completed a three-hour maiden flight at Everett, Washington. It has also been fully outfitted with Lufthansa's cabin. As the first to receive a 777X, Lufthansa will get its jet into revenue service first, but will have to serve as the aircraft type's pioneer.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Korean Air sits further back in the delivery queue when compared with early customers like Emirates, Qatar Airways and Cathay Pacific. It won't receive its 777Xs as soon as the aircraft enters service, and may have to wait a year or more depending on the speed of production.

#6177. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?
