#6175. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit.

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

#6172. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

#6168. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

#6167. How Emirates Safeguards Its Longest Airbus A380 Route With A Little-Known Fallback

Operating the world's longest Airbus A380 route is an achievement that demands far more than simply assigning the aircraft with the greatest passenger capacity. Every flight between Dubai International Airport (DXB) and Auckland Airport (AKL) requires careful planning, significant fuel reserves, favorable weather conditions, and enough operational flexibility to cope with changing winds across thousands of miles of ocean and remote airspace.

While the nonstop service often attracts attention because of its remarkable duration, the supporting strategy behind it is equally noteworthy. Since launching the route in 2016, Emirates has quietly maintained an alternative network that allows passengers to reach New Zealand even when the airline adjusts nonstop operations.

Rather than relying exclusively on a single ultra-long-haul flight, the Dubai-based carrier has preserved one-stop connections through Australia, creating a practical fallback that strengthens resilience while giving planners greater freedom to respond to operational challenges and changing market demand.

The nonstop route between DXB and AKL has occupied a unique position within Emirates' network since its introduction in March 2016. Covering approximately 8,800 miles (14,162 km), the flight represents the airline's longest scheduled A380 operation and remains among the longest commercial flights operated anywhere in the world.

Although the eastbound journey from Auckland to Dubai is lengthy in its own right, the westbound flight usually presents the greater challenge because of prevailing winds across the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia. Under favorable conditions, the journey can be completed in a little over 17 hours, but strong headwinds have regularly extended block times to around 17 hours and 25 minutes.

This makes every departure a carefully planned balancing act involving payload, fuel, weather forecasts, and air traffic considerations. These operational realities mean that dispatchers cannot simply schedule the same aircraft performance every day throughout the year. Seasonal wind patterns influence fuel requirements, while unexpected weather systems may require revised routings that add additional flying time.

Even relatively small changes become significant on flights lasting well over 17 hours, where every additional minute increases fuel consumption and operational complexity. Despite these challenges, Emirates has continued to assign the A380 exclusively to the route.

This highlights the carrier's confidence in the aircraft's capabilities. The double-decker provides substantial passenger capacity across premium and economy cabins while also offering the range needed for one of commercial aviation's most demanding missions.

While the nonstop route receives the majority of public attention, Emirates has never depended on it as the sole means of serving Auckland. Instead, the airline has continued operating extensive services into Australia's largest cities, allowing passengers to connect onward to New Zealand whenever necessary.

Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) has traditionally played the most prominent role within this strategy thanks to its extensive schedule from Dubai and its large volume of connecting passengers. Emirates also maintains significant operations into Melbourne Airport (MEL) and Brisbane Airport (BNE), creating multiple pathways for travelers heading toward Auckland without requiring the airline to depend entirely on the nonstop service.

This approach gives Emirates an established backup within its broader network rather than requiring special contingency planning whenever operational conditions become less favorable. If schedules change or nonstop frequencies are reduced, passengers can still travel between Dubai and Auckland through Australian gateways using connections that have long been integrated into the airline's system.

The arrangement also benefits customers originating outside Dubai, as Emirates carries passengers from across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia through its Dubai hub before distributing them across its long-haul network. Having several onward routing options increases flexibility throughout the reservation system and helps minimize disruption when demand patterns shift.

Flights lasting more than 17 hours leave little room for operational uncertainty. Airline planners must consider aircraft performance, passenger loads, cargo demand, weather forecasts, alternate airports, and regulatory fuel requirements before every departure. Unlike shorter international routes, adjustments cannot easily be absorbed once the aircraft is airborne because diversion options remain limited across large stretches of ocean.

Headwinds represent one of the most important variables affecting Dubai-Auckland operations, and strong winds opposing the aircraft increase fuel burn and can reduce operational margins, particularly on the westbound sector. As a result, planners continuously evaluate expected atmospheric conditions before finalizing payload and fuel calculations.

Maintaining one-stop alternatives through Australia provides an additional layer of flexibility within this process, as rather than insisting that every passenger travel nonstop regardless of operating conditions, Emirates can adapt schedules according to seasonal requirements while continuing to offer reliable service between Dubai and New Zealand.

The strategy also supports efficient fleet utilization. A380 examples represent valuable assets that must be allocated carefully across the airline's global network. Having multiple routing options allows Emirates to deploy aircraft where demand is strongest while preserving connectivity even when operational priorities evolve during different times of the year.

Four out of the seven routes use the Boeing 787.

Although the Australian connection strategy remains in place, passenger demand has increasingly favored the nonstop option. As international travel continued to recover and long-haul markets strengthened, Emirates gradually expanded nonstop operations between Dubai and Auckland.

A significant milestone arrived earlier this year, when the airline increased the route to daily A380 service. The schedule expansion reflected confidence in sustained demand while demonstrating that the economics of operating one of the world's longest flights remained attractive despite its considerable operating costs.

Even with daily nonstop flights, however, the underlying network philosophy has not changed. The Australian gateways continue serving an important role by providing additional capacity, supporting passengers whose itineraries involve Australian destinations, and preserving operational resilience whenever circumstances require adjustments. Rather than replacing the connecting model, the expanded non-stop schedule complements it.

Together, both options create a network that can accommodate different passenger preferences while allowing Emirates to respond to changes in demand without sacrificing connectivity across the region. The result is a system that balances efficiency with redundancy, ensuring that one of the airline's most ambitious routes remains supported by a broader operational framework rather than existing in isolation.

Many airlines have reduced or retired A380 fleets over the past decade, yet Emirates has remained firmly committed to the type as the flagship of its long-haul operation. No carrier operates more A380s, and the aircraft continues serving numerous high-demand destinations throughout Europe, Asia, Australia, and North America.

The Dubai-Auckland route showcases many of the aircraft's strengths. Its combination of long range and high seating capacity allows Emirates to transport hundreds of passengers on a single flight while offering premium products that include onboard lounges and shower spas for first-class travelers.

Operating such a large aircraft on an ultra-long-haul route also improves efficiency when passenger demand supports high load factors. Instead of scheduling multiple smaller aircraft, Emirates can concentrate capacity into a single daily departure while maintaining a consistent onboard product across the route. The airline's continuing investment in cabin refurbishment programs further reinforces the importance of the A380 within its future plans.

Updated interiors, refreshed premium cabins, and modernized economy seating help ensure that the aircraft remains competitive despite its age, particularly on flights where passenger comfort becomes increasingly important after more than 17 hours in the air. As detailed in the table above, Emirates currently has a total of 116 Airbus A380s in its fleet, according to ch-aviation.

Why the Airbus A350-1000’s range, efficiency, and comfort can make it the ideal aircraft for Emirates’ ultra-long-haul global network.

From a passenger perspective, the non-stop Dubai-Auckland service appears to be a single record-setting flight linking two distant cities. Behind the scenes, however, it functions as one component within a much larger network built around flexibility, redundancy, and efficient aircraft utilization.

The continued availability of Australian connections demonstrates that successful ultra-long-haul operations depend as much on network planning as aircraft performance. By maintaining multiple routing options through Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane, Emirates reduces dependence on any single schedule while preserving service continuity across the broader region.

This philosophy has allowed the airline to adjust non-stop frequencies over time without abandoning the market or compromising connectivity. Whether operating fewer non-stop flights during certain periods or increasing the service to daily A380 departures when demand supports expansion, Emirates retains an established fallback that has been part of its strategy since the route first launched in 2016.

Rather than viewing the Australian services as competitors to the non-stop flight, Emirates has positioned them as complementary components of a broader network. That combination enables the airline to continue operating one of commercial aviation's most demanding Airbus A380 routes while maintaining the operational resilience needed for flights that regularly spend well over 17 hours in the air.

#6165. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6164. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

#6162. $12,000 Buffalo–New York Fares Making Headlines—I’m Finding Nonstops For $337 Roundtrip

A $12,203 airfare between Buffalo and New York about 300 miles each way – is going viral as evidence of how expensive it’s gotten to fly home for the holidays. The TikTok video that started it off though shows a roundtrip price (not one-way) and connecting both directions in Florida (not non-stop). Meanwhile, nonstops on that route seem to start at $337 roundtrip. Kristen Mirand says she was trying to get home to Buffalo and received a notification for a $200 flight from New York. Then she looked at returning, and found five-figure prices with connections in Orlando and Fort Lauderdale. She joked that she’d start walking. The New York Post ran with “Flight from Buffalo to NYC reportedly reached $12K — as holiday airfare hits an all-time high” and suggests higher fuel costs and holiday demand are involved here. ZeroHedge describes a “roughly 90 minute flight,” and launches into airlines keeping fares high after fuel prices fall. It ends with the prospect of airlines “laughing all the way to the bank.” Look at the flights actually displayed in the video: $11,400 roundtrip, returning through Orlando. These are 7 and 9 hour trips from Buffalo to JFK. $12,203 roundtrip, returning through Fort Lauderdale. These are 7 and 8.5 hour trips. Every price is labeled round trip. you’re seeing the cost of the whole ticket when you select a return. This wasn’t a $12,000 nonstop and none of these itineraries gets you there in 90 minutes. I’m seeing nonstop roundtrips around $337 on Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, United Airlines and American Airlines, checking across the New York airports. Even if you want to connect in Florida, Frontier Airlines can be as low as $210 roundtrip. She doesn’t show her dates, but at those prices be flexible! My guess is that the pricing is breaking somewhere as the system puts together this unnatural itinerary. A fare between Buffalo and New York comes with rules about how you can travel and Florida connections aren’t usually included in the routing rules. A search can wind up combining separate fares for different pieces of the trip instead of using the simple fare between the two cities. Bad fare combining or an error putting together the outbound and return can cause weird outcomes. While the last seats on a flight can be expensive, “last seat available” doesn’t seem like the explanation for a $12,000 Buffalo–New York price. Airfares are up. Hopper’s says Thanksgiving domestic roundtrips average $402, up 31%, and Christmas $452, up 23%. With millions of fare quotes being generated, even a tiny error rate is going to produce outlier results. Mistake fares can be fares that are too high, not just too low. Faced with a fare like this, I’d: Search for nonstops on the date I actually want. Start with the trip I’d choose to take before considering a seven-hour detour. Check JFK, LaGuardia and Newark. Restricting the search to one airport leaves out alternatives that may work just as well. Search the airline websites directly. See whether the airline produces the same price, rather than treating one Google Flights result as the answer. Start a fresh search and compare one-ways with the roundtrip. Check the dates, cabin, passenger count and currency. Separate searches can get you away from whatever combination generated the nonsense price. For this route I’d also price Amtrak’s Empire Service between Buffalo and New York. Those Florida connections already consume most of the day before you add getting to the airport, security and the trip into Manhattan. #6161. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

For small-business owners who love to fly with American Airlines, the (see rates and fees) should be in your crosshairs.

It's an affordable card with no annual fee for the first cardholder year (then a $99 annual fee; this fee increases to a $150 annual fee for renewals after Jan. 24, 2027). That gives you a chance to try out its free checked bags, preferred boarding and bonus miles on several common business expenses without committing to a fee for the first year.

But because it overlaps heavily with the airline perks on personal American Airlines cards, it makes the most sense for side hustlers and small businesses that don’t already carry a similar credit card or those looking to add to their mileage balance through business spending. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

The offers a moderate set of benefits without the treasure trove of partner offers, elite status boosts and lounge perks found on more premium cards.

This card's benefits favor travelers who prefer to fly with American Airlines, but it doesn't require a full commitment to the airline thanks to its manageable annual fee (after the first cardholder year).

In addition to the benefits just mentioned, cardholders have access to these perks:

The is a mid-tier airline card with standout perks like free checked bags, no-additional-fee employee cards and Loyalty Points on spending.

Given that checking bags with American costs at least $45 per bag one-way, you can practically recoup this card's annual fee after the first cardholder year by checking a bag on three one-way flights. If you travel with an employee or another companion, it becomes easy to extract even more value — assuming you would otherwise pay for checked bags.

You'll need to spend $30,000 in a cardholder year to earn a companion certificate ($99 plus taxes and fees). That's an incredibly high spending requirement for a mid-tier card that earns just 1 mile per dollar on nonbonus purchases.

The card includes basic business management resources, but its benefits still lean heavily toward American Airlines travel rather than premium business tools.

You won’t get statement credits for business partners or other features offered by more robust business cards. From a perks standpoint, the Citi / AAdvantage Business is extremely similar to the personal , though the earning rates are better suited to business spending.

The earns miles in a relatively broad selection of categories. Cardholders earn:

Starting Jan. 24, 2027, the card is undergoing a refresh that will add two new bonus-earning categories.

There aren't many cards that offer bonus earnings on telecommunication services, so the AAdvantage Business is a viable option for those expenses. Cardholders could also get a lot of value out of the choice category once it launches in 2027. You'll be able to select your preferred earnings category and can change it once a quarter, if you prefer. All the options overlap nicely with common business purchases.

Ironically, this card may not be the best option for American Airlines airfare. Some cards outearn it, such as the .

Remember that you'll earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent on all purchases, helping you get closer to elite status with American.

When it's time to redeem the miles you earn, your best bet is to book award flights. In addition to flights operated by American Airlines, you can use your miles on partner airlines such as Alaska Airlines or Finnair.

TPG credit cards writer Becky Pokora recently redeemed 55,000 miles for a one-way trip from Johannesburg (JNB) to Berlin (BER) in business class on Oneworld partner Qatar Airways for travel in 2027. That’s more than 14 hours in a premium cabin for fewer miles than you can earn through the card’s introductory offer.

You can also use your AAdvantage miles for flight upgrades, hotels, car rentals, vacation packages, cruises and Admirals Club passes. Aside from cabin upgrades on flights, these options generally provide less value than award flights.

The Citi / AAdvantage Business will become more useful after its 2027 refresh, but its annual fee is rising from $99 to $150. That makes it harder to justify if you don’t use the new inflight or Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credits.

Most purchases will still earn just 1 mile per dollar, and only one of the three selectable business categories can earn 2 miles per dollar at a time.

Related: Which AAdvantage card is right for you? Here are 3 options you should consider

The AAdvantage Business and Platinum Select share most of their airline perks, so the decision comes down to whether you need a business account, which bonus categories fit your spending and whether you value the Business card’s companion certificate or the Platinum Select’s new lifestyle perks.

The Platinum Select, though, has stronger rewards on restaurant spending and will add bonus spending categories for select streaming services, electric vehicle charging and eligible rides and rails purchases beginning Jan. 24, 2027.

You'll still get free checked bags, preferred boarding, Loyalty Points on card spending and inflight savings with the Platinum Select.

Choose the Citi / AAdvantage Business if you want to separate your business expenses, add employee cards and earn bonus miles on more business-specific purchases, like telecommunications, U.S. advertising, U.S. shipping or office supplies.

The Platinum Select is the better fit if you don’t need a business account. Because their core American Airlines benefits overlap, most travelers won’t need both.

The Citi / AAdvantage Business is worth it for small-business owners who fly American often enough to use the airline benefits. The addition of statement credits toward eligible inflight purchases could provide more value to offset the annual fee, even though that cost is going up in 2027.

At $150 after the first year, it will be less compelling for cardholders who already receive similar American Airlines perks from another card or via elite status. It’s also not ideal as an everyday spending card, since most purchases earn just 1 mile per dollar spent.

For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. This offer is the highest we've seen in the card’s recent public offers, making it an excellent time to apply.

According to TPG's November 2026 valuations, these bonus miles are worth $1,088.

Before submitting your application, make sure to consider Citi's application rules.

I've already mentioned the Platinum Select as a strong competitor, but here are some other options to think about:

For additional options, check out our picks for the best American Airlines cards and the best travel rewards cards.

The upcoming refresh will make the Citi / AAdvantage Business more versatile—but also more expensive. Its new business bonus category and statement credits can justify the upcharge for frequent American flyers who will use them naturally. The free checked bag benefit can also offset the annual fee, especially when employees or companions travel on the same reservation.

If you already have an AAdvantage card, you might not find the AAdvantage Business as compelling. But if this is your first foray into American Airlines' cards, it's worth giving the AAdvantage Business a shot.

#6157. Former China Eastern Chairman Jailed In $10+ Million Bribery Scandal

The former chairman of China Eastern Airlines has been sentenced to 14 years in jail, as he accepted more than $10 million in bribes in his official role. Yowzers!

A court in China’s Liaoning Province has sentenced former China Eastern chairman Liu Shaoyong to prison. The court ruled that he accepted over $10 million in bribes in his official capacity as chairman of one of China’s largest airlines.

The court found that between 2002 and 2023, Liu abused his position at the airline to provide assistance to companies and individuals in business operations, project contracts, and flight route management. Liu has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and has been ordered to pay a fine of $600K, plus his illicit gains and related proceeds have to be recovered.

While the court ruled that his conduct constituted bribery “in an exceedingly large amount,” the sentence he got was actually lighter than it could’ve been, due to mitigating circumstances. These include his confession, voluntary disclosure of previously unknown offenses, and expression of remorse and cooperation in recovering illicit gains.

Make of this what you will, but it’s interesting to note that this is all part of China’s “anti-corruption campaign,” targeting officials at various levels, including executives of state-owned enterprises.

In June 2025, Liu had been placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision, for violations of party discipline and state laws. In January 2026, he was expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), after investigators found that he had abused his authority for personal gain, and he was formally charged in May 2026.

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, after he admitted to taking over $10 million in bribes in his official role. This came as part of a larger crackdown by the government, which also saw the executive expelled from the Communist Party of China.

Over the years we’ve seen a decent number of airline executives charged with corruption — after all, they control a lot of spending, and in some cases, might get influenced for the wrong reasons.

What do you make of this punishment for China Eastern’s former chairman?

#6154. Air Serbia Flight To Moscow Diverts After Politician Reportedly Skips Security

An Air Serbia flight that was supposed to fly from Serbia to Russia ended up turning around over Lithuania, in order for additional security checks to be carried out on passengers. The circumstances surrounding this sure are unusual, given who was onboard.

This incident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and involves Air Serbia flight JU134, scheduled to fly from Belgrade (BEG) to Moscow (SVO). The 1,074-mile flight was operated by an Airbus A320 with the registration code YU-APH. The flight was scheduled to depart at 6:25PM and land at 11:40PM, with a two hour time change, so it was blocked at 3hr15min.

The plane took off at 6:48PM, basically on schedule, and it started flying north, over Hungary, Slovakia, Poland, and then Lithuania. However, around 90 minutes after takeoff, while more than halfway, the plane u-turned, and flew back toward Belgrade.

The plane ended up landing in Belgrade at 9:57PM local time, a little over three hours after it first departed. The plane ended up once again taking off in the early morning hours of November 4, departing at 1:56AM, and landing at 6:43AM, over seven hours behind schedule.

Diversions happen, though it’s definitely unusual for a flight to turn around to the origin when it’s already more than halfway to its destination, especially when maintenance wasn’t to blame. Officially, the airline has shared that the decision to divert was made “in accordance with the instructions received and all applicable security rules.” That’s obviously really vague, though… so what really happened?

Here’s where the story gets really interesting. Onboard this Air Serbia flight were a few associates of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, who just recently lost an election. One of the people onboard was Aleksandar Vulin, who served as deputy prime minister until 2025, and is viewed as being very pro-Russia. The US had even imposed sanctions on him due to his close ties with Russia.

Media reports in Serbia suggest that the reason for the diversion was that security camera footage at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport had been reviewed, and it was determined that someone had helped him avoid security checks. Now, I understand the need to carry out security checks, though I’m also not sure the point of diverting when you’re already more than halfway to your destination.

Vulin denies that he was the reason that the plane diverted, claiming that it was instead a political showdown. After the diversion, he went on national TV in Serbia, to say the following:

“It’s all a lie, an act of violence and an attempt to prove to these new authorities how ready they are here at the airport, how much they are on the defensive of their ideology. So, of course it’s all a lie, of course it’s all utter nonsense. I’m really sorry and uncomfortable, so many people have returned, their lives are being ruined, their obligations are being ruined because of the attempt to politically deal with me.”

“I am completely calm, I know that I am in the right. And you know, I did not go to Moscow as a tourist, I went on business. I am going there to fight for the extension of the gas agreement. Not for me and you, but for all citizens of Serbia.”

He also said he was asleep at the time of the diversion, and had no clue what was going on until the plane landed back in Belgrade:

“We just woke up, to be honest, I fell asleep. I was sleeping on the plane, I wake up, they say: You are in Belgrade. How are you in Belgrade? When we went outside, I see the police, the special forces gathered. I say: ‘Colleagues, have you come for me?’ They laugh. They say: ‘We are not, Minister.’ I go down with all the other passengers. I go through the procedure with all the other passengers again. I go through another procedure by myself. And now, I am standing and waiting for them to let us get on the plane again.”

An Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Moscow turned around while over halfway to its destination. The decision to divert was made in accordance with “applicable security rules,” and all passengers were screened when the plane landed back in Serbia.

While it’s believed that a pro-Russia Serbian politician who was onboard may have avoided security checks at the airport, the politician denies that, and claims this was a political move.

What do you make of this unusual Air Serbia diversion?

#6151. Is World Of Hyatt Points + Cash Worth It? The Value Varies Wildly

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night redemptions, the program also has a Points + Cash option, whereby you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay.

The reality is that the value of Hyatt Points + Cash has fluctuated significantly over the years. Going back a decade, it was the primary way that I redeemed my points. Then it was devalued significantly, and then some value was brought back. So I’d like to take a look at the current state of things… is Hyatt Points + Cash worth considering nowadays?

As the name suggests, with Hyatt Points + Cash, you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a Hyatt stay. More specifically, you’ll redeem 50% of the points required for a stay, and will receive a 30-50% discount off the standard rate for the room type chosen.

Now, there are some important things to be aware of:

Just as a reminder, below is the standard room World of Hyatt award chart, which shows the award pricing for a free night hotel stay based on which of the five pricing tiers applies for a particular night (lowest, low, moderate, upper, or top).

When booking Points + Cash, you’d pay half of the points, plus 50-70% of the flexible revenue rate, so below is that chart.

With the basics of Hyatt Points + Cash out of the way, let’s do some number crunching. Let me state upfront that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each, though I usually get quite a bit more value out of them in comparison to what a hotel stay would cost with cash.

For the purposes of the below examples, I’ll simply be comparing the cost for a free night redemption to the cost of a Points + Cash redemption. This doesn’t consider the outright cost of a stay if paying cash, so for more on that, see my post about when you should redeem points for a hotel stay.

I picked six hotels at random, belonging to different brands and in different regions. I picked totally random dates, so let’s take a look at what I found.

For the night I picked, the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay is charging 15,000 points per night, or 7,500 points plus $103 ($116 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 7,500 extra points to save $116, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.55 cents each.

The Park Hyatt Los Cabos is charging 55,000 points per night, or 27,500 points plus $500.50 ($680.68 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 27,500 extra points to save $680.68, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.48 cents each.

The Hyatt Studios Mobile is charging 3,000 points per night, or 1,500 points plus $61 ($71.98 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 1,500 extra points to save $71.98, which is like buying Hyatt points for 4.8 cents each.

The Thompson Rome is charging 35,000 points per night, or 17,500 points plus $281.20 (that includes taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 17,500 extra points to save $281.20, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.61 cents each.

The Hyatt Centric Dubai Jumeirah is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $115 ($145.14 including taxes & fees). You’re spending $145.14 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.45 cents each.

The Grand Hyatt Seoul is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $221 (that includes taxes & fees). You’re spending $221 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.21 cents each.

As you can see, the value of Hyatt Points + Cash varies significantly. In the above six examples I randomly pulled up, you’re essentially “buying” Hyatt points for anywhere from 1.45 cents to 4.8 cents each (these aren’t actually points in your account, but rather you’re spending some amount of cash in lieu of points).

So the idea is that if the “purchase” price on points were relatively low, it could be worth booking Points + Cash, rather than just redeeming outright. On the low end of the spectrum, some people might find this to be worthwhile, though I think on the high end of the spectrum, we can all agree this represents an awful deal.

Before you make a final decision, just keep in mind:

Lastly, let me just mention that in many cases Points + Cash is a better value compared to redeeming points outright in situations where the cash rate is lower than usual, and a hotel is in low season. In those situations it might not make sense to redeem points at all. This comes down to how reimbursement for these awards works between World of Hyatt and individual hotels.

For example, the single best Points + Cash deal above is at the Hyatt Centric Dubai, but if you look at the cash rate, you’ll see that redeeming points isn’t a great deal in the first place. There’s no reason to redeem 20,000 points (or 10,000 points plus $115) when the cash rate in the first place is well under $200.

Hyatt Points + Cash lets you redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay. While it’s nice to have the flexibility of this redemption opportunity, more often than not it doesn’t represent a good deal, in my opinion.

The value you’re getting per point through Points + Cash does vary wildly, but one thing that’s fairly consistent is that you won’t get outsized value. In a majority of situations where Points + Cash represents a good deal compared to the outright points cost, it’s a hotel where a points redemption isn’t a good deal in the first place.

Personally, I avoid Points + Cash redemptions, though it’s always worth checking and crunching the numbers.

What’s your take on Hyatt’s Points + Cash option? Do you ever use it?

#6148. Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points Double Dip Explained

The single best way to earn American AAdvantage Loyalty Points with credit card spending often flies under the radar, so I’d like to talk a little more about that in this post, especially since this tends to cause some confusion. Furthermore, this was recently made an “official” card perk, rather than something that just unofficially applied to most cardmembers.

Link: Double dip your Loyalty Points earning with the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

With the American AAdvantage Loyalty Points program, you can typically earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on a co-branded American credit card. However, there’s one card that’s an exception, and by far the best.

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more) is the co-branded Citi and American Airlines business card. There’s a quirk to the card, though, when it comes to authorized user rewards. On the surface, the authorized user ordinarily earns the Loyalty Points for their spending, and not the primary cardmember, which is an unusual policy for a small business card.

However, through December 31, 2028 (and it’s possible this will be extended again, as it has been in the past), both the primary cardmember and the authorized user earn Loyalty Points for authorized user spending. It basically means you earn two Loyalty Points per dollar spent, just in different accounts. Just to be abundantly clear here:

So the key is for the spending to be on the authorized user’s card, so that this spending unlocks double Loyalty Points (spread across two accounts).

Either way, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers several valuable perks, and also has an excellent welcome bonus, making it a good time to apply. So if you are eligible, I’d consider applying even if the double Loyalty Points opportunity doesn’t work out (though hopefully it does).

Personally, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points double dip is how I qualified for AAdvantage elite status last year. I had a hard time justifying putting spending onto co-branded American cards compared to some other cards out there, when I was only earning one Loyalty Point per dollar.

But if I can qualify for elite status for two people at once, and earn the corresponding Loyalty Point Rewards perks, the math on that spending starts to look much better:

For example, earning 250,000 Loyalty Points per account could potentially earn you a combined total of 12 systemwide upgrades or 170,000 bonus miles. That’s a pretty substantial reward, beyond just the miles you earn for spending and the status!

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers an easy opportunity to double dip Loyalty Points earning through authorized user spending. This opportunity is available to all cardmembers, and is currently valid through December 31, 2028 (though has the potential to be extended beyond that). This is a great opportunity, so if you’re pursuing AAdvantage elite status, I’d highly recommend this method.

Have you been taking advantage of this Loyalty Points double dip opportunity?

#6147. Senator Chris Murphy “awake and alert” after suffering a stroke

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized after suffering a stroke Saturday afternoon while attending his son’s hockey game, his office announced Sunday.

The 53-year-old senator began experiencing numbness in his arm and was taken to a local hospital, where doctors determined he had suffered a stroke. He was subsequently transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for further monitoring.

“He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment,” Murphy’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said in a statement.

Chris Murphy’s chief says the 53-year-old Democratic senator had a stroke.

“Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”

“The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” she added.

Murphy is actually the fourth Senate Democrat to suffer a stroke in recent years. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland both suffered strokes in 2022 and subsequently recovered. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania also suffered a stroke that year while campaigning for office and now uses live-captioning technology to assist with auditory processing during Senate proceedings.

Murphy, who has represented Connecticut in the Senate since 2013, has emerged as a prominent Democratic voice on gun control and immigration. He is also considered a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The senator has spent recent weeks campaigning for Democratic candidates ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. He was scheduled to appear Sunday in New Hampshire alongside Democratic candidates Chris Pappas and Stefany Shaheen. Murphy is not on Tuesday’s ballot.

Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont, who campaigned alongside Murphy on Friday, said he and his wife were keeping the senator and his family in their prayers.

Lawmakers from both parties also expressed support, including Sens. John Fetterman, D-Pa., and Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa.

Murphy’s office has not announced a timeline for his release from the hospital.

#6146. Hotel CEOs Reveal Where They Think Travel Is Headed—But AI Could Make Them Lower Room Prices

GHA Discovery asked hotel CEOs what will shape their business over the next few years, and 87% expect AI assistants to be among the most important booking channels by 2030. They expect hotel websites and loyalty programs to matter more than online travel agencies. Hotels would love to stop paying commissions to Expedia and Booking.com. But I think they’re overlooking how much harder a sufficiently capable AI will make it to charge customers more than they need to pay. Hotels may get more direct bookings while earning less from each guest booking direct. The short GHA Hotel Brand CEO Outlook 2027 is worth reading. GHA Discovery connects about 60 brands and 1,000 hotels, including Kempinski, Anantara, Capella, Pan Pacific, NH and smaller groups like Lore. I think the program gets far less attention than it deserves and I’ve had some fantastic stays. What Hotel CEOs Expect This was an August survey of 30 CEOs from GHA brands: They’re worried, but still expect growth. 90% named geopolitical instability among their biggest challenges over the next five years. Nearly half expect like-for-like hotel revenue to grow at least 5% in 2027. (Notably, GHA itself is based in Dubai.) International leisure travel is the growth engine. 73% expect international demand to outperform domestic, and 90% expect international leisure travel to increase. India is almost as widely cited as the United States. 53% named the U.S. as a source of international growth, versus 50% for India and 40% each for China and the U.K. AI is expected to dominate hotel discovery. For influence on bookings in 2030, AI assistants scored 87%, hotel websites and apps 50%, loyalty platforms 47%, and online travel agencies 30%. Loyalty matters, and recognition leads their list of differentiators. 83% consider loyalty critical or very important to revenue growth. Recognition was selected by 70% as a factor distinguishing successful programs, versus 57% for personalization and 47% for rewards. India is significant, a small share of a very large population crossing the income threshold for international travel produces a lot of customers. India had 32.83 million departures by Indian nationals in 2025, up 6.3%. And the number of people there worth more than $30 million grew 63% between 2021 and 2026. The opportunity comes from the number of people who can afford to travel, rather than population numbers themselves. The finding in the report I’m skeptical of is only 13% selecting price as a leading influence on hotel decisions in 2030. Unless money just no longer matters in a post-AGI world (!) this seems implausible. Hotel brand also scored just 13%, compared with 43% for loyalty benefits. An AI recommendation can be based on price. Putting “AI recommendations” and “price” in separate buckets doesn’t establish that price stops mattering to the AI. Hotels Can Lose Pricing Power Even As More Guests Book Direct Online travel agencies do two things that hotels value. They bring customers. Someone may not know the hotel exists, may not have a preferred chain, or may want to compare properties across chains. Expedia, Booking.com and others supply an audience the hotel doesn’t reach on its own. They help hotels charge different customers different prices. A hotel wants to sell rooms that would otherwise sit empty without cutting the price for everyone who would’ve paid more. Packages, restricted membership rates and opaque offers can let them discount without putting the same lower rate on their own site. I’ve written about how hotels distribute discounted inventory outside their public rates, and why a card travel portal can sometimes beat the hotel’s own member price. Booking direct isn’t automatically the cheapest option. The hotel has room to be more generous when it isn’t spending on the OTA commission. It can give some of that money to the guest as a lower price, rewards or benefits. The agency has its own operating costs and profit to cover. It seems like a chain could undercut the third party. But today’s room rate isn’t fixed while AI just redistributes the savings. If AI can find the right small hotel even though I’ve never heard of it, that’s less reason to start with Expedia and more reason to book direct. But it’s also less reason to pay a premium for the familiar hotel I would’ve booked without doing much research. And where there are opaque offers the AI may find those too. It could ask several suitable hotels for their best offer, comparing cash discounts with credits and benefits, and without my needing to spend time negotiating. This already matters in my own choices. In Venice, I wanted a location that worked for my family, rather than staying on Murano just to use Hyatt. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi, GHA status helped me with early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout. An assistant that knows my family’s needs can compare that entire package against the alternatives. It can consider a different neighborhood, a different destination, or different dates, rather than just finding another website selling the same room. It can also work through offers that are currently tedious to find. Opaque hotels become less opaque if the assistant can identify them from their amenities, location and photos. Still, knowing about a corporate rate doesn’t make you eligible for it. I’d expect pressure on direct booking margins because consumers have the intelligence in their pockets that just solved math. They may avoid OTA commissions but get rates competed down, and while lower commissions apply only to a limited piece of their business, the lower rates would affect the entire hotel. An unknown hotel may gain enough customers to come out well ahead. A unique property on a sold out night has pricing power. But more direct bookings may or may not mean greater profits. Recognition Doesn’t Replace Rewards The report’s loyalty finding interests me because I’ve been writing about recognition and reward as the twin pillars of loyalty for more than a decade. They’re different things, and a good program does both. Recognition can be the thing a traveler values most. But if getting it means giving up the rebate they’d earn elsewhere, they’re actually having to pay for that recognition. A guest may care more about their treatment but that’s holding rewards constant. GHA addressed this when it relaunched Discovery in December 2021. Previously, it offered status benefits and Local Experience awards. Those awards could be great, but a business traveler working all day often had no use for the experience on offer. Discovery Dollars gave members a flexible rebate they could put toward a hotel bill. The CEO survey asks what will differentiate successful programs. That’s compatible with rewards being something customers already expect. It doesn’t mean you can take the rewards away. And in GHA’s separate research among more than 9,000 members this year, generosity was the leading program attribute. Ease of earning and spending Discovery Dollars and hotel benefits both rated highly. Why I Value GHA Discovery I’ve called GHA my second favorite hotel loyalty program, after Hyatt. Hyatt still has the advantages of confirmed suites at booking, guaranteed late checkout at most properties and a more consistent breakfast benefit. GHA gives me interesting hotels where I still receive real benefits. At Riggs in Washington, D.C., I wound up in the suite that used to be the bank’s boardroom, with a dining table for 12. I’d booked through Chase’s The Edit and stacked its benefits with GHA status. At Kempinski Cancun, I combined American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts with GHA and received an oceanfront suite and club access. Members earn 4% to 7% back in Discovery Dollars on eligible spending, depending on status. One Discovery Dollar is worth one U.S. dollar toward eligible spending at participating hotels. Titanium earns 7%, with those regularly earned dollars valid for 24 months. Promotional dollars can expire sooner. Titanium includes a two-category upgrade, 11 a.m. early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability. Breakfast for two is included at participating brands on direct bookings. You can earn Titanium with 30 eligible nights, $15,000 in eligible spending, or stays at three qualifying brands in a calendar year. The last route can mean just three one-night stays (NH Hotels, NH Collection and nhow count together as one brand). At the Lyle in D.C., the staff arranged fresh coffee for me at 5 a.m., two hours before room service opened. It arrived at exactly 5 a.m. That’s the sort of thing I remember and go back for. I’ve also covered their unusually accessible status matches. The current offer runs through November 30, 2026, with approved status lasting through December 31, 2027: Platinum: $100 application fee, with D$50 back. Titanium: $150 application fee, with D$75 back. There’s no stay challenge. Hilton Diamond, Hyatt Globalist, Marriott Platinum and above, and IHG Platinum and above are among the statuses that match to Titanium. Eligible airline and cruise status, and some credit cards, qualify too. The gift dollars expire after 12 months, and the terms allow only one GHA status match. For someone with an upcoming stay at one of these hotels, $150 with $75 back in hotel spending can be a very good way to get treated better. I’d like my future travel assistant to notice that before it tells me I’ve saved $20 booking the same hotel without benefits through Expedia. Online travel agencies do two things that hotels value. They bring customers. Someone may not know the hotel exists, may not have a preferred chain, or may want to compare properties across chains. Expedia, Booking.com and others supply an audience the hotel doesn’t reach on its own. They help hotels charge different customers different prices. A hotel wants to sell rooms that would otherwise sit empty without cutting the price for everyone who would’ve paid more. Packages, restricted membership rates and opaque offers can let them discount without putting the same lower rate on their own site. I’ve written about how hotels distribute discounted inventory outside their public rates, and why a card travel portal can sometimes beat the hotel’s own member price. Booking direct isn’t automatically the cheapest option. The hotel has room to be more generous when it isn’t spending on the OTA commission. It can give some of that money to the guest as a lower price, rewards or benefits. The agency has its own operating costs and profit to cover. It seems like a chain could undercut the third party. But today’s room rate isn’t fixed while AI just redistributes the savings. If AI can find the right small hotel even though I’ve never heard of it, that’s less reason to start with Expedia and more reason to book direct. But it’s also less reason to pay a premium for the familiar hotel I would’ve booked without doing much research. And where there are opaque offers the AI may find those too. It could ask several suitable hotels for their best offer, comparing cash discounts with credits and benefits, and without my needing to spend time negotiating. This already matters in my own choices. In Venice, I wanted a location that worked for my family, rather than staying on Murano just to use Hyatt. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi, GHA status helped me with early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout. An assistant that knows my family’s needs can compare that entire package against the alternatives. It can consider a different neighborhood, a different destination, or different dates, rather than just finding another website selling the same room. It can also work through offers that are currently tedious to find. Opaque hotels become less opaque if the assistant can identify them from their amenities, location and photos. Still, knowing about a corporate rate doesn’t make you eligible for it. I’d expect pressure on direct booking margins because consumers have the intelligence in their pockets that just solved math. They may avoid OTA commissions but get rates competed down, and while lower commissions apply only to a limited piece of their business, the lower rates would affect the entire hotel. An unknown hotel may gain enough customers to come out well ahead. A unique property on a sold out night has pricing power. But more direct bookings may or may not mean greater profits. Recognition Doesn’t Replace Rewards The report’s loyalty finding interests me because I’ve been writing about recognition and reward as the twin pillars of loyalty for more than a decade. They’re different things, and a good program does both. Recognition can be the thing a traveler values most. But if getting it means giving up the rebate they’d earn elsewhere, they’re actually having to pay for that recognition. A guest may care more about their treatment but that’s holding rewards constant. GHA addressed this when it relaunched Discovery in December 2021. Previously, it offered status benefits and Local Experience awards. Those awards could be great, but a business traveler working all day often had no use for the experience on offer. Discovery Dollars gave members a flexible rebate they could put toward a hotel bill. The CEO survey asks what will differentiate successful programs. That’s compatible with rewards being something customers already expect. It doesn’t mean you can take the rewards away. And in GHA’s separate research among more than 9,000 members this year, generosity was the leading program attribute. Ease of earning and spending Discovery Dollars and hotel benefits both rated highly. Why I Value GHA Discovery I’ve called GHA my second favorite hotel loyalty program, after Hyatt. Hyatt still has the advantages of confirmed suites at booking, guaranteed late checkout at most properties and a more consistent breakfast benefit. GHA gives me interesting hotels where I still receive real benefits. At Riggs in Washington, D.C., I wound up in the suite that used to be the bank’s boardroom, with a dining table for 12. I’d booked through Chase’s The Edit and stacked its benefits with GHA status. At Kempinski Cancun, I combined American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts with GHA and received an oceanfront suite and club access. Members earn 4% to 7% back in Discovery Dollars on eligible spending, depending on status. One Discovery Dollar is worth one U.S. dollar toward eligible spending at participating hotels. Titanium earns 7%, with those regularly earned dollars valid for 24 months. Promotional dollars can expire sooner. Titanium includes a two-category upgrade, 11 a.m. early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability. Breakfast for two is included at participating brands on direct bookings. You can earn Titanium with 30 eligible nights, $15,000 in eligible spending, or stays at three qualifying brands in a calendar year. The last route can mean just three one-night stays (NH Hotels, NH Collection and nhow count together as one brand). At the Lyle in D.C., the staff arranged fresh coffee for me at 5 a.m., two hours before room service opened. It arrived at exactly 5 a.m. That’s the sort of thing I remember and go back for. I’ve also covered their unusually accessible status matches. The current offer runs through November 30, 2026, with approved status lasting through December 31, 2027: Platinum: $100 application fee, with D$50 back. Titanium: $150 application fee, with D$75 back. There’s no stay challenge. Hilton Diamond, Hyatt Globalist, Marriott Platinum and above, and IHG Platinum and above are among the statuses that match to Titanium. Eligible airline and cruise status, and some credit cards, qualify too. The gift dollars expire after 12 months, and the terms allow only one GHA status match. For someone with an upcoming stay at one of these hotels, $150 with $75 back in hotel spending can be a very good way to get treated better. I’d like my future travel assistant to notice that before it tells me I’ve saved $20 booking the same hotel without benefits through Expedia. I was not quite sure what this article was about. Is it about GHA? You were right in a previous post, I know little about it. Maybe I should find out.

If it is about booking directly, Nike’s attempt to force everyone to buy their shoes directly was a disaster. Booking engines provide visibility, even to major brands. I still use Agoda to book in Asia, even though it is now owned by Booking Holdings. For small hotels, like a nice family hotel with dinky clean rooms I stayed in Tokyo or the great one bedroom suite with a free breakfast in Phnom Penh, Agoda opens up a world market.

If it about AI, AI might help. However, (1) My iphone AI news app has decided that I want to read food and recipe, celerity, puzzles. I cannot figure out how to turn off the feed of crap stories. (2) My Youtube app has decided to push a steady stream of AI generated content, that mostly is taken from Wikipedia and shorts. I cannot seem to turn it off, so I turned off all suggestions and search. (3) My Netflicks app has decided I like Korean movies (I have no idea why), and sends me pages of suggestions. I cannot get it to stop. It gives me a headache, and I don’t watch anything. I might cancel Netflicks (4) Don’t get me started about customer service AI. Until I see AI working in my own life, I am naturally skeptical that AI will solve my hotel choices any time soon.

The main problem is incentives. Hotel operators actual customers are not guests; it’s property owners. Rarely do these corporations own the underlying real estate. So, they don’t really care about consumers so much as shareholders, property owners, and their own executive compensation. Fix the incentives; magically, consumers will be treated better. At the very least, better guardrails to protect from outright fraud, deceptive practices, please.

Yeah, just charge a resort fee and for parking in the middle of Nebraska hotels.

This article is clearly a pitch for GHA, which quite frankly, is lame. Pass.

@Gene — What is it with Gary (and Ben) promoting GHA?! Like, never heard of it before these guys… bah!
