#6130. Ali Velshi is on the Big Board now

Six years ago, Donald Trump dropped â11th Hourâ host Ali Velshiâs name at several campaign rallies as an example of the so-called âfake news mediaâ getting what the president thought he deserved: a taste of âlaw and order.â

In May 2020, while covering the Minneapolis protests that arose in response to the murder of George Floyd, MSNBCâs live coverage caught Velshi being struck in the knee by one of the rubber bullets police fired into the crowd.

Months later, Trump referred to the incident multiple times on the campaign trail as âthe most beautiful thing,â earning laughter and applause from supporters. But an emotional Velshi recalled that moment differently in June 2026, as he said goodbye to his old weekend showâs audience.

In that moment and others, he told âVelshiâ viewers that democracy, fairness, transparency and accountability took yet another hit. âThis is how it unfolds. Not always with legislation, not always with imprisonment. Sometimes with a rubber bullet. Sometimes with a police escort. Philosophy repeated until enough people believe it. . . and they believe that the next step becomes possible,â he said. âThe press is not the enemy of the people. The press is the peopleâs guarantee that they will know what is done in their name.â

Then, he reminded everyone watching that the midterm elections were 148 days away.

When I spoke with him last Thursday, the veteran journalist repeated his belief in the pressâ witnessing role, unshaken by the massive changes occurring in the news industry.Â  One of those changes places him at the networkâs famous Big Board as the chief data reporter for MS NOWâformerly MSNBCâcarrying on an election-night tradition made famous by Steve Kornacki.

Velshiâs on-air analysis will be augmented by an additional feed called VelshiCast, a behind-the-scenes look that will stream on MS NOWâs YouTube channel.

Other aspects of MS NOWâs live coverage remain familiar to longtime MSNBC viewers, with Rachel Maddow leading the channelâs supergroup of Nicolle Wallace, Chris Hayes, Jen Psaki, Lawrence OâDonnell, Stephanie Ruhle, Michael Steele, Symone Sanders Townsend, Ari Melber and Peter Alexander.

As for Kornacki, he became NBC Newsâ chief data analyst after NBCUniversalâs owner, Comcast, spun off MS NOW along with USA Network, Syfy, E!, and its other cable channels into a venture known as Versant.

Journalism is in a precarious time, but this administration has placed particular pressure on TV newsrooms. With Paramount Skydanceâs acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, CNNâs and CBSâ teams are facing rounds of buyouts and return-to-office orders to thin their ranks. Meanwhile, Status reported that October 2026 is Fox Newsâ lowest-rated month since December 2023, with the network averaging 1.1 million total-day viewers.

Velshi remains optimistic about his profession, as he said in our wide-ranging conversation about his plans to make the Big Board even more essential on this midterm election night.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Salon: A lot of coverage cited what you said in your farewell message for your last weekend show. One of them, and I think this is important, is that you were reminding people that the show was ending 148 days before the midterm elections.

Well, weâre here now. Youâve started your weekday show, and Iâm curious to hear your impressions of how you think things are going, in terms of that dialogue with viewers and whatâs coming up about Tuesday from a data perspective.

Thanks for actually thinking that through because there is a real through line. I miss my old show a lot, but you know, that moment was so important. What I was trying to do that night, and what Iâve been trying to do since, is convey the idea that this isnât about partisan politics. This is about civic engagement. This is about democracy, and nobodyâs going to do that for you, right? Democracy is not something you pick off a shelf. It is work for all of us all the time, and I donât think weâll ever be free of a moment when democracy is on autopilot.

And so, right now, everybodyâs responsibility is to participate actively. I have a sense that pretty much all of our regular viewers, certainly people in our MS NOW community, are heavily engaged. Theyâre big consumers of news and information. They probably already voted. If not, theyâre planning to, because some people just like voting on election day because itâs exciting. But this moment wants more of us. It needs us not just to vote, but to be engaged in the dialogue, to commit to democracy, to help other people vote, to feel like we are in community with each other, to save democracy.

This doesnât matter whether youâre a Democrat or Republican or an independent, or you donât even think politics matters to you. And I will say that since that day that I left the show, Iâve only felt stronger about this, and Iâve only felt that people are understanding their assignment very, very well. And weâre seeing this from a data perspective.

Every single day, we get new data that shows early voting and advance voting. It is remarkable. At the low end, the states are up 20% compared to the last midterm elections in 2022. Weâre not even bothering to compare it to a presidential election because theyâre different beasts. In some states, early voting is up 40%. Now, what would possibly explain that? Itâs enthusiasm amongst voters. So people are going out and theyâre taking the assignment very, very seriously. Iâm very heartened by that.

So letâs talk about your new role and what you do with the data, and the conversation you have with people about that. Because I think that especially around elections, some of our pessimism and optimism comes from polling, but not necessarily from data.

Youâre 100% right. Thank you for that question too. I led the show on Monday night with three people: Kabir Khanna, whoâs our head of data and analytics; Dave Wasserman from the Cook Political Report; and Larry Sabato from the University of Virginiaâs Crystal Ball. These are the three data nerdiest guys around.

I think itâs important to understand that raw data is of no use to anyone. Even slightly interpreted data is of no use to anyone. You have to be able to look at it holistically. You have to look at polls and also understand their margins of error. You have to understand trends in polling so that even if a poll is good, meaning itâs statistically sound, that doesnât mean itâs correct. Polls have errors, and then the decision about how an election goes depends in part on polling, in part on trends, in part on the weather, in part on the news cycle, in part on whether your decision in an election is because youâre voting in favor of someone youâre excited about or youâre voting against someone youâre mad at.

I think raw data without analysis should be a crime â¦ OK, in this world where people make crimes out of everything, Iâm not sure thatâs the right thing to say. But my point is, itâs really bad. Itâs bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope that they interpret it. Itâs also bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope they follow it. Like, what am I trying to tell you? If I tell you these races are all ahead, I may not be giving you useful information for you.

So part of it is also managing expectations amongst voters. A âblue waveâ or a âbig blue wave,â I donât use that terminology . . .Â  But Iâll give you a range. Iâll tell you that as of today, the Democrats are likely to win a minimum of eight seats in the House and a maximum of probably in the mid-30s. Thatâs probably the range. Might I be wrong? Absolutely. But thatâs what I want people to understand. And then Iâm going to give you the clues to understand how I got there, so that you can follow along with me. Iâd rather make a data interpreter out of everybody who watches us than be their data interpreter.

â[P]eople are understanding their assignment very, very well.â

In terms of the election night and you being at the BigÂ  â are you guys still calling it the Big Board?

We are. Yes. I tried to call it The Magic Board of Wisdom, but no one took to that.

What you and Kornacki were doing at the Big Board really became a thing over the last decade or so.

People learned to consume election night coverage based around it. I know a lot of folks who may not necessarily watch every single moment of coverage, but keep an eye on developments with the sound off, based on whatâs going on with the Big Board. Itâs kind of like a lot of folks might go into a restaurant or a bar with the TV tuned to a game, but on mute. Iâd like to know how you feel about that mode of consumption.

Well, look: The bottom line is, scientifically, peopleâs visual consumption is their No. 1 source of information consumption. I mean, you can make the argument that smell is actually more important for your survival, but weâre not talking about survival here. The visual component hits before the auditory component does, so thatâs never going to change.

What may change is whether people watch it on their phone or their TV or, you know, through AI glasses, but the visual component is still stronger for everyone than anything else. So we spend a lot of time adjusting the size of the boxes on TV and deciding whether there are too many of them, and whether this is helpful information or confusing information. We want to make it very obvious that this is complicated information, and weâre working hard because itâs our job to present this to you in a way that is consumable and accessible. Which, by the way, has been sort of my stock in trade for my entire career.

So Iâm committed to making this the most visually easy experience. If you donât have audio, and if youâre sitting in a bar or sitting on a plane or wherever, and you canât hear me, youâll still understand everything thatâs going on.

In this election, thereâs emotional sentiment, psychological underpinnings, and consumer sentiment to account for. How much are you able to go into those factors on election night? Because each is also locally dependent. We have a lot of reporting determining the key races, but if you look down the ballot beyond the candidates, you have initiatives and other legislation driven by sentiment.

So we have two ways of measuring sentiment. One is in what we call our voter poll. Thatâs what you would know of as an exit poll, right? We do that in partnership with others. Itâs probably 1000 questions that really allow you to put meat on the bones of the result you just saw.

And I actually think thatâs one of the sad things about fast-moving election coverage, is that you sometimes donât get to sit there and say, âLet me explain to you. We actually know. We asked these voters why they made the decision they made, and they actually told us. So we donât have to extrapolate. We donât have to, you know, twist ourselves into pretzels. We actually have that information.â

âOur capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.â

So I will tell you, a lot of that will happen prior to polls closing. So people think to themselves, âYour coverage always starts before the polls close, or before the polls close in the place that I care aboutâ â thatâs actually where you get the most context. So weâre going to start early in the evening on Tuesday with our exit polls. I think we release them at 5 oâclock, and thatâs great information.

And then subsequently, we are covering every one of those ballot measures. In fact, thatâs part of what Iâm studying today. Iâm studying both the exit polls and the ballot measures today to really understand how theyâre going to correlate with the results.

You know, Iâm an economics reporter, so things like consumer sentiment are really, really clear to me. You know, people keep saying the economy is the most important thing in this election. I remind people the economy is the most important thing in pretty much every single election there is, with the exception of an actual war in which Americans have troops on the ground or an international threat. Thatâs the truth. People care most about how this affects them.

I think thereâs an interesting intersection in this election between people who care about the things that affect them, like the economy, gas, things like that, and people who care about democracy deeply. The second one can be a bit of an extra abstraction for people. The first oneâs absolutely not. So I have to measure how I tell those stories.

So Iâm going to take a little bit of a 30,000-foot view here and look at this in terms of MS NOWâs position in the news industry. On one side, you have Fox, part of a massive media conglomerate, with ratings declining right now, days before the election.

And on the other, CNN. Thereâs a lot of restructuring going on there related to the Skydance merger, a lot of conversation about that. And then thereâs you guys. Iâm wondering if, at this point, things feel different, just in terms of what youâre able to do.Â  I donât necessarily mean just kind of financial resources, but also what kind of backing Versant is giving you this time versus when you were part of the larger NBC Universal structure.Â  I realize this is still a very new situation, but again â Iâm curious about the pros and cons.

At the moment, itâs all pros. So first of all, weâre the scrappy, leaner player in the game now. . . Can we compete with other people? Yes, we can, and weâre doing it very well. As I said, the things that matter â the ability to conduct the analysis, and I donât mean that just for the big board â weâre able to do that. We are going to match everybodyâs expertise and probably exceed it.Â  Our capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.

No. 2, weâre literally the tip of the spear for the conversation that is happening in America right now around what country do we want to be. How is this solvable? Weâre right there.

And Iâm sorry for the folks around us who are dealing with these structural issues and trying to figure out what they are and how to represent themselves in this moment of turmoil, but weâre not struggling with this at all.

But we are not one thing, right? We are covering the story with all the complexity of an electorate that is spread out along the political spectrum. Iâm sure there are some of our viewers who love the idea that the [Democratic Socialists of America] is ascendant, and there are some of our viewers who love the fact that there are ex-conservatives, ex-Republicans like David Jolly running for governor in Florida. Or that there are some Republicans who are running for office because theyâve demonstrated their ability to be independent thinkers. We have the ability at MS NOW to have those discussions across the political spectrum. Weâre very comfortable with it.

In 2024, I interviewed Lawrence OâDonnell right before the election, and we talked a lot about the state of journalism, and specifically how effective the media was in terms of questioning Trump and holding him accountable. I think weâve seen shifts since then, but Iâd love to know whether youâve seen any shift one way or another.

I think so. Once in a while, maybe even daily, Iâll see some headline from a mainstream news organization that makes me cringe. That makes me think: Are these reporters and editors not understanding the moment that weâre in? Are they not understanding that that weirdly neutral headline that you just wrote doesnât actually communicate what just happened? It doesnât capture the fact that your reader and your viewer and your listener are shocked and possibly outraged and really struggling with whatâs going on. But you just wrote a headline that looks like this is just a governmental development, something that the Department of Justice did.

I think most of us are better at this than we were in 2024, and certainly better than we were in 2020 and 2016. Yes, weâve all gotten a lot better. There are still remnants in mainstream media of journalists who treat the activities of this government and this administration as normal, and thatâs not a journalistically difficult thing to unwind, right? Itâs not.

Itâs not difficult to say that journalism exists for two reasons: to bear witness for those of our consumers who cannot bear witness on their own because they canât travel to go see the scene, they canât go to the protest and they canât go to the press conference. We are there to bear witness, and we are there to hold power to account. Thatâs it. If you are not doing those two things every single day, you are not doing your job.

And there are still some members of the mainstream media who are not doing their job. This has nothing to do with what your opinion is or where you are in the political spectrum. Are you bearing witness and are you holding power to account? I think we are generally better at that. Now, what that has done is result in lawsuits. It has resulted in bans for some of us from the White House. Thatâs the consequence of doing your job properly, and thatâs okay. We will meet and face the consequences. Weâll fight back, and we will fight for our right and our viewersâ and our listenersâ and our readersâ rights to get the information that they deserve. Thatâs how you can tell weâre doing a better job at this. When they come for you, it means youâre doing your job.

MS Nowâs live election coverage begin at 6 p.m. ET/ 3 p.m. PT on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

#6129. American Airlines Says AAdvantage Is Its Edge—These 10 Changes Would Make That True

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom calls AAdvantage one of the airline’s strongest competitive advantages. I agree. I still find more value in American’s program than in most of its competitors. Alaska can be better for single-partner awards, including domestic American Airlines flights. American itself can offer terrific deals on its own flights, alongside some truly terrible ones. One of AAdvantage’s best features is that the partner award chart hasn’t been devalued since 2016. But a good price for an award you can’t book doesn’t get you very far. American improved its Million Miler program in 2025, and has more changes coming there. But that’s really the only real improvement I can think of in the past few years. In the meantime, it eliminated fixed-price mileage upgrades and took seat selection and upgrade benefits away from elites buying Basic Economy. Some of my major complaints about the program: American offers paid upgrades to anyone on the flight while elite members wait and usually do not get upgraded. Systemwide upgrades are nearly impossible to use. Upgrades were once the major benefit of status but can no longer meaningfully be factored, of course dependent on route and dates of travel. When you aren’t upgraded, at least elites can confirm extra legroom seats – but American has far too few of those. And when you exclude exit row seats (not eligible with young children), I often have to pick my flights carefully because there just aren’t extra legroom seats available. American says they’re adding more – but won’t start until 2028. When they first introduced Main Cabin Extra they did the whole fleet in a matter of months! Scarce partner business class awards. British Airways guarantees award space for those redeeming Avios (whether their own, Finnair’s, Qatar’s, etc.) but those guarantee seats are unavailable for AAdvantage redemption. Qantas reserves premium cabin awards for its own members (they didn’t before the pandemic). Cathay Pacific does the same. Qatar limits access to its own premium cabin awards to those redeeming their points or those in other Avios programs. Etihad heavily limits redemptions by partners, to name just a few. These are all new restrictions in the past few years that make AAdvantage miles less valuable. Same day changes are highly restrictive. Elites can confirm changes to their bookings, but can’t change the routing – they can’t connect through a different hub than their original reservation. What’s the use of having the best domestic network when customers aren’t allowed to use it? And from many cities there aren’t multiple flights to a given hub, effectively eliminating the benefit entirely. Here are ten changes that would make earning American miles and status more worthwhile. Most have precedents at other airlines. Some are things American has already done, and could simply bring back. Give the best customers better award pricing. American doesn’t offer a standing award discount for its top elites or credit card customers. They used to have extra availability at the saver level for Executive Platinums – by phone only – but they eliminated this when dropping the idea of saver awards for their ow flights and going all-dynamic pricing. They also used to offer an award option of a 15% redemption rebate at 175,000 Loyalty Points but they dropped this for 2024. It only applied to one American Airlines award trip, for up to two passengers, with a claim process after travel. Bring it back, make the rebate automatic, and let members use it on the awards they actually book. An annual mileage cap would control the cost without requiring a narrowly defined roundtrip. American still offers award rebates at million-plus Loyalty Point milestones. Delta and United have elite or cardmember redemption discounts. Delta mostly seemed to just raise prices on everybody else, while United’s has actually opened up more saver awards and discounts even compared to the old saver level at times. American doesn’t have anything comparable, but should. In my ideal – I don’t expect American to budget for this – I’d love to see Executive Platinum and ConciergeKey members have a limited number of opportunities to open award space each year. British Airways Gold Guest List members have “jokers” that can release awards from specified paid inventory. It doesn’t have to mean last seat avialability on every flight. It could be capacity controlled with a certain level of revenue inventory. Make partner awards easier to get, including when schedules first open American’s partner chart is very good (10 years ago the devaluation was brutal, but many airlines have devalued more since then). The challenge now is access to partner award space, with so many partners withholding inventory from American. British Airways shares revenue with American in a transatlantic joint venture that’s supposed to make them indifferent about whose aircraft a passenger flies. Yet Avios programs even outside the joint venture can get British Airways award space that American can’t. Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Qatar Airways and Etihad also give their own members or selected partners access that AAdvantage doesn’t get. American should negotiate for access, pay for additional inventory, and make reciprocal access part of its partnership discussions. Start with British Airways, despite draconian fuel surcharges that some other partners don’t even charge, simply because their close commercial relationship should produce a better result for customers – otherwise why are we allowing antitrust immunity in the first place? And keep the existing partner chart, don’t use this better inventory as an excuse to reprice the seats. American should also stop making members wait for its own booking calendar to open. American books up to 331 days ahead, while Finnair opens awards 360 days out. When a partner releases seats earlier, AAdvantage members should be able to book them then. Nearly a month’s head start matters when there are only a couple of business class awards. Many years ago that was the practice at Alaska Airlines – you could book the partner award right away, and call up later to add Alaska connecting flights when their own scheduled loaded. Give top elites priority for an empty middle seatI argued for this in 2020. It would be even more useful now, with complimentary upgrades harder to count on and not enough Main Cabin Extra seats. When a Platinum Pro, Executive Platinum or ConciergeKey member sits in a window or aisle seat in regular coach, hold the adjacent middle seat out from seat assignments. Have AgentAssist automatically release it at the gate when needed. The airline would keep selling the flight. It wouldn’t turn away a paying passenger to preserve an empty seat. Families who need to sit together and operational requirements could take priority. But when some middle seats are going to wind upempty anyway, ensuring the empty seat is beside the airline’s best customers simply makes sense. American could deliver a meaningful comfort benefit with very little displaced revenue. Make confirmed upgrades from paid premium economy a permanent option American has already tested this twice. In March and again in September, it offered promotions where a member could buy premium economy and apply a systemwide upgrade to confirm business class without the usual upgrade inventory. Make that a regular feature of systemwide upgrades: buy premium economy, spend a certificate, and confirm business class when a seat is still for sale. If American needs a short, published list of blackout dates, that’s fair enough. The existing ability to upgrade from coach should stay. This would give members an additional way to use their certificates, with certainty in exchange for buying a more expensive ticket. Give top elites 20% off paid upgrades, and let them earn upgrade creditsAmerican sells seats that once would have gone to complimentary upgrades. They value the tens of dollars more than rewarding the customer who spends tens of thousands. But upgrades were the key reason to earn status, which is the key driver of cobrand card spend. Give Platinum Pro and higher members 20% off the paid upgrade offers they see. American already has AA20 discounts for employees and eligible family members on airfare and awards. A comparable discount on upgrade offers for top customers isn’t an out of sample idea. The price before the discount needs to be the same offer the customer would otherwise receive. And American might collect more money from members who currently decline a buy-up because they’re waiting for a free upgrade. Some existing buyers would pay less while some people who never buy would start. Elites would get a better deal on excess premium inventory than once a year flyers. Add upgrade credits at Loyalty Point Reward milestones, usable toward these offers. That would provide something useful even when a systemwide upgrade won’t clear. Let top elites use the route network for same-day changes American has a huge network. Its same-day change rules prevent members from making full use of it. Under American’s rules, a replacement itinerary needs the same airports and routing. If you’re connecting through Charlotte, an earlier option through Dallas doesn’t necessarily help you. Neither does a nonstop replacing your connection. I was writing about this problem in 2015. The same-routing restriction already existed then, though agents had often been willing to waive it. Let Platinum Pro and higher members confirm a same-day change between the same origin and destination using any reasonable American routing with seats available in the cabin they’re entitled to occupy. Keep it to the day of travel, so this doesn’t become a way to buy a cheaper itinerary weeks ahead and immediately swap into an expensive one. Let an already-purchased upgrade carry over when the new flight has room in that cabin. A meeting ends early, the member gets home sooner, and American gives a frequent traveler a real benefit for their loyalty. Bring back stopovers on awards. Alaska allows free stopovers on one-way awards. Air France KLM’s Flying Blue offers them, too. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 additional points for an eligible stopover. American should let members stop at a connecting city on an international award that prices based on the partner redemption chart. Spend several days in Tokyo on the way to somewhere else in Asia, or visit Helsinki, London or Madrid before continuing through Europe. This should be free for top elites, but consider charging 5,000 miles for everyone else. Count award flights toward status and Million Miler balancesAmerican encourages members to earn miles through credit cards, shopping, hotels and other partners. When they finally redeem those miles and fly, the award trip doesn’t earn Loyalty Points. Publish a simple rate of Loyalty Points per mile redeemed. Include partner flights booked with AAdvantage miles. American issued the ticket and knows what the member redeemed. It could begin with its own flights if that’s easier to administer, but that shouldn’t be a permanent limit. Actual distance flown on awards should count toward Million Miler status as well. Delta already counts award travel toward its lifetime totals. Let elite households pool miles for free and share benefits easilyA family can collectively have enough miles for an award while each individual account comes up short. American should let an elite member establish a household pool, with no charge for combining miles. LifeMiles makes family pooling an elite benefit. Other programs manage pooling, too. Require verified members, put limits on how often people can join or leave, and give the household head redemption authority. Restricting the benefit to elites should make some forms of abuse less attractive, though it wouldn’t eliminate fraud. But the optimal amount of fraud is not zero anyway. American already lets members give someone status for a day. Make that benefit work like a trip benefit: select the traveler and reservation, then have the eligible seating and airport benefits apply immediately. The current terms require selecting the usage day at least seven days ahead Give Million Milers a benefit every yearAmerican deserves credit for adding lifetime Platinum Pro at four million miles and Executive Platinum at five million. It has also announced more choices for Million Miler milestone rewards. The next improvement should be something that arrives every year, including years when the member doesn’t cross another million mile threshold. Alaska gives Million Milers an annual head start toward status, which keeps them flying rather than retiring from engagement after they hit their threshold. American could also let a Million Miler share status with a designated household member, as competing programs do, or choose an annual benefit such as upgrade credit. Delta’s higher lifetime tiers bring recurring Choice Benefits. I’d start with the annual Loyalty Points. Someone who has already flown American a million miles shouldn’t have to begin every year’s pursuit of higher status at the same zero as someone who just joined. What do you feel American Airlines AAdvantage is missing, and how does it compare to other programs today? I see only Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards as comparable among U.S. airlines, believing both American and Alaska’s programs to be better than United’s. Some of you will disagree! And Alaska’s has its own challenges, including inventory for award redemption on its own flights and combining different partners on the same award ticket. Which of these changes I’ve suggested would move the needle for your own loyalty? And what am I missing from this list? In my ideal – I don’t expect American to budget for this – I’d love to see Executive Platinum and ConciergeKey members have a limited number of opportunities to open award space each year. British Airways Gold Guest List members have “jokers” that can release awards from specified paid inventory. It doesn’t have to mean last seat avialability on every flight. It could be capacity controlled with a certain level of revenue inventory.

British Airways shares revenue with American in a transatlantic joint venture that’s supposed to make them indifferent about whose aircraft a passenger flies. Yet Avios programs even outside the joint venture can get British Airways award space that American can’t. Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Qatar Airways and Etihad also give their own members or selected partners access that AAdvantage doesn’t get. American should negotiate for access, pay for additional inventory, and make reciprocal access part of its partnership discussions. Start with British Airways, despite draconian fuel surcharges that some other partners don’t even charge, simply because their close commercial relationship should produce a better result for customers – otherwise why are we allowing antitrust immunity in the first place? And keep the existing partner chart, don’t use this better inventory as an excuse to reprice the seats. American should also stop making members wait for its own booking calendar to open. American books up to 331 days ahead, while Finnair opens awards 360 days out. When a partner releases seats earlier, AAdvantage members should be able to book them then. Nearly a month’s head start matters when there are only a couple of business class awards. Many years ago that was the practice at Alaska Airlines – you could book the partner award right away, and call up later to add Alaska connecting flights when their own scheduled loaded. Give top elites priority for an empty middle seatI argued for this in 2020. It would be even more useful now, with complimentary upgrades harder to count on and not enough Main Cabin Extra seats. When a Platinum Pro, Executive Platinum or ConciergeKey member sits in a window or aisle seat in regular coach, hold the adjacent middle seat out from seat assignments. Have AgentAssist automatically release it at the gate when needed. The airline would keep selling the flight. It wouldn’t turn away a paying passenger to preserve an empty seat. Families who need to sit together and operational requirements could take priority. But when some middle seats are going to wind upempty anyway, ensuring the empty seat is beside the airline’s best customers simply makes sense. American could deliver a meaningful comfort benefit with very little displaced revenue. Make confirmed upgrades from paid premium economy a permanent option American has already tested this twice. In March and again in September, it offered promotions where a member could buy premium economy and apply a systemwide upgrade to confirm business class without the usual upgrade inventory. Make that a regular feature of systemwide upgrades: buy premium economy, spend a certificate, and confirm business class when a seat is still for sale. If American needs a short, published list of blackout dates, that’s fair enough. The existing ability to upgrade from coach should stay. This would give members an additional way to use their certificates, with certainty in exchange for buying a more expensive ticket. Give top elites 20% off paid upgrades, and let them earn upgrade creditsAmerican sells seats that once would have gone to complimentary upgrades. They value the tens of dollars more than rewarding the customer who spends tens of thousands. But upgrades were the key reason to earn status, which is the key driver of cobrand card spend. Give Platinum Pro and higher members 20% off the paid upgrade offers they see. American already has AA20 discounts for employees and eligible family members on airfare and awards. A comparable discount on upgrade offers for top customers isn’t an out of sample idea. The price before the discount needs to be the same offer the customer would otherwise receive. And American might collect more money from members who currently decline a buy-up because they’re waiting for a free upgrade. Some existing buyers would pay less while some people who never buy would start. Elites would get a better deal on excess premium inventory than once a year flyers. Add upgrade credits at Loyalty Point Reward milestones, usable toward these offers. That would provide something useful even when a systemwide upgrade won’t clear. Let top elites use the route network for same-day changes American has a huge network. Its same-day change rules prevent members from making full use of it. Under American’s rules, a replacement itinerary needs the same airports and routing. If you’re connecting through Charlotte, an earlier option through Dallas doesn’t necessarily help you. Neither does a nonstop replacing your connection. I was writing about this problem in 2015. The same-routing restriction already existed then, though agents had often been willing to waive it. Let Platinum Pro and higher members confirm a same-day change between the same origin and destination using any reasonable American routing with seats available in the cabin they’re entitled to occupy. Keep it to the day of travel, so this doesn’t become a way to buy a cheaper itinerary weeks ahead and immediately swap into an expensive one. Let an already-purchased upgrade carry over when the new flight has room in that cabin. A meeting ends early, the member gets home sooner, and American gives a frequent traveler a real benefit for their loyalty. Bring back stopovers on awards. Alaska allows free stopovers on one-way awards. Air France KLM’s Flying Blue offers them, too. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 additional points for an eligible stopover. American should let members stop at a connecting city on an international award that prices based on the partner redemption chart. Spend several days in Tokyo on the way to somewhere else in Asia, or visit Helsinki, London or Madrid before continuing through Europe. This should be free for top elites, but consider charging 5,000 miles for everyone else. Count award flights toward status and Million Miler balancesAmerican encourages members to earn miles through credit cards, shopping, hotels and other partners. When they finally redeem those miles and fly, the award trip doesn’t earn Loyalty Points. Publish a simple rate of Loyalty Points per mile redeemed. Include partner flights booked with AAdvantage miles. American issued the ticket and knows what the member redeemed. It could begin with its own flights if that’s easier to administer, but that shouldn’t be a permanent limit. Actual distance flown on awards should count toward Million Miler status as well. Delta already counts award travel toward its lifetime totals. Let elite households pool miles for free and share benefits easilyA family can collectively have enough miles for an award while each individual account comes up short. American should let an elite member establish a household pool, with no charge for combining miles. LifeMiles makes family pooling an elite benefit. Other programs manage pooling, too. Require verified members, put limits on how often people can join or leave, and give the household head redemption authority. Restricting the benefit to elites should make some forms of abuse less attractive, though it wouldn’t eliminate fraud. But the optimal amount of fraud is not zero anyway. American already lets members give someone status for a day. Make that benefit work like a trip benefit: select the traveler and reservation, then have the eligible seating and airport benefits apply immediately. The current terms require selecting the usage day at least seven days ahead Give Million Milers a benefit every yearAmerican deserves credit for adding lifetime Platinum Pro at four million miles and Executive Platinum at five million. It has also announced more choices for Million Miler milestone rewards. The next improvement should be something that arrives every year, including years when the member doesn’t cross another million mile threshold. Alaska gives Million Milers an annual head start toward status, which keeps them flying rather than retiring from engagement after they hit their threshold. American could also let a Million Miler share status with a designated household member, as competing programs do, or choose an annual benefit such as upgrade credit. Delta’s higher lifetime tiers bring recurring Choice Benefits. I’d start with the annual Loyalty Points. Someone who has already flown American a million miles shouldn’t have to begin every year’s pursuit of higher status at the same zero as someone who just joined. What do you feel American Airlines AAdvantage is missing, and how does it compare to other programs today? I see only Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards as comparable among U.S. airlines, believing both American and Alaska’s programs to be better than United’s. Some of you will disagree! And Alaska’s has its own challenges, including inventory for award redemption on its own flights and combining different partners on the same award ticket. Which of these changes I’ve suggested would move the needle for your own loyalty? And what am I missing from this list? Excellent article, and I agree with most of it. However, you are leaving out one major miss in AA’s Million Miler program. The highest level, CK, is unachievable, unlike all their domestic competitors. Until they change that, their Million Miler program simply isn’t competitive. If you can’t chase the top tier, you’re chasing mediocrity (especially on AA today).

Excellent list. They need more MCE on their planes – it’s a competitive disadvantage compared to UA and DL. It’s the main perk of elite status these days. Software to auto-upgrade you to an MCE seat only works if there are, you know, more MCE seats.

Other than that, while most of this list would be nice to have, #1 on your list (discount award tickets for elites and cardholders) is also a need to have. It’s a competitive disadvantage compared to UA in a meaningful way, and DL in a still meaningful but somewhat more theoretical way given their often sky high redemption rates.

Bravo! Making the most of your strengths makes more sense than struggling with improving your weaknesses. I agree with all of these proposals especially better SWU options, million miler accrual and loyalty points for award tickets, and special perks for Platinum Pro and above. I’d be surprised if American adopts any of them, however.

In the business of monetizing elite programs (ie. liquidating the goodwill assets for short term gain). Typical hustles: (1) Hey, the other airline is worse. (2) Our downgrades are actually improvements if you look at it right.

@Peter — When I saw the post; I knew to look for you (and MCE!)

Once again, I wish our “elites “ would just quit whining about their sorry state of life. Want first, buy first. After all, from each according to their ability (to pay).

Have 1,300,000 miles but can not book a trip to South Africa or South in Business! Thanks BA 🙂 Same with South America and many places in EU.

@jcil open up your wallet and bus something other then Basic. You really should go to WN , you must miss Spirt

Given how hard it is to find premium award inventory in general, I wish they would make it easier to combine award segments with paid segments. I’m sometimes willing to buy a ticket DCA to CLT so I can then use the business class award from CLT to LHR, for example. But the airline doesn’t see both segments as part of one itinerary and doesn’t protect me if my first segment takes a delay and I misconnect. They also won’t let me check my bags all the way through. I’m literally willing to pay for part of the trip out of pocket to make it work, but the airline makes it very risky and difficult by not acknowledging that.

Lack of MCE is a big deal. I’m a lowly Gold on UA and can almost always book into Economy Plus. Flying AA this week to burn some miles earned on BA and the seat map on both flights has so few MCE seats. I booked a month out and there were none available.

Make Exec Platinums feel more valued, as there’s currently little reason to strive for the top tier given the decline in upgrade benefits.

Award discounts, additional AA inventory, and additional partner access would be a great way to do that.

Plus one on the discount award tickets for elites I have EXP on AA and Gold on UA. I just booked tickets to Europe outbound on AA and return on UA because of the very competitive elite discount on UA. I even bought additional UA miles so that I could snag multiple tickets at the discount rate I have done similar on Flying Blue also

Gary, I agree 100%!! FYI #3 (shadow blocking middle seat) is done by BA for their top tier members automatically by their reservation system software. Of course, I would also like to see AA match United and give lifetime Exec Plat at 4M miles and Concierge Key at 5M (or 10M – at least give something to shoot for)

Great ideas Gary. As an EXP flying out of DFW, the benefits I currently derive are almost non-existent. I’d be pleasantly shocked if AA were to implement any of these suggestions.

Better SDC changes. There’s a real no-brainer and going to make life easier for everyone including the reps.

@Common Sense — So wild to see you go “no politics” on here; at least you’re pretending to save-face by still showing up. The rest needed to submit a sick-day, apparently. (Oh, poor @This comes to mind; at least much of the rest of Ohio did their part.)

I find the 330 day calendar combined with limited partner availability to be especially galling

Confirmable SWU space at booking if seats are available for sale. Otherwise, there’s no material increased benefit for EP over Plat Pro. It’s incredibly frustrating to select a benefit that goes to waste (that used to be very valuable and therefore drive spending behavior to AA flights and CC’s). On a recent flight LAX-LHR I booked PE and was offered a paid upgrade price to biz class of ~$420 or ~42k miles. I’m Plat Pro and there was no confirmable space to use SWU’s on this flight despite the low paid upgrade offer, so this does not drive me to continue spending towards EP and higher LP threshholds. Upgrades were the sole reason I made sure I hit EP in the past and directly drove my spending behavior.

You make superb arguments that would strengthen AAdvantage and make more people likely to earn and retain loyalty status with American. That is valid, sensible, and would pay huge long term dividends to American. Therefore they won’t enact these badly needed changes. As a multi year EXP that’s highly unfortunate.

The issues with partner premium cabin awards is the biggest issue facing AAdvantge. American has considerable leverage here but choses not to use it. You to code share with us? Cool, our members get access to your premium cabin awards. You want to be in one of our JVs? Sweet – give us that award access. You want my booking engine to steer my passengers to your connecting flights? Wonderful – show me the award seats.

I negotiate contracts for a living and understand leverage. Give me one month and I’d have this problem solved.

Of all the celebrities Iâd bet on botching their Halloween getup, Martha Stewart would have been the longest shot. The doyenne of gracious livingâs holiday game is legendary, which NBCâs âTodayâ acknowledged by hosting her on Oct. 30 as half of an Olympics-themed couples costume, with Craig Melvin dressed as Snoop Dogg.

The next day, Stewart, who has an estimated net worth of $400 million, proudly showed off on Instagram that in 2026, she decided to cosplay a poor person. Not just any old poor, a dirty one. Stewart smudged her face with gray makeup, cut a few rips in her least-loved jeans, sliced up a gleaming white cardigan and held up a clipboard that read, âI Am Hungry Help Me!!â

Stewart soon took down the post, but the internet never forgets. She has now apologized twice: First, she postedÂ a Sunday statement to NBC News saying, âI am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention.â

In addition to Stewartâs ill-conceived effort to raise awareness of the unhoused crisis, the offending image was part of a carousel promoting her QVC candle collection, which she touted as âperfect for Halloween!!!â

Timbre, in a reply to her Instagram mea culpa. Heâs right. Where was her daughter Alexis? Was Snoop too high to talk her down from this mishap?

Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Earn 2 Delta Comfort Flight Certificates + 50K Miles

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Client dinners, catered lunches and team celebrations can add up quickly. The right business credit card can turn those restaurant bills into a meaningful haul of points, miles or cash back.

From high category bonuses to uncapped flat-rate rewards, the best credit cards for dining can make every business meal work harder.

Here's how our top picks compare based on their dining returns, annual fees and reward flexibility.

The information for the U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus Visa Signature Card and the U.S. Bank Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

To determine the best business cards for dining, I looked for cards with an estimated return of at least 3% on restaurant purchases, based on TPG's valuations. I focused on ongoing earnings rather than welcome offers or dining credits, then selected cards serving distinct use cases, including high category bonuses, uncapped transferable rewards and no-annual-fee options.

Other cards that don't earn at least 3% back in value based on our valuations may still be good fits for your business within a broader rewards strategy, but are less competitive when restaurant earnings are the primary goal.

The American Express Business Gold earns valuable Membership Rewards points. Cardmembers earn 4 points per dollar spent in their top two spending categories each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in bonus category spending per year, then 1 point per dollar), with dining and restaurants falling under an available category.

That means businesses that max out their cap could earn 600,000 points each year. Even if you don't come close to that cap, 4 points per dollar is still a significant return on spend, especially when they come with all the potential of Membership Rewards.

Just be careful: Since Amex rewards extra bonus points on your top spending categories each billing cycle, if other eligible expenses overtake dining, restaurant purchases may earn only 1 point per dollar. You can use that to your advantage when your restaurant spending is low one month, but it could also catch you off guard.

To learn more, read our full review of the Business Gold.

Apply here: American Express Business Gold

The U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus earns 5% cash back in the cardholder's top eligible spending category each month on up to $200,000 in annual eligible purchases, automatically. Dining is one of the qualifying categories, and the cap is high enough that most businesses won't have to worry about it. All purchases outside the top category earn at least 2% cash back, which is also a generous return.

The $295 annual fee makes this card best for businesses with substantial, consistent restaurant spending. Otherwise, a no-annual-fee option may provide better value overall.

If you're looking for a card with no annual fee, The Blue Business Plus earns 2 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on all purchases (for the first $50,000 in spending each year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The simplicity of this card means you don't need to keep track of spending categories; it's just as great for your dining purchases as it is for shipping, advertising and other business expenses. For businesses that can stay below the cap and earn 2 points per dollar spent on all their spending, the combination of transferable points and no annual fee is difficult to beat.

To learn more, read our full review of the Blue Business Plus.

Apply here: The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express

Like the Blue Business Plus, the Capital One Venture Business earns 2 miles per dollar spent on dining and other purchases. Unlike the Amex card, however, that earning rate is unlimited. This makes Venture Business a stronger fit for businesses that expect to spend more than $50,000 each year and can take advantage of double miles well above that spending threshold, despite the $95 annual fee.

Capital One miles are highly versatile, with options to transfer to 15-plus airline or hotel partners, book travel without blackout dates through Capital One Travel and more. In fact, a different set of transfer partners could make the Venture Business a more compelling solution than an Amex, depending on your business's redemption preferences.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Business Credit Card

The Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card earns 3% cash back on eligible restaurant purchases with no annual fee, and there's no cap on total rewards.

It can't match the Business Essentials Plus card's 5% return, but there's no annual fee to recoup. A business would need to spend about $14,750 annually on dining for the 5% rate to make up for the $295 fee versus the Triple Cash card's no-annual-fee 3% return. Therefore, if you're looking for simple cash back but have more moderate restaurant spending, the Triple Cash is a stronger fit.

To learn more, read our full review of the U.S. Bank Triple Cash.

The Marriott Bonvoy Business Amex is a good fit for businesses that frequently entertain clients, host events at Marriott properties or incur dining expenses while traveling. It earns 4 points per dollar spent on eligible restaurant purchases worldwide, which represents a 3% return at TPG's November 2026 valuations. Since it doesn't impose a spending cap on its restaurant rewards, businesses can earn consistently throughout the year.

The card becomes especially valuable for businesses that regularly stay with Marriott and can put both its hotel benefits and Bonvoy rewards to use.

Of course, loyalty to one hotel brand won't work for everyone. Businesses that prioritize more flexible redemptions may prefer a card that includes Marriott as a transfer partner rather than choosing a cobranded card specifically.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bonvoy Business Amex.

Apply now: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card

The right business card option depends on more than earning rates. You'll also need to account for how much your business spends, whether you prefer cash back or travel rewards and whether you're willing to pay an annual fee.

Start with the net value, not the largest number in the table. The Amex Business Gold and Business Essentials Plus only deliver their highest dining returns when restaurant purchases rank among the business's top eligible categories. But cards that earn lower rates of return on dining might be a better value once you factor in annual fees and spending caps.

In addition to considering the type of rewards best for your business, think about what else these cards offer. Secondary benefits like travel protections, cellphone insurance, lounge access or elite status might make up for a lower earning rate on meals when you consider the whole package.

A large welcome offer can improve a card's first-year value, but it shouldn't outweigh its long-term fit. Compare ongoing rewards after the annual fee, along with the protections, credits and other benefits your business will realistically use. That said, when two or more cards are equally strong long-term fits, a welcome bonus can be a useful tiebreaker. Especially since some credit cards currently offer welcome bonuses of 100,000 points or more.

Lastly, confirm your spending will count toward elevated earning rates if the bonus rate affects which card you pay with. Dining bonuses depend on how the merchant categorizes the purchase, and not all food vendors are considered a restaurant. For example, a hotel cafe may code as travel, while a bar might code as nightlife or entertainment.

The Amex Business Gold offers the highest potential dining return based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, but its earning rate alone likely doesn't settle the decision. Spending caps, annual fees, redemption flexibility and other card benefits will also factor into which card delivers the most value for your business.

Businesses with large, predictable restaurant expenses will come out ahead by choosing premium cards, even after budgeting for an annual fee. When your dining spending is more moderate or inconsistent, though, a no-annual-fee card may produce the same net value with less monitoring. Don't pay for an earnings rate your business won't regularly trigger.

Related: The best no-annual-fee business credit cards

#6124. Southwest’s New Platinum Status Adds Too Little—10 Ways Rapid Rewards Should Fix Its New Program

Southwest Airlines is adding Platinum status to Rapid Rewards, but someone who already has A-List Preferred and Companion Pass won’t get much new. A third checked bag, earlier boarding, and a higher advertised earning bonus (offset by lower base-earning on higher fares) are very modest additions considering they’re launching a new top tier. Gold, the replacement for A-List Preferred, already gets the same seats. The 2027 overhaul makes things simpler by unifying qualification for elite status and Companion Pass. And they’re adding award travel on Icelandair, China Airlines and Etihad Airways beginning in the spring, including in premium cabins. We don’t yet know redemption pricing, rules or surcharges, so we don’t know how much value those will deliver. I’ve argued that Southwest’s changes follow from one another. Broader distribution puts their fares alongside everyone else’s. That creates pressure to unbundle with basic economy and paid seats and bags. Selling better seats requires assigned seating. Once they’ve given up the old differences, they need more of the benefits that make other airlines worth choosing. Southwest is inexorably becoming like the rest of the industry, but – they insist – with friendler crews. They at least need to become like everyone else without offering less. I offered ten ways to improve Rapid Rewards in 2022. Some, including partner airline redemptions and stronger credit card earning toward status, are finally being addressed. Here’s what I’d do next. Deliver Elite Members’ Bags First Southwest baggage delivery can be slow. That was easier to tolerate when checking bags was free for everyone. Once they’re charging for the service, standing around a carousel feels different. They should offer priority baggage handling for elites, with Gold and Platinum bags among the first delivered. This requires actually sorting and loading the bags so they come out first, not just a colored tag. And back it with a delivery guarantee. Delta offers 2,500 miles when checked bags take more than 20 minutes from gate arrival to the carousel. Alaska has a similar guarantee (and was actually first). Southwest could start with a guarantee for its top elites. I’d rather get my first bag promptly than have a free third one. Give Platinum Members Priority For An Empty Middle SeatSouthwest doesn’t have first class upgrades to offer. It can still make sitting in coach better. When a Platinum member selects a window or aisle in a regular legroom row, hold the adjacent middle seat out of routine seat assignments until it’s needed. Keep selling the flight, and release the seat at the gate if passengers need it. This would determine who gets the empty seat when a flight isn’t full. Someone is going to have extra space beside them. Give the customer who earned the highest status the best chance of being that person. Limiting this to ordinary coach would avoid taking some premium seats they’re trying to sell out of inventory. An empty middle can be better than a few additional inches of legroom. Introduce Lifetime Elite StatusAmerican, Delta, United and Alaska all recognize lifetime flying. Southwest now should, too. I’d base on miles or flight segments since Southwest has never had a long haul netowrk to rack up 20,000 flown miles on a roundtrip. For instance, 1,000 one-way trips could earn lifetime Silver, 2,000 could earn lifetime Gold, and 3,000 lifetime Platinum. I don’t know whether Southwest has the database to support historical flying like this. Give Elites An Award Rebate Make points worth more to the customers who earn status. A 10% rebate on Southwest awards for Gold and 15% for Platinum would make their points more valuable, and could be more easily managed than an award discount. Some Southwest credit cards already provide annual 10% or 15% discount codes. This is especially important because the new program cuts earning on expensive fares. As I laid out in comparing the new tiers, a Choice Extra ticket earns an A-List Preferred member 28 points per eligible dollar today, versus 22 for a Platinum member next year. Let Families Pool Points Free Southwest sells family travel and has one of the best benefits for traveling with someone else. Yet its program rules prohibit members from pooling points. Let a household combine its balances without paying a transfer fee. You can already use your points to book someone else’s ticket. The problem is having enough points across several accounts, but not enough in any one account for the award you want. JetBlue has offered free pooling for groups of up to seven people for years. United has family accounts, and this is a big feature in international progams. Count Award Flights Toward Status A flight paid for entirely with Rapid Rewards points doesn’t count as a qualifying flight. Southwest should change that, like Delta and Alaska do, and include partner awards as that part of the program develops. Southwest wants people to earn points from its credit cards and partners, then use them to fly. Treating that journey as less valuable to the airline makes no sense. Make Companion Pass More Useful When Traveling With Different People Companion Pass remains Southwest’s strongest benefit. But the new program keeps the old restrictions: one designated companion at a time, three changes per calendar year, and existing companion reservations must be canceled before switching people. Let Platinum members designate a small group, perhaps three people, and choose one companion for each trip. A spouse on one trip, a child on another. Still one companion per flight, still traveling with the member, with limits on changing the roster. I’d also let Platinum members use Companion Pass for an adjacent empty seat when traveling alone, an idea I included in my earlier wishlist. This would be a confirmed seat reservation, consuming inventory just as a companion booking does. A member whose travel is mostly business shouldn’t need to bring another person on the trip to get substantial value from the program’s biggest reward. Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares Southwest already lets elites use their seating benefits on Basic. That’s a real advantage over competitors, and it extends to family members on the same reservation. But even the new Platinum tier won’t receive free confirmed same-day changes on Basic. Members can stand by. They need to buy Choice or higher to confirm the change without paying a fare difference. Give Gold and Platinum confirmed changes into available seats on the day of travel, regardless of their original fare. Keep the same origin and destination, and let the member choose an available itinerary that gets them there sooner or works better with their schedule. Southwest already provides the service on more expensive fares, here earned status would supply it. Make Southwest Status Useful On Its Airline Partners The international redemption announcement addresses not being able to use Southwest points for long haul travel. The awards need solid pricing and inventory. I expect that we’ll eventually see reciprocal status recognition, but that needs to come quickly: priority check-in, baggage allowances, boarding and seat benefits and lounge access would make Gold and Platinum valuable even when member travels beyond Southwest’s route map. Give Platinum A Choice Of Benefits Southwest is building Icon Lounges, with openings planned to begin in late 2027. Access has been announced through a forthcoming premium Chase card. They haven’t announced a Platinum lounge benefit. Give members an annual choice when they earn Platinum: perhaps some lounge passes which could encourage them to try the product and get the card, or to share the passes with others. They might choose a travel credit or certificates that let friends and family select extra legroom seats when the member isn’t traveling. Southwest is already introducing two milestones, at 20,000 and 95,000 qualifying points which are below Platinum. The earlier milestone’s Preferred seat certificates aren’t extra legroom upgrades and can’t be gifted, so certificates for a friend to choose a better seat would add something different. They should continue with milestones above platinum, and continue offering choice benefits. Southwest Airlines is remaking itself in the image of the rest of the airline industry – with the same kinds of restrictions, but also adding many of the same amenities. They will have three elite tiers, but those tiers need to be competitive. I want Southwest to succeed. Are these things that would do it for you? What’s missing from my list? The earlier milestone’s Preferred seat certificates aren’t extra legroom upgrades and can’t be gifted, so certificates for a friend to choose a better seat would add something different. They should continue with milestones above platinum, and continue offering choice benefits. Southwest Airlines is remaking itself in the image of the rest of the airline industry – with the same kinds of restrictions, but also adding many of the same amenities. They will have three elite tiers, but those tiers need to be competitive. I want Southwest to succeed. Are these things that would do it for you? What’s missing from my list? Let Platinum members designate a small group, perhaps three people, and choose one companion for each trip. A spouse on one trip, a child on another. Still one companion per flight, still traveling with the member, with limits on changing the roster.

I’d also let Platinum members use Companion Pass for an adjacent empty seat when traveling alone, an idea I included in my earlier wishlist. This would be a confirmed seat reservation, consuming inventory just as a companion booking does. A member whose travel is mostly business shouldn’t need to bring another person on the trip to get substantial value from the program’s biggest reward.

Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares Southwest already lets elites use their seating benefits on Basic. That’s a real advantage over competitors, and it extends to family members on the same reservation. But even the new Platinum tier won’t receive free confirmed same-day changes on Basic. Members can stand by. They need to buy Choice or higher to confirm the change without paying a fare difference.

Give Gold and Platinum confirmed changes into available seats on the day of travel, regardless of their original fare. Keep the same origin and destination, and let the member choose an available itinerary that gets them there sooner or works better with their schedule. Southwest already provides the service on more expensive fares, here earned status would supply it.

Make Southwest Status Useful On Its Airline Partners The international redemption announcement addresses not being able to use Southwest points for long haul travel. The awards need solid pricing and inventory.

I expect that we’ll eventually see reciprocal status recognition, but that needs to come quickly: priority check-in, baggage allowances, boarding and seat benefits and lounge access would make Gold and Platinum valuable even when member travels beyond Southwest’s route map.

Give Platinum A Choice Of Benefits Southwest is building Icon Lounges, with openings planned to begin in late 2027. Access has been announced through a forthcoming premium Chase card. They haven’t announced a Platinum lounge benefit.

Give members an annual choice when they earn Platinum: perhaps some lounge passes which could encourage them to try the product and get the card, or to share the passes with others. They might choose a travel credit or certificates that let friends and family select extra legroom seats when the member isn’t traveling.

Southwest is already introducing two milestones, at 20,000 and 95,000 qualifying points which are below Platinum. The earlier milestone’s Preferred seat certificates aren’t extra legroom upgrades and can’t be gifted, so certificates for a friend to choose a better seat would add something different. They should continue with milestones above platinum, and continue offering choice benefits. Southwest Airlines is remaking itself in the image of the rest of the airline industry – with the same kinds of restrictions, but also adding many of the same amenities. They will have three elite tiers, but those tiers need to be competitive. I want Southwest to succeed. Are these things that would do it for you? What’s missing from my list? So what you’re saying is that if I spend $75k on the CSR I can get the amazing benefits that come with Southwest A-List / Silver status?

>Count Award Flights Toward Status Southwest has done this a couple times in past years. It makes sense because Southwest has been paid for the points and Southwest recognizes revenue when they are flown.

>Introduce Lifetime Elite Status I would like to think my 2000+ flights count for something, even though I know they don’t.

>Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares This would be great but it won’t happen because it would reduce revenue by up to 50% on short haul trips booked in advance. Southwest has fired its loyal low-fare customers and does not want to re-hire them.

One improvement unrelated to elite status would be to eliminate or somehow mitigate expiration of travel funds. I have been booking on points to avoid having to worry about funds expiration. If funds expiration were eliminated I would have booked those flights on cash fares. I believe that Southwest is foolish to count breakage as revenue without accurately estimating how many cash fare sales are lost because of funds expiration.

Do they fly DC to Shreveport? Asking for a frenemy who has a lawn business he needs to get back to…

Also, do they fly from Beverly Hills to Miami? I presume Bill Maher will soon move to Florida, as well. (Oh, and gonna need a direct from Rochester Hills, Michigan, to Florida, or Tel Aviv, you know, for Haley and her fiancé.)

We have companion thru end of 2027. After that we’ll cancel our SW credit card and focus on United. No point in sticking with, as even the planned international partnerships are of no interest. My spouse has been ALP for over 15 years. I’ve had Companion for over 10. There’s really no place SWA goes that other airlines don’t that we need to get to.

#6123. Booking.com Bets It Can Close the Trips That ChatGPT and Gemini Start

AI may own the start of the trip, but Booking.com is betting trust and payments decide who gets the booking. Its experience with superapps, where daily use never became travel spending, suggests generative chatbots may face the same problem.

Booking.com is okay with travelers starting their trip planning with AI. It just wants to be the platform to close things.

Travelers are increasingly researching trips with AI, but that doesn’t mean the booking follows. Booking.com frames its challenge in Asia-Pacific as staying relevant at the moment people are ready to pay, wherever they may begin.

A Booking.com survey conducted earlier this year found that 64% of travelers in the region use AI to plan trips. Yet Booking Holdings, its parent company, has said recently that traffic referred directly by large language models is rare, representing well under 1% of room nights.

Laura Houldsworth, Booking.com’s vice president for Asia-Pacific, told Skift the gap exists because travelers don’t stay in one chatbot. “They might be searching on Claude one minute, ChatGPT another, Gemini, then rounding out with Google, and then coming to us directly,” she said. Booking.com's Asia-Pacific chief, Laura Houldsworth, told Skift the company is comfortable with travelers starting trip research inside AI chatbots as long as the booking still closes on Booking.com. A Booking.com survey earlier this year found 64% of travelers in Asia-Pacific use AI to plan trips, while parent Booking Holdings has said traffic referred directly by large language models accounts for well under 1% of room nights. Houldsworth attributes the gap to travelers moving between Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google before coming to Booking.com directly, so no single assistant gets credit. Her argument is that trust decides where the money lands — 400 million reviews, secure payments, and customer service that chatbots don't offer. The same logic shapes her view of superapps: daily usage hasn't translated into big-ticket travel spend, so Booking.com is plugging into platforms travelers already use rather than competing with them, starting with WhatsApp as a booking channel in India. Houldsworth also called intra-Asia the fastest-growing travel corridor in the world, with domestic room nights in Asia growing at a low double-digit rate against mid-single-digit growth companywide, which has cushioned softness in the Europe–Asia corridor tied to Middle East conflict. Alternative accommodation is about 37% of global room nights, with regulation the main risk, and the connected trip strategy depends on local payments landing first.
